blaster-master-1988:
Jason steers the frog-shaped tank SOPHIA through side-view ruins in Blaster Master (1988) before dropping into an overhead cavern. Sunsoft's American booklet makes him a boy chasing a pet, while the Japanese board Metafight tells a war story on that same cartridge.

SOPHIA's cannon clears the horizontal tunnels, then Jason climbs out on foot when a ladder opens a top-down chamber. Gun upgrades found in those chambers change the tank's shot before the next corridor begins.

Metafight's pilot and science-fiction briefing never show up in the American manual. Both editions still alternate the same two viewpoints, tank run then cavern, on one board.
dragons-lair:
Don Bluth animated Dirk the Daring's deaths for Dragon's Lair, and the 1983 laserdisc only lets a joystick pick the next scene. Daphne waits in a castle the player never walks freely, because the cabinet is playing film, not a simulated body.

A late sword swing or a missed jump cuts to a filmed Dirk dying on that disc. The scene then resumes only if the chosen path was the one the animators drew.

The NES cartridge reuses Dirk's name and then asks for ordinary jumps and swings. Anyone waiting for Bluth's filmed timing will not find that laserdisc inside the cart.
dragonstrike:
Dragonback combat is the whole of DragonStrike, SSI's Advanced Dungeons & Dragons flyer about fighting other dragons from the saddle. Breath, a lance, and the rider's aim replace a party marching on foot.

The computer original laid out that aerial duel first. In 1990 the design already existed on machines with keyboards before any console board was considered.

The NES edition shrinks the same dragonback idea into a smaller adaptation. It keeps the mounted fight and drops much of the computer game's wider campaign.
the-simpsons-bart-vs-the-space-mutants:
Purple objects give the aliens their harvest in The Simpsons: Bart vs. the Space Mutants, so Bart has to disguise them before the count is finished. Acclaim's first licensed Simpsons cartridge sends him through Springfield ahead of the later Bart games.

Family members and shop props become tools for covering the purple targets on each street. Maggie, Lisa, and the rest of the household are part of that scavenger hunt rather than a fighting roster.

The NES release arrived in 1991, with the space-mutant plot already on the box. Later Bart cartridges are separate licenses, not extra stages of this disguise hunt.
spider-man-return-of-the-sinister-six:
Doctor Octopus regroups his villains in Spider-Man: Return of the Sinister Six, LJN's side-scrolling NES comic license. Web shots and a short crawl carry Peter Parker from one member of that team to the next.

The 1992 cartridge tells its own Marvel story on an 8-bit board. Sandman, Electro, and the other lieutenants appear as stage bosses rather than as a tournament lineup.

Sixteen-bit Spider-Man brawlers use different stages and a different publisher's design. This cart does not share their levels, even though the mask is the same.
xevious:
Solvalou bombs the ground and fires ahead at once in Xevious, Namco's shooter whose ship never chooses just one layer. Nazca-like markings on the desert scroll under the blaster while aircraft peel in from above.

The 1982 coin-op made that double attack the identity of the game. A Famicom conversion carried the same Solvalou, the same ground targets, and the same air threats home.

A much later reissue is not the game people mean by the name. The cabinet, and the Famicom port of that cabinet, are the shooter itself.
gunsmoke:
A lone gunman walks up the street in Gun.Smoke, Capcom's Western where the shots fan in several directions. Bandits step out of doorways while the bounty hunter keeps moving toward the top of the screen.

The 1985 coin-op built that upward march and the multi-way fire. Wagons, rooftops, and named outlaws break the walk into a series of showdowns.

An NES conversion later kept the same cowboy premise and the same up-the-screen aim. It is that Western shooter brought home, still about one gun and several directions of fire.
dragon-quest-ii-1987:
Midenhall's prince sets out with two cousins in Dragon Quest II (1987), Enix's quest drawn by Akira Toriyama and scored by Koichi Sugiyama. The prince of Cannock and the princess of Moonbrooke join him, so the party is a family rather than a hired band of strangers.

Toriyama's monsters and Sugiyama's marches give the road its look and its sound. Caves, ships, and a widening map ask the three cousins to share equipment instead of one hero carrying everything.

North America later received the same journey as Dragon Warrior II. The cousins, the Toriyama bestiary, and Sugiyama's themes are the journey either box is selling.
sky-destroyer:
Behind the fighter is the whole view in Sky Destroyer, Taito's rail shooter locked to a World War II plane's tail. Enemy aircraft and ground targets rush toward the guns while the pilot never banks into a free sky.

Taito published that chase in 1985, and the same design was issued as an arcade machine as well as a Famicom cartridge. The home board is not a Western-born original with a new campaign.

Tracers and approaching wings are the threat, seen always from the rear seat of the chase. Players who know only a later console library are still looking at that Famicom and coin-op design.
top-gunnes:
Carrier landings decide the sortie in Top Gun (1987), Konami's jet game taken from the Tom Cruise film. Dogfights can go well and the mission still fails if the approach to the deck is missed.

The F-14 has to match the carrier's speed and height in that landing window. A bad angle dumps the plane, and the successful air combat before it does not save the run.

Konami built the notoriety of those approaches into the NES design on purpose. The film's call signs and carrier setting are the wrapper around a landing that many players remember better than the missiles.
nintendo-world-cup:
Kunio's soccer becomes a foul-heavy match in Nintendo World Cup, the Western release of a Technos Nekketsu game. Nintendo published that version in 1990, while the Japanese name keeps the tie to the high-school brawler series.

Shoulder charges and sliding tackles matter as much as a clean pass. The teams play a full pitch, but the tone is the Nekketsu habit of turning a sport into a scrap.

Technos built the match, and the Western box put Nintendo's name on the foul-friendly rules. It is Kunio-kun soccer with international teams, not a restrained simulation of a real cup.
micro-mages:
Four wizards share one television in Micro Mages, Morphcat Games' new NES platformer made for the original hardware. It is not a remake of an older hit, and the cartridge was built in 2019 to run on the console itself.

Each wizard fits in a handful of pixels so four players can occupy the same single screen. Spells and jumps have to be readable at that size, which is the trick the board was rarely asked to do.

Morphcat shipped it as a contemporary game on an old connector, not as a reissue with a new label. The shared screen, the four mages, and the new stages are the whole point of the cart.
batman-return-of-the-joker:
Sunsoft followed its own Batman cartridge with Batman: Return of the Joker, a fast NES sequel that does not retell the film Batman Returns. The Joker is the villain on the box, and the stages stay in Sunsoft's demanding style.

Walls, pits, and quick enemy patterns ask for the same sharp timing as the studio's earlier Batman cart. The 1991 release stands in that line, beside the first Sunsoft Batman, rather than beside a movie-script adaptation.

A Game Boy edition exists as well, but the NES board is the one that continues Sunsoft's console Batman. Batman Returns, the film, is a different story with a different villain focus and no claim on these stages.
punch-out:
Little Mac reads every tell from behind his gloves in Punch-Out!!
Glass Joe's slow windup and King Hippo's open mouth are lessons in a ladder of cartoon boxers. Doc Louis shouts from the corner while Mac waits for the pattern instead of mashing.

Nintendo's NES boxing career is the one later Punch-Out games are measured against. The view stays over Mac's shoulder, so the opponent's face is the puzzle and Mac's own body is mostly arms and a star punch.

A missed pattern ends the round faster than a wild swing can save it. The bracket of rivals, from the glass-jawed opener to the champion, is the campaign.
home-alone:
Kevin McCallister wires the house against Harry and Marv in Home Alone, the NES license Bethesda Softworks developed for THQ. Traps in the hallways and on the stairs are the weapons, and the burglars are the Wet Bandits from the film.

The 1991 cartridge keeps Kevin inside that booby-trapped house. Items picked up in one room become the next gag when a burglar steps on the right tile.

The Super Nintendo release is a separate production from another team, with its own rooms. The NES cart is Bethesda's version of the house, not a shared design copied onto the later machine.
marble-madness:
Mark Cerny designed the isometric race Marble Madness for Atari Games, a trackball cabinet that rolls one marble down ramps. Rails, catapults, and acid pools punish a marble that leaves the narrow course.

The 1984 arcade machine made the trackball the way the marble was steered. Speed and a short timer matter as much as staying on the geometry.

Home versions followed that cabinet, including an NES port of the same courses. The marble, the isometric drop, and Cerny's ramps are the game, whether the control is a trackball or a pad.
california-games:
Beach events fill California Games, Epyx's collection of surfing, half-pipe skating, and BMX. Each event has its own timing, from a wave face to a ramp lip to a dirt jump.

The computer sports collection arrived in 1987, with those beach and street contests already the lineup. Judges, crashes, and a score for style sit beside simply finishing the run.

An NES port later brought the same event list home. Surfing the wave, skating the half-pipe, and riding the BMX course remain the three set pieces Epyx is known for here.
antarctic-adventure:
Penta waddles toward the South Pole in Antarctic Adventure, Konami's ice trek across floes and fishing holes. The penguin's slide has a time limit, and falling through a gap costs the trip.

Konami's arcade version of that polar run dates to 1983, with fish already leaping from holes in the ice. Penta's line toward the South Pole fails if a floe gap takes him under.

The Famicom cartridge is a home version of that arcade trip, not a later original with a new route. Penta, the floes, and the South Pole goal are the whole journey.
soccer:
Overhead pitches and small teams define Soccer, Nintendo's black-box match sold beside the company's early baseball and tennis carts. The view looks down on a simple field, and the players are generic squads rather than licensed stars.

The Famicom match dates to 1985, in the same early sports line as those other two carts. Passing and shooting are direct, with little of the foul theater later soccer games added.

It is Nintendo's own overhead soccer, not a Konami arcade port and not an EA title. The black-box presentation and the plain diamond of play are how the cartridge presents a match.
side-pocket-1986:
Nine-ball racks and a trick-shot challenge share the table in Side Pocket (1986), Data East's pocket billiards. English on the cue ball and the order of the rack are the skills, not a fictional athlete's story.

Arcade cabinets came first and established the table, the nine-ball sets, and the trick-shot mode. A missed cushion or a scratched shot ends the problem the way a real table would.

NES and later 16-bit versions kept that same table rather than inventing a new rule set. Data East's billiards is the through-line, from the cabinet to the home carts.
dragon-quest-iii-1988:
Class changes and a hero who builds a party define Dragon Quest III (1988), the Enix RPG Enix shipped on a Wednesday in Japan so students would not skip school. Akira Toriyama's monsters fill a world that opens more widely than the two quests before it.

The hero recruits companions, picks their classes, and later changes those classes after the party has already traveled. That second vocation is the system people remember, alongside Toriyama's bestiary.

Enix treated the Wednesday release as a way to keep the Famicom launch from emptying classrooms. The class-changing hero and those monsters made this the series' Famicom peak.
robocop:
Murphy's cyborg walks and shoots through Data East's RoboCop, a side-scrolling arcade game taken from the film. ED-209 and street thugs break the march into shooting galleries with the film's armored silhouette.

An NES cartridge followed that coin-op, keeping the cyborg's slow advance and his pistol. The 1989 arcade design is the one the console board is adapting.

Ocean's computer versions are a separate set of licenses, not this coin-op and not this NES cart. Data East's side-scrolling Murphy is its own RoboCop, with the film's look and a different studio's stages.
bomberman-ii:
Fresh mazes extend the bomb-and-brick formula in Bomberman II, Hudson Soft's single-screen blaster on the NES. Soft blocks hide exits and power-ups, and the blast still travels in a straight cross.

Hudson released those new maze stages in 1991, and the robot still has to outrun his own fuse. A soft block hiding the exit is the usual prize inside each single screen.

Super Bomberman later turned the idea into a party line with its own rules and its own machine. This cartridge stays a single-screen blaster, one maze at a time, rather than that later party design.
qbert:
Coily the snake and bouncing balls intrude while Q*bert hops a pyramid and flips the color of each cube. Gottlieb's arcade character swears in symbols when he lands wrong or meets a creature on the same block.

The 1982 coin-op made the pyramid and that color-flipping hop famous. Ugg and Wrong-Way complicate the edges, but Coily is the chase players remember.

The character reached the NES long after the cabinet had already made him a name. The home board still asks for the same hop, the same cubes, and the same avoidance of Coily.
defender-of-the-crown:
Saxon lords joust, raid, and take territory in Defender of the Crown, Cinemaware's Robin Hood-era strategy game. A tournament can win land and gold, and a night raid can steal what the joust did not.

The Amiga original of 1986 is famous for those painted scenes between the strategic choices. Castles, garrisons, and the map of England give the raids a place to happen.

The NES port is a reduced take on that computer original. The joust, the raid, and the territory struggle remain, with less of the Amiga presentation around them.
mighty-final-fight:
Chibi fighters shrink Metro City's brawl into Mighty Final Fight, Capcom's super-deformed NES spinoff. Mike Haggar and the street fight against the Mad Gear gang are recognizable, and the proportions are not the arcade's.

Capcom released that spinoff in 1993, after the arcade Final Fight had already defined the city. The NES cast keeps the mayor and the kidnappers, drawn with oversized heads and short stages.

It is neither the arcade Final Fight nor the Super Nintendo sequels. Those are separate builds with their own move lists, while this cart is the super-deformed detour.
strider-1989:
Hiryu climbs a futuristic mountain with a tonfa in Strider (1989), Capcom's arcade action about a specialized agent. The weapon swings in wide arcs, and the climb uses the tonfa and Hiryu's grip on the cliff machinery.

The NES cartridge ports that coin-op, including the mountain and the organization's bases. It is the arcade Strider brought home, not a new plot written only for the console.

The Genesis Strider is a different and much longer game, with its own route. Players comparing the two are looking at two Strider designs, and the NES cart is the one tied to the arcade mountain.
the-immortal:
Isometric corridors full of sudden traps form The Immortal, the dungeon adventure Electronic Arts published from an Apple IIGS original. A wrong step on a pressure plate or a missed clue in a room can end the descent immediately.

The computer game is the original design. In 1990 that Apple IIGS quest already had its wizard's search, its pits, and its room-by-room map.

The NES edition is a later port of that computer quest. The isometric view and the lethal rooms are the part that survived the move, even with a smaller presentation.
shadow-of-the-ninja-1990:
Two ninjas take on a future emperor in Shadow of the Ninja (1990), Natsume's NES action about a seized city. Grapples, short blades, and rooftop routes carry the pair toward that ruler's stronghold.

European boxes retitle the same cartridge Blue Shadow. The stages and the emperor do not change with the box, only the name printed on it.

Natsume's future setting, with guns and a dictator rather than a historical warlord, is the backdrop. The two playable ninjas and the European retitle are the facts that separate this cart from other ninja names on the shelf.
rushn-attack-1985:
Knife rushes across a military base define Rush'n Attack (1985), the Western name for Konami's arcade game Green Beret. Soldiers advance on foot, and the knife is the default weapon when a dropped gun runs dry.

The coin-op sends the commando through gates, trucks, and missile yards. A grenade or a rocket, when one is found, is a brief upgrade rather than a new character.

An NES port followed that cabinet and kept the on-foot assault. Green Beret is the Japanese arcade name, and the Western title is the one printed on this cartridge.
elite:
Wireframe traders and wanted ratings fill Elite, the open space game David Braben and Ian Bell created on the BBC Micro. A Cobra ship docks at stations, buys cargo, and risks Thargoid encounters when the rating climbs.

The 1984 computer original is where that trading loop began. Braben and Bell fit a galaxy of stations into a machine with very little memory, using wireframe ships instead of painted scenes.

A Famicom edition came later and did not invent the design. Elite did not begin on Nintendo hardware, and the BBC Micro trading game is the one the name refers to.
guerrilla-war-1987:
Guevara is the Japanese name of Guerrilla War (1987), SNK's top-down shooter that puts Che Guevara and Fidel in command. The Western release keeps the jungle shooting and drops those two names from the briefing.

Two soldiers advance through camps, barracks, and hostages who can be rescued or caught in the fire. Grenades clear bunkers while the pair moves up the screen.

SNK's Japanese version is explicit about the historical pair. The Western cartridge is the same style of shooting without putting Che and Fidel on the title screen.
ultima-iii-exodus:
Exodus demands a mixed party in Ultima III: Exodus, Richard Garriott's chapter for Origin where fantasy races share one team. Fighters, wizards, and other callings march together instead of a single avatar solving every lock.

Origin published that party-based chapter in 1983, when Exodus required several races on one team. Sosaria's mixed party marks the chapter against the solo journeys around it.

Pony Canyon and FCI later brought a licensed version to the NES. The home cart carries Garriott's party and the Exodus crisis, adapted from the computer original rather than written as a new quest.
shinobi-1988:
Joe Musashi rescues kidnapped children in Shinobi (1988), the home cartridge of Sega's arcade mission. Shuriken and a short jump carry him through hostage rooms that the coin-op had already staged.

Sega's arcade Shinobi arrived in 1987, and that cabinet is the first appearance of Musashi's rescue. The home title's parenthetical date marks the port, not the birth of the mission.

Hostages in the line of fire change how a room is cleared. The cartridge is a port of the coin-op, and the children Musashi is there to save are the objective the arcade already used.
alien-3:
Several licenses share the name ALIEN³, spun from the film and published by LJN, and they are not one shared design. Ripley's prison colony supplies the creature and the setting, while each machine got its own stages.

The Genesis version earned the stronger reputation among those licenses. The Super Nintendo game is a separate design, with its own maps, rather than a straight copy of that Genesis cart.

A 1993 film tie-in boom produced this split, and the NES and Game Boy boards sit in the same crowded name. LJN's label covers the licenses, but playing one of them does not teach the layout of the others.
dragon-quest-iv:
Chapter cards introduce other heroes before the main quest in DRAGON QUEST IV, Enix's Famicom RPG led again by Horii, Toriyama, and Sugiyama. Ragnar, Alena, Torneko, and the twin fortune-tellers each travel before the hero's own chapter begins.

Those opening chapters are playable stories, not a menu of biographies. Toriyama's characters and Sugiyama's motifs change with the hero of the hour, then the party finally converges.

The 1990 Famicom release used that structure, and the US name was Dragon Warrior IV. Psaro's threat sits over all of the chapters, but the early hours belong to the side heroes.
home-alone-2:
Hotel lobbies and a toy store replace the first film's house in Home Alone 2, with Kevin loose in a big city. Traps and thrown props follow him from the sequel's plot, and the setting is no longer a suburban hallway.

NES and Super Nintendo carts are separate early-1990s licenses, not one game resized for two machines. Each team staged the hotel and the streets in its own way.

The 1993 releases sit beside the film's New York trip, including the toy store where Kevin rearms. Playing the NES cart does not reveal the Super Nintendo rooms, because they were never one shared build.
kung-fu-master:
Floor by floor, Thomas climbs toward Sylvia in Kung-Fu Master, the Irem arcade fighter Japan called Spartan X, a tower of knives and grippers. Each landing plays like a Hong Kong action reel.

The arcade climber dates to 1984, with five floors and a boss at each landing. Thomas's kick and punch are the whole move list, and Sylvia is the reason the elevator keeps going up.

Nintendo's NES release retitles that coin-op Kung Fu. The 1985 home cart is the building climb under a new name, not a different tower.
tom-jerry-the-ultimate-game-of-cat-and-m:
Jerry crosses side-view rooms while Tom tries to catch him in Tom & Jerry: The Ultimate Game of Cat and Mouse!
The MGM cartoon's chase is the whole plot, with the mouse solving a path and the cat acting as the hazard. Household props, from furniture to thrown objects, change how a room is crossed.

The NES chase dates to 1991, and Jerry is the one the player steers through the house. Tom's grab ends the attempt when the mouse is cornered behind the furniture.

It is a cartoon license built as a side-view pursuit, not a versus match where both animals are equal fighters. The title's claim is the chase itself.
little-nemo-the-dream-master:
Candy bribes sleeping animals so Nemo can ride them in Little Nemo: The Dream Master, Capcom's adaptation of the Slumberland film and comic. A fed frog, a mole, or another dream creature lends its movement until the stage's logic changes.

Capcom brought that ride-the-animal idea to the NES in 1990, crossing Slumberland by borrowed bodies. A polite dream garden and a harsher nightmare room need different creatures, because Nemo's own jump is rarely enough.

The candy is both key and timer, because the animal wakes or wanders if the feeding is mishandled. Nemo's own small jump is rarely enough, which is why the sleeping creatures matter.
worms:
Andy Davidson turned artillery duels into cartoon worms for Team17's Worms, on landscapes that blow apart under the shot. A bazooka, a grenade, or a ninja rope changes who can even see the other team after the dirt is gone.

The design started on the Amiga. Team17's 1995 release made the squirming army and the destructible hill a familiar match rather than a grim hex war.

Nintendo machines got ports after that Amiga original. The ninja rope and the crumbling bridge are the toys those ports are carrying, not a new ruleset invented for a console.
wolfenstein-3d:
B.J. Blazkowicz moves through a Nazi castle in Wolfenstein 3D, id Software's maze of guards, push-walls, and locked doors. The pistol and the stolen guns are simple, and the castle's right angles did a lot to popularize first-person shooting on PC.

id released that castle crawl in 1992, hiding secret rooms behind push-walls. A player who checks every panel finds more than the marked doors of the Nazi fortress.

The Super Nintendo port censors much of the original imagery. Swastikas, gore, and some of the castle's explicit props are altered, so the home version is not a perfect copy of the PC floors.
mortal-kombat:
Digitized actors and graphic finishing moves announced Mortal Kombat when Midway put it in arcades. Scorpion's spear and Sub-Zero's freeze are performed by photographed fighters, and Goro towers over the human-sized roster.

The arcade arrival was in 1992, and the finishing moves were the detail that traveled by rumor. Liu Kang, Johnny Cage, Sonya, and Kano fill out a cast that looks like photos rather than drawings.

On the Super Nintendo the blood became sweat, a recolor that fed the violence debate. The sweat substitute is the Super Nintendo version's scar, not a feature of the arcade cabinet.
doom-2:
Shareware spread the first episode of DOOM far beyond store shelves after id Software released it on PC. Mars, the UAC complex, and a shotgun in a tight corridor became the picture of the game even for people who never bought a boxed copy.

That PC debut was in 1993, with imps and a cyberdemon already in the episode players passed around. The shareware slice was enough to teach the doors, the secrets, and the circle-strafing habit.

Super Nintendo and later Game Boy Advance versions are reduced conversions, not the debut. Smaller windows and cut content mean those carts are adaptations of id's PC game, not the version that spread first.
final-fantasy-vi:
An ensemble casts magic against an empire in Final Fantasy VI, and the second half lets the player choose who walks point. Terra's magic, Magitek armor, and Kefka's cruelty set the first half, then the World of Ruin scatters the cast.

Square's story does not stay with one swordsman. Celes, Locke, and the rest can lead after the catastrophe, which is the structural break the blurb is pointing at.

North America first knew this Super Nintendo game as Final Fantasy III. The 1994 Japanese numbering is the sixth, and the American box used a different count for the same opera, the same empire, and the same ruined world.
super-mario-world:
Super Mario World hides a second map, the Star Road, behind exits that a straight run to Bowser never needs. Many stages have a normal exit and a secret one, and only the secret exit redraws the map.

It was a launch title for the Super Nintendo, directed by Shigeru Miyamoto with Takashi Tezuka, and it introduced Yoshi as a mount that can eat enemies and, with a shell color, gain a new ability. A cape replaces the raccoon tail and lets Mario fly if the player builds speed.

The ghost houses, the forest of illusion, and the secret exits made the world map a puzzle of its own. Koji Kondo's overworld theme is the melody most people still hum when they picture the game.

Later 2D Mario games, from Yoshi's Island to the New Super Mario Bros. line, keep answering this map, this dinosaur, and these exits. This page is the original Super Mario World, not those follow-ups.
super-mario-bros:
Super Mario Bros. turned a running jump, a fire flower, and a flagpole into the pattern later Mario games still answer. Pipes, brick blocks, and a flagpole at the end of a short stage became the language of the series.

Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka built it at Nintendo with Koji Kondo's looping themes, after the team had already made the single-screen Mario Bros. arcade. Warp zones, a hidden 1-Up in a block, and the minus world glitch gave players secrets to trade in schoolyards.

The princess-rescue plot is short on purpose. The design work is in the enemy mix: Goombas, Koopa Troopas that become shells, and Bowser's false bridges. A timer forces the run to stay short, which is why speedrunners still treat the cartridge as a measured dash.

Nintendo later folded the same stages into Super Mario All-Stars and into handheld remakes. Those editions are other entries. This page is the original side-scrolling Super Mario Bros.
a-link-to-the-past:
The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past splits Hyrule into a light world and a dark world that share one map. A tool you win in one dungeon is the key that makes an earlier screen suddenly traversable.

Nintendo's team, with Shigeru Miyamoto producing and Takashi Tezuka directing, built each dungeon around a single tool: a hookshot, a hammer, a cane. The Master Sword is the hinge of the story, pulled once the three pendants are found, and then the same kingdom turns hostile.

The opening, with Link woken in the rain and sent after Zelda through the castle sewers, is more plotted than the first Zelda, yet the player can still wander. The flute, the magic medallions, and the bottle collection became the series' inventory language.

A Game Boy Advance port added a small extra quest. The 2019 Link's Awakening remake and the 2013 A Link Between Worlds are different games. This page is the Super Nintendo original.
chrono-trigger:
Chrono Trigger lets a festival accident throw a small party across several eras of one planet. The fair, the trial, and the ruined future are the same planet arguing with itself.

Square assembled an unusual team: Hironobu Sakaguchi, Yuji Horii, and Akira Toriyama on the story and character art, with Yasunori Mitsuda writing most of the score until health forced him to share the last tracks. Battles take place on the field, and where a character stands changes what a tech can hit.

New Game+ keeps levels and gear so a second journey can reach endings the first clock would not allow. The trial at the start of the future, the reptite past, and the ruined dome are one timeline arguing with itself.

A Nintendo DS port later added extra dungeons and a monster arena. This page is the Super Nintendo Chrono Trigger, the version whose ending count and soundtrack made it the RPG people recommended for a decade.
super-mario-bros-3:
Tanooki suits and a world map turn short stages into a toy box in Super Mario Bros. 3, with airships parked between the levels. Raccoon tails, frog suits, and hammer overalls sit in the inventory for those short runs.

Koopalings hold those airships, and Boom Boom waits in the fortresses. A warp whistle, found rather than earned by a straight clear, skips whole regions of the map.

The game reached players in 1988 and became the third side-scrolling Mario, a cornerstone of the 8-bit lineup. Picking a suit and wandering the map matter as much as reaching any single flagpole.
eye-of-the-beholder:
Waterdeep's sewers hide a beholders' lair in Eye of the Beholder, the first-person Advanced Dungeons & Dragons crawl Westwood developed for SSI. A party of four moves on a grid, and the portrait of each adventurer shows who is still standing.

The computer game is the original, with the city's underworld and the beholder at the end of the descent. Spells and melee are chosen from the portraits while the view stays in the corridor ahead.

A Super Nintendo port came afterward and carries that grid crawl home. The 1990 computer release under Waterdeep is the one the port is following, not a quest written for the console first.
final-fantasy-v:
Job tablets let the cast change classes in FINAL FANTASY V, Square's Super Famicom RPG built around that freedom. Bartz and his companions can leave a knight's path for a mage's, and the wind crystal's shattering is what starts the need.

Square released the job system on the Super Famicom in 1992, and Faris, Lenna, and Galuf share one class menu. A pirate and a princess can end up with the same skill if the player insists.

No official English edition existed until long after the Japanese release. The jobs, the crystals, and the Super Famicom original are what players mean when they talk about this chapter rather than a later translation.
super-metroid:
Super Metroid opens with Samus delivering a baby metroid to researchers and then returning to a station that has already gone wrong. An item counter on the map screen invites a second pass through rooms you already survived.

Yoshio Sakamoto directed the Super Nintendo sequel as a quiet map: almost no dialogue, an item percentage on the map screen, and rooms that only make sense after a later upgrade. The planet Zebes is explored again, but the route is a web of missile tanks, a shinespark, and doors sealed with colored gates.

Sequence breaks became part of the game's reputation. Players learned to leave the intended path with mockball tricks and early ice-beam routes, and Nintendo's own map still functions when they do. The final escape, with a timer and a last look at the baby metroid, is the scene the series keeps echoing.

Metroid Fusion and Metroid Dread continue Samus's story from this ending. The Prime games move the same idea of isolation into first person. This page is Super Metroid itself.
earthworm-jim:
A robotic suit turns a worm into a run-and-gun hero in Earthworm Jim, launched by Shiny Entertainment and David Perry. New Junk City opens with a cow used as a living projectile, and Psycrow wants the suit back.

The first release was on the Sega Genesis in 1994, with the cartoon frames and the whip-like worm body already in place. Princess What's-Her-Name is the excuse for the trip, but the suit's guns and the worm's stretch are the verbs.

Super Nintendo and handheld versions followed that Genesis original. They are ports of Shiny's cartoon, not the place the cow, the suit, or Psycrow were invented.
another-world:
Lester Chaykin, a physicist, is stranded with almost no readable text in Another World, Eric Chahi's rotoscoped adventure published by Delphine. A cage, a whip, and an alien ally replace a tutorial, and the player learns by dying.

Delphine published that silent planet in 1991, with rotoscoped figures that move like filmed bodies. The beast in the opening is a lesson in timing rather than a stat check.

North America called the same game Out of This World. The physicist, the alien buddy, and the near-absence of words are the work, under either title.
donkey-kong-country:
Pre-rendered fur and a mine-cart ride define Donkey Kong Country, Rare's jungle where Diddy covers ground the big ape cannot. Rambi the rhino, Expresso the ostrich, and other animal buddies change the speed and the attack of a stage.

Rare and Nintendo shipped the pre-rendered look as a Super Nintendo showcase. Barrels, rope swings, and the mine cart are the set pieces, and King K. Rool's Kremlings are the army in the way.

The game arrived in 1994 and restarted the ape as a platform-game lead after years of cameo duty. Rare's first Donkey Kong Country is the cartridge those mine carts and that rhino belong to.
disneys-aladdin-1993:
Hand-drawn cels of the film's cast distinguish Virgin Interactive's Disney's Aladdin, the Genesis platformer known for that animation. Abu, the Carpet, and the Genie appear as drawn frames, and Agrabah's streets are built around that look.

Virgin's version arrived in 1993 and is not the only Aladdin on Nintendo shelves. Capcom's Super Nintendo Aladdin is a different game, with its own stages and its own handling of the lamp.

The NES and Game Boy editions differ again, each a separate production. Virgin's hand-drawn Genesis cart is the one the animation reputation belongs to, while Capcom's console version has to be judged on its own rooms.
ultimate-mortal-kombat-3:
Extra kombatants revise the roster in Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3, where Midway adds fighters beyond the first Mortal Kombat 3 cabinet. Classic ninjas return, and animalities join a finishing-move list the earlier board did not have.

The cabinet itself is the 1995 revision, one update past the first MK3 lineup. Kitana, Jade, and Scorpion are among the names the update puts back on the select screen.

A Super Nintendo port followed that cabinet. It is the updated roster and the added stages, not the original MK3 board with a new sticker.
prince-of-persia-nes:
Rotoscoped leaps and a one-hour dungeon define Prince of Persia (1989), Jordan Mechner's Apple II game of traps and sword fights. Mechner filmed his brother for the prince's run, and the spikes and closing gates expect that weight.

Broderbund published the timed escape, with the princess and the vizier's hourglass already running. A loose tile or a late sword parry costs seconds the dungeon does not refund.

NES, Super Nintendo, and Game Boy ports came after that computer original. The rotoscoped run and the traps are Mechner's Apple II design, and the console carts are later carriers of it.
tetris-1984:
Falling tetrominoes lock into complete lines in Tetris (1984), the puzzle Alexey Pajitnov designed in Moscow. A straight bar, a square, and the awkward S shapes are the whole vocabulary, and a filled line is the only way to breathe.

Pajitnov's first version is the one this title points at. The Soviet design stacks the pieces until the well overflows, with no Nintendo mascot in the well.

Nintendo's Game Boy edition is a later licensed hit, not this first version. The Moscow stacking game and the handheld phenomenon share the tetrominoes and do not share a birthplace.
super-mario-bros-2:
Subspace vegetables and a four-person cast define Super Mario Bros. 2, the Western sequel built from a different Japanese game. Mario, Luigi, Toad, and Peach pick up Shy Guys and throw them, and Birdo spits eggs that can be thrown back.

Peach's float and Luigi's jump make the same stage a different route. Wart waits at the end of Subcon, and the dream framing explains why the enemies are not Goombas.

The game sits between the original and Super Mario Bros. 3, and it later returned inside Super Mario All-Stars. It reached players in 1988, already a reskin of Yume Kojo: Doki Doki Panic rather than a harder copy of the first Mario.
earthworm-jim-2:
Puppy Love, the stage where a puppy must be bounced to safety, sits inside Earthworm Jim 2 among Shiny's continuing cartoon levels. The worm, the suit, and the inflated absurdity of the first game return with new gags rather than a straight repeat.

Shiny continued the series in 1995, and Sega hardware led again. The bounced puppy is one of the stages people describe when they separate this sequel from the first cart.

Nintendo ports followed the Sega lead, as they had with the first worm. The bounced puppy and the new level toys are the sequel's own material.
super-mario-kart:
Banana peels and a red shell define Super Mario Kart, the Mode 7 racer whose handling stays slippery on purpose. Lakitu fishes a fallen driver back onto Rainbow Road, and Donut Plains hides a jump that a straight line will miss.

Nintendo's first Mario Kart uses the Super Nintendo's Mode 7 to rotate the track under the kart. A mushroom is a burst of speed, and the shell is a weapon, not scenery.

The game arrived in 1992 and is the original, not a later title that reused the cast. Slippery corners and those items are the rules later karts still answer.
earthbound:
Onett's baseball bats and psychic flashes open EarthBound, the modern-dress journey of Ness and his friends. Paula, Jeff, and Poo join across a country of suburbs, cultists, and department stores, and Giygas waits at the end of that odd map.

Ape, HAL Laboratory, and Nintendo stand behind the cartridge, with Shigesato Itoi's writing in the tone of the battles. PSI and a bat replace a medieval sword, and a hamburger can matter more than a potion.

The Super Nintendo release in 1994 is the Mother game many players met through later reissues and the series' reputation. Saturn Valley's Mr. Saturns and the photo at the end belong to this cult RPG.
super-mario-world-2-yoshis-island:
Crayon hills and a flutter jump carry Baby Mario in Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island, where the eggs are both ammo and a way to hit a distant post. Kamek's toadies snatch the baby when the timer after a hit runs out.

Yoshi's aim with a thrown egg solves puzzles a stomp cannot. The crayon shading and the pastel enemies are the look of the stages, and Baby Bowser is the reason Kamek interferes.

The game arrived in 1995 as a Super Nintendo Yoshi platformer, a spin on Mario World rather than a kart or a party board. The egg, the flutter, and the baby on the saddle are the verbs.
mortal-kombat-3:
A run button and cybernetic ninjas arrive with Mortal Kombat 3, Midway's arcade lineup that lets fighters dash. Cyrax and Sektor bring the metal masks, and the run changes the spacing of the older spear-and-freeze game.

Midway put that cabinet out in 1995, with the cyber ninjas and the dash as the mechanical news. Shao Kahn's invasion is the story the roster is built to serve.

Home editions, including the Super Nintendo one, followed that cabinet. The run button and the cyber bodies are what this entry adds on top of the earlier tournaments.
mortal-kombat-2:
Blood codes unlock the red pixels in Mortal Kombat 2 on the Super Nintendo, reversing the first home version's sweat substitute. Kitana's fans and Kung Lao's hat join a roster much wider than the original arcade cast.

Midway's sequel reached the Super Nintendo in 1993 with that code available to players who wanted the arcade's gore back. Friendships and babalities sit beside the older finishing moves, so the tone is broader than a single fatality.

The widened roster is the other half of the news. Kitana, Mileena, and Kung Lao are reasons to pick the sequel even before the code is entered.
donkey-kong-country-2:
Dixie's ponytail spins like a helicopter in Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest, and she and Diddy are the ones doing the rescuing. Donkey Kong himself is the prisoner, so the lighter pair has to cross tighter stages than the first jungle asked for.

Animal buddies return with new jobs, and the bramble and the beehives punish a sloppy jump. Kaptain K. Rool holds the ape, and the map is a pirate's route rather than a straight replay of the first island.

Rare and Nintendo released this second Country game in 1995, and players who want harder levels often name it. Dixie's hover and Diddy's speed are the tools those tighter stages expect.
the-lion-king:
Wildebeest gorge turns a stampede into a platform test in Disney's The Lion King, Virgin's difficult adaptation of Simba's life. Young Simba's roar and the adult Simba's pounce are different move sets, and the gorge is the stage players warn each other about.

Virgin built the film's timeline as a platformer, from the presentation of the cub through the later fights. Scar's shadow sits over the story, but the difficulty is in the jumps and the animal hazards.

Genesis and Super Nintendo copies led the release in 1994, with the wildebeest run as the notorious test. The shift from cub Simba to adult Simba is the spine of those 16-bit carts.
battletoads-double-dragon:
Toads meet the Lee brothers in Battletoads & Double Dragon, Rare's crossover published by Tradewest. Rash, Zitz, and Pimple share a roster with Billy and Jimmy, and the Dark Queen's plot is the excuse for the team-up.

The crossover arrived in 1993, and the NES, Super Nintendo, and Game Boy editions are not the same build. A trick learned on one machine may be missing from another's move list.

Tradewest's name is on the publishing side, and Rare made the meeting. The speeder habits of the toads and the brawler habits of the Lees have to live in whatever version is in the slot, and those versions were built separately.
the-chaos-engine:
Victorian mercenaries fight through a corrupted Britain in The Chaos Engine, The Bitmap Brothers' moody shooter sold in the US as Soldiers of Fortune. Two guns-for-hire share the screen, and the machine of the title is what has twisted the alleys.

The Amiga original dates to 1993, with the brown-and-brass look already in place. A partner can be a friend or a computer ally, and the levels are mazes of gates and monsters rather than a straight trench.

A Super Nintendo port exists of that Victorian science-fiction world. Soldiers of Fortune is the American name, and the Bitmap Brothers' Amiga design is the source.
super-3-d-noahs-ark:
Food pellets, fired from a launcher, calm the animals in Super 3-D Noah's Ark, Wisdom Tree's unlicensed Super Nintendo game. The viewpoint and the maze owe a debt to a Wolfenstein-style engine, but the targets are goats and ostriches that need feeding.

Wisdom Tree released the cartridge in 1994 outside Nintendo's approval. The cart bypassed the lockout chip, which is how an unlicensed board could boot at all.

Noah's errand is the story pasted on that engine: stock the ark by stunning creatures with food rather than by killing guards. The lockout bypass and the food launcher are the two facts that identify the cartridge.
rock-n-roll-racing:
Licensed riffs punch in between heats in Rock n' Roll Racing, the isometric combat race Silicon & Synapse made for Interplay. Cars drop weapons on a diagonal track, and the song stings play in the pause before the next planet's grid.

Silicon & Synapse, later known as Blizzard, built that mix. The 1993 Interplay release treats the soundtrack as part of the event, not as a menu that can be ignored.

Isometric cars, mines, and rockets make a clean first place hard to hold. The rock cues between events are as much a signature as the weapons.
super-mario-rpg:
Geno joins Mario, Bowser, and Peach in a turn-based party in Super Mario RPG, the story Square built with Nintendo. Smithy's gang shatters the Star Road, and Mallow the cloud-creature fills out a group that should not share a battle menu.

Timed hits reward a button press as the weapon lands, so the turn-based fight still asks for rhythm. Bowser as a party member, rather than the last boss, is the casting joke the alliance depends on.

Square and Nintendo released the game in 1996 on the Super Nintendo. A separate remake from 2023 has its own page in this catalog, and Smithy's story here is the original party.
lemmings:
Blocker lemmings and a builder's staircase keep the crowd off the cliff in Lemmings, DMA Design's puzzle published by Psygnosis. Each creature walks until a job, assigned one at a time, digs, builds, or stops the line.

The Amiga original is the famous one. Psygnosis published it in 1991, with the green hair and the doorway exit already the picture players draw from memory.

Nintendo ports came later and carry the same job list. The builder, the blocker, and the cliff are DMA's puzzle, and the ports are how that puzzle reached a console.
mega-man-x:
Armor capsules and a dash move Mega Man into a faster future in Mega Man X, where a wall jump replaces the older ladder habit. Zero fights beside him, Sigma commands the Mavericks, and Dr. Light's hidden tanks upgrade the armor.

Capcom opened the X series on the Super Nintendo with that speed. The dash and the wall cling change every corridor that a classic robot-master stage would have walked.

The game arrived in 1993 and stays separate from the numbered NES Mega Man line. Sigma's revolt and Zero's saber belong to this future, not to Dr. Wily's earlier gauntlet.
final-fantasy-iv-1991:
Cecil Harvey's dark-knight guilt drives Final Fantasy IV (1991), the Super Famicom story that introduced the Active Time Battle gauge. Kain, Rosa, and Rydia join and leave, and Golbez's hold on the crystals is the threat above Baron.

The gauge fills even while the player is reading a menu, so a slow choice is a real delay. Cecil's path from dark knight toward paladin is the character arc the battles are hung on.

North America retitled this game Final Fantasy II. It is the real fourth story, Cecil's, and not a sequel to the American numbering that had skipped chapters.
super-star-wars:
Landspeeder chases use Mode 7 in Super Star Wars, the LucasArts and Sculptured Software adaptation of A New Hope. Luke, Han, and the Death Star trench each get a form, from a side-view blaster run to a into-the-screen race.

The Super Nintendo game opened a trilogy of film tie-ins on that console. Tatooine's cantina hazards and the Death Star's corridor sit beside the landspeeder's Mode 7 stretch.

Sculptured Software and LucasArts shipped it in 1992, opening a trilogy of film tie-ins. Later carts reused the blaster stages and the Mode 7 vehicle scenes, with this A New Hope board as the first of the three.
simcity-2000:
Isometric zoning and a newspaper of disasters define SimCity 2000, Maxis's follow-up to its city builder. Underground pipes and subways sit on a layer beneath the streets, and the paper reports the fires and the crashes the mayor failed to prevent.

Will Wright's studio switched the view off the plain top-down map. Arcologies and the underground view give the mayor a vertical problem the first game did not draw.

The computer original arrived in 1993, and a Super Nintendo port followed that PC design. Isometric blocks and the newspaper of disasters came along in the console version.
theme-park:
Ride prices and path layouts decide whether guests wander happy in Theme Park, Bullfrog's management game associated with Peter Molyneux. A roller coaster's intensity, a burger's cost, and the distance to a bin are all levers.

Bullfrog's computer original lets the player watch individual guests move, not only a spreadsheet. Shops, queues, and research into new attractions fill the park lot.

The management game dates to 1994, and a Super Nintendo port followed. Molyneux's association and Bullfrog's guest-watching model are the computer game the port is based on.
darkwing-duck:
Gas-gun theatrics and a cape define Disney's Darkwing Duck, Capcom's NES continuation of its Disney platformers. The cartoon duck who poses as a superhero gets stages built around that gas gun and a short glide.

Capcom placed the cart in 1992, after the studio's earlier Disney jumps on the same machine. St. Canard's criminals are the bosses, and the pose is the character's joke even when the pit is serious.

A Game Boy version was released as well. The NES stages are the main Capcom treatment, still in the line of the studio's Disney platformers rather than a new genre for the duck.
ninja-gaiden:
Ryu Hayabusa clings to walls between cinema scenes in Ninja Gaiden, Tecmo's NES action that cuts to a story after each stage. The cling, the slash, and the wind scroll of those cutscenes became the trilogy's language.

Jaquio's cult and the statues Ryu climbs are the first game's obstacles. A knocked-down Ryu restarts the climb with little mercy, which is why the wall grip matters.

Tecmo released the game in 1988, and the NES trilogy starts here. This is the home run the catalog treats as the original, the one the later Tecmo sequels are answering.
ice-climber:
Popo hammers ice blocks while Nana climbs beside him in Ice Climber, and a condor waits at the top of each mountain. Vegetables sit in the bonus gap under the bird, and a polar bear patrols the bricks.

The hammer both breaks a floor and bonks a creature nesting in it. A missed jump sends a climber sliding, and the condor flies off if the pair is too slow.

Nintendo's compact mountain dates to 1985 and stayed recognizable through later cameos. Popo, Nana, the hammer, and that condor are the whole loop.
final-fantasy-ii-1988:
Weapon practice raises a stat in Final Fantasy II (1988), Square's game that grows characters by the actions they take. Firion and his allies do not collect the usual experience levels, and the Emperor is the tyrant at the end of that experiment.

Using swords makes a swordsman, and taking hits makes a sturdier body. Maria, Guy, and Leon are caught in the same system, so the player's habits become the build.

The American Super Nintendo game called Final Fantasy II is actually IV. This cartridge is the real second game, the one with the use-based growth and the Emperor.
super-contra-1988:
Overhead jeep sections alternate with side-view runs in Super Contra (1988), Konami's arcade sequel. The vehicle stretches of the coin-op and the on-foot alien bases are both part of the cabinet, not a single camera.

Bill and Lance return to a larger invasion than the first run. Turrets, overhead roadways, and vertical bases change the shape of the shooting from stage to stage.

The NES game Super C is a later, rearranged home edition, not this cabinet. Konami's arcade Super Contra is the one with the original overhead-and-side split, and Super C rebuilds that idea rather than copying every yard.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-ii-the-arca:
Foot soldiers march in the coin-op stages of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: The Arcade Game, Konami's NES port for two players. Leonardo, Donatello, Michelangelo, and Raphael each bring a weapon, and Shredder waits at the end of the arcade's route.

Bebop and Rocksteady appear as they did in the cabinet, with April's rescue along the way. The port's job is those arcade stages, not a new overworld.

Konami released the NES port in 1990, so two players could share the Foot-clan brawl the coin-op had already drawn. The subtitle names the arcade because those stages, not a new overworld, are the cart's job.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-tournament-:
One-on-one shells and a tournament bracket replace the brawler in Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Tournament Fighters. Konami built a fighter, and the NES and Super Nintendo cartridges of that name are different games.

Neither cart continues the earlier side-scrolling sewer fights. Health bars, special moves, and a versus screen are the structure, with the turtles and their rivals as duelists.

The split between the two 1993 cartridges matters, because a combo on one machine is not a combo on the other. Konami treated the NES board and the Super Nintendo board as separate fighters that happen to share a title.
super-mario-bros-the-lost-levels:
Poison mushrooms and gusts of wind harshen Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels, the Japanese Super Mario Bros. 2 later retitled abroad. Luigi's higher jump and slipperier stop make the same gap a different commitment.

Warp pipes and castle gates return, but the mushroom that looks helpful can cost a life. The wind pushes a jump that the first quest would have left alone.

The game dates to 1986 and, in this catalog, is the NES sibling of the original, not the Western throw-the-vegetables sequel. That vegetable quest is a different game with a different enemy cast.
mega-man-3-1990:
Rush the dog joins the support gear in Mega Man 3 (1990), and Proto Man takes a role in the story beyond a distant whistle. Rush Coil, Rush Jet, and Rush Marine change how a pit or a water stretch is crossed.

Capcom's new gear sits under the usual robot-master weapons. A coil spring, a flight, or a marine form is chosen before the hazard, which the first two games solved with the arm cannon alone.

Proto Man's appearances tie the stages together as a plot, not only a boss list. The dog and that rival are what set this NES chapter apart from the opening pair.
track-field:
Button-mashing dashes and a long jump share Track & Field, Konami's Olympic button-hammer known in Japan as Hyper Olympic. The 100-meter run asks for speed on the buttons, and the javelin asks for an angle a moment later.

Konami's arcade events date to 1983, from hurdles to the hammer throw. The controller takes a beating, and the on-screen athlete is only as fast as the taps.

Home versions, the NES one included, kept that rapid tapping. Hyper Olympic is the Japanese name, and the Western box is Track & Field for the same button-driven meet.
double-dragon-ii:
Marian's loss sends Billy and Jimmy Lee back into the gang in Double Dragon II: The Revenge, and the NES edition rebuilds that plot with its own stages. Technos had already told the revenge in arcades before the home cart rearranged the rooms.

New moves and new alleys mean an arcade pattern does not solve the NES climb. The brothers still punch, kick, and throw, but the layout is a home design.

The arcade version arrived in 1988, and the NES board followed with its own revenge geography. Billy, Jimmy, and Marian's absence are the story, told twice in two different sets of rooms.
paperboy:
Handlebar cabinets steer the bicycle in Paperboy, Atari Games' route past dogs, skateboards, and broken windows. Subscribers on one side of the street want the paper, and a smashed pane on the other side is a different kind of point.

The 1985 arcade machine made the handlebars part of its identity. The paper has to hit the porch, and a missed throw or a collision ends the morning.

The NES port has none of those handlebars. It keeps the suburban street, the dogs, and the windows, and it leaves the cabinet's unique control behind.
castlevania-iii-draculas-curse:
Trevor Belmont can take Sypha, Grant, or Alucard onto branching roads in Castlevania III: Dracula's Curse. The pirate's climb, the mage's spell, and the dhampir's attack rewrite a corridor the whip alone would fail.

Konami forks the map so a chosen partner locks some stairs and opens others. The clock tower and the marsh are not a single mandatory march, which is the expansion beyond the first castle.

The game arrived in 1989 and is often treated as the peak of the 8-bit entries. Trevor's whip remains the spine, and the partner is what makes this late NES Castlevania wider than a straight ascent.
adventure-island-1986:
Skateboards and thrown axes carry Master Higgins in Adventure Island (1986), Hudson's Famicom game based on Sega's Wonder Boy. Fruit keeps a hunger timer at bay, and the skateboard turns a flat stretch into a faster risk.

The licensed arcade design supplies the axes and the board. Hudson's hero wears the island setting, but the skeleton of the run is the Wonder Boy cabinet it was drawn from.

A missed fruit or a dropped axe changes the next screen more than a higher score would. Higgins's name is the Hudson dressing on that licensed chase toward the captured girl.
tiny-toon-adventures:
Buster Bunny leads the Acme Acres kids in Tiny Toon Adventures, Konami's NES cartoon platformer. Plucky and Hamton appear in a cast built from the afternoon show, and the stages are gags rather than a grim fortress.

Konami shipped this cartridge in 1991, on a different board from the later Super Nintendo Buster game. The NES rooms and that later cart do not share a layout.

Acme Acres' sight gags, from silly enemies to Buster's ears as a glide, are the NES version's texture. Konami's first Tiny Toons cart on this machine is the one those Acme streets belong to.
circus-charlie:
Fire hoops, tightropes, and a balancing ball make the acts in Circus Charlie, Konami's clown show. Charlie rides or walks through each specialty, and a fall from the rope or a missed hoop ends the trick.

The arcade act dates to 1984, with lions, flames, and the high wire as separate events. The bill feels like a variety show rather than one continuous stage.

The Famicom port is a home version of that coin-op. The clown, the hoops, and the tightrope are Konami's circus, moved from the cabinet to the cartridge.
castlevania-ii-simons-quest-1987:
Daylight fades into a dangerous night in Castlevania II: Simon's Quest (1987), and the whip's journey becomes a countryside search. Towns sell garlic and clues, and Dracula's scattered remains are the objects Simon Belmont is trying to assemble.

Mansions replace a single straight castle march. A villager's cryptic line is often the only hint toward the next body part or the next hidden stair.

Konami opened the sequel into that day-night map. The towns, the clues, and the cycle of light are the structure, not a corridor of candelabras ending at one throne.
joust:
Ostrich knights score by striking from above in Joust, Williams' duel of lances and wings. A buzzard rider is the enemy, and the lava pit's hand punishes anyone who drifts too low.

The arcade cabinet dates to 1982, and flapping keeps the ostrich aloft. The higher lance wins the collision, which is the rule that makes the chaos readable.

An NES port arrived years later. The cabinet is the original, with the ostriches and the buzzards, and the home cart is a later carrier of that same higher-lance rule.
mega-man-4:
Charged buster shots and a false patron define Mega Man 4 (1991), which sends the hero against Dr. Cossack before the usual Wily twist. Pharaoh Man and the other new masters still drop weapons, and the charge is available even before those weapons are taken.

The arm cannon can be held until the shot grows, a habit the earlier games did not ask for. Cossack's citadel looks like the final stop until the plot turns back toward Dr. Wily.

Capcom kept the side-view robot run and added that charge and that misdirection. The NES chapter is still a master-weapon loop, with Cossack as the detour.
batman-the-video-game:
Grappling lines and wall jumps move Batman through original stages in Batman: The Video Game, Sunsoft's NES game that borrows the 1989 film's look without retelling the movie. Gotham's warehouses and mechanical shafts are new routes, not a walk through the film's scenes in order.

The wall jump and the grappling line are the verbs. A shot from the gadget and a cling to the brick replace a straight brawler's punch.

Sunsoft built those stages for the NES, and a Game Boy version exists beside them. The film supplies the silhouette, while the wall jump and the line are how this Batman actually travels.
lode-runner:
Gold bars sit inside diggable brick in Lode Runner, the puzzle Hudson brought from Broderbund to the Famicom. Guards chase the thief, and a dug hole traps them only until they climb back out.

The US edition followed in 1987, and every piece of gold has to be taken before the exit matters. A buried guard is a temporary tool rather than a permanent kill.

Hudson's home version keeps the dig, the trap, and the gold. Broderbund's computer puzzle is the source, and this cartridge is the Famicom and NES life of that chase.
galaxian:
Diving flags peel out of formation in Galaxian, Namco's shooter that sends aliens down at the player instead of only marching in rigid rows. The Flagship splits into escorts, and a dive is more dangerous than the formation's slow advance.

Namco's cabinet dates to 1979, and leaving the row to swoop was the step past locked ranks. The Flagship's dive is the cabinet's real threat.

The NES release is a much later port of that arcade shooter. The diving escorts and the Flagship are the coin-op's idea, and the home cart is carrying them across a long gap.
ducktales-2:
Pogo cane hops return with Scrooge McDuck in Disney's DuckTales 2, Capcom's second NES treasure hunt. The cane's bounce is still the way to cross spikes and stun a foe, and the new routes are a sequel's maps rather than a redraw of the first cart.

Capcom shipped the follow-up in 1993, with Huey, Dewey, Louie, and Launchpad still in Scrooge's orbit. The stages are new hunts rather than a redraw of the first cart's maps.

It is a sequel to the studio's first DuckTales cartridge, not a remake with a new coat of paint. The pogo cane is the inherited tool, and the new treasure maps are the reason to treat it as its own game.
wild-gunman-1984:
Zapper duels against drawing outlaws structure Wild Gunman (1984), Nintendo's Famicom light-gun game. The opponent's hand twitches, and the shot has to land in the window after the draw, not before.

An earlier Nintendo electromechanical arcade of the same name dates to the 1970s. That older machine and this cartridge share a title and a showdown, and they are not the same hardware.

The Famicom game wants the Zapper and a television, with the outlaws on the cartridge. The 1970s electromechanical cabinet is the ancestor of the name, not the board in this slot.
felix-the-cat:
A magic bag turns into vehicles and weapons in Felix the Cat, Hudson Soft's platformer of the classic cartoon. The bag's transformations carry Felix across stages that would be impossible on his ordinary walk.

Hudson released NES and Game Boy versions in the early 1990s, with the 1992 NES cart among them. The bag is the inventory and the vehicle, not a cosmetic nod to the cartoons.

This is not an Adventure Island spinoff wearing a cat's face. Felix's bag of tricks is its own Hudson platformer, on both the NES and the handheld.
mega-man-5:
Gravity Man's hold and Gyro Man's blades headline Mega Man 5 (1992), alongside a charge shot and the usual special weapons. Proto Man's apparent betrayal is the story hook that makes the stages feel like a setup.

Capcom keeps the side-view robot masters and adds the suspicion about the rival. Gravity Hold changes a room's jumps, which is a stranger gift than a simple spread shot.

The charge shot remains available beside those borrowed weapons. Proto Man's seeming turn is the NES plot, and Gravity Man and Gyro Man are the bosses that announce this chapter.
space-invaders-1978:
Descending invaders and destructible bunkers define Space Invaders (1978), the Taito game designed by Tomohiro Nishikado. A mystery saucer crosses overhead for bonus points while the formation steps down toward the cannon.

Nishikado's march helped make arcade games a mass business. The bunkers wear away under both the aliens' bombs and the player's own shots, so cover is temporary.

The NES cart is one of many later ports of that formation. Taito's original march, the saucer, and the bunkers are the game, and the home cartridge is a later carrier.
contra-force:
Swappable operatives replace the usual pair in Contra Force, Konami's NES spinoff with no arcade original. The player can change members during a run-and-gun stage, and each member's weapon changes the next room.

Konami released the task-force story in 1992, with no coin-op whose stages this cart is trying to copy. That missing cabinet is what separates it from the earlier Contra boards.

Switching bodies mid-stage is the mechanical hook. The task force, rather than the famous duo, is who shows up on the select screen.
pool-of-radiance:
Phlan's ruins host the first Gold Box party in Pool of Radiance, SSI's Advanced Dungeons & Dragons game set in the Forgotten Realms. A party approaches the city's cursed blocks, and combat uses the Gold Box formation rather than a single hero's slash.

SSI published that computer RPG in 1988, set in the occupation of Phlan. Gold Box party tactics, not a single hero's slash, decide the ruined blocks.

The NES version adapts that party combat. Phlan and the Gold Box rules are the source, and the cartridge is the console adaptation of the same ruined city.
yie-ar-kung-fu-1985:
Oolong faces a queue of armed fighters in Yie Ar Kung-Fu (1985), Konami's early arcade bout. Each opponent brings a weapon, so a chain, a star, or a club changes the distance Oolong has to keep.

The one-on-one line is the structure, not a walk through a side-view fortress. Winning advances to the next specialist, and losing restarts the duel.

The NES edition is a home port of those bouts. Oolong and the weapon-users are Konami's arcade roster, moved onto the cartridge without becoming a different sport.
balloon-fight-1985:
Flapping balloons and a hungry fish define Balloon Fight (1985), Nintendo's duel that owes an obvious debt to Joust. Popping a rival's balloons drops them toward the water, and the fish waits for anyone who falls in.

Balloon Trip mode drops the rival fighters for a scrolling course of sparks. The flaps still keep the player aloft, but the goal becomes a long survival rather than a duel.

Nintendo kept both the Joust-like combat and that spark course on one cartridge. The fish, the popped balloons, and Balloon Trip's sparks are the two ways the cart is played.
donkey-kong-jr:
Junior climbs vines to free his father while Mario holds the cage in Donkey Kong Jr., and the first arcade story is reversed. The carpenter is the captor, and the son is the one dodging Snapjaws and pushing keys.

Nintendo's coin-op dates to 1982, with vines, chains, and keys on the path to the cage. Mario's traps sit between Junior and Donkey Kong.

A real NES port later carried that reversal home. The vines and the caged father are the arcade idea, and the console cart is a port of it rather than a new father-and-son plot.
road-fighter:
Fuel gauges end the drive when they hit empty in Road Fighter, Konami's overhead arcade racer. Other cars are hazards, but running out of fuel is the loss even if the road is clear.

Konami's coin-op dates to 1984, and fuel pickups along the overhead lanes matter as much as threading traffic. A fast line that misses the can still fails when the gauge hits empty.

The Famicom version is a port of that coin-op, not a later console-born racing series. The overhead view and the fuel limit are the cabinet's rules, kept on the home board.
jurassic-park:
Separate park licenses share the film's name and not a single design in Jurassic Park. Ocean's Super Nintendo cart is mostly overhead exploration of the grounds, while the NES game is a side-scroller through dinosaur set pieces.

The 1993 film is the common source, and the machines did not share one map. A raptor encounter on the NES side-scroller is not the same scene as Ocean's overhead search.

Game Boy and later handheld boards add still more variants under the same title. Ocean's overhead Super Nintendo game and the side-scrolling NES game are the clearest split.
galaga-1981:
Tractor beams capture a ship in Galaga (1981), and a rescued second fighter doubles the fire. Namco followed Galaxian with that kidnapping, so losing a ship to the beam can become an advantage if the player wins it back.

Challenging stages break the formation for a bonus pattern. The dual fighter, once recovered, fills the screen with a wider shot than the single cannon.

The NES version is a later port of that arcade shooter. The tractor beam and the doubled ship are Namco's sequel idea, and the home cart is carrying the beam across years.
ghosts-n-goblins-1985:
Arthur's armor falls away after one hit in Ghosts 'n Goblins (1985), leaving him in his underwear among graveyard monsters. Capcom's knight still throws lances, but the second hit is death, and the graveyard does not apologize.

Both the arcade cabinet and the fierce NES port expect the quest to be beaten twice. A first clear is not the end, and the return trip is part of the design.

The kidnapped princess is the reason Arthur walks into that cemetery. The underwear rule and the second loop are what players mean when they call the NES port fierce.
mega-man-6:
Mr. X stands in for the usual villain in Mega Man 6 (1993), and Rush adapters fuse with the hero before the mask comes off. Capcom closes the original NES run with those fused forms, a jet and a power suit built from Rush.

The tournament excuse lets new robot masters appear under Mr. X's banner. Late in the game the alias gives way to the villain players already expect.

The fusion adapters are the new support trick, different from simply calling Rush as a separate pet. This is the last of the original NES robot-master line, with Mr. X as the late-game disguise.
lode-runner-1983:
Doug Smith wrote the gold-collecting puzzle Lode Runner (1983), and Broderbund's computer release made the diggable brick a hit. Guards follow the thief through holes he digs, and every bar of gold has to be cleared.

The design predates any Nintendo port. Computer players already knew the trap-the-guard rhythm before a console board existed.

Broderbund's release is the hit this title refers to. Hudson's later Famicom life of the puzzle is a descendant, and Smith's computer game is the earlier chase.
bubble-bobble-1986:
Bub and Bob trap foes in bubbles they can burst in Bubble Bobble (1986), Taito's rescue of two kidnapped girlfriends. Fukio Mitsuji directed the cave of dinosaurs, potions, and fruit that falls when a round is cleared quickly.

The two brothers, transformed into dinosaurs, blow bubbles and then pop them to turn a captured pest into a bonus. A potion changes the bubble's effect, which is how a stuck room gets a new verb.

The NES port keeps that two-dinosaur rescue. Bub, Bob, the bubbles, and the girlfriends are Mitsuji's arcade scene, carried onto the cartridge.
mother:
Ninten leaves home with a baseball bat and psychic tricks in Earthbound Beginnings, the English name of Shigesato Itoi's Famicom RPG Mother. Magicant and Queen Mary's crisis sit beyond the suburbs, and a planned NES localization of that journey was cancelled.

The Famicom game itself dates to 1989, and the official English name arrived decades later. Many players met the quest under the Mother title first because that localization had been cancelled.

Itoi's modern-dress battles and the cancelled localization are the history around the cartridge. Earthbound Beginnings is that later English name for the same Famicom quest, not a new story written in the translation years.
ultima-v-warriors-of-destiny:
Blackthorn's reign replaces Lord British in Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny, and the Avatar has to oppose the usurper. Richard Garriott's virtue-based world continues, with the Shadowlords pressing the same Britannia the earlier quest had asked players to embody.

Origin published the computer RPG in 1988, and the codex and the shrines give Blackthorn's law a system. The tyranny is more than a dark castle on the edge of Britannia.

The NES port carries that computer story forward. The Avatar, Lord British's absence, and Blackthorn are the political crisis the cartridge is adapting.
golf-1980:
Iwata's swing meter and a stroke-play course define Golf (1980), the Famicom game designed with Shigeru Miyamoto and programmed by Satoru Iwata at HAL. Club selection, wind, and the lie of the ball decide the shot, and the parenthetical date on the title is not the cartridge's release.

The Famicom board reached players in 1984, with HAL's programming and Miyamoto's involvement already attached. The NES later received that same stroke-play game.

A year printed beside the name can be a catalog convenience rather than the day the first drive was sold. Iwata's meter and Miyamoto's role are the credits that identify the cartridge.
super-c:
Rearranged bases, not a one-for-one copy of the arcade yards, fill Super C, the North American title of Konami's Famicom run-and-gun follow-up. Bill and Lance return, and the cart rebuilds the sequel's invasion instead of tracing every arcade corridor.

The NES release of that rearrangement came in 1990, with overhead stretches and side-view forts in a home-made order. Their shape is a new map rather than a tracing of every arcade yard.

Konami's Famicom follow-up is the source of the American name Super C, and players coming from the arcade sequel will find familiar guns. The map under those guns is the home cart's own arrangement.
life-force:
Living caverns inside a planet form Life Force, the Western name for Konami's Salamander, a shooter spun off from Gradius. Organic walls and biomechanical bosses replace a purely mechanical fortress, and the NES version adds a Gradius-style power bar.

Konami's spinoff dates to 1986, and the living planet is the setting. The power bar on the NES cart lets the ship upgrade in the Gradius manner while the scenery stays organic.

Salamander is the name on the Japanese side of that idea. Life Force is the Western title for the same living-planet shooter, with the NES power bar as the home version's twist.
after-burner:
Tilting cockpits roll with the jet in After Burner, Yu Suzuki's Sega arcade machine. Missiles and a machine gun clear waves of fighters, and the deluxe cabinet physically banks when the plane banks.

Suzuki's coin-op dates to 1987, and the public identity of the game is that tilting cabinet. Afterburner speed and lock-on missiles belong to the machine that rolled under the player.

Home ports exist, including an NES edition, but they cannot be the machine that moved under the player. The jet, the lock-on missiles, and the rolling seat are the arcade facts.
monster-in-my-pocket:
Toy figurines of famous creatures become a side-scrolling license in Monster in My Pocket, Konami's NES adaptation of the pocket-sized toy line. The similar phrase people later used for a different creature game is a coincidence of words, not a shared design.

Konami brought the toys to the NES in 1992, with small monsters and a horror-figure roster. The stages are a side-scrolling license aimed at that toy line's cast.

It is unrelated to the later Pokemon games despite the echo in the wording. The pocket toys and Konami's side-scrolling stages are the cartridge.
rampage:
George the gorilla, Lizzie the lizard, and Ralph the wolf smash buildings in Rampage, Bally Midway's arcade destruction. Eating a bystander and punching a skyscraper are both scoring methods, and the army eventually arrives to stop the movie monsters.

The coin-op dates to 1986, and three monsters can ruin a city block at once. George, Lizzie, and Ralph punching the same skyline is the cabinet's party trick.

The NES cart is a port of that arcade destruction. George, Lizzie, and Ralph are the same three monsters, brought home without becoming a new species.
nuts-milk:
Milk chases across single-screen mazes in Nuts & Milk, Hudson Soft's early Famicom game also sold on Japanese computers. One character flees with the food while the other tries to catch up before the screen is solved.

Hudson's maze dates to 1984, with ladders and short platforms on a single screen. The food and the chase repeat across those screens rather than scrolling into a larger world.

The computer editions and the Famicom cart share that chase. Nuts and Milk are the pursuer and the meal, and the maze is Hudson's early puzzle-action.
chase-hq:
Radio briefings name the suspect in Chase H.Q., Taito's arcade drive about ramming a car before the timer expires. Nancy's dispatch sets the target, and the bumper has to wreck the fleeing vehicle while the clock still has time.

Taito's cabinet dates to 1988, and traffic is only an obstacle. The win condition is wrecking the suspect's car before the timer expires.

Home ports include an NES edition of that ram-the-suspect structure. The radio briefing and the crashing finish are the coin-op's identity, kept on the home board.
spy-hunter-1983:
Oil slicks, smoke, and missiles arm the car in Spy Hunter (1983), Bally Midway's overhead highway set to a Peter Gunn-style theme. A weapons van drops the next armament if the driver can meet it without crashing.

The theme and the van are as famous as the guns. Boats and cars both appear as the road changes, and the oil is for the pursuers behind.

The NES port keeps the overhead highway combat of the arcade cabinet. The Peter Gunn-style music, the smoke screen, and the weapons van are the cabinet's signature, carried onto the cartridge.
wrecking-crew-1985:
Foreman Spike competes with Mario and Luigi as they knock out walls in Wrecking Crew (1985), where deadly doors and bombs complicate the job. The golden hammer turns a demolition screen into a puzzle more than a rescue.

Nintendo's Famicom game asks the brothers to destroy every listed wall without trapping themselves. Spike wanders the same screen and undoes a clean plan.
