It is not the later Wrecking Crew '98, and the golden hammer belongs to this earlier demolition. Spike and the brothers are the wreckers on these trap-filled screens.
samurai-pizza-cats:
Dub titles and a Japanese series meet in Samurai Pizza Cats, the English name of the anime Kyatto Ninden Teyandee. The Famicom game uses that Japanese cartoon about samurai cats, and the pizza-delivery joke belongs to the English dub rather than to a new mascot.

The license dates to 1991 on the Famicom. Cat warriors, not an original animal hero invented for the cartridge, are the cast.

It is a cartoon license, and the box name English speakers know is the dub's title. The cartridge itself follows Kyatto Ninden Teyandee.
paperboy-2:
Papergirl routes join the morning run in Paperboy 2, a home sequel that lets the rider be a girl or a boy. The suburban hazards remain, and the sequel moves the delivery onto consoles without needing a new famous cabinet.

The home release dates to 1991, with obstacles, subscribers, and broken glass still on the route. The new choice is who rides the bike, a papergirl or a paperboy.

It is a home sequel, not a celebrated new arcade machine. The papergirl option and the console-first follow-up are what separate it from the handlebar cabinet.
silent-service:
Periscope hunts and torpedo solutions fill Silent Service, the World War II submarine simulation Sid Meier designed for MicroProse. Convoys, depth charges, and a limited spread of torpedoes are the problems, on home computers in the mid-1980s.

Meier's design asks for patience under the waves rather than a fast arcade pattern. The map and the periscope are the two views a patrol lives in.

The NES cartridge is a later port, not the original release. MicroProse's computer submarine, and Meier's name on it, are the simulation the cart is adapting.
bucky-ohare:
Toad warships and a hare captain fill Bucky O'Hare, Konami's NES adaptation of the comic-and-cartoon crew. Blinky, Dead-Eye Duck, and the others join Bucky across side-view stages that fans still rate among Konami's stronger licenses.

Konami released the cart in 1992, and the Toad Empire is the enemy across the side-view stages. Bucky's crew changes how a room is crossed because their bodies are not interchangeable.

It is a licensed action game with a reputation out of proportion to the obscurity of the show. Bucky and his crew, not a generic mascot, are the team on the cartridge.
spy-vs-spy-2:
White spy and black spy rig one split screen in Spy vs. Spy, First Star Software's adaptation of Antonio Prohias's Mad magazine strip. A trap on a door or a bomb in a drawer waits for the other spy, and the suitcase is the prize.

The computer game dates to 1984, with the two rooms visible at once. First Star's design is the magazine duel turned into traps, and it later reached the NES.

It is not the Island Caper sequel. The suitcase, the furniture traps, and Prohias's two spies are this game, and the island follow-up is a different entry.
rc-pro-am:
Upgrade wrenches and missiles sit on an overhead oval in R.C. Pro-Am, Rare's race of tiny radio-control cars. A better tire or a stronger engine, collected on the track, changes the next heat more than a perfect line alone.

Rare built the miniature motorsport for the NES. Letters and parts scattered on the asphalt are the prize, and a missile is how a rival's tiny car leaves the groove.

The game arrived in 1988 and is a step on the way to Rare's later Nintendo racing and sports work. The overhead view and the upgrade parts are this racer's identity.
gauntlet-1985:
Food warnings from a narrator announce a dying hero in Gauntlet (1985), Ed Logg's four-player dungeon for Atari Games. Wizard, Valkyrie, Warrior, and Elf each shoot or swing in a different pattern, and the voice names who is about to fall.

Generators keep spawning grunts until they are destroyed. The "needs food" bark is as famous as the potion or the key, because health is a constant tax.

Logg's cabinet is the original four-class maze. The NES cart carries those classes and that narrator's warning, adapted from the arcade dungeon.
blades-of-steel-1988:
Dropped gloves turn a hockey stoppage into a punching match in Blades of Steel (1988), Konami's arcade ice game. The fight is a separate screen, and the winner of the fists returns to the period with the momentum.

Fast periods and body checks keep the match short and rough. A penalty brawl is not a menu statistic, because the player throws the punches.

The NES port keeps those fast periods and the glove-drop fights. Konami's cabinet made the boxing detour part of hockey, and the home cart preserves it.
shatterhand:
Cyborg fists and satellite drones define Shatterhand, the NES brawler American players got through Jaleco. In Japan the same game licenses the tokusatsu series Tokkyuu Shirei Solbrain, a name the American box does not use.

Natsume's side-view punches can assemble little robot allies from collected parts. The cyborg hero's arms are the weapon, and the Japanese license explains the armored look.

Jaleco's American release arrived in 1991, while the Solbrain connection stayed a Japanese identity. Cyborg brawling is what both boxes actually play.
tetris-tengen:
Unlicensed carts and a competitive mode distinguish Tetris (Tengen), the NES puzzle Tengen shipped under Atari Games' label. Two players can race the same well, a feature Nintendo's licensed cartridge did not treat as the point.

Tengen was forced to pull the cart from stores after the rights fight. Nintendo won the case in 1989, and its own licensed cartridge stayed on shelves while the Tengen boards were withdrawn.

The competitive mode and the unlicensed label are why this version is remembered separately. Pajitnov's falling pieces are the shared puzzle, and the lawsuit is this cart's own history.
rygar-1987:
Diskarmor swings on a chain in Rygar (1987), Tecmo's weapon that is both shield and yo-yo. The NES game stretches that tool across a large side-view adventure, with a map far wider than the short looping arcade original.

The arcade Rygar repeats a brief course. The NES quest keeps the chain shield and then adds temples, fields, and a longer road for the warrior.

Tecmo's home version is the one players describe as an adventure. The diskarmor is the shared weapon, and the size of the NES map is the difference.
terminator-2-judgment-day:
Light-gun cabinets and side-view carts share only a film in Terminator 2: Judgment Day. Midway's arcade machine is a light-gun shooter aimed at the T-1000's pursuits, while the NES and Game Boy cartridges are separate side-view licenses.

The 1991 film's liquid-metal villain and Cyberdyne imagery appear across those products without making them one design. A shot in the arcade gun game is not a jump in the NES stages.

Several different games took the title, and they should not be treated as ports of one board. Midway's light gun is the cabinet, and the NES cart is its own side-view license.
mitsume-ga-tooru:
Sharaku's forehead hides a third eye in Mitsume ga Tooru, Natsume's Famicom adaptation of Osamu Tezuka's manga The Three-Eyed One. The eye, when uncovered, changes the boy who otherwise looks harmless.

Natsume released the Japanese action game in 1992, using Tezuka's character and the temple imagery. The cartridge did not receive a contemporary English release.

Players outside Japan met the manga long before they could meet this board in translation. The third eye and Sharaku are the manga facts the Famicom game is using.
tiny-toon-adventures-2-trouble-in-wackyl:
Wackyland warps around Buster Bunny in Tiny Toon Adventures 2: Trouble in Wackyland, Konami's NES follow-up set in the cartoon's broken park. Gogo Dodo's territory supplies the illogical platforms, and Buster is still the one being steered.

Konami continued its first NES Tiny Toons cart with this trip in 1992, and it is not the Super Nintendo Buster game. That later cart has its own stages and its own priorities.

The warped park is the setting the subtitle names. Konami's second NES Tiny Toons cartridge is the one that takes Buster into Wackyland.
kings-quest-v:
King Graham walks a point-and-click kingdom in King's Quest V, Roberta Williams's Sierra adventure that moved the series to VGA graphics. Mordack the wizard has taken the royal family, and Crispin's wand is part of Graham's tools on the computer original.

Sierra's mouse-driven design and the painted VGA scenes date to 1990, with a desert, a yeti, and Mordack's castle. The computer game presents those scenes through the point-and-click interface.

The NES port is a notorious, stripped-down version of that computer adventure. Graham and Mordack remain, and the presentation that made the computer game famous does not survive intact.
adventures-of-lolo-1989:
Jewel chests sit behind monsters that must be sealed or baited in Adventures of Lolo (1989), HAL Laboratory's Eggerland puzzle. Lolo and Lala push blocks, turn some creatures into eggs, and cross water only where a block makes a bridge.

Each room is a single screen with one jewel chest as the exit's key. A Medusa's gaze or a Don Medusa's shot punishes a rushed push.

HAL's NES chapter belongs to a longer Eggerland line. Lolo, Lala, the blocks, and the chest are the puzzle, repeated until the castle's rooms run out.
yoshi:
Stacked enemies vanish in matched pairs while a dinosaur hatches underneath in Yoshi, Nintendo's puzzle sold in Japan under an egg title. Mario shuffles the falling Goombas and Bloopers so a pair lines up, and the egg at the bottom cracks into Yoshi.

The puzzle appeared on the NES and Game Boy. Yoshi no Tamago, the egg title, is the Japanese name for the same stacking.

Nintendo released it in 1991, and the hatching dinosaur under the stack is the prize. Pair-clearing is the toy, not a side-view ride through a Yoshi stage.
space-harrier-1986:
Checkered plains rush toward a flying hero in Space Harrier (1986), Yu Suzuki's super-scaler arcade shooter. Dragons, cyclops, and a chant of "Get ready" fill a cabinet whose scaling hardware defined the ride.

An NES port exists and cannot match that cabinet. The checkered ground and the into-the-screen speed depend on the arcade board Suzuki's team built.

Sega's super-scaler machine is the identity of the game. The home cart is a reduced echo of the plain, the dragons, and the flying pose.
elevator-action-1983:
Stolen documents sit behind colored doors in Elevator Action (1983), Taito's arcade spy game of lifts and shoot-outs. The agent rides an elevator, ducks into a hallway, and has to leave with the papers before the building's guards finish the job.

Red doors hide the files. A missed shot in a narrow hall is as dangerous as a bad choice of floor.

The NES cartridge is a home port of that building raid. Taito's elevators, doorways, and documents are the coin-op, carried onto the cart.
crystalis:
Elemental blades of wind, fire, water, and thunder arm the hero in Crystalis, SNK's NES quest set after a disaster. The swords are not cosmetic, because a dungeon often demands the element that matches its hazard.

SNK released the action RPG in 1990 as an original quest, not a port of a computer RPG. The four elemental swords were written for this board.

The post-disaster towns and the four swords are the structure. Combining the blades' power is the long-term goal of a journey SNK wrote for this machine.
adventure-island-3:
Takahashi Meijin, Hudson's famous spokesman, stars in Takahashi Meijin no Bugutte Honey, a Famicom mix of side-scrolling and Breakout-style rooms. Bricks break under a shot while other stretches play as a run, and Master Higgins is not the lead.

Hudson Soft released the Japan-only game in 1987, and the spokesman's rapid-fire reputation is the joke. Brick-breaking rooms supply the mechanical twist beside the side-scrolling stretches.

It is not an Adventure Island sequel wearing a strange name. Higgins's island carts are a different series, and this board belongs to Takahashi Meijin and the breaking bricks.
toy-story:
Woody rides stages built from Andy's room and beyond in Toy Story, the platformer Traveller's Tales made from the Pixar film. Buzz Lightyear's levels use a different toy's movement, and the 16-bit versions on Super Nintendo and Genesis are the main production.

Traveller's Tales aimed those stages at the film's 16-bit moment. A Game Boy edition exists, but it is not the same production as those Super Nintendo and Genesis rooms.

The film's release and the game's own arrival share 1995, with Woody and Buzz as the two playable toys of the 16-bit platformer. The handheld board should not be mistaken for that same set of stages.
indiana-jones-and-the-last-crusade-1991:
Circus trains and tiered train roofs open Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade: The Action Game, US Gold's platformer of the film. It is separate from Lucasfilm's point-and-click adventure, which uses puzzles instead of these jumping set pieces.

The circus train is the film's opening chase turned into platforms. Later screens stand in for other set pieces, still as an action game rather than as an inventory puzzle.

US Gold's platformer dates to 1989, and the whip and the circus train belong to this action license. The tiered screens are not the inventory puzzles of the graphic adventure that shares the film.
urban-champion-1984:
Flower pots drop from windows while two fighters shove each other in Urban Champion (1984), Nintendo's simple Famicom fistfight on a sidewalk. A manhole and the street itself wait for whoever loses the pushing contest.

The moves are a high punch and a low punch, and the round is about position more than a long health bar. Nintendo's early catalog often cites this among the company's slighter games.

The sidewalk, the pots, and the shove toward the curb are the entire sport. It is a Famicom boxing-on-the-pavement idea, small on purpose.
mega-man-3:
Slide kicks and a rival robot join the master-weapon loop in Mega Man 3, where Proto Man's whistle interrupts the chase. The slide fits under barriers the first two games made the player jump.

Capcom's third NES chapter is often ranked beside the second. The slide is a movement change, not only a new gun, and the rival gives the stages a stalker.

The cartridge reached players in 1990, with Rush's help and the new masters around that slide. Players arguing the NES line often put this chapter next to Mega Man 2 for the tightness of the weapon answers.
fantastic-dizzy:
Egg folklore and the Oliver twins' hero fill Fantastic Dizzy, Codemasters' puzzle adventure in the Dizzy line. The yolkfolk's missing friends and an overworld of small puzzles are the computer game's shape.

Codemasters released that adventure in 1991, and it did not start as a Nintendo product. The egg hero already had a line of games on other machines before Camerica's cart.

Camerica later sold an unlicensed NES version. The Oliver twins' Dizzy and the puzzle overworld are the source, and Camerica's cart is an unlicensed carrier rather than the birthplace.
rockin-kats:
Spring-loaded punches from a cartoon cat's gun clear the stages in Rockin' Kats, an original Atlus platformer. The extendable fist grabs ledges and hits foes, and the cat is not a licensed Saturday-morning star.

Atlus shipped the game in 1991, with jazz-cartoon framing and the spring-gun as the identity. No television series supplied the model sheets.

It is Atlus's own platformer. The punching gun and the cat protagonist were made for the cartridge, not borrowed from a show's model sheets.
adventure-island:
Dinosaur mounts carry Master Higgins across Adventure Island III (1992), Hudson's third Western island cart. A ridden dinosaur changes the attack and the jump, and the lineage still runs back to the Wonder Boy-derived original.

Hudson continued Higgins's crossing with those mounts and a new set of island hazards. The third Western entry is not a renumbering of the Japanese spokesman game that shares none of this plot.

The skateboard-and-axe ancestor remains the root. Higgins and the dinosaurs are the third Western chapter of that line.
baseball-1983:
Behind-the-plate framing shows a simple diamond in Baseball (1983), Nintendo's early Famicom sports game. The pitcher, the batter, and a small field are drawn without licensed teams or a season-long franchise mode.

The view from behind the plate makes the pitch's height and the swing's timing the whole at-bat. Fielders are few, and the diamond is the entire stadium.

The later Game Boy Baseball is another cartridge in Nintendo's sports line, not this same code. The Famicom behind-the-plate game is its own early diamond.
ultima-4-quest-of-the-avatar:
Eight virtues, from honesty to humility, are the quest in Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar, Richard Garriott's demand that the player live the code. Lord British's Britannia asks for conduct, not only for a lich's death, and the Codex of Ultimate Wisdom waits on that conduct.

Origin published the computer RPG in 1985, and shrines and mantras teach the virtues as systems. The party's example matters more than a closing paragraph about a dead lich.

The NES port is a later adaptation of that computer RPG. The Avatar, the eight virtues, and Britannia are Garriott's design, carried onto the cartridge afterward.
battletoads:
Turbo Tunnel speeders smash careless riders in Battletoads, Rare's NES brawler that changes vehicles and gimmicks every few stages. Rash, Zitz, and Pimple climb, punch, and then get dropped onto a speeder that does not forgive a late dodge.

The Dark Queen is the kidnapper behind the shifting levels. A surfboard stretch and a climbing rope sit beside the tunnel, so the next stage may abandon fists entirely.

Rare's original arrived in 1991 and is the Battletoads people mean, long before later reimaginings. The Turbo Tunnel is the brutal speeder sequence the reputation rests on.
pac-man:
Blinky, Pinky, Inky, and Clyde chase the dot-eater in Pac-Man, Toru Iwatani's maze for Namco. A power pellet turns the chase around for a few seconds, and the fruit is a bonus between the pellets.

Namco's arcade craze dates to 1980, and Iwatani's design is the public identity of the yellow shape. The four ghosts, not a console debut, are what the name meant first.

The Famicom port came years later. Wakawaka corridors and the ghosts are the cabinet's phenomenon, and the home board is a later carrier of that craze.
the-legend-of-zelda:
The Legend of Zelda hands you a sword in a cave and then refuses to tell you which dungeon comes next. Burning a bush or bombing a wall is often the only hint the game is willing to give.

Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka wanted a game that felt like wandering the hills behind Miyamoto's childhood home. The American gold cartridge included a battery so the overworld, the bombed walls, and the collected triforce pieces survived after the console was switched off.

Link burns bushes, pushes tombstones, and learns the whistle mostly by rumor. A second quest rearranges the same Hyrule once the first is finished, which was a rare trick on a cartridge of that size. The manual's map, often drawn on by the owner, became part of how people played.

Every later Zelda borrows the mix of a wide map, a tool for each dungeon, and a final Ganon. The side-view sequel that followed is a different game with its own page.
battle-city:
Shared tanks and destructible bricks fill Battle City, Namco's Famicom game descended from Tank Battalion. Two players can occupy one screen, shooting walls to open a lane and defending the base at the bottom.

Namco released it in 1985, and it was a Japanese hit. Many Western players met the bricks and the two-player screen only in later reissues, not as a contemporary NES blockbuster.

Tank Battalion is the ancestor of the cannon-and-brick rules. Battle City is the Famicom game that put two tanks on that shared screen.
contra-1987:
Spread shots and the famous extra-life code define Contra (1987), the run-and-gun Europe called Gryzor. Bill and Lance advance through a jungle and an alien base, and the NES version became a co-op benchmark.

Konami rearranged the arcade stages for the home cart rather than copying every yard. The code that grants extra lives is tied to this board in players' memories.

The jungle, the waterfall, and the alien heart are the campaign's images. Gryzor is the European name, and the rearranged NES stages are the co-op game the code belongs to.
alwas-awakening:
Physical boards and a PC edition both carry Alwa's Awakening, a new adventure written for the old console rather than a rerelease of a licensed 1980s hit. The heroine's staff and the dungeon maps were made in the modern indie wave and then also pressed as a cartridge.

The release arrived in 2017, with the physical NES cart as a real product beside the computer version. It is new software, not a relabel of someone else's old stages.

Playing it on the original hardware is the point of that cartridge pressing. The new dungeon adventure and the dual release, PC and NES board, are the facts that place it.
double-dragon:
Marian waits at the end of a gang's alley in Double Dragon, Technos' side-scrolling brawler about punching through the Black Warriors. Billy and Jimmy Lee use elbows, kicks, and throws, and Abobo is the giant who blocks an early stretch.

The NES port is the home version many players met first. The cabinet exists, but a large audience learned the Lees and Marian's kidnapping from the cartridge.

Technos's brawler reached that NES audience in 1988, and the gang, the brothers, and Marian's kidnapping are the plot. The home cart is how a lot of players threw the first punch.
castlevania:
Medusa heads drift across the stairs while Simon Belmont's whip cracks in Castlevania. Candles drop hearts and holy water, and Dracula's castle leaves very little room for a sloppy landing.

Konami's first castle in this line sets the whip, the stairs, and the boss rooms as the language later games quote. Simon's advance is a straight assault, not a countryside search.

The game arrived in 1986 and starts Konami's long run on Nintendo hardware. The whip and the castle, with Simon at the door, are the beginning.
chips-challenge:
Bit Busters membership waits behind keys and computer chips in Chip's Challenge, Chuck Sommerville's top-down puzzle. Teeth, fire, and water block the grid, and a stolen chip is the ticket through a socket.

Sommerville's game debuted on the Atari Lynx in 1989, and the Bit Busters trials are the fiction. Monsters and keys are the rules of each single-screen room.

Microsoft later bundled it in a Windows Entertainment Pack. The Lynx original and that PC bundle are the lives of Sommerville's chips, beyond any one console port.
metal-gear:
Cardboard boxes hide Solid Snake in Metal Gear, Hideo Kojima's sneaking mission that began on the MSX2 rather than as a straight shooter. Outer Heaven's guards raise an alert if they see him, and the transceiver delivers the next order.

Kojima's MSX2 game dates to 1987, with the cardboard box, the card keys, and the alarm as the tools. Big Boss's frequency on the transceiver is the story's turn.

The NES version changes maps and bosses, and Kojima has distanced himself from that port. Snake and Outer Heaven begin on the MSX2, and the NES board is a different layout of the sneak.
zelda-ii-the-adventure-of-link:
Experience points and side-view swordplay make Zelda II: The Adventure of Link the odd Zelda, closer to an action RPG than the first overhead quest. Link talks in towns such as Ruto, raises a level, and then fights in palaces drawn from the side.

A magic cost and a down-thrust change the combat the first game resolved with a stab and a boomerang. Dark Link waits as the shadow at the end of that road.

Nintendo released the experiment in 1987, and it is the second Zelda on the NES. People cite it when they talk about how far the series later swung back toward exploration.
duck-hunt-1984:
A laughing dog mocks a missed shot in Duck Hunt (1984), Nintendo's Zapper game of ducks and clay pigeons. The dog holds a successful kill and laughs when the sky stays empty, which is the joke players remember.

The cartridge shipped in the Action Set beside Super Mario Bros., and that pack-in status made the clay pigeons a shared memory. People who bought the console with the bundle met the laughing dog on day one.

The Zapper is required for the shot, and the dog is the audience. Ducks in the grass and the flying discs are the two hunts on the cart.
metroid:
Metroid drops Samus Aran into the caverns of Zebes with a weak beam and doors that will not open until the right upgrade is found. Missiles, a morph ball, and ice beam are found by getting lost, not by following a marker.

Yoshio Sakamoto, Hiroji Kiyotake, and Gunpei Yokoi shaped it at Nintendo as an exploration game rather than a stage-by-stage shooter. Kraid, Ridley, and Mother Brain guard the path, and a password system stands in for a battery save.

The ending that removes Samus's helmet, if the player is fast enough, was a genuine surprise in an era when the hero was assumed to be a man. That reveal is why the series' identity starts here and not with a later comic.

Super Metroid, Fusion, and the Prime games all reuse the loop of getting lost, finding a morph ball or a missile tank, and opening an earlier door. They are separate works. This page is the first Metroid.
chip-n-dale-rescue-rangers:
Thrown crates and enemies become weapons in Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers, Capcom's NES platformer of the Disney Afternoon series. Chip and Dale pick up almost anything, including a foe, and throw it, which is the verb that replaces a simple stomp.

Fat Cat's crime spree is the plot. Gadget, Monterey Jack, and Zipper belong to the show, and the stages turn those characters' world into throwable clutter.

Capcom released the cart in 1990, and the throw, more than a mascot walk, is why it is remembered. A crate or a foe in Dale's hands solves the room.
final-fantasy-1987:
Light Warriors cross a bridge that breaks behind them in Final Fantasy (1987), Hironobu Sakaguchi's Famicom RPG that launched the series. Four crystals, Garland's corrupted knight, and Chaos at the end of time are the quest Square bet the company on.

The party is four named roles rather than one silent wanderer. The crystals of earth, fire, water, and wind are the objectives scattered across the continents.

North America received Nintendo's localization two years later. Sakaguchi's four Light Warriors and Square's Famicom original are the launch of the line.
mega-man-2:
Metal blades from Metal Man answer whole rooms in Mega Man 2, where eight robot masters can be challenged in any order. Their weapons answer one another, so a stage that looks impossible becomes simple after the right boss falls.

Capcom's NES chapter is the Mega Man most players mean when they talk about the series. Crash Man, Flash Man, and the rest form a loop of weaknesses, and Dr. Wily's castle follows the eight.

The game arrived in 1988 with that free order already the structure. The metal blade and the chosen route are the reasons this chapter became the reference point.
mega-man:
Cut Man's shears and the Yellow Devil's shifting blocks open Mega Man, a shorter and harder robot-master gauntlet than the sequel that made the formula famous. Elec Man, Ice Man, Fire Man, Bomb Man, and Guts Man complete a six-boss loop with no slide and no charge shot.

Capcom's first NES set is the one later games are softening and extending. Dr. Wily and Dr. Light are already the plot, and the Yellow Devil is the fortress hazard players still cite.

The cartridge arrived in 1987 and opens the original line on Nintendo's 8-bit console. The six masters and the Devil's blocks are the first gauntlet, before the sequel's eight-boss menu.
mario-bros:
POW blocks flip every pest on a single screen in Mario Bros., the cooperative attic game about bumping creatures from below. Shellcreepers, Sidesteppers, and Fighter Flies have to be hit from underneath and then kicked before they right themselves.

Mario and Luigi share the pipes and the platform, and a bumped brother also knocks the other plumber down. It is the arcade-born game on the NES, not Super Mario Bros.

Nintendo's single-screen cooperation dates to 1983, before the side-scrolling Mushroom Kingdom. The POW block and the bump-from-below rule are the whole sport.
chip-n-dale-rescue-rangers-2:
Between-stage shops sell the acorns of a finished level in Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers 2, Capcom's NES return of the throwing chipmunks. The shop is new, and the hook of picking up an enemy and throwing it remains from the first Disney Afternoon cart.

Capcom brought the pair back in 1993, and Fat Cat's schemes continue. Crate-throwing still solves a room that a jump cannot.

The shop between stages is the sequel's added beat. Throwing foes, the first cart's verb, is still how Chip and Dale fight.
dyna-blaster:
White Bomber places a bomb and runs in Bomberman (1983), Hudson Soft's maze that began on computers and became a Famicom staple. Soft blocks hide the exit, and the blast travels in a cross that the robot can be caught in.

Europe often sold later entries under the Dynablaster name. The Famicom robot and the computer maze share the bomb-and-run idea this first title names.

Hudson's early board is the staple later party games are expanding. The single robot, the cross-shaped blast, and the brick maze are the start.
kirbys-adventure:
Inhaled enemies become copy abilities in Kirby's Adventure, the long NES journey that gave Kirby a hat for each stolen power. A sword, a fireball, or a hammer replaces the plain puff, and King Dedede is no longer the only thing the inhale is for.

HAL Laboratory and Nintendo built the follow-up to Dream Land around that copy. Masahiro Sakurai's hero still floats, but the stolen ability is the new identity.

The game arrived in 1993 and set the copy-ability identity later Kirby games keep. Nightmare and the Fountain of Dreams sit at the end of a much longer map than Dream Land had.
excitebike:
Overheated engines force a cooler line in Excitebike, Nintendo's side-view dirt-bike race where temperature matters as much as the jumps. Mud strips and uneven ramps cost speed, and a too-hot bike loses power before the finish.

A design mode lets a player place the ramps and the mud for the next heat. The side view shows the whole jump, including the landing that overheats a sloppy rider.

Nintendo's racer dates to 1984 and is a name later Excite sequels kept alive. The temperature gauge and the track builder are the original's own tools.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-iii-the-man:
Manhattan sidewalks and a raised city host Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles III: The Manhattan Project, Konami's NES brawler that is not a port of the arcade game. The turtles fight through the city instead of repeating the coin-op's stages.

Konami built that story for the NES in 1991, and Shredder's plot uses a Manhattan setting original to this cart. The punches resemble earlier brawls, but the city stages are not the coin-op's route.

It does not copy the arcade route that a different cartridge had already ported. The Manhattan Project's city stages are their own brawler.
dr-mario:
Megavitamin capsules fall into a bottle to clear colored viruses in Dr. Mario, Nintendo's puzzle about matching red, blue, and yellow. A pair of capsule halves has to land so three of a color line up, and the viruses do not move on their own.

The bottle is the well, and the doctor is Mario in a lab coat. Speed rises as the bottle clears, which is the pressure the puzzle adds to a simple match.

Nintendo's NES puzzle arrived in 1990 and started the Dr. Mario line. The viruses and the megavitamins are the first version of that bottle.
ducktales:
Moon treasure and a pogo cane define Disney's DuckTales, Capcom's NES hunt starring Scrooge McDuck. The cane's bounce crosses spikes and stuns foes, and the Moon is one of the places the treasure maps send him.

The Amazon, the Himalayas, and Transylvania sit beside that Moon as separate expeditions. Launchpad flies Scrooge between them, and Huey, Dewey, and Louie wait in the hub.

Capcom released the hunts in 1989, and the cane plus the Moon kept the cart famous. It remains one of the best-known Disney games on that console.
altered-beast-1988:
Spirit balls turn a risen centurion into beasts in Altered Beast (1988), Sega's arcade game that opens with a call to rise from the grave. Enough orbs change a wolf form or a dragon form, and the cabinet was also a Genesis pack-in.

Zeus's resurrection and the beast transformations are the coin-op's spectacle. Punching spirits out of enemies is how the form advances.

The NES cart is a later port of that grave-and-beast idea. The arcade machine and the Genesis pack-in are the versions that made the call to rise famous, and the NES board follows them.
the-jungle-book:
Mowgli swings through levels built around the film's songs in Disney's The Jungle Book, Virgin Interactive's platformer. Baloo, Kaa, and King Louie supply the set pieces, and the songs are the scaffolding of the stages rather than a menu extra.

Virgin's Genesis and Super Nintendo versions are the main 16-bit releases. Shere Khan waits as the threat the film already taught, while the platforms are Virgin's.

The adaptation dates to 1993, and Mowgli's vine swings carry the song-built levels. NES and handheld variants sit beside the main 16-bit carts rather than replacing them.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-1989:
Dam corridors, swimming sections, and a top-down overworld make Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (1989) a demanding NES adventure. The turtles search for April and fight the Foot on a map, then drop into side-view missions that include the notorious dam.

Konami's cart is not the arcade beat 'em up. That coin-op was ported by a later cartridge, and this one has the overworld, the water, and the dam instead.

The swimming and the dam are the stretches players still describe as the wall. The top-down map and the mission stages are Konami's NES adventure, separate from the cabinet brawl.
maniac-mansion:
Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick built Maniac Mansion at Lucasfilm Games around a verb menu and a haunted house. Players pick a pair of kids, and each kid's quirks open different jokes inside Dr. Fred's rooms.

SCUMM, the scripting system written for that 1987 project, let later Lucasfilm adventures reuse the same engine. A meteor, a kidnapped cheerleader, and a purple tentacle give the house its plot.

Jaleco's NES cartridge keeps the room layout while censoring some of the computer version's jokes. The mansion is still explored by swapping characters rather than by fighting through a corridor.
arkanoid-1986:
Taito turned Breakout into Arkanoid (1986) by putting the player in a ship called the Vaus. Capsules fall from cracked bricks and briefly change the Vaus, the ball, or the barrier.

A short escape story frames the bricks as a prison the Vaus is trying to leave. The energy ball still has to clear every tile, so the old brick-breaking rhythm sits underneath the capsules.

The NES edition can swap the ordinary pad for a dedicated paddle controller. That paddle lets the Vaus track the ball the way the arcade dial did.
star-trek-25th-anniversary:
Interplay treated Star Trek: 25th Anniversary as a silver-jubilee voyage with two very different shapes. The computer game is a point-and-click tour of the Enterprise, and the CD edition uses the original cast.

Kirk's crew still takes the bridge in that computer version, while the NES cartridge plays as an action-led tie-in. Phaser fights and corridor runs replace the mouse-driven conversations of the CD voyage.

A Game Boy cartridge sits beside the NES one in the same jubilee window, around 1991 already. Neither of those carts is the talking adventure that put the television cast on disc.
the-little-mermaid:
Ariel swims and then walks in Capcom's The Little Mermaid, a stage design drawn from Disney's film. Bubbles are her underwater shot, and dry land makes her hop across decks and caves.

Capcom shipped those swimming and walking stages in 1991, with Ursula's film as backdrop rather than a scene-for-scene script. Pearls, eels, and the change of posture between sea and shore carry each course.

This is not the Genesis Little Mermaid, which came from another developer. The two licenses share the film and almost nothing about how Ariel moves.
battle-chess:
Interplay kept ordinary chess laws in Battle Chess and then staged every capture as a fight. A queen does not vanish quietly; she duels the piece she takes, and the board waits until the animation ends.

The 1988 computer original sold the joke of living pieces on a medieval board. Knights, rooks, and pawns each get their own combat sketch, while checkmate still follows the standard rules.

The NES version is a home port of that computer novelty. The same animated captures play on the cartridge, slowed by how much cartoon the console can show.
popeye:
Olive Oyl tosses tokens down to the sailor in Nintendo's Popeye, while Bluto patrols the platforms. Spinach is a short power-up that lets Popeye punch the bully instead of fleeing him.

The 1982 arcade license is a single-screen chase: hearts and letters have to be caught before they hit the water. Miss too many gifts, or let Bluto land a grab, and the round is over.

An NES port of that coin-op is real, and a Game Boy edition followed the same license. Both still turn on spinach, Olive's falling gifts, and Bluto's reach.
dig-dug-1982:
Taizo Hori pumps enemies until they pop in Dig Dug (1982), or he drops rocks onto them. Pookas and Fygars chase him through tunnels he carves in the dirt.

The pump is the whole weapon: inflate a monster to bursting, or leave it half-full while another closes in. Rocks lodged in the soil fall once the dirt beneath them is dug away.

Later games treat this digger as Mr. Driller's father. The original rounds stay small underground arenas, not the falling puzzle columns those descendants use.
captain-america-and-the-avengers:
Data East put the Marvel team into an arcade brawler called Captain America and The Avengers. Captain America leads the punches, and the cabinet treats the heroes as selectable fighters against a shared villain wave.

The 1991 coin-op is a side-view brawl with health bars and grabs, not a bracket of one-on-one duels. Iron Man joins the same street-level fights when a second player steps in.

NES and Super Nintendo releases are separate home versions, not one identical port. A Game Boy cartridge is a third, smaller cut of that Marvel license.
hillsfar-1993:
Forgotten Realms errands fill SSI's Hillsfar (1993), a walled city of arena fights and lockpicking. The hero rides into town, takes odd jobs, and steps into an arena when the city wants a duel.

It started on computers in the late 1980s, with the same mix of mini-tasks inside one town. Picking a lock is a timed challenge of its own, separate from the arena's weapon swings.

The NES edition is a later cartridge of that computer spinoff. Guild jobs, the arena, and the city's gates remain the three ways a visit gets spent.
dragon-quest-1986:
Yuji Horii, with Akira Toriyama, Koichi Sugiyama, and Chunsoft, made Enix's Dragon Quest (1986) the template for Japanese console RPGs. A lone hero crosses a top-down land, buys better gear in town, and grinds slimes until a cave is survivable.

Menu battles, a king who sends you outward, and the Dragonlord at the end became the pattern other parties copied. Alefgard's bridges are small, and the danger comes from how hard a random encounter hits.

North America received it in 1989 as Dragon Warrior. That renamed release is the same cave-to-castle march, slime and all.
double-dragon-3-the-rosetta-stone:
Billy and Jimmy Lee hunt relics in Double Dragon III: The Sacred Stones (1991), and Technos changed more than the wording. The arcade subtitle was The Rosetta Stone, while this home quest builds its own route.

The brothers still punch, kick, and grab weapons, but the stages and goals are not a straight dump of the cabinet. Enemy lines and pickups remain, arranged as a longer cartridge journey.

A Game Boy edition carries the Sacred Stones name as well. Both home versions stay apart from the Rosetta Stone coin-op they branched away from.
smash-tv:
Eugene Jarvis staged Smash TV as a lethal game show for Williams, played with twin sticks and a studio full of guns. Contestants clear a room, snatch prizes, and step through a door into the next armed set.

The 1990 cabinet throws keys and cash onto the floor while mutants pour in from every wall. A mocking host keeps score, and the map is a grid of those rooms rather than one scrolling street.

NES and Super Nintendo ports followed the cabinet's room-by-room prize grab. Both home versions keep the two-direction shooting, even when a pad has to fake the second stick.
game-1942:
Capcom sent a lone fighter called the Super Ace over the Pacific in 1942, the first of the studio's wartime 19XX shooters. The plane loops to dodge, and the view scrolls vertically through waves of enemy aircraft.

That arcade sortie dates to 1984, with a small set of power-ups that widen the Super Ace's guns. Formations and a short fuel-like tension keep each stage brief and repeatable.

The NES port keeps the looping Super Ace and the same vertical scroll. It does not rebuild the Pacific run as a side-view campaign.
ms-pac-man:
General Computer Corporation built Ms. Pac-Man for Midway, giving the hero a bow and mazes that wander. Ghosts still chase, but the walls change from round to round instead of repeating one fixed board.

It followed Pac-Man in the early 1980s and was not a Namco design. Bouncing fruit, four roaming layouts, and the bow are the sequel's own additions.

Nintendo ports on the NES, Super Nintendo, and Game Boy arrived much later. Those cartridges inherit Midway's shifting mazes rather than a Namco blueprint.
robocop-versus-the-terminator:
Dark Horse published the comic that RoboCop Versus The Terminator adapts, a crossover that never happened on film. RoboCop fights a future in which his own technology helps the machines, and the stages follow that plot.

Virgin's Genesis game is the best-known version of the license. Super Nintendo and NES editions are separate carts, each with its own levels cut from the same comic premise.

The 1993 tie-in therefore splinters by hardware. A Game Boy cartridge is yet another small version, not a shrink of the Genesis shooter.
kid-icarus:
Pit climbs out of the underworld in Kid Icarus with a bow that starts weak and strengthens if his health stays high. Hearts dropped by monsters pay for gear in the shops of Angel Land.

Nintendo built that climb in 1986 through vertical fortresses, sideways worlds, and a last sky maze. Medusa waits at the end, and falling off a vertical shaft drops Pit back down the room.

Later handheld and 3DS games in the series look back to this NES original. They reuse the angel and the growing bow, yet each of those later quests is a separate work.
jackal-1986:
Konami drove a jeep behind enemy lines in Jackal (1986), a mission also called Top Gunner. The view is overhead, and the point is to load prisoners and carry them out to a waiting helicopter.

A mounted gun and tossed grenades clear the barracks while the jeep stops to take captives aboard. Leave a prisoner behind and the rescue, which is the whole sortie, fails.

The NES version is a port of that overhead arcade shooter. The same jeep, the same pickup, and the same escape helicopter define the cartridge.
ninja-gaiden-iii-the-ancient-ship-of-doo:
Ryu Hayabusa closes Tecmo's NES trilogy in Ninja Gaiden III: The Ancient Ship of Doom (1991) already. Cinema-style scenes still play between stages, the format the series used to tell his story.

The ship of the subtitle is the destination, reached through wall jumps, pits, and armed corridors. His sword and a small stock of lives are the tools, and a missed jump is usually fatal.

The US cartridge is stricter about continues than the Japanese one. That continue limit is what players cite when they compare the two releases of the same ship.
wolverine:
LJN put the clawed Marvel mutant on a cartridge in Wolverine, a side-view trek from 1991 already. Adamantium claws are how he gets through soldiers and beasts, and the comic license is the reason the cart exists.

It belongs with that publisher's comic-book games, not with later fighting-game appearances. There is no tournament bracket and no versus screen, only a course of jumps and slashes.

Health and enemies behave like an obstacle run rather than a superhero duel. The X-Men name brings players in, while the stages themselves are pits, thugs, and the claws.
final-fantasy-iii-1990:
Square gave four orphans a full job system in Final Fantasy III (1990), and that Famicom game had no English release in its own era. Onion Kids change class at a shrine, and the new role rewrites their commands.

Black mages, dragoons, and other jobs are spell-and-gear kits, not costumes. A floating continent and a war with darkness give those jobs a world to cross, still in Japanese on the original cartridge.

The cartridge North America once called Final Fantasy III is actually VI. Anyone hunting the job shrine has to look for the Famicom original, not that later English number.
adventure-island-ii-1991:
Master Higgins gains dinosaur companions in Hudson's Adventure Island II (1991) already. Each mount changes how he crosses a side-view island, whether that means a burst of speed or a way over a gap.

It is the first sequel, still an island trek rather than a new kind of game. The timer and the scrolling hazards remain, and the dinosaurs are the new company on that run.

A Game Boy edition carries the same Higgins-and-dinosaur idea. The NES cartridge is the one where those companions first joined the islands.
karateka-1986:
Jordan Mechner made Karateka (1985) on the Apple II before Prince of Persia, and Broderbund published it. A fighter runs toward a palace, and every guard is a one-on-one bout that ends when one stance breaks.

The computer original is from 1984, with punches Mechner filmed and traced into the animation. Charge the captive princess in a fighting stance and she kicks the rescuer, so the last door is a test of manners.

An NES port came later. The palace duels, the rotoscoped strikes, and that final mistake with the princess remain the scene people mean by the name.
rushn-attack:
Konami brought the arcade Green Beret home as Rush'n Attack, a base assault fought largely with a knife. Soldiers pour in from both sides of a military yard, and the blade is the weapon that never runs out.

A dropped gun helps until its shots are gone, then the knife is all that remains. Alarm troops make the yard suddenly crowded, which is why the timing of a stab matters more than a firearm you might miss.

The American name is the one printed for the NES, and the coin-op predates that cartridge. The 1988 home version keeps the barracks, the bridges, and Green Beret's knife.
robocop-3:
Two different cartridges licensed the third film as Robocop 3, and the NES and Super Nintendo editions do not play alike. Each one builds its own stages around that movie, so one is not a scaled copy of the other.

Both are early-1990s tie-ins from the 1992 film window. Robocop still faces armed streets and corporate enemies drawn from the picture, but jumps, weapons, and bosses diverge after the title screen.

Neither cart is Data East's earlier arcade RoboCop. That coin-op is a separate brawler, and these film licenses do not reuse its rooms.
kunio-kun-no-nekketsu-soccer-league:
Technos kept Kunio-kun no Nekketsu Soccer League on the Famicom, a 1993 match inside the Kunio-kun series. Teams settle arguments with fists as well as with goals, which is the Nekketsu habit.

It stayed in Japan. Nintendo World Cup had already exported an earlier Nekketsu soccer title, so this league never took that overseas trip.

Play is a pitch where a foul can become a brawl, not a calm table of league statistics. Kunio's name ties the ball to the schoolyard series, and scoring is only half of the match.
ninja-gaiden-ii-the-dark-sword-of-chaos:
Wind-tossed platforms and new blades join Ryu's climb in Ninja Gaiden II: The Dark Sword of Chaos (1990) already. Cinema-style scenes still interrupt the action, the way Tecmo told the NES story.

The dark sword of the subtitle is the new threat, and gusts shove a jump off its line. Ryu Hayabusa returns with sword arts the first cartridge did not give him.

Tecmo kept the habit of a story scene, then a deadly corridor. Players cite the wind platforms when they separate this middle quest from the other two NES chapters.
donkey-kong-3:
Stanley the exterminator replaces Jumpman in Donkey Kong 3, spraying bugs at Donkey Kong inside a greenhouse. The ape hangs from vines, and the spray can pushes both insects and the ape upward.

The arcade original is from 1983 and is the odd third coin-op, not another climbing rescue. There is no barrel run and no captive to reach; a round ends when the ape is driven to the top.

Nintendo's home cartridge follows that greenhouse fight. A later Game Boy Advance release repeats the sprayer and the bees rather than restoring Mario's ladders.
gradius:
Vic Viper's selectable power bar is the system Konami introduced in Gradius, also sold as Nemesis. Speed, missiles, a double shot, a laser, an Option satellite, or a shield waits in a queue until the pilot arms it.

The 1985 arcade shooter scrolls left to right through cores, volcanoes, and bacterian fleets. Dying empties the bar, which is why a fresh life feels suddenly fragile.

The NES port is real and keeps that left-to-right upgrade path. Options still trail the Vic Viper, and the same bar still decides what the next capsule will arm.
lunar-pool:
Compile built oddly shaped tables and a friction knob into Lunar Pool, called Lunar Ball in Japan. Pockets sit at strange angles, and high friction makes the cue ball die before a long rail.

The 1985 billiards game began on Japanese computers before the Famicom and NES releases. There is no named rival across the felt; the opponent is the table's geometry.

Each layout asks for a different aim because the cushions do not form a rectangle. The friction setting is the other skill, and a slippery cloth turns a gentle hit into a long carom.
micro-machines-old:
Codemasters raced Galoob's tiny cars across household clutter in Micro Machines (Old). A school desk, a pool table, and breakfast leftovers each count as a full circuit.

The 1991 racer reached the NES as an unlicensed Camerica cart. Falling off a table edge is the usual crash, because the camera stays tight on toy-sized vehicles.

Later Micro Machines games add features this first tabletop set does not have. The Camerica cartridge is the one built from those desks, baize, and leftover meals.
the-flintstones-the-rescue-of-dino-hoppy:
Fred Flintstone sets out after a kidnapped dinosaur and hopparoo in The Flintstones: The Rescue of Dino & Hoppy. Taito built the NES trek from the Hanna-Barbera cartoon, and the United States release arrived in 1991 already.

Dino and Hoppy are the captives, so the stages send Fred through Bedrock gadgets, clubs, and stone vehicles. Barney and the quarry sit behind a rescue plot, not a bowling-night sketch.

The hopparoo and the dinosaur are the goal at the end of that march. Fred's stone-age weapons are the means, and the cartoon town is the license's scenery.
tetris-1989:
Nintendo's licensed cartridge Tetris (1989) is the one that remained after the Tengen lawsuit. Alexey Pajitnov's falling blocks are here, but this cart is the official Nintendo edition, not his original computer design.

Tetrominoes drop in a well, and a line vanishes when it fills. The unlicensed Tengen cart was pulled off shelves, which is why players were left holding Nintendo's well.

It is distinct both from Pajitnov's original and from that pulled cart. Rotation, a rising drop speed, and the official license are what separate this cartridge from the one that disappeared.
tennis:
HAL Laboratory helped program Nintendo's Tennis, a Famicom game of singles and doubles from 1984 already. Mario umpires from the net post, and serve, volley, and smash depend on timing more than on a season's stats.

The NES cart came from that design. A doubles partner covers the far side of one court, and nothing like a tournament calendar wraps the match.

A separate handheld edition followed later. Mario's chair and the simple swing are what that NES cartridge copies from the Famicom original.
hogans-alley-1984:
Cardboard gangsters pop up in Hogan's Alley (1984), and Nintendo's Zapper is supposed to spare the innocents. Shoot a lady or a professor cutout and the drill scolds you; shoot the gunman and it continues.

It shared the Famicom light-gun lineup with Duck Hunt and Wild Gunman. The alley is a range of panels, not a free-roaming street.

Another mode pans targets across the screen, still with the same rule about who must not be hit. The Zapper, the gangster panels, and those innocent bystanders are the entire lesson.
simcity:
Will Wright's SimCity, from Maxis in 1989, is a city builder about zoning, power, and disasters that started on computers. Residential, commercial, and industrial zones grow only when the wires and the roads reach them.

Nintendo later published an NES port and a richer Super Nintendo edition. That Super Nintendo version adds a Bowser attack among its disasters and an advisor named Dr. Wright, beside the fires and floods the computer game already knew.

The mayor never walks the streets as a brawling hero. Taxes, power plants, and a monster downtown are the decisions, and a blackout undoes a block faster than a park repairs it.
the-addams-family:
Gomez Addams searches a house in Ocean's The Addams Family, a platformer based on the film. The NES cartridge is a separate, smaller license, and it is not the huge mansion people mean when they praise the Super Nintendo game.

That Super Nintendo version is remembered as a large, difficult house full of secret rooms. Family members such as Wednesday and Thing change the goals, while Gomez does the jumping.

The 1990 film supplies the names and the creepy estate. Ocean's NES cart is the shorter trek, and it should not be mistaken for the bigger mansion cartridge.
river-city-ransom:
Alex and Ryan spend recovered cash on stats and food in River City Ransom, Technos' open-town brawler. Mall shops sell burgers and books that raise punch power, and gangs fill the streets between those shops.

It sits in the same family as Double Dragon, yet it plays closer to a small role-playing quest. The town can be wandered, and the last boss is reached by getting stronger, not by surviving one corridor.

The 1989 release lets two players cooperate through that town. Coins dropped by students are the economy, and a meal matters as much as a new pair of shoes.
joe-mac:
Data East's club-swinging pair is Joe & Mac, also known as Caveman Ninja, a dinosaur brawl from the 1991 arcades. They smash through pterodactyls and rolling boulders while cavewomen wait to be rescued.

Clubs, thrown stones, and a roast are the tools, and a dinosaur is often the platform as well as the threat. Two players can batter the same prehistoric stage side by side.

The Super Nintendo version became the best-known home edition. NES and Game Boy releases sit beside it, but the living-room reputation belongs to those Super Nintendo clubs and dinosaurs.
snake-rattle-n-roll:
Rattle and Roll swallow Nibbley Pibbles until they weigh enough to ring a bell in Rare's Snake Rattle 'n' Roll. The view is isometric, and each snake grows fatter as the nibbles go down.

A bell on a scale blocks the exit until a body is heavy enough to depress it. Tongue strikes collect the pibbles, and enemies on the diamond grid can knock a snake off a ledge.

Rare also produced a Game Boy version in that same 1991 season. The NES original is the isometric pair, the pibbles, and the weight-activated bell.
resident-evil-2:
Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield cross a ruined Raccoon City in Resident Evil 2 (1998) already. Capcom's PlayStation release splits the outbreak between the rookie cop and Chris Redfield's sister, and their routes meet at the police department.

Zombies, a licker, and the station's locked doors shape a hunt for keys and ammunition. Ink ribbons record a save on the original discs, and each character sees rooms the other misses.

The Nintendo 64 port is famous for fitting that two-disc game onto one cartridge. A GameCube release followed later, still the same Leon-and-Claire outbreak rather than a new city.
quake:
id Software's Quake, from 1996, is the fully 3D follow-up to DOOM, with a soundtrack credited to Trent Reznor. A ranger steps through a Slipgate into rooms that can be circled, not flat corridors pasted with sprites.

Nailguns, grenades, and a rocket launcher punish crowds in gothic bases and strange caves. Shamblers and ogres replace the earlier demon roster, and the physics allow a bunny hop between ledges.

A Nintendo 64 port came after the PC original. The cartridge keeps the Slipgate campaign, with a pad in place of the keyboard and a smaller set of deathmatch options.
worms-armageddon:
Team17 stuffed a deep editor and a huge weapon list into Worms Armageddon, widely treated as the high point of the flat artillery series. Worms take turns lobbing shots across a hill that crumbles, and wind tugs the slower bombs.

That 1999 computer design is what the Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color editions carry over. Holy hand grenades, sheep, and air strikes sit on the weapon list, and the editor can store a custom hill.

A team is finished when its last worm drops into the water. The Game Boy Color cart cannot offer the full computer editor, yet the craters and the turn order remain the joke.
quake-2:
The Strogg wage an industrial war in id Software's Quake II, on an alien world invaded in 1997 already. A marine is dropped into that campaign, and the levels connect as one push instead of isolated episodes.

Strogg facilities, a prison block, and a great gun on the horizon structure the march. Metal corridors and harsher lighting replaced the first game's gothic stone.

The Nintendo 64 release is a later port, with its own compromises in lighting and geometry. Those cuts change how a hallway reads, even when the Strogg and the mission order stay recognizable.
ocarina-of-time:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time uses a lock-on camera so a sword fight can exist inside a 3D Hyrule. Songs played on the instrument change the hour, call a horse, or warp to a place you have already earned.

Shigeru Miyamoto produced it and Eiji Aonuma directed the dungeons, with Koji Kondo writing the ocarina themes the player performs to open doors and change the time of day. Link is a child in Kokiri Forest, then an adult after the Master Sword seals him, and the same temples exist in both ages.

Epona, the hookshot, and the iron boots are tools that rewrite earlier rooms. The Water Temple's iron-boots puzzle is the one players still argue about. A trading sequence that ends with Biggoron's sword is optional and long, which fits a game that treats side errands as part of the world.

The Nintendo 3DS revision changes the iron boots, the hints, and the graphics, and it has its own page. The iron boots and the Water Temple arguments belong to this version, not the later handheld revision.
daikatana:
Ion Storm shipped John Romero's Daikatana to PCs in 2000 after years of hype, and it became a notorious critical failure. The blade in the title is supposed to carry a fighter across separate eras, with companions trailing behind.

Kemco's Nintendo 64 port followed and was received even more harshly. Players who had already rejected the computer release found the cartridge's cramped rooms and slower fights harder to excuse.

The advance talk had promised a revolutionary sword. What arrived, on the computer and on the cartridge, was a shooter people cited when they warned about unfinished design.
super-mario-64:
Super Mario 64 puts a castle full of paintings between Mario and Bowser, and each painting is a sandbox with several stars. Stars can be collected out of order once the castle doors begin to open.

Shigeru Miyamoto and Yoshiaki Koizumi used the Nintendo 64's analog stick to make Mario run, tiptoe, long-jump, and wall-kick. Peach's castle is the hub: the more stars collected, the more doors open, and the order of courses is loose after the first few.

A hundred and twenty stars exist, including stars that only appear after a course is already beaten. Yoshi on the roof is the prize for finishing the set. The camera, often fought as much as the enemies, taught a generation how a 3D platformer should be framed.

Later 3D Mario games, from Sunshine to Odyssey, still use a hub and a loose goal list. A limited compilation on Switch included this game for a time. Peach's castle, the analog stick, and the roof Yoshi belong to this original sandbox.
banjo-kazooie:
Gruntilda's rhyme opens Rare's Banjo-Kazooie, in which a bear and a bird collect musical notes and jiggies. Spiral Mountain leads into themed worlds, and each jiggy opens another door in the witch's lair.

Notes raise the hit points, while jiggies are the keys. Mumbo's hut can transform the pair, and the jokes sit on signposts, in the voices, and in Gruntilda's couplets.

The 1998 collect-a-thon sits beside Mario 64 on that shelf of Nintendo 64 exploration. Banjo's backpack and Kazooie's eggs are the moves that make each world traversable.
turok:
Acclaim and Iguana brought the comic hunter to foggy jungles in Turok: Dinosaur Hunter, an early Nintendo 64 showpiece from 1997 already. Dinosaurs and armed poachers share the mist, and the draw distance fades into that fog.

The campaign is a first-person trek with a bow, firearms, and keys for ancient doors. Health plants and ammunition caches are the reason to leave the main path and search a ravine.

It was one of that console's early demonstrations of a first-person view. The comic hero, the fog, and the dinosaur packs are what the cartridge was bought to show.
starcraft:
Blizzard set Terran marines, Zerg swarms, and Protoss templars against one another in StarCraft. Bases are mined, barracks are built, and a real-time war spreads across a fogged map until one force is gone.

The computer release arrived in 1998 and became the strategy game people meant when they named those three factions. Each side's units are not simple color swaps: a Zerg rush and a Protoss gateway produce different fights.

Nintendo published a Nintendo 64 port that adds a console-only episode. That extra episode is the cartridge's own story, beside the Terran, Zerg, and Protoss campaigns brought over from the computer.
turok-2-seeds-of-evil:
Acclaim darkened the hunt in Turok 2: Seeds of Evil, and the cerebral bore became the weapon players still name. Iguana developed it as a sequel, not a fresh license, so the dinosaur corridors continue rather than start over.

The 1998 levels are meaner, with more cramped interiors and a wider arsenal than the first foggy jungle. The cerebral bore is a charge that locks onto a foe's head, which is a different fantasy from a simple rifle.

Nintendo 64 owners met that sequel on the same console as the first hunter. Seeds, the bore, and the gloomier maps are how this chapter separates itself from the earlier cartridge.
majoras-mask:
A falling moon and a three-day clock rule The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask, Nintendo's darker follow-up to Ocarina of Time. Link plays the Song of Time to rewind Clock Town before the moon finishes its descent.

Masks change how he moves: a Deku scrub hops, a Goron rolls, and a Zora swims the coast of Termina. Skull Kid wears the cursed mask that drives the cycle, and side quests in Clock Town only make sense if you learn the schedule.

The 2000 quest is the one with that doomed week. A 3DS version is a separate entry, so the moon, the masks, and Clock Town's bomb shop belong to this Nintendo 64 cycle.
hexen-for-windows-95:
Raven Software followed Heretic with HeXen: Beyond Heretic, a fantasy shooter of three character classes and hub levels. A fighter, a cleric, and a mage do not share the same weapons, so the same hub plays differently in each pair of hands.

The 1995 computer release links stages around a central map instead of a straight line of maps. Switches in one wing open doors in another, and the class you chose decides whether the answer is a hammer or a spell.

The Nintendo 64 version is a later port of that hub design. It is not a new sequel, and the three classes remain the reason to replay a fortress.
perfect-dark:
Joanna Dark takes rare gadgets into Perfect Dark, Rare's spy shooter and follow-up to GoldenEye. The Farsight rifle can see through walls, and a laptop gun unfolds into a turret that holds a hallway.

Bots called simulants fill custom matches, and a counter-operative mode lets a second player inhabit the campaign's enemies. Carrington Institute missions sit beside that match setup, with objectives closer to a spy checklist than a straight corridor.

It was the studio's last big first-person game of the Nintendo 64 era, released in 2000 already. GoldenEye's split-screen parties are the ancestor, while Joanna's gadgets and the counter-operative slot are this cartridge's own tricks.
doom-64:
Midway built Doom 64 as an original campaign, not a straight port of the computer episodes. New maps replace the familiar knee-deep stations, and a more ambient score sets the mood apart from the Super Nintendo DOOM cartridge.

The 1997 Nintendo 64 release still uses a shotgun, a chaingun, and demons in brown corridors, but the layout is its own. Colored keys and switch hunts follow a new route, with a Mother Demon waiting past the last gate.

Players who wanted the old episode select do not find it here. The ambient music and the new maps are the reasons this campaign stands beside, rather than inside, the earlier DOOM releases.
spider-man-2000:
Stan Lee narrates Neversoft's Spider-Man (2000), a third-person web-swing published by Activision. It launched on PlayStation and also reached the Nintendo 64, and it is not the later movie game.

Doc Ock and a frame-up drive the story while Spider-Man crawls over rooftops and into sewers. Combat is a brawl of punches and web, and the narration keeps breaking in with Lee's asides.

The Nintendo 64 edition follows that PlayStation design rather than inventing a new villain. Anyone looking for the film tie-in has a different game in mind; this one is the narrated rooftop quest.
banjo-tooie:
Larger connected worlds and new egg types continue the hunt in Banjo-Tooie, Rare's sequel still made in the studio's Nintendo years. Banjo and Kazooie can split up, and a pad in one region opens a door that the pair already walked past.

Clockwork eggs, grenade eggs, and other new shots join the moves Gruntilda's return demands. Jamjars teaches those moves from a bunker, replacing the first game's mole teacher with a drill sergeant.

The 2000 Nintendo 64 worlds bleed into one another instead of resetting at a lair door. That connection, plus the egg roster and the split-up, is how the sequel outgrows the first collection of jiggies.
tony-hawks-pro-skater-2:
Neversoft added the manual and custom parks to Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2, extending a timed trick run into linked lines. A manual balances between grinds so the score does not drop when the skater leaves a rail.

The design reached players in 2000, with the Nintendo 64 version following the PlayStation one. Real skaters still fill the roster, and a created park can be the whole session once the goals in a real city are done.

The Game Boy Color edition is a separate flat game, not a shrink of those 3D lines. Manuals, the park editor, and the Nintendo 64 goals belong to the console design, not to that handheld card.
star-wars-rogue-squadron-3d:
Factor 5 flew Rebel missions in STAR WARS: Rogue Squadron 3D, published with LucasArts as a Nintendo 64 combat flyer. Speeder runs on a planet and starfighter sorties in space share one campaign of pilots.

The 1998 missions quote battles from the films, then grade the pilot on time, accuracy, and optional targets. An A-wing handles differently from an X-wing, and a snowspeeder's cable is the tool for a walker.

Medals send the player back to earn a better rank on a world already survived. The speeder tow cable and the starfighter hangar are the two halves of that Factor 5 campaign.
shadow-man:
Mike LeRoi crosses between Liveside and Deadside in Acclaim's Shadow Man, a 1999 adaptation of the Valiant comic. The Nintendo 64 is among the platforms, and the two worlds do not play as the same kind of place.

Liveside is a grim Louisiana of bayous and a bar, while Deadside is a corpse-strewn afterworld of temples. A mask changes LeRoi into the Shadow Man, and dark souls collected in the afterworld raise his strength.

The comic's voodoo hero is the lead, not an original soldier dropped into a maze. Switching at a gate between the bayou and Deadside is the structure of the quest.
mario-kart-64:
Mario Kart 64 took the Super Nintendo racer's drifting and built courses that climb, drop, and hide shortcuts for four players on one television. A shortcut you learn on a couch still decides a cup, because the catch-up is weaker than in later karts.

Nintendo EAD made it for the Nintendo 64, with four-player split screen as the feature living rooms actually used. Wario and Donkey Kong joined the roster. Items like the blue shell, new here, punish the leader in a way the first game did not.

Rainbow Road, Yoshi Valley's maze of bridges, and the train on Kalimari Desert became the tracks people memorized. Because there is no rubber-band catch-up as strong as later entries, a good shortcut still decides a cup.

It is the second Mario Kart. The later games on GameCube, Wii, Wii U, and Switch each have their own pages, including the Wii U and Switch editions that reuse some of these ideas without being this cartridge.
rayman-2-the-great-escape:
Michel Ancel and Ubisoft moved Rayman into 3D in Rayman 2: The Great Escape, and the Nintendo 64 edition is among the best regarded. A pirate prison opens the journey, which already separates it from the original side-view Rayman.

Globox, walking shells, and a handful of lum creatures give the floating islands someone to talk to. Rayman's fist still flies on a tether, now aimed in a 3D space of swamps, canopies, and a slave-ship hall.

The 1999 design is a different game from the first Rayman's drawn levels. Players who remember only the side-view chase are not remembering this escape from the pirate fleet.
star-wars-shadows-of-the-empire:
Dash Rendar fills the gap between films in LucasArts' Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire, a 1996 multimedia project that includes a Nintendo 64 campaign. The Battle of Hoth opens that campaign, with a snowspeeder against walkers before the story moves on.

Dash's ship, the Outrider, carries him through sewer chases and a space brawl that the movies do not show. IG-88 and bounty hunters crowd a story set after The Empire Strikes Back and before Return of the Jedi.

The novel, the comics, and this cartridge were planned as one gap-year project. On the cartridge, Hoth and the Outrider are the parts a player actually steers.
super-smash-bros-1999:
Masahiro Sakurai and HAL Laboratory knock familiar heroes off the stage in Super Smash Bros. (1999) instead of draining a life bar. Damage climbs as a percent, and a strong hit sends Mario, Link, Pikachu, or whoever is lighter flying past a blast line.

It is the first game in the series and a Nintendo 64 original. The starting roster includes Samus, Fox, Donkey Kong, Yoshi, Kirby, and the rest of that first dozen, each with a few moves rather than a long command list.

Items drop onto floating platforms, and a home-run bat can end a stock in one swing. Later Smash games change the physics and the roster; this cartridge is the percent-and-platform original.
mortal-kombat-4:
Midway took the tournament into polygons in Mortal Kombat 4, the first main entry to leave sprites behind. Fighters stand as 3D models on a 2D line, and a weapon can be pulled off the wall of the arena.

The arcade shift dates to 1997, with fatalities still ending a match after the life bar empties. Goro's era of painted sprites gives way to chunkier limbs and a new set of combo dials.

The Nintendo 64 version is a home port of that arcade change. A Game Boy and a Game Boy Color edition sit further off to the side, while the polygon cast is what the Nintendo 64 cart was translating.
goldeneye-007-1997:
Rare's GoldenEye 007 (1997) turned a film license into a split-screen shooter that console parties played longer than the story. Objectives are checklists inside film locations, and the watch magnet matters as much as the gun.

Martin Hollis led a small Rare team, with David Doak among the designers and Grant Kirkhope on the score. Missions quote the movie's locations, from the dam to the facility, but the objectives are checklists: plant a covert modem, photograph a scientist, escape on a time limit.

Stealth is optional and often abandoned. The watch magnet, the Klobb, and the proximity mines exist because the team was inventing console aiming with a single stick. Multiplayer maps such as Facility and Temple, and modes like Slappers Only, are why the cartridge stayed in the console.

A later Wii reimagining and a Switch-era remaster are different products. This page is Rare's Nintendo 64 GoldenEye 007 (1997).
paper-mario:
A folded Mario turns sideways for timed hits in Paper Mario, the storybook quest Intelligent Systems made with Nintendo. Goombario and other partners join the turn order, and a button press inside the attack window raises the damage.

The 2000 battles still use jump and hammer, but the timing is the skill. Star Spirits and a paper theater frame a map of towns where Mario is flat enough to slip through a crack.

It is the start of this paper line, before the GameCube sequel and later spin-offs. The sideways turn, the partner puzzles, and the timed hammer belong to this Nintendo 64 storybook.
disneys-tarzan:
Vine swings carry Disney's Tarzan, a 1999 trek based on Disney's animated film rather than a straight pass through the Burroughs novels. The Nintendo 64 and PlayStation editions stage the movie's set pieces, from the jungle canopy to a confrontation with Clayton.

Tarzan moves by swinging, sliding, and surfing a branch, and the film's songs sit behind those traversal tricks. Jane, Terk, and the gorilla family are story markers, not a roster of selectable leads.

The Burroughs books have a different plot and a different tone. This tie-in follows the animated picture's vines and its villain, on those two consoles.
carmageddon:
Stainless Games made Carmageddon a car-combat race notorious for running over pedestrians, and SCI published it. Points come from checkpoints or from the crowd, and a wrecked car can still crawl if the driver keeps moving.

The 1997 computer game is the original. A Nintendo 64 port exists and was censored in some regions, which changes how the pedestrians look even when the demolition racing stays.

Repair pads and a timer push the driver to hit something, whether that is a rival car or the people on the course. The computer version is the uncut source of that idea; the cartridge is the later, sometimes censored, edition.
pokemon-snap:
Professor Oak sends a photographer down a rail in Pokemon Snap, and the score depends on the framing, not on a battle. HAL Laboratory built the on-rails safari with Nintendo, and apples, pester balls, and a flute provoke the creatures into a better pose.

The Zero-One vehicle never leaves its track, so the skill is when to snap. A Pokemon Sign lures subjects into the center, and a boring shot of a distant back scores worse than a close, active pose.

The 1999 Nintendo 64 safari is this rail and this camera. New Pokemon Snap, much later on Switch, is its own entry and not a level pack inside the Zero-One.
tony-hawks-pro-skater-3:
A revert links a vert trick back into a manual in Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3, the move Neversoft added with a deeper park editor. The revert is the glue: land a ramp trick, revert, and the combo does not die before the next grind.

PlayStation 2 led the 2001 release. The Nintendo 64 edition is a later, reduced version of that same skating design, with a smaller slice of the parks and goals.

Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance editions are flatter takes, and a GameCube version sits closer to the lead design. The revert and the thicker editor are the ideas the Nintendo 64 cart only partly had room to hold.
star-fox-64:
Branching paths and cockpit chatter carry Star Fox 64, the on-rails shooter that replaced the Super Nintendo game's chip-drawn look. Fox McCloud still flies an Arwing, and Peppy's bark about a barrel roll is now a spoken line.

Nintendo built the 1997 missions so a saved teammate or a found shortcut opens a different next world. All-range mode lets the Arwing turn around inside a space brawl, which the strict corridor stages do not allow.

Slippy, Falco, and Peppy call out damage from the wing. A 3DS remake later revisited this campaign, and that remake is a separate release from the Nintendo 64 chatter and medals.
donkey-kong-64:
Rare brought DK, Diddy, Tiny, Lanky, and Chunky to Donkey Kong 64, and the cartridge demands the Expansion Pak. Each Kong has a color of banana and a set of moves, so a door that refuses Diddy may open for Lanky.

The 1999 collect-a-thon follows the Country series into 3D rather than porting the arcade barrels. King K. Rool's island hides blueprints, golden bananas, and a switch that only one Kong's instrument can strike.

It is not a climbing remake of the coin-op. The five Kongs, the colored fruit, and the Expansion Pak requirement are the cartridge's own terms.
star-wars-episode-i-racer:
LucasArts spun podracing out of The Phantom Menace as STAR WARS: Episode I Racer. Anakin's podracer and Sebulba's larger engine share tracks full of tusken fire and falling rock, and a boost melts the engines if it is held too long.

Nintendo 64 and PC versions are the main 1999 releases. The Game Boy Color cart is a much simpler spinoff, without the same engine-heat tension or the wide anti-gravity courses.

Repairing a pod between races spends the winnings on better parts. The film's Boonta Eve idea is the license; the heat meter and the part shop are the game's own loop.
tony-hawks-pro-skater:
Neversoft turned real skaters and a two-minute timer into Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, published by Activision. The Warehouse is the session people learned first: gaps, a halfpipe, and a tape that ends whether or not the goals are done.

It debuted on PlayStation in 1999, and the Nintendo 64 version followed. Manuals were not in yet, so each trick line has to be rebuilt after the wheels touch flat ground.

A Game Boy Color edition is a separate, smaller game. The timed Warehouse run and the named skaters belong to the console design Activision shipped that year.
pokemon-stadium:
Rental teams and a Transfer Pak feed 3D battles in Pokemon Stadium, Nintendo's console companion to the Game Boy creatures. Gym cups climb in difficulty, and a minigame break sits between the stadium nights.
