Players who brought pocket-monster teams from the handheld can fight with those imported sets. Without a cartridge in the Pak, a rental roster still lets a cup begin, though the personal team is the reason the adapter exists.

The 1999 Nintendo 64 battles are not a mainline handheld journey. There is no long walk through a region; the play is the cup, the minigames, and the link to the Game Boy teams.
animal-crossing:
Tom Nook hands over a house and a debt in Animal Crossing, a town that runs on a real-time clock. Neighbors move away if the days pass without you, and letters arrive in place of any win screen.

Nintendo's first Western release of the series is the GameCube town, dated to 2001 already. K.K. Slider plays on Saturday nights, shops close in the evening, and a fossil in the ground waits for the museum rather than for a combat reward.

New Horizons and the handheld towns are separate games. This clock, these neighbors, and Nook's loan are the Western town's own rituals, including the Japanese Nintendo 64 original that shares the same idea under an earlier name.
indiana-jones-and-the-infernal-machine:
LucasArts sent Indiana Jones after a Soviet dig in Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine, a 3D adventure that debuted on PC. The Infernal Machine is the artifact at the center of the chase, and the levels are tombs and jungle bases rather than a menu of fistfights.

A Nintendo 64 port arrived in 2000 already. Whips, revolvers, and climbable ledges carry over, with the compromises of a cartridge controlling a PC-born camera.

It is not one of the earlier Last Crusade games. Those older Grail adventures are different works; this one is the machine, the Soviet rivalry, and the 3D tombs.
earthworm-jim-3d:
Earthworm Jim 3D moves the worm into a Nintendo 64 space in 1999, made by a different team than Shiny's side-scrollers. The cow, the pocket, and the cartoon violence of the flat games give way to a polygonal playground that reviewers treated much more coldly.

Reviews were harsher than they had been for the 16-bit run. Jumping puzzles and a lost-in-his-own-mind frame replace the tight stages Shiny had built around a plasma gun and a hamster.

The name on the box is the worm people already knew. The team, the camera, and the colder reception are what separate this 3D outing from those side-view cartridges.
donkey-kong-country-3:
Rare sent Dixie and Kiddy north in Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble! Donkey and Diddy are missing, so the search crosses a colder map than the earlier Country islands.

Kiddy is the heavy partner, and Dixie's helicopter hair still crosses gaps the toddler cannot. Barrel cannons and animal buddies return in that northern world, with a mill and a lake in place of the first game's beaches.

It closes the Super Nintendo Country trilogy, late in the console's life, in 1996 already. The missing heroes and the northern trek are the reasons this last cartridge is not another visit to Donkey Kong Island.
super-mario-all-stars-1993:
Nintendo remade four Mario cartridges as Super Mario All-Stars (1993), and the result is a compilation rather than a new adventure. Super Mario Bros., the Japanese Lost Levels, Super Mario Bros. 2, and Super Mario Bros. 3 all sit on one Super Nintendo cart with redrawn sprites.

A save file replaces the password habits of the older NES releases. World maps, warp whistles, and Birdo still behave as they did, now in the later console's colors.

Lost Levels, once withheld from North American NES shelves, is the inclusion that surprised players. The compilation does not add a fifth quest; it preserves those four, including the lost one.
the-lost-vikings:
Silicon & Synapse, later Blizzard, switched players among Erik, Baleog, and Olaf in The Lost Vikings, published by Interplay. Erik's jump and headbutt, Baleog's arrow, and Olaf's shield solve different doors in the same room.

The 1993 puzzles are unwinnable with the wrong Viking in the lead. A pit that eats Erik may be a safe drop for Olaf's shield, and a target only Baleog can shoot sits over a switch.

Tomators and alien machinery kidnap the trio out of a Viking village. The tool split, not a shared sword swing, is the reason the three have to travel as a set.
super-castlevania-iv:
Simon Belmont's whip swings in eight directions in Super Castlevania IV, and Konami redrew the castle for 16-bit hardware. A tap sends the leather across stairs and chandeliers, which the stiffer NES whip could not do.

It is a retelling rather than a straight port of the NES game. Rotating rooms, a treasure-room waltz, and crumbling bridges are new staging for Dracula's same invitation.

The 1991 castle still ends at Dracula, but the path there is a different architecture. Players who wanted the NES room order do not find it in these multi-directional halls.
street-fighter-2:
Capcom revived arcade one-on-one fighting with Street Fighter II: The World Warrior (1991) and a six-button layout. Ryu's hadouken, Chun-Li's spinning kick, and Guile's sonic boom each demand their own motion, and blocking is a deliberate hold.

The World Warrior roster, from E. Honda to Dhalsim, defined the match people copied. A round is still best of three, and a dizzy foe can be punished if the special move comes out clean.

The Super Nintendo port became a landmark home version of that roster. Six face buttons on the pad finally matched the cabinet's punches and kicks.
secret-of-mana-1993:
Square's ring menu and a party of three define Secret of Mana (1993), known in Japan as Seiken Densetsu 2 on the Super Famicom. Combat happens on the field, and each hero's weapon gains levels that change the charge attack.

Cooperative play is the feature people still cite: a second and third player can take the girl and the sprite while the boy leads. The ring pauses the field and sorts magic, items, and weapons into a circle instead of a vertical list.

A mana sword that grows and a cannon-travel network tie the regions together. The three-player ring is why this Super Famicom quest stayed in the conversation.
populous:
Peter Molyneux and Bullfrog let a deity raise land in Populous so a population can expand and fight. Lower a coast and the little settlers drown; lift a hill and they build farther from the enemy's book.

The 1989 computer original is the god game people named first. Walks of the faithful, papal magnets, and floods are divine interventions spent from a mana bar while two civilizations race.

Console ports, including the Super Nintendo, followed that computer original. The raised land and the tiny wars remain the play, even when the mouse becomes a pad.
flashback-1992:
Paul Cuisset led Delphine's Flashback: The Quest for Identity, a cinematic trek about an amnesiac named Conrad. Rotoscoped running and a holocube of lost memory set the tone after the studio's Another World.

Conrad wakes in a jungle in 1992 and pieces together a ticket back to Titan. Shields, a pistol, and ledge grabs are one-shot precise, and a wrong landing restarts the screen.

The game was strongest on computers and the Genesis. The Super Nintendo edition tells Conrad's same memory hunt with its own limits on how smooth that rotoscoped run feels.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-turtles-in-:
Konami reworked an arcade brawler into Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles IV: Turtles in Time, and the Super Nintendo cart adds stages the cabinet never had. Leonardo, Donatello, Raphael, and Michelangelo still clear Foot soldiers, now across a time-hop that includes a prehistoric scrap and a future train.

The 1992 beat-em-up is a high point of the studio's turtle brawlers. A throw into the screen, a Technodrome showdown, and Shredder at the end keep the comic-strip violence of the arcade while the extra eras are the home cart's gift.

Two players share the same sidewalks and the same pizza health. The additional time periods are why players treat this cartridge as more than a straight copy of the coin-op.
drakkhen:
Infogrames brought Drakkhen from late-1980s computers to an early North American Super Nintendo release. Four heroes cross an overworld drawn with a three-dimensional view that was unusual for role-playing games of that moment.

The 1988 computer design uses that receding landscape instead of a flat icon map. Dragon rulers hold the story, and random attacks interrupt the walk between their islands of architecture.

Entering a palace drops the view to a closer confrontation. The strange overworld perspective, more than any single spell, is what made the Super Nintendo edition feel unlike its neighbors on the shelf.
desert-strike:
Electronic Arts opened Desert Strike on the Genesis in 1992, a helicopter campaign inspired by contemporary desert warfare. An Apache-style gunship takes missions from a map, and fuel and armor limit how many tanks a single outing can burn.

The Super Nintendo version ports that isometric mission map. Co-pilots winch survivors while the cannon and the missiles have separate ammunition, so a noisy approach can leave the chopper dry.

A Game Boy and a later Game Boy Advance edition shrink the same war. The isometric map and the winch are the campaign's identity, born on the Genesis before those other carts.
cannon-fodder:
Sensible Software joked that war has never been so much fun, then sent named soldiers to die for good in Cannon Fodder. Jon Hare's team made it first for the Amiga in 1993, and a hill of graves fills with every private the player spends.

The tiny troopers shoot, grenade, and split into squads across a scrolling field. A soldier who falls does not respawn; the next mission recruits a fresh name, and the old one stays on the hill.

The Super Nintendo cartridge and a much later Game Boy Color edition carry that same cruel joke. The phrase, the graves, and the unreturning privates are the design, not a realistic officer school.
fatal-fury-special:
SNK upgraded Fatal Fury 2 into Fatal Fury Special, adding fighters and combo routes on Neo Geo in 1993 already. Terry Bogard remains the lead, and the new arrivals widen a roster that already had his brother Andy and Joe Higashi.

Lane switching, a habit of the Fatal Fury line, still lets a fighter hop to the far plane. Special's extra combo routes reward players who already knew the second game's motions.

The Super Nintendo version is a home port of that revision. It is not a new tournament with a new plot; it is the Neo Geo upgrade, brought to the pad.
samurai-shodown:
Haohmaru's sword and a rage gauge define SNK's Samurai Shodown, a weapon-based Neo Geo fighter from 1993 already. A heavy slash is slower than a kick, and the rage gauge changes the duel once a fighter has taken enough damage.

Slash or bust, the choice of stance, alters reach. Genjuro and Nakoruru bring different blades and speeds, so the match is about spacing a weapon, not throwing an identical punch.

Super Nintendo and Game Boy ports followed the arcade game. The rage gauge and Haohmaru's upper slash are what those ports were trying to keep.
sunset-riders:
Konami posted bounty targets between towns in Sunset Riders, a Wild West run-and-gun from 1991 already. Four players can ride in the arcade cabinet, while the Super Nintendo version trims that posse to two.

Steve and his fellow bounty hunters shoot through saloons, trains, and cattle stampedes. A wanted poster names the next boss, so the towns are a checklist of rewards rather than one endless desert.

The home version is a port, not a new license. The posters, the two-player limit on the Super Nintendo, and the four-player cabinet are the split players still mention.
pushover:
G.I. Ant topples a chain of dominoes in Ocean's Pushover, and the last tile has to land on a trigger. Shove the wrong domino and the chain collapses short of the switch, which means the room starts over.

Computer editions tied the puzzles to Britain's Quavers snacks. The Super Nintendo version swaps that branding for money bags, so the ant is collecting cash rather than crisp packets.

The 1991 puzzle is still the same physics: one push, a long fall, and a door that opens only if the sequence was legal. G.I. Ant's walk and the money bags are the cartridge's visible difference from the snack-branded computer editions.
star-fox:
Fox McCloud leads an Arwing wing in Star Fox, and the Super FX chip draws the on-rails space combat. Slippy, Peppy, and Falco chatter over the radio while Andross's forces fill a corridor the player cannot freely turn around in.

Nintendo and Argonaut shipped that chip-driven flyer in 1993 already. A wingman's shield call is not flavor alone; saving or ignoring a teammate changes how crowded the next trench feels.

It is distinct from the Nintendo 64 follow-up Star Fox 64 and its branching paths. The polygonal Super FX corridors, the Arwing's laser, and this first radio crew belong to the Super Nintendo cartridge.
f-zero:
Captain Falcon's Blue Falcon is one of a small roster in F-Zero, a hovercraft race that showed off Mode 7 speed. Mute City, Death Wind, and Port Town are tracks, and a machine that kisses the railing loses boost energy.

Nintendo's 1990 original pits those few hulls against one another on a flat course that scales toward the horizon. The league table is short, and falling off the track is a harsher penalty than a simple slowdown.

Later entries on Nintendo 64 and GameCube add cups and machines this roster never had. Mute City and the Blue Falcon's first league remain this Mode 7 cartridge.
sid-meiers-civilization:
Sid Meier's Civilization, from MicroProse in 1991, starts a people in the ancient world and aims them toward space. Settlers found cities, and a technology such as the wheel or gunpowder rewrites what those cities can build.

Wars, wonders, and a palace the player designs sit beside the research path. A rival civilization will arrive with chariots while you are still on bronze if the science slider is ignored.

The Super Nintendo edition is a later port of that computer strategy game. The same march from hut to starship is the goal, squeezed onto a pad.
castlevania-rondo-of-blood-2:
Richter Belmont and Maria Renard star in Konami's Castlevania: Rondo of Blood, a 1993 PC Engine Super CD game. Maria's doves and Richter's whip are two different campaigns through Dracula's town, and a secret path can recruit her.

It is not the Super Nintendo cartridge. That machine received the different Dracula X instead, with its own stage list and without this disc's arranged soundtrack.

Item crashes and a branching street of stages belong to the PC Engine release. Players who own only Dracula X have not played Maria's route or Richter's CD version.
boogerman-a-pick-and-flick-adventure-199:
Interplay aimed burps and nose flicks at the enemies of Boogerman: A Pick and Flick Adventure. The hero's health and ammunition are bodily, and a gross-out gag is the actual attack rather than a skin on a normal punch.

The Super Nintendo and Genesis cartridges shipped in the mid-1990s, and the gross-out fuss belongs to 1996 rather than to a later sequel. Mud pits, toilet tunnels, and a cape made of something unmentionable fill the stages.

Jumping still matters, but the flick and the burp are why the cart has its reputation. Both home versions share that joke, and neither pretends to be a polite mascot trek.
wwf-wrestlemania-the-arcade-game:
Midway digitized real wrestlers for combo strings in WWF WrestleMania: The Arcade Game, a 1995 federation license. A grapple opens into a chain of hits more like a fighting game than a simulation of a pay-per-view card.

Doink, Bret Hart, and the rest appear as photographed sprites, and a combo meter rewards the longer string. There is no season and no contract screen; the match is the whole product.

It is an arcade fighting take, not a booking sim. The Super Nintendo port brings those digitized combos home without turning them into a calendar of real shows.
zombies-ate-my-neighbors-1993:
Zeke and Julie sprint through suburban horror sets in LucasArts' Zombies Ate My Neighbors (1993) already. Neighbors trapped in hedges, basements, and pools are the score, and a squirt gun is a serious weapon against a pod person.

Super Nintendo and Genesis were the original pair of releases. Chainsaws, soda grenades, and a martian all show up as movie jokes, and a two-player rescue shares the same frantic map.

The goal is the neighbor count, not a boss rush for its own sake. Leave too many victims and the stage fails, even if Zeke and Julie are still standing.
kirby-super-star-1996:
HAL and Masahiro Sakurai packed several shorter games onto Kirby Super Star (1996), including The Great Cave Offensive. A copied ability can become a helper who fights beside Kirby, which a single-player inhale never did on the earlier carts.

Spring Breeze retells a tiny Dream Land, while The Great Cave Offensive is a long treasure hunt. Milky Way Wishes hands out powers from a menu instead of from an enemy, a break in the usual inhale rule.

Japan calls the collection Kirby of the Stars Super Deluxe. The helper, the cave, and that Japanese title are the reasons this Super Nintendo anthology is not one more short Kirby stroll.
street-fighter-alpha-2:
Capcom added custom combos to Street Fighter Alpha 2, a prequel series set before Street Fighter II. Fill the gauge, then spend it on a free-form chain that does not follow the old target-combo limits.

The arcade release is from 1996, with Alpha counters and a returning Sakura among the cast. Air blocking and the custom gauge are the systems players were learning on top of hadoukens they already knew.

The Super Nintendo port is a late, dense conversion of that arcade fighter. It arrives near the end of the console's life, still trying to hold those custom strings on a pad.
contra-iii-the-alien-wars:
Konami armed two soldiers for Contra III: The Alien Wars, known in Japan as Contra Spirits. Mode 7 spins a top-down street while missiles lock on, and the side-view stages still let a second player join the gunfire.

The 1992 Super Nintendo run-and-gun uses bombs, a hold-and-charge shot, and a mid-air swap of weapons. Red Falcon's return is the story excuse for robots, alien hives, and a last climb.

Smart bombs clear a screen the rifles cannot. The Mode 7 street and the two-player crawl are the set pieces players quote when they name this Spirits cartridge.
syndicate:
Bullfrog drugged corporate agents and sent them across a world map of hostile cities in Syndicate. The 1993 computer design is a tactics game: equip a squad, then walk them through pedestrians who can be persuaded or shot.

A research tree sells better cyborg parts, and the map paints rival syndicates as territories to seize. Gauss guns and a persuasion view make a mission either a massacre or a quiet recruitment.

The Super Nintendo cartridge ports that computer design. The same agents, the same city blocks, and the same corporate map are the port's job to carry.
mickey-mania:
Traveller's Tales walked Mickey through classic cartoons in Mickey Mania, and Europe later called the PlayStation release Mickey's Wild Adventure. Steamboat Willie is one of the stops, with the black-and-white deck rebuilt as a course of hazards.

The 1994 trek hit Super Nintendo and Genesis first, under the Mania title. The Mad Doctor and a moose hunt show up as further shorts, each with Mickey's hammer or a thrown object suited to that reel.

The PlayStation name is a regional retitle, not a different plot. The cartridge people mean is the earlier Mania tour through those old reels.
jungle-strike:
A hovercraft joins the gunship in Jungle Strike, Electronic Arts' isometric follow-up to Desert Strike with extra vehicles besides the helicopter. A motorcycle, a hovercraft, and the familiar gunship share the 1993 war against a drug lord and a nuclear plot.

Super Nintendo and Game Boy versions came after the Genesis lead. Passengers, fuel, and armor still limit a sortie, and the extra chassis are what separate this campaign from the desert-only predecessor.

The map remains a menu of missions rather than one open country. Choosing the hovercraft for a river and the chopper for a fortress is the new decision.
batman-forever:
Acclaim tied Batman Forever to Joel Schumacher's 1995 film, on Super Nintendo and Game Boy carts that share the movie rather than Sunsoft's earlier Batman games. Two-Face and the Riddler supply the villain imagery, and the stages are an action license of that picture.

Gadgets from the film, including a grapple, structure the jumps. The Game Boy edition is a smaller cut of the same license, not a level-select inside the Super Nintendo cart.

Sunsoft's NES and Genesis Batman games are different stories and different studios. Schumacher's Gotham, the Riddler, and Two-Face mark this pair of Acclaim carts.
mega-man-x2:
Zero's parts decide the ending of Mega Man X2, and Capcom's X-Hunters carry the pieces that let him return to help. A hunter fought in a stage may drop a piece, and missing it leaves X without his partner for the ending stretch.

The 1994 Super Nintendo sequel continues the X series' wall cling and charged buster. Sigma's influence lingers, but the X-Hunters are the new pursuers holding Zero's body.

Armor capsules still hide in optional corners. The part hunt, more than a new buster color, is the decision that makes this chapter different from the first X.
populous-2-trials-of-the-olympian-gods:
Bullfrog moved the god game into Greek myth with Populous 2: Trials of the Olympian Gods. Divine effects and a pantheon of rivals replace the first game's more abstract books, and an earthquake or a tidal wave is a named Greek power.

The 1991 computer design lets the player climb a ladder of gods by devastating the opposing believers. Buildings still rise on raised land, but lightning, baptism, and volcanoes are the new interventions.

A Super Nintendo port carries those Olympian trials. The pantheon, not a simple repeat of the first land-raising matches, is the reason this sequel has its own name.
super-ghoulsn-ghosts:
Arthur dashes through a harsher monster gauntlet in Capcom's Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts (1991) already. Japan knows the same quest as Chou Makaimura, and it follows the arcade Ghouls 'n Ghosts rather than starting Arthur's story over.

Double jumps and a magic weapon join the boxer-shorts panic of the earlier games. A princess to rescue and a graveyard opening are familiar, while the new armor spells change the projectile.

The Super Nintendo difficulty is the reputation: two passes through the gauntlet, and a chest that can curse as easily as it arms. Chou Makaimura's name on the Japanese box is the same Arthur, the same dash, the same cruel chests.
street-fighter-ii-turbo-hyper-fighting:
Capcom sped the cast up and added new special moves in Street Fighter II Turbo: Hyper Fighting, an arcade revision from 1992 already. Chun-Li gains a fireball, and the faster walk speed changes how soon a throw is in range.

The Super Nintendo port let players use that faster ruleset at home. It is not the earlier World Warrior timing; jumps, dashes, and specials come out at the Hyper Fighting pace.

Cabinet players already knew the roster. The home attraction was having that accelerated ruleset, new specials included, on a pad.
shin-megami-tensei-ii:
Atlus continued the apocalypse in Shin Megami Tensei II, with an underground Tokyo and alignment choices, in 1994 already. The Center, the Valhalla district, and a messiah plot sit under the ruins, and law, chaos, or neutrality still rewrite the ending.

It is a mainline sequel, not the school spinoff If. Demon negotiation and fusion return, now in a buried city rather than the first game's open Tokyo.

A party can be built from fused demons whose alignments tug the hero's path. The underground map and the messiah role are what keep this chapter from being a second school story.
mario-paint:
Nintendo bundled a mouse with Mario Paint, a 1992 drawing toy for the Super Nintendo. Stamps, animation frames, and a music composer share the cartridge with a fly-swatting minigame.

The composer grids notes the way a tiny piano roll would, and a stamp of Yoshi or a flower can be planted on a canvas. Animation is a flipbook of those drawings, not a side-scrolling level editor.

Gnat Attack, the fly swatter, is the only competitive corner. The mouse, the stamps, and the composer are why the cartridge shipped as a toy rather than as another Mario rescue.
ultima-vi-the-false-prophet:
Richard Garriott's Avatar meets a gargoyle conflict in Origin's Ultima VI: The False Prophet, a 1990 computer quest. The gargoyles are not a mindless camp; the plot asks whether the Avatar has been attacking a people with its own shrine.

The Super Nintendo release is a later, heavily altered home version. Conversations shrink, and the mouse-driven party of the computer game becomes something a pad can manage.

Britannia's shrines and the gargoyle side of the war are the story being altered, not replaced with a different hero. Players of the computer original meet a changed interface and a cut script on the cartridge.
star-ocean:
tri-Ace and Enix opened the series with Star Ocean, a 1996 Super Famicom mix of real-time fights and private actions in town. A private action is a small scene between party members that can change a relationship if you leave them alone in the right shop.

Battles move on a field without a separate encounter screen. Skills assigned from a menu fire while the hero runs, and a town's optional scenes are easy to miss.

It stayed Japan-only until much later remakes. Those remakes are other releases; the Super Famicom original is the first private-action system and the first real-time sword swings of the line.
disneys-aladdin:
Capcom built its own stages for Disney’s Aladdin (1993), a different production from Virgin's Genesis Aladdin. Abu, the carpet, and Agrabah appear, but the obstacle order is Capcom's, not Virgin's animation-heavy design.

Virgin's cart is remembered for fluid drawn frames. Capcom's Super Nintendo version plays more like the studio's other leaping heroes, with its own boss pattern and its own carpet moments.

Owning one does not mean you have played the other. The Genesis animation reel and Capcom's separate stage list are two Aladdins from the same film.
wild-guns-1994:
Natsume set a steampunk Wild West on one screen in Wild Guns (1994), and two players can share that gallery. Guns aim with a cursor while the cowboys dodge on foot, which makes it a gallery shooter rather than a light-gun port of an older coin-op.

It is an original Natsume design. Mechanical bosses, a wanted duel, and a bomb that clears bullets are the cartridge's own toys.

The Super Nintendo pad moves both the body and the crosshair. That split, plus the steam-age props, is the whole shootout.
starfox-2:
Argonaut and Nintendo finished Starfox 2 for the Super Nintendo in the mid-1990s, then shelved it. A strategic map lets the Arwing intercept invading forces, which already differs from the first game's strict corridor choice.

The official release finally came in 2017 on the Super NES Classic Edition. Until that plug-and-play box, the finished cartridge did not have a wide public launch.

Fox still leads, and the shelved map is the reason historians separate this follow-up from the original Super FX trenches. The Classic Edition is how most players finally flew that map.
super-bomberman-2:
Hudson's story mode in Super Bomberman 2 is about capturing the bomber, on a 1994 Super Nintendo maze cart. Multitap matches remain the reason people kept the cartridge after the rescue plot was finished.

Bombs still blast along a grid and kick down a corridor. The captivity plot gives the single-player side a villain and a cage, which a pure battle mode never needed.

Four-player taps were the living-room habit. The story of the captured bomber is the single-player excuse; the multitap is why the cart stayed plugged in.
international-superstar-soccer:
Konami's International Superstar Soccer on the Super Nintendo, from 1994, is the celebrated first game in that soccer line. Set pieces, a radar, and a faster pace set it apart from slower top-down pitches of the same years.

Later consoles received their own follow-ups rather than one unchanged port. A Nintendo 64 or Game Boy entry with a similar name is a later design, not this Super Nintendo match copied forward.

The celebration belongs to this first one: the feel of a through ball and the roster of international sides. Subsequent hardware got sequels, and those sequels are not this cartridge.
venomspider-man-separation-anxiety:
Acclaim followed Maximum Carnage with Venom/Spider-Man: Separation Anxiety, again starring the symbiote pair. Software Creations developed the mid-1990s Super Nintendo and Genesis versions, and the two still brawl as a side-scrolling pair.

Venom and Spider-Man can both be on screen, which the title's separation theme keeps threatening to undo. Symbiote tendrils are the extra reach, and the enemies are the same street-level comic chaos Carnage had already staged.

The 1995 beat-em-up is a sequel, not a fresh license. Maximum Carnage is the previous cart; this one is the separation story and the same two hosts.
dungeon-master:
FTL Games made Dungeon Master a real-time first-person crawl, and it became a hit on the Atari ST in 1987 already. Four champions stand in a party grid, and a spell is drawn with runes while monsters keep moving.

Food, water, and a torch are resources, not flavor. The ST game is the one that shook the genre, because the dungeon did not wait for the player's turn.

A Super Nintendo port arrived years later. The rune spells and the champion portraits are what that later cartridge inherits from the ST original.
super-bomberman-3:
Hudson let five players onto Super Bomberman 3, and the 1995 stages are themed around world cities. A multitap is assumed, and a match in a city arena is the reason to invite the extra bombers.

It continues the party design of the earlier Super Bomberman carts. Louies still appear as mounts, and a bomb kick can betray the friend who thought the tile was safe.

Story stages exist, but the five-player city bowls are the cartridge's reputation. The world-city dressing is new; the betrayal-by-bomb is the habit Hudson was extending.
shin-megami-tensei-if:
Atlus trapped a class inside Shin Megami Tensei If... A demon-invaded high school is the whole dungeon, and that school premise later fed the Persona series.

The 1994 Super Famicom spinoff is not a mainline apocalypse in Tokyo's streets. Classmates can join or fall, and fusion still produces the demons pacing the halls.

Persona inherits the school and the summoning, then becomes its own line. This cart is the invaded campus, the If title, and the first time the series held class indoors.
front-mission:
Square fielded customizable wanzer mechs in Front Mission: The First (1995), a Super Famicom strategy game of parts and pilots. Legs, arms, and a body are separate components, so a slow cannon build and a fast melee build can share a squad.

Later remakes reused the subtitle The First for this same story. The Huffman conflict and the wanzer garage are the campaign those remakes keep retelling.

A mission is a grid of mechs, not a menu of soldier sprites. Swapping an arm after a bad drop is the customization the subtitle's story is built around.
pilotwings-1990:
Lesson certificates, not combat sorties, structure Nintendo's Pilotwings (1990) already. A biplane, a hang glider, and a skydiving drop each demand a score, and Mode 7 draws the island while the student tries to hit the landing pad.

It is a Super Famicom launch title. Points come from a target circle, a ring in the air, or a gentle touchdown, and a failed landing sends the student back to the instructor.

There is no enemy ace to shoot. The flight school, the three vehicles, and the Mode 7 runway are the whole cartridge.
sailor-moon:
Angel sent the Sailor Soldiers through side-scrolling fights in Bishoujo Senshi Sailor Moon (1993) already. Sailor Moon, Mars, Mercury, and the rest of the class are selectable, and the stages follow the anime's early monsters rather than a one-on-one bracket.

A later R follow-up added a versus mode this first cart lacks. The original is a brawler: health bars, a special attack, and a path from the street to a boss youma.

The Super Famicom release is that cooperative-feeling lineup of soldiers, even when one player holds the pad. The missing one-on-one mode is what the R cartridge later supplied.
fatal-fury-king-of-fighters:
Terry Bogard entered SNK's King of Fighters tournament in Fatal Fury: King of Fighters, the 1991 Neo Geo fighter that started the line. Geese Howard waits at the end in South Town, and a two-plane stage lets Terry hop away from a fireball.

The Super Nintendo version ports that first Fatal Fury, not a later KOF entry. Andy Bogard and Joe Higashi are already on the roster, but the huge team format of The King of Fighters has not arrived.

Lane changes and Geese's stage are the cabinet's signature. The home port is trying to keep South Town, not the ensemble tag matches that borrowed the tournament's name afterward.
pirates-of-dark-water:
Ren's quest for scattered treasures is the plot of Pirates of Dark Water, a 1994 Super Nintendo license of the Hanna-Barbera series. It is a cartoon tie-in, not an original pirate design with its own ship and lore.

The Dark Water itself is the threat from the show, swallowing islands while Ren gathers the prizes that can stop it. Side-view fights and swims follow that episode logic.

No separate studio legend is required to explain the swords. The cartoon's Ren, the spreading stain, and the treasure hunt are the cartridge.
gods:
The Bitmap Brothers built ornate rooms and a shop between levels in Gods, a 1991 trek that began on the Amiga. Weapons and potions are bought with loot, and a key puzzle in a Greek temple is as important as the next monster.

Smooth animation and a dense background were the studio's reputation, and this game spends both on statues, traps, and a climbing route. A bought weapon changes the next hall more than a found heart does.

A Super Nintendo port came later. The shop, the Amiga-born animation, and the temple traps are what that port was copying.
fifa-international-soccer:
Extended Play Productions developed EA Sports' first association-football game, FIFA International Soccer, and consoles received it in 1993 already. An isometric pitch stood out from the top-down soccer that had dominated pads.

The camera angle shows more of the field's depth, and a through ball reads differently than it did on a flat overhead view. International sides, not a club season, fill the first menus.

That isometric debut is the whole identity of this first FIFA. Later numbered seasons add leagues and licenses this opening pitch did not yet carry.
ogre-battle-the-march-of-the-black-queen:
Yasumi Matsuno and Quest marched squads in real time across Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen, a 1993 Super Famicom strategy game. Moral alignment shifts with the battles you choose and the towns you liberate or exploit.

It is the first Ogre Battle, not Tactics Ogre. Units walk a map, meet the enemy, and resolve a fight on a separate field according to formation and class.

Tarot cards and a reputation meter color the ending. The march, the alignment, and the squads are this game; the later tactical grids are a different Quest release.
tiny-toon-adventures-buster-busts-loose:
Konami sent Buster through sports-mad stages in Tiny Toon Adventures: Buster Busts Loose! A football finale caps the cartridge, after levels that already behave like obstacle sports.

It is separate from Konami's NES Tiny Toons carts. Those NES outings are different stages and a different Buster; this Super Nintendo run has its own map and the football close.

The 1992 release leans on the Warner cartoon's slapstick and on Buster's dash. The finale on the gridiron is the scene that separates it from a plain hop through Acme acres.
bubsy:
Michael Berlyn's bobcat became Accolade's heavily promoted mascot in Bubsy, fully titled Claws Encounters of the Furred Kind. The 1993 Super Nintendo and Genesis versions sell speed: long drops, yarn, and a mouth that will not stop talking.

Later, the same mascot was widely mocked, which is part of the cartridge's history as much as the promotion. Extra lives scatter through levels that punish a mistimed leap off a high branch.

The furred-kind subtitle is the full name on the box. Speed, the bobcat's patter, and that rise-and-fall reputation belong to this first encounter, not to a later sequel's excuses.
super-star-wars-the-empire-strikes-back:
Hoth opens LucasArts' Super Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back, and Sculptured Software again built the action between the film's set pieces. A snowspeeder run and a wampa cave sit beside platform stretches with Luke, Han, and the others.

The 1993 Super Nintendo chapter continues the film trilogy the studio had started on the console. Blasters, lightsabers, and a Mode 7 moment translate a scene, then drop the player into a side-view fight the movie never timed.

It is the middle film, so the carbonite plot is the destination. Sculptured Software's corridors are the part you play between those famous shots.
the-lost-vikings-2:
Blizzard reunited Erik, Baleog, and Olaf in The Lost Vikings 2, also called Norse by Norsewest, and taught them new skills. The 1997 Super Nintendo sequel is much later than the first game's launch, not a companion released beside it.

A new tool on an old Viking changes puzzles that the original trio could not have solved. The alien kidnappers and the swap-between-three structure return, with fresh animations and fresh gaps.

Norse by Norsewest is the other name on the box. The new skills, not a simple rerelease of the first tombs, are why this sequel exists.
art-of-fighting-1992:
Ryo Sakazaki's spirit gauge powers special moves in SNK's Art of Fighting (1992) already. Spend the gauge on a fireball and the next special is weaker until it refills, which makes a desperate attack a real cost.

Robert Garcia shares the Neo Geo roster of that first entry. A zooming camera closes in when the fighters step apart, a flourish the cabinet used to show the sprite work.

The Super Nintendo port is a home version of that first entry. The spirit gauge and Ryo's kyokugen style are the systems the port had to teach on a pad.
spider-man-1995:
Webs and a side-scrolling punch define Spider-Man (1995), one of several mid-decade carts that share the hero's name. It is a Super Nintendo action course based on Marvel's wall-crawler, and it is not Neversoft's later 3D Spider-Man.

No Stan Lee narration and no open rooftops structure this one. Stages run left to right, with thugs, pits, and a boss at the end of a street.

The shared name is the trap. The year on the box and the flat perspective are how this cart stays separate from the third-person game that arrived afterward.
soul-blazer:
Freeing a trapped soul rebuilds a house, a villager, or a shop in Soul Blazer, Quintet's top-down quest published by Enix. Empty rooms fill in as the sword clears the monster that held the soul, so combat and town repair are the same act.

It is the first of Quintet's Super Nintendo action quests from Enix, ahead of Illusion of Gaia and Terranigma. The Master's servant is the hero, sent back to a world that has been stripped of its people.

A 1992 release, the sword, and the repopulating rooms are the whole loop. Later Quintet games inherit the mood, but the soul-by-soul restoration starts in this town.
stargate:
Williams and Eugene Jarvis followed Defender with Stargate in 1981, a space shooter later sold as Defender II. Humanoids still need rescuing, and the ship still faces a planet's surface rather than a castle's corridors.

It is not a Super Nintendo platformer and not the 1994 film that reused the name. Landers, mutants, and the warp gate belong to the arcade sequel, with the same frantic reversal of direction Defender taught.

The film's Egypt and the cartridge people might imagine from the title are unrelated. Jarvis's gate, the astronauts, and the Defender-style planet are the actual machine.
fatal-fury-2-1992:
Terry and Andy Bogard return to a larger Neo Geo roster in SNK's Fatal Fury 2 (1992) already. New challengers join the South Town tournament, and the two-plane lane system remains from the first game.

Super Nintendo and Game Boy ports brought that sequel home. The Game Boy edition is a severe shrink of the sprites, while the Super Nintendo cart tries to keep the new fighters' specials.

Wolfgang Krauser and the expanded lineup are the sequel's excuse to exist. The ports are how players without a Neo Geo cabinet met that lineup.
aero-the-acro-bat:
Iguana Entertainment put a circus bat to work in an amusement park, and Sunsoft published Aero the Acro-Bat in 1993 already. Aero dives, drills through a platform, and rides star-shaped platforms across a funhouse.

Super Nintendo and Genesis versions share the bat and the park. Spikes, cannons, and a magician's traps are the hazards, and a missed dive is the usual way a life ends.

The unlicensed-feeling mascot push of the era sits on a fully licensed Sunsoft box. The drill attack and the circus setting are what the two home versions were selling.
nhl-98:
EA Sports branded NHL 98 a year ahead of its window, and a late Super Nintendo edition sits beside the 32-bit games. It belongs to EA's NHL line, not to Nintendo's Ice Hockey, so the teams, the season, and the presentation follow the annual rather than a simple pond match.

The cover's 98 is the branding, while the release window itself is 1997 already. Checking, shooting, and a season mode are the hockey, even on hardware that was leaving the spotlight.

Nintendo's own Ice Hockey is a different, older cartridge. This annual is the EA one, arriving late on the Super Nintendo while newer machines carried the same year's branding.
biker-mice-from-mars-1994:
Throttle and the other animated mice license a motorcycle brawl in Biker Mice from Mars (SNES), a 1994 Super Nintendo combat racer. The hardware tag in the name marks this 16-bit cart, not a later remake.

Limburger's machines are the opposition, and weapons mounted on the bikes matter as much as the racing line. The cartoon's Chicago-in-space tone is the license, translated into laps and combat.

A later game with the same mice would be a different product. This cartridge is the one whose title wears the console, and whose races are the 16-bit ones.
blast-corps:
Rare clears a path for a runaway nuclear carrier in Blast Corps by smashing every building in its way. Dump trucks, a robot that leaps and pounds, and a train-like ram are the tools, and a single standing wall means failure.

The 1997 Nintendo 64 original comes from the studio behind GoldenEye, and it is not a licensed disaster film. Levels time the demolition against the carrier's slow approach across a town, a bridge, or a set of blocks.

J-Bomb's stomp and the dump truck's slide are different answers to the same wall. The carrier, the timer, and those vehicles are the whole emergency.
glover:
Hasbro Interactive gave a magic glove its own hero role in Glover, a 1998 Nintendo 64 trek about guiding a ball. The ball can change form, and bowling it, bouncing it, or carrying it are three different solutions for a gap.

A wizard's glove is the character, so there is no sword and no gun. The ball as a crystal, a bowling ball, or a fragile orb changes whether a slope is safe.

Play revolves around keeping that ball out of the water and onto a socket. Those shifting forms, the carry, and the bowl are the puzzle.
40-winks:
Eurocom's 40 Winks sends a child through dream worlds to rescue spirits called Winks, and it shipped on PlayStation in 1999 already. Pillow forts, nightmare bosses, and a cooperative second dreamer structure the rescue.

A Nintendo 64 version was cancelled at the time and only surfaced many years later. The released PlayStation game is the one players could buy in stores; the cartridge was the missing twin.

Winks are the collectible victims, not power-ups with a combat use. The cancellation is why a Nintendo 64 copy, when it appears, is a curiosity beside the PlayStation original.
castlevania-1998:
Reinhardt Schneider and Carrie Fernandez enter a 3D castle in Konami's Castlevania (1999), often called Castlevania 64 by players. It is a new quest, not a port of Symphony of the Night, and the villa, the hedge maze, and the vampires are built for a 3D camera.

Reinhardt uses a whip, while Carrie fights with magic, so the same hall is a different danger for each hunter. Contractual vampires and a nitro-fueled skeleton chase sit among the early rooms.

Symphony's inverted castle and Alucard's sword are absent. This pair of hunters and this polygonal estate are the Nintendo 64 chapter.
pokemon-puzzle-league-2000:
Nintendo applied Panel de Pon matching to Pokemon characters in Pokémon Puzzle League (2000) already. Blocks rise in a well, and a match of three clears them, with Ash and the 4Kids cast calling the shots on the American cartridge.

The United States version uses voices from the 4Kids anime dub. Team Rocket's taunts and Pikachu's cheer replace the silent panels of the Japanese puzzle game it is built on.

Garbage blocks still punish a slow match. The Pokemon skins and those dub voices are what turn Panel de Pon into this Nintendo 64 league.
nuclear-strike:
Shaped terrain replaces the flat strike map in Nuclear Strike, the 1997 campaign where the helicopter series steps into fuller flight. A campaign of rotorcraft missions follows the PlayStation and PC releases, and the Nintendo 64 version came after those.

The desert-map abstraction of the earliest Strike games gives way to shaped terrain and a more continuous flight. Fuel, armor, and winch goals still decide whether a sortie succeeds.

It remains a Strike game: a military helicopter, a mission select, and a limited vehicle. The fuller 3D world is the step Nuclear Strike takes, and the Nintendo 64 cart is the later passenger.
nhl-99:
Skaters hit a 3D rink in NHL 99, the annual EA Sports carried onto the Nintendo 64 under 1998 season branding. Skaters, a season, and 3D rinks follow EA's presentation, and the game is not a sequel to Konami's Blades of Steel.

Blades of Steel is an older arcade-style scrap with its own fights and its own teams. This annual belongs to the EA line, with the season's branding on the cover and a console roster to match.

Checking and a breakaway are the on-ice decisions. That season label sits on the box; the Nintendo 64 ice is one of the places that annual landed.
cruisn-usa-1996:
Midway's cross-country dash in Cruis'n USA (1996) is the racer Nintendo also shipped on the Nintendo 64 near that console's launch. The arcade cabinet came before the home cart, with landmarks rolling past a windshield at a rising speed.

Checkpoints gate the next state, and a crash is a brief crunch rather than a wreck that ends the trip. The home version keeps that coast-to-coast idea, reduced to what a cartridge could draw.

It is a launch-window companion to the new hardware, not a simulation of real touring-car rules. The cabinet's route and the early Nintendo 64 release are the same race in two buildings.
world-cup-98-2:
France hosts the licensed finals in World Cup 98, the tournament game EA Sports built around that summer. National sides, a tournament bracket, and the summer's teams are the content, on Nintendo 64 and Game Boy beside the PlayStation and PC releases.

The 1998 finals supply the badge and the roster. A Game Boy edition is a much smaller kickoff, while the Nintendo 64 version tries to hold the tournament structure.

It is the official tie-in of that French summer, not a generic street soccer cart. France, the license, and the national teams are the reason the title wears the tournament's name.
micro-machines-v3:
Codemasters moved the toy-car races into 3D in Micro Machines V3, still across kitchen tables and workshop floors. The 1997 entry is the third main one, and the Nintendo 64 version is one of several home ports.

A pool table's pockets are hazards again, now with a camera that swings in three dimensions. Tiny vehicles still fall off the edge of a real-world surface, which remains the series' crash.

It is not the flat overhead of the earliest tabletop sets. The 3D household and the port to the Nintendo 64 are V3's place in the line.
pilotwings-64:
Hang gliders, gyrocopters, and rocket belts cross photoreal islands in Pilotwings 64, the Nintendo 64 sequel to the Super Nintendo flight school. Paradigm worked with Nintendo, and the game was a launch title, so the islands were a showpiece for the new hardware.

A cannon shot and a skydiving target return as lessons with new aircraft. Cartoon pilots take the tests, and a rocket belt's fuel is the limit on how long a hover can last.

The 1996 launch lessons are this sequel, not a redraw of the Mode 7 biplane. Gyrocopters, the belt, and the photo-based islands are the new syllabus.
batman-beyond-return-of-the-joker:
Terry McGinnis wears the future suit in Batman Beyond: Return of the Joker, a 2000 Nintendo 64 game based on the animated film. It is not Sunsoft's earlier NES Return of the Joker, which belongs to a different Batman and a different decade.

The futuristic Gotham, the red-and-black suit, and the Joker's return follow the film. Side-view fights and gadgets from the series are the play, not a blocky 8-bit corridor from Sunsoft's book.

Confusing the two Joker titles is easy and wrong. Terry, the Beyond setting, and the film are this cartridge; the NES Joker is someone else's revenge.
forsaken:
Probe built Forsaken as a six-degrees-of-freedom shooter in the vein of Descent, and Acclaim published it in 1998 already. A craft pitches, rolls, and slides through tunnels, with no floor that can be called down for long.

The Nintendo 64 version is a home port of that PC and PlayStation design. Doors, reactor cores, and a hostile security system structure the floors, and the hover is the skill.

Descent is the ancestor of the free rotation, not a level pack inside this box. Forsaken's tunnels and Acclaim's port are the Nintendo 64 way into that weightless gunfight.
mystical-ninja-starring-goemon-1997:
Goemon pilots the giant robot Impact on a musical stage in Konami's Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon (1997) already. Fans still quote that robot concert, and the rest of the quest is a 3D wander through a fantastic Japan with Ebisumaru in tow.

The United States release followed the Japanese Ganbare Goemon cart. Impact's stage is a rhythm fight, while towns hide jokes, meals, and a castle that would not fit a straight brawler.

A later side-view sequel is a different shape. This cartridge is the 3D Goemon, the robot, and the song.
castlevania-legacy-of-darkness:
Cornell the werewolf joins a revised castle in Konami's Castlevania: Legacy of Darkness, an expansion of the Nintendo 64 quest from 1999 already. It works as both a prequel story and a reworking of the earlier 3D game, with levels rebuilt rather than merely relabeled.

Cornell's beast form and a new set of keys change how a familiar hall plays. Carrie and Reinhardt's routes are still in the package, altered by the rework.

Cornell's chapter is the one to seek if the goal is the werewolf and the revised maps. The earlier 3D cart lacks Cornell's chapter and these rebuilt rooms.
sin-punishment:
Treasure fired a rail shooter down a ruined future in Sin and Punishment - Successor of the Earth. Saki's sword and a gun sight share the same stick, and the Nintendo 64 game was published in Japan in 2000 already.

Western players got an official English release later, including a 2007 Virtual Console edition. Until that translation, the rail, the sword, and the Earth-successor story were much harder to read.

The sight-and-sword combination is Treasure's idea of a shooter. The Japanese cartridge and the later English Virtual Console are the two official ways that idea left the studio.
tiggers-honey-hunt:
Tigger bounces after honey pots in Disney's Tigger's Honey Hunt, a 2000 trek based on Disney's Winnie the Pooh characters. The Nintendo 64 and PlayStation editions send him through levels spun from the Hundred Acre Wood rather than from a new plot.

Roo, Piglet, and Pooh appear as the neighbors of that hunt. Springs, honey trails, and a bounce that can overshoot a ledge are Tigger's way of moving, which a Christopher Robin walking tour would not use.

The film and television Pooh stories supply the faces. Honey, the bounce, and those two home versions are the licensed chase.
gauntlet-legends:
Atari Games rebuilt the four-hero dungeon crawl as a 3D arcade quest in Gauntlet Legends, and the Nintendo 64 version ports that sequel rather than the 1985 cabinet. Warriors, valkyries, wizards, and archers still need food, but the dungeons now recede in perspective.

The late 1990s arcade update adds a campaign of realms instead of one endless floor. Generators still spawn the hordes, and a voice still mocks a fallen hero, now over a 3D hall.

It is not the flat 1985 cabinet with its original four classes and nothing else. Legends, the realms, and the Nintendo 64 port are the sequel's shape, from a 1999 push to bring that hall home.
south-park-rally:
Acclaim put the Comedy Central cast into karts for South Park Rally, a 1999 racer separate from the earlier South Park first-person game. Cartman, Kenny, Kyle, and Stan drive snowy South Park streets, and a weapon from the show replaces a plain banana peel.

The first-person license is a different Nintendo 64 product about the same town. Rally is laps and items, not a corridor of terrorists and cows.

That kart is the one with the starting grid of fourth graders. Confusing it with the shooter means expecting a gun where the box put a steering wheel.
monster-truck-madness-2:
Microsoft followed its earlier truck game with Monster Truck Madness 2, a 1998 racing sequel of licensed monster trucks and muddy tracks. Bigfoot and other named trucks bounce through holes that would stop an ordinary stock car, and the series lives on Windows.

Mud, hills, and a crushed car are the scenery of that Windows line. It began with Monster Truck Madness and continues here with a larger garage of licensed bodies.

The tracks are the point: a pit of mud, a ramp, and a truck tall enough to survive both. Office-computer players met those trucks here, in the sequel's garage.
mischief-makers:
Marina Liteyears grabs an enemy and shakes it in Mischief Makers, Treasure's side-scrolling robot girl and her grab, built for the Nintendo 64 pad. A shake shakes out coins, a stunned foe, or a throw she can aim back into the crowd.

The 1997 cult favorite is not a Nintendo-made platformer. Treasure's grab, the hover, and Marina's "shake shake" habit are the moves, in a bright world of clan balls and Professor Theo.

Grabbing is the verb, more than jumping. The robot girl, the professor, and the shake are why the cartridge has a cult rather than a broad Nintendo-hero reputation.
ogre-battle-64-person-of-lordly-caliber:
Quest continued the squad battles on the Nintendo 64 with Ogre Battle 64: Person of Lordly Caliber, first released in Japan in 1999 already. Real-time units still meet on a map, now wrapped in a larger class story of a soldier rising through a revolution.

Classes and a moral lean change how the army is judged. A unit's formation still resolves the clash, and the lordly caliber of the subtitle is the hero's climb, not a single duel.

The Japanese release is the original home of that class tale. Western carts followed, but the squads and the revolution start with Quest's Nintendo 64 continuation.
killer-instinct-gold:
A practice dummy defines Killer Instinct Gold, Rare's Nintendo 64 version of Killer Instinct 2 with a practice room attached. Combo breakers still interrupt a long string, and the 1996 training mode lets a player drill those breakers without a tournament match.

It covers the sequel, not the earlier Super Nintendo Killer Instinct cart. Orchid, Fulgore, and the new fighters belong to the second arcade cast, which Gold is translating.

The training mode is the home addition players cite. Gold is that second roster plus the practice room, not a reprint of the Super Nintendo combo tape.
tonic-trouble:
Ubisoft, the Rayman team, spilled a magic drink across Earth in Tonic Trouble and followed the clumsy alien who dropped it. The 1998 3D worlds drew much harsher reviews than Rayman 2, and the comparison stuck.

Ed, the alien, stretches and misfires through kitchens and gardens warped by the tonic. The drink is the plot device, and the camera and the jokes never found the goodwill Rayman's pirate escape earned.

Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color versions carry that same spill. The harsher reviews and the clumsy alien are the reputation, next to a studio that had just shown it could do better.
bomberman-hero-1998:
Hudson took the bomber off the maze grid in Bomberman Hero (1998) and made him jump through Nintendo 64 stages. Bombs still clear a path, but the camera follows a hero course of rails, enemies, and gaps instead of a single-screen arena.

It is a spinoff, not a numbered Super Bomberman port. Multitap battle is not the reason this cart exists; a health bar and a forward path are.

Louie's absence from the old party format is the point. Hero stages, the jumping bomber, and the abandoned maze are the spinoff's terms.
quest-64:
Imagineer's lone hero walks a Nintendo 64 world without a traditional party in Quest 64's quiet overworld. THQ published it in the United States in 1998, and Europe received the same quest as Holy Magic Century.

Spirit collection replaces a party of fighters. Brian, the boy with the staff, captures elemental power from defeated foes, and there is no shop-bought roster of companions to fill a back row.

It is one of the few role-playing quests on that console, and a divisive one. The solo staff, the spirit wells, and the two regional names are the whole offer.
ready-2-rumble-boxing:
Afro Thunder and other exaggerated boxers headline Midway's Ready 2 Rumble Boxing, a cartoon bout from 1999 already. A rumble meter fills as punches land, and spending it unleashes a flurry that a simulation's stamina bar would never allow.

Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color versions followed the arcade-style original. The Game Boy Color card is a smaller ring, while the Nintendo 64 version keeps the big gloves and the taunts.

Afro Thunder's hair and the lettered specials are the personality. The meter, the taunt, and those cartoon bodies are the sport Midway was selling.
snowboard-kids:
Atlus mixed item attacks into a downhill dash in Snowboard Kids, a 1998 Nintendo 64 racer that plays more like a cartoon kart than a simulation of the sport. Snowmen, projectiles, and a course through a theme park replace a realistic gate run.

Slash, Nancy, and the other kids draft and shove on the way to a lodge. A well-timed item matters as much as a clean carve, which is the kart habit showing through the snow.

It is not a licensed winter-sports annual. The items, the kids, and the playful courses are Atlus's downhill.
hydro-thunder-1999:
Boost starts and huge jumps define Midway's Hydro Thunder (1999), an arcade powerboat racer. A full boost meter at the horn is the difference between a clean first corner and a wall of wake.

The Nintendo 64 version is a home port of that cabinet, not an original Nintendo water game. Tracks such as a Greek ruin or an arctic cut are fantasies, and missing a jump throws the boat into a reset.

The cabinet came first. The cartridge's job is those boost starts, those jumps, and the same overpowered boats.
army-men-air-attack:
3DO put plastic-green helicopters over a backyard in Army Men: Air Attack (1999) already. Tan enemy plastic, a garden hose, and picnic furniture are the battlefield, and the helicopters are a spinoff of the toy-soldier series.

The Nintendo 64 edition is one home port of that aerial spinoff. Machine guns and a winch share the cockpit, while a magnifying glass or a match can be as dangerous as the tan guns.

It is not the foot-soldier campaign of the main Army Men line. Green plastic rotors, the backyard, and the tan army are this helicopter's war.
duke-nukem-zero-hour:
Eurocom gave Duke a time-travel plot in Duke Nukem: Zero Hour, a 1999 Nintendo 64 third-person shooter published by GT Interactive. Eras change the guns and the enemies, from a Victorian street to a future alley, while Duke's boot remains the melee option.

It is not Duke Nukem 64, the port of Duke Nukem 3D. That other cart is the first-person Build engine brought over; Zero Hour is a behind-the-back camera and a time machine.

GT Interactive's box is the third-person one. The eras, the camera, and Eurocom's stages are how this Duke stays a different cartridge.
ready-2-rumble-boxing-round-2:
Midway enlarged the roster and kept the exaggerated boxing in Ready 2 Rumble Boxing: Round 2 with a louder undercard. The sequel arrived in 2000, and the Nintendo 64 version continues those cartoon bouts with new faces beside Afro Thunder.

The rumble meter and the taunts return, now with more boxers who do not resemble a sanctioned athlete. A letter-graded special still breaks a realistic jab-cross pattern on purpose.

Round 2 is the larger card, not a balance patch alone. New challengers, the same rubbery punches, and the Nintendo 64 ring are the sequel.
excitebike-64-2000:
Left Field Productions built a dirt-bike follow-up, published by Nintendo, in Excitebike 64 (2000) already. A track editor and stunt racing keep it from being a simple remake of the NES Excitebike's side-view heats.

Riders crash in 3D ruts, and a saved custom track can be the whole evening. The spirit of the NES game is the dirt and the jumps, not the flat sprite of a bike on a single plane.

Temperature and a crash that costs time return as ideas, rebuilt for a 3D hillside. The editor is the feature the original heats never offered.
turok-3-shadow-of-oblivion:
Danielle and Joseph take the rifles in Acclaim's Turok 3: Shadow of Oblivion, the chapter that closes the Nintendo 64 trilogy. It follows Seeds of Evil rather than restarting the comic license, and the 2000 release puts the two hunters in place of the earlier solo lead.

Oblivion's enemies and a darker corridor continue the series' gun-and-dinosaur mix. Each sibling has a different loadout, so the same gate is not identical in both campaigns.

Seeds of Evil's arsenal is the ancestor. Danielle, Joseph, and the decision to end the trilogy here are this cart's own terms.
extreme-g:
Probe mounted weapons on futuristic motorcycles for Extreme-G, and Acclaim published the Nintendo 64 racer in 1997 already. A boost, a mine, and a laser share the handlebars, and sequels on the same console followed this first grid.

The track is a tube of neon and tunnels, not a dirt circuit. Falling off the racing line into a wall at that speed is the usual retirement.

It is the first of those weaponized bike games from Probe and Acclaim. The later Extreme-G sequels add riders and tracks; this one is the original armed grid.
bomberman-64-the-second-attack:
Hudson returned to adventure stages and bombs in Bomberman 64: The Second Attack, the 2000 Nintendo 64 sequel. In Japan it is known as a numbered follow-up to Bomberman 64, and the story shares space with the series' explosives.

Pommy, a companion, and a gravity belt change how a bomb is thrown across a 3D room. The maze party of the Super Nintendo multitap is not the center; an exploration map is.

The Second Attack name is the Western label for that numbered follow-up. Adventure rooms, the bombs, and the companion are the sequel's mix.
goemons-great-adventure:
Konami shifted to a side-on view in Goemon's Great Adventure, the 1998 follow-up to Mystical Ninja. Japan knows it as a Ganbare Goemon sequel, and the jokes, the meals, and Impact-sized nonsense remain.

Goemon and his friends now travel a scrolling stage rather than a free 3D town. A mech sequence can still interrupt, but the camera stays lateral for the villages and the castles.

That side-on camera is the break from the earlier 3D wander. Players who wanted another open castle will find a scroll, a punchline, and a different Goemon instead.
battlezone-1998:
Activision reworked the Atari name into tank combat plus base building in Battlezone (1998) already. Satellites are captured, factories are dropped, and a tank the player built rolls out to hold the moon or a scrap of Mars.

The Nintendo 64 release is a later, less famous port of that remake. The computer game is where the builder-and-tank idea was fully at home, with a mouse on the construction menu.

It is not the 1980 vector cabinet, which had no base to build. Factories, the satellite grid, and the constructed tank are the remake's rules, and the cartridge is the quieter echo.
rugrats-in-paris-the-movie:
The babies take the Nickelodeon film's Paris trip in Rugrats in Paris: The Movie, a 2000 license with a Nintendo 64 version among the tie-ins. Chuckie's wedding story, a giant Reptar, and the city replace an earlier Rugrats game-show setting.

Minigames and short adventures follow the movie's beats rather than a quiz bowl. The Eiffel Tower and the wedding are scenery the game-show cart never needed.

It is the film's Paris, not the previous television-studio license. That Paris trip, Reptar, and the Nintendo 64 tie-in belong to this movie.
animaniacs:
Yakko, Wakko, and Dot share Konami's Animaniacs, and the 1994 Super Nintendo and Game Boy cartridges are not the same game. The Warner Bros. cartoon supplies the siblings, the water tower, and the slapstick, while each cart builds its own stages.

A mallet, a chase, and a movie-lot hazard fit the Super Nintendo run. The Game Boy edition cannot hold that same map, even though the three faces on the box match.

Treating the two cartridges as one game is the mistake. Yakko's commentary and the lot are the license; the stage lists diverge as soon as the hardware does.
breath-of-fire-ii:
Ryu's dragon forms return between visits to a township the party is building in Capcom's Breath of Fire II (1994) already. The Super Famicom sequel lets the hero found a town, staff its shops, and leave again on the world map.

It continues the dragon-transformation line started by the first game. A fused shaman and a township upgrade sit beside the church, and the dragon breath is still the family's weapon.

Township is the feature players cite when they separate this quest from a straight dungeon march. The town, the transformations, and the church are the sequel's own camp.
trials-of-mana-2:
Trials of Mana asks you to field three companions chosen from Duran, Angela, Kevin, Charlotte, Hawkeye, and Riesz. Square first published that six-hero roster on the Super Famicom under the name Seiken Densetsu 3 in 1995.

Switching the starting trio changes which towns open their doors and which class change appears after the light and dark forks. Battles pause on a ring menu, and a full gauge spends a technique before the enemy bar fills.

The Super Famicom cartridge left Japan without an English script. A much later remake took Trials of Mana as its public title and finally translated the six-hero scenario for players who had known only Secret of Mana.
goof-troop:
Goofy and Max share every room in Goof Troop, Capcom's cooperative puzzle adventure drawn from the Disney series. Two players shove blocks, trade keys, and keep Pete's traps from splitting the pair on the Super Nintendo in 1993.

One Goof must lift the other onto a ledge a single body cannot reach, and a hook fires only while the partner stands on the switch. The pace follows a room-by-room rescue, closer to a shared brainteaser than to Capcom's punch-heavy cartoon brawlers.

Max's fishing rod and Goofy's grappling hook divide the labor inside each house. Clearing a stage means both characters reach the door with the crates already shoved, not with a boss meter emptied.
live-a-live:
Takashi Tokita directed Live A Live as chapters that refuse to share a century. Square released that anthology on the Super Famicom in 1994, long before an official English script existed.

A prehistoric wrestler, the ninja Oboromaru, a kung-fu pupil, the gunman Sundown, a present-day grappler, the boy Akira, and the robot Cube each receive a self-contained scenario. The medieval knight Oersted waits until those chapters are finished, then binds their survivors into one last castle.

Contact battles and floor traps replace a roaming encounter rate in several of those eras. The HD-2D remake is what finally carried an official English script, decades after the Super Famicom chapters.
castlevania-dracula-x:
Richter Belmont climbs a castle in Castlevania: Dracula X that is not the PC Engine CD's Rondo of Blood. Konami's Super Nintendo release in 1995 keeps the whip and the final duel with Dracula while drawing its own stages.

Item crashes and Maria Renard's route, both central to the CD game, do not chart this cartridge. The corridors are stricter, and the music is a fresh arrangement rather than the disc's audio tracks.

Players who hoped for a straight transfer of Rondo meet a shorter path to the throne room. Richter still ends the night against Dracula, yet every hall along the way was built for this Super Nintendo project.
columns-1990:
Columns (1990) drops jewels in vertical stacks of three, and a line of matching gems clears. Sega's puzzle, remembered on the Genesis as a rival to falling-block games, began as a computer and arcade design.

Cycling the order of the three stones, then sliding the stack, is the entire decision before they lock. A magic gem can erase one color, a tool that behaves nothing like rotating a tetromino into a gap.

The Super Nintendo cartridge is a later home edition of that jewel rain. Genesis players already knew the rising speed and the same three-stone column.
final-fight-2:
Haggar returns to Metro City in Final Fight 2 with Maki and Carlos walking beside him. Capcom built this Super Nintendo sequel in 1993 and never produced an arcade cabinet for it.

Maki's tonfa reach and Carlos's sword cover lanes Haggar's pipe cannot, and a second player may pick any of the three. Mad Gear remnants still pour from doorways, but the streets were drawn for a controller rather than a cabinet panel.

A co-op walk is the original way to see this plot, because no coin-op Final Fight 2 exists. Anyone who learned the first Metro City rescue will find a new partner pair and a route that started on the cartridge.
ultima-vii-the-black-gate:
Richard Garriott opens Ultima VII: The Black Gate on a murder beside a moongate in Britannia. Origin shipped that mouse-driven PC chapter in 1992, and the Super Nintendo game using the subtitle is a much simpler adaptation.

On the computer the Avatar drags crates, bakes bread, and walks a continuous map while the Fellowship spreads. The console edition compresses that simulation into menus, so conversation and combat lose the freedom of the mouse cursor.

The Black Gate conspiracy remains the threat both versions name. Garriott's PC world is the original chapter, and the Super Nintendo cart is a reduced retelling of the same Fellowship plot.
super-bomberman:
Four bombers crowd one television in Super Bomberman once a multitap is plugged into the Super Nintendo. Hudson's 1993 cartridge is the cart that made Bomberman a living-room fixture on that hardware.

Soft blocks hide extra bombs, longer flames, and a remote detonator that lets a player choose the moment a charge explodes. The last Bomber standing wins the grid, and a kicked bomb can rebound off a wall into its owner.

A solo route exists, yet the picture people remember is four hands on the multitap. That party grid, more than any single boss, is why this Hudson cartridge stayed in the Super Nintendo lineup.
fifa-97:
EA Sports aimed FIFA 97 at the 1996 season and kept an isometric pitch on the Super Nintendo. The camera looks down the grass at an angle, so a through-ball reads differently from the sideline view in Konami's International Superstar Soccer.

National sides fill the menus, and one outfield runner stays under the controller at a time. Set pieces and a small radar are the tools for a match that resolves in a few minutes.

The annual stays inside EA's FIFA line of soccer games. International Superstar Soccer keeps its own teams, its own camera, and its own Konami match on a separate cartridge.
toy-story-1995:
Woody crosses rendered dioramas in Toy Story (1995), the platformer Traveller's Tales built from the Pixar film. Super Nintendo and Genesis editions share those pre-rendered rooms, while the Game Boy cart is a separate, smaller tie-in.

Andy's bedroom, Sid's mutant toys, and the moving van each become a stage built around Woody's pull-string attack. The backgrounds were painted to resemble the film's sets, an unusual look for a licensed hop on those consoles.

A stage select keeps the film's order from Andy's room onward. Players who only held the Game Boy edition met a shorter, different version of Woody's trip.
captain-commando:
Captain Commando leads Ginzu, Mack the mummy, and Baby Head's mech through a future city. Capcom's arcade brawler from 1991 received a Super Nintendo port of that same coin-op.

The Captain's electric gloves, Ginzu's blade, Mack's reach, and the baby's mech missiles each clear a different crowd. Sidewalks fill with criminals, and a second player can grab any partner for the same street.

The home cartridge follows the arcade route rather than inventing a new plot. Learning which of the four fighters breaks a particular guard is the skill the cabinet already demanded.
final-fight-3:
A super-move gauge glows on the HUD throughout Final Fight 3, Capcom's Metro City continuation. Haggar fights beside new allies in this 1995 Super Nintendo game, and like Final Fight 2 it never had a matching arcade cabinet.

Lucia's speed and Dean's grapples cover space the mayor's pipe cannot, and a full gauge spends a screen-clearing special. Mad Gear holdouts still arrive in waves, yet every street was composed for the Super Nintendo controller from the start.

Co-op on this cartridge is the original way to walk the new route, because no cabinet exists. Players who finished the Maki and Carlos adventure meet a different partner roster and that extra gauge.
top-gear-2:
Weapons bolt onto the cars in Top Gear 2, the Super Nintendo racing sequel. Kemco published the series, known in Japan as Top Racer, and this 1993 season runs longer than the first game's country tour.

Mines, a boost, and a front skid change how a split-screen rival is passed on tracks that cross more regions. A password still marks the season, so a wrecked machine can be repaired before the next national round.

The earlier Top Gear was a clean two-player drive under the same Kemco banner. Here that shared road adds an arsenal, and a lead can be shot away before the finish banner.
nba-jam-1994:
Mark Turmell's two-on-two at Midway is NBA Jam (1994), the basketball game where a hot streak sets a player on fire. Arcades came first, and the home versions became a major hit in 1993.

Turbo into a dunk from beyond the lane is the spectacle, and the announcer shouts once the streak holds. Shoving a defender out of the air is legal, which is why a match feels like a brawl that happens to own a hoop.

Super Nintendo and Game Boy editions carried that announcer and the flaming head. The cabinet is where the phrase landed first, and the home carts spread the same two-on-two rules.
doom-troopers-mutant-chronicles:
Doom Troopers: Mutant Chronicles sends armored soldiers down a run-and-gun drawn from the Mutant Chronicles tabletop setting. The shared opening word sits beside a different license from id Software's DOOM, and this Super Nintendo cartridge arrived in 1995.

Corporate factions and the Dark Legion's creatures define the targets, and the troopers carry heavy guns through side-view corridors. A second player can join the push, which fits a squad skirmish more than a lone patrol on Mars.

What the crosshair finds here are mutants from that science-fiction setting. The cartridge's title begins with a familiar syllable and then names Mutant Chronicles on purpose.
mighty-morphin-power-rangers:
Mighty Morphin Power Rangers licenses Saban's television series, and the Super Nintendo edition from 1994 is a one-on-one fighter. The Game Boy release is another, smaller tie-in with its own screen layout.

Rangers morph and trade special moves in a versus match, closer to a duel than to a belt-scrolling episode of the show. A monster can close a round, but the television call to morph is what the license is selling.

The handheld cart retells the same colored suits on a much smaller set of screens. Both editions borrow the Saban costumes, and each one plays by a different set of rules.
adventures-of-batman-robin:
Batman shares rooftops with Robin in Konami's The Adventures of Batman and Robin, based on the animated series. Platform streets alternate with Batmobile runs in this 1994 Super Nintendo game, a separate Gotham from Sunsoft's NES Batman carts.

Grapple points, batarangs, and a highway stage against the animated rogue's gallery give the cart its shape. Tall shadows and the Batmobile's long fins follow the look of that television series.

Sunsoft's earlier NES outings used a different studio and a different map of the city. Konami's tie-in builds its own sequence of alleys and a chase in the car.
battletoads-in-battlemaniacs:
Rare's Battletoads in Battlemaniacs keeps the series' sudden difficulty spikes on the Super Nintendo. Rash and Zitz still smash through a stage that changes shape mid-level, and this 1994 episode stands apart from the NES original and from the Double Dragon crossover.

A hover-bike rush sits beside a climb that ends on one mistimed jump. Two players can take the pair, yet a single missed cue in the speeder section stops the attempt cold.

The NES and Game Boy Battletoads maps use different corridors and different jokes. Battlemaniacs builds its own run of one-hit traps for the 16-bit machine.
final-fantasy-mystic-quest-1992:
Final Fantasy Mystic Quest (1992) is Square's simplified role-playing quest aimed at North American players. Japan received the same journey as Final Fantasy USA: Mystic Quest, and it sits outside the numbered main line.

Benjamin's path runs through short dungeons where a weapon doubles as a field tool, and encounters arrive more gently than in a typical numbered Final Fantasy. Allies rotate in as the walk moves from the Focus Tower toward Doom Castle.

The Western box used the Final Fantasy name to welcome newcomers to menus and towns. Collectors keep Benjamin's quest beside the numbered games, as its own cartridge.
maui-mallard-in-cold-shadow:
Donald Duck wears a shirt and a hard-boiled glare in Maui Mallard in Cold Shadow, Disney's platformer. Super Nintendo and Genesis versions of this 1996 adventure exist, and some US boxes lead with Donald's name.

A staff for close hits and a bug-loaded gun give the duck two stances he can swap mid-stage. Hawaiian shores, a mansion interior, and a mud-soaked underworld break the journey into distinct sets.

The Game Boy cartridge is a smaller companion to those console versions. Shoppers who picked up the US box sometimes met Donald's name first, with Maui Mallard as the detective he is playing.
demolition-man:
