John Spartan thaws into corridor fights in Demolition Man, a Super Nintendo action game based on the Sylvester Stallone film. Shooting mixes with brawling in this 1994 movie license, a separate product from Midway's arcade treatment of the same picture.

Simon Phoenix's crew fills a cryo-prison hall and a sanitized future street. A short ammo count pushes Spartan from the firearm back into punches when the clip runs dry.

Stallone's thawed cop and the film's chase supply the premise. The stages were drawn as a film adaptation, with their own rooms rather than a trace of a Midway cabinet layout.
super-street-fighter-ii-the-new-challeng:
Cammy, Dee Jay, T. Hawk, and Fei Long join the roster in Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers. Capcom's update reached the Super Nintendo in 1993 with those four newcomers intact.

Cammy's spiral arrow, Dee Jay's max out, T. Hawk's storm hammer, and Fei Long's rekka each demand their own spacing. The grand masters still anchor the cast, and a mirror match can pit a new challenger against a copy.

Home players who owned only the earlier Street Fighter II carts met the new four here. The arcade cabinet introduced them, and this cartridge is the Super Nintendo place to practice those matchups.
wing-commander:
Chris Roberts mixes cockpit sorties with a branching carrier plot in Wing Commander. Origin released the PC original in 1990, and the Super Nintendo port is a later, simplified adaptation of those flights.

A lost mission can change the next briefing aboard the Tiger's Claw, and a Kilrathi ace may return if the guns miss. Shipmates' portraits react to the war's direction between dogfights.

The console version keeps the Kilrathi war while trimming the PC simulation's detail. Roberts's branching briefings, not a pure score attack, are what the name describes.
the-simpsons-barts-nightmare:
A sleeping Bart tumbles through sketch-like dreams in The Simpsons: Bart's Nightmare. Acclaim's Super Nintendo game from 1992 stands apart from the NES plot of Bart vs. the Space Mutants.

Homework pages blow along a Springfield sidewalk, and catching one drops Bart into a dream with its own rules, including a giant Bartzilla stomping buildings. Each dream ends by dumping him back on that windy street.

Space Mutants on the NES is a separate Springfield episode about costumes and collectibles. This nightmare is its own night, built from disconnected dreams rather than that earlier mission.
international-superstar-soccer-deluxe:
More national sides and a tighter match define International Superstar Soccer Deluxe. Konami's Super Nintendo update from 1995 builds on the first ISS game and stays outside EA's FIFA line.

A one-two, a lob, or a sliding tackle comes from different button holds, and the camera sits nearer the sideline than FIFA's isometric view. Exhibition, league, and scenario modes give the extra squads somewhere to play.

The first International Superstar Soccer established Konami's style of close control. Deluxe adds teams and small tuning on top of that earlier cartridge.
mechwarrior-3050:
A Mad Cat walks an isometric field in BattleTech: A Game of Armored Combat, the Super Nintendo label for a design other boxes call MechWarrior 3050 instead. In 1994, Activision published this BattleMech game set in FASA's universe.

Torso twists aim the weapons while the legs face another direction, and missile racks fire apart from the lasers. Enemy 'Mechs and turrets dot the mission map under that Mad Cat cursor.

The BattleTech wording is what this cartridge's label uses. The pilot's machine remains the Mad Cat even when another box prints the MechWarrior number.
asterix-obelix:
Asterix and Obelix defend a potion-fueled Gaulish village against Rome in Asterix & Obelix. The Super Nintendo and Game Boy games from 1995 are tie-ins to that French bande dessinée, not to an American cartoon.

Menhirs, Roman camps, and a wild-boar chase supply the obstacles, and Obelix shoulders tasks Asterix handles with speed. Getafix's cauldron is why the small village holds off the legions in the albums these carts adapt.

Goscinny and Uderzo's speech balloons are the source of the jokes. Both Nintendo editions draw on that same village fence and the same druid's brew.
secret-of-evermore:
A boy and a shape-changing dog cross fabricated worlds in Secret of Evermore. Square's Redmond studio developed this action role-playing game in 1995, outside Japan, and the cartridge was not released there.

Alchemy mixes ingredients into spells, and the dog can become a beast that soaks a hit the boy would dodge. Podunk, a prehistoric jungle, and an antique marketplace are among the regions the pair walk.

Secret of Mana's real-time attacks are the model, translated by the Redmond team. Because the quest was designed outside Japan and never shipped there, it stands as Square's American Super Nintendo experiment.
x-men-mutant-apocalypse:
Wolverine and Cyclops brawl in side view throughout X-Men: Mutant Apocalypse. Capcom's Super Nintendo game from 1995 is a scrolling action cartridge, separate from the later arcade fighter X-Men: Children of the Atom.

A claw dash, an optic blast, or a teammate's teleport clears a different patch of Apocalypse's forces. Switching which mutant leads a stage changes the route through those strongholds.

Children of the Atom is a versus fighter with its own posed introductions. Mutant Apocalypse keeps the camera on a side-view battlefield and a cooperating Marvel team.
sim-city:
Dr. Wright advises the mayor in Nintendo's Super Nintendo edition of Sim City, and Bowser can strike the skyline as a disaster. It is a special edition of Will Wright's city builder from 1989, distinct from the plainer NES port.

Zones for homes, shops, and factories still demand power lines, and a rail link raises land value the way Wright's model did. The advisor's portrait pops up when traffic or crime turns sour.

Bowser's attack is a Nintendo-only calamity alongside fires and floods. The NES port lacks that king and that advisor, so this Super Nintendo city is its own municipal toy.
top-gear:
Kemco's Top Gear splits one television between two cars for a country-by-country season. A password saves a place in that 1992 Super Nintendo tour, and Japan knows the same racer as Top Racer.

Nitro boosts and a glance at the rival's bumper are the tools on tracks that cross one nation after another. This first season carries no weapon rack, which keeps the drive cleaner than the armed sequel.

The password string lets a wrecked campaign resume at the next border. Split-screen is the reason two people sat down with Kemco's cart.
actraiser-1990:
Quintet's ActRaiser (1990) alternates side-view sword fights with a god's-eye view where a civilization grows. Enix published this Super Nintendo original from that studio.

The Master clears a monster lair, then the overhead map lets villagers raise homes and send offerings that strengthen the angel. Those offerings change the next side-view battle, tying the two cameras together.

A sword stage and a town offering are the cartridge's two rhythms. Enix's link with Quintet is how that combination reached players.
lufia-ii-rise-of-the-sinistrals:
Neverland filled Lufia II: Rise of the Sinistrals with puzzle rooms that are the dungeon, not a side errand. Taito published this Super Famicom prequel in 1995, and the US release kept those puzzles as a main draw.

Maxim's party shoves crates, rides moving blocks, and steps on switches before a monster is even the point. Capsule monsters can join the humans, and the Ancient Cave stands as a separate challenge tower.

The earlier Lufia told a later war against the Sinistrals. This prequel spends its hours on intricate rooms, which is why the US box still led with the puzzles.
prehistorik-2-1993:
Titus brought Prehistorik 2, a European caveman platformer, to the Super Nintendo and Game Boy. The club-wielding hero of this 1993 sequel belongs to Titus's line, a different prehistoric joke from Data East's Joe & Mac.

Meat hung over a pit, a dinosaur used as a step, and a belly that needs feeding give the stages their slapstick. The club bonks a foe into the dirt, which is the attack this caveman carries.

Joe & Mac's twin hunters and their egg hunts live on Data East's cartridges. Titus's hero keeps his own levels on both the Super Nintendo and the Game Boy.
prince-of-persia-2-the-shadow-and-the-fl:
Jordan Mechner's Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame continues the careful swordplay inside a palace intrigue. The DOS sequel arrived in 1993, a Super Nintendo port exists, and the PC game remains the original.

A betrayed prince flees across deserts, and the shadow he casts can turn against him. Single-step jumps, hanging ledges, and a duel that punishes a hasty slash all return from Mechner's first palace.

The flame of the subtitle is a power later battles call on. Mechner's DOS version is the edition his team built first, with the Super Nintendo cart as the later adaptation.
romancing-saga-2-2017:
Square's Romancing SaGa 2, led by Akitoshi Kawazu, follows an empire handed across generations. This Super Famicom role-playing game from 1993 did not receive a contemporary English release.

A ruler falls and an heir inherits the throne, the researched spells, and the unfinished war against the Seven Heroes. Classes appear as the centuries pass, so the party that ends the campaign need not have been born when it began.

The generation skip is the system players remember. English-speaking audiences waited years before an official edition carried Kawazu's empire outside Japan.
spider-man-and-venom-maximum-carnage:
LJN's Spider-Man and Venom: Maximum Carnage adapts the comic crossover as a beat 'em up on the Super Nintendo and the Genesis. A red cartridge and the symbiote team-up are the public hooks of this 1994 release.

Spider-Man and Venom trade the lead while Carnage tears down a street, and a guest hero from the crossover can spend a special attack. Thugs and a health bar define each block of the scrolling brawl.

The red plastic made the Super Nintendo box easy to spot on a shelf. Both home versions retell that comic event with the symbiote pair in front.
mega-man-x3-1995:
Capcom's Mega Man X3 (1995) continues the X series under Dr. Doppler, and some versions let you deploy as Zero. It is the third X adventure, still a 16-bit run before later disc ports.

X borrows a weapon after a Maverick falls, and Doppler's laboratory waits at the end of that hunt. Zero's saber, on versions that include him, cuts with a different rhythm from the buster.

The first two X cartridges set the Maverick stages and the armor upgrades. Doppler's plot is the layer this third Super Nintendo cart adds.
umihara-kawase:
Umihara Kawase swings on a stretchy fishing line that grabs a wall, hooks a fish, and climbs a gap. This Super Famicom platformer from 1994 stayed in Japan on its first edition and later gathered a cult following.

The cord bends, snaps, and slings the girl across kitchens and docks full of hostile sea life. A mistimed hook drops her, so the rubber line is both the path and the hazard.

No official translation shipped with that first Japanese cartridge. Players who found the line physics years later are the audience that turned the Super Famicom original into a cult favorite.
clock-tower:
Human Entertainment's Clock Tower (1995), directed by Hifumi Kono, follows Jennifer through a point-and-click night with the Scissorman. Panic, a hiding spot, and a cursor replace a weapon, so the Super Famicom game plays as suspense.

Jennifer moves through the Barrows mansion room by room, and a door helps only if she reaches it before the blades. Several endings depend on which clues she gathers and whether her nerve holds.

Kono's horror uses a pointer and a stalker. The Scissorman's footsteps are a threat the cursor cannot answer with a subweapon.
cool-spot:
Virgin's Cool Spot puts the 7 Up mascot, a red dot in sunglasses, onto bright ledges. This hopper from 1993 reached both the Genesis and the Super Nintendo, and the stages began as a soda advertisement.

Spot gathers cool points, bounces on a bubble, and rides a yo-yo line between platforms. Candy-colored rooms follow the drink's mascot rather than a film's sets.

Genesis and Super Nintendo editions share that red hero and the same brand. The yo-yo and the floating bottles are what turn the logo into a stage.
tactics-ogre-let-us-cling-together:
Quest's Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together, directed by Yasumi Matsuno, fights on a grid. This Super Famicom tactical game from 1995 uses turns, a different clock from the real-time marches of Ogre Battle.

Denam's choices on Valeria shift who stays loyal, and a unit's facing changes who can be struck. Archers, knights, and wizards act in a strict order across those tiles.

The subtitle belongs to Matsuno's campaign of hard choices. Players who knew only Ogre Battle's flowing battlefield meet a turn-based war on this cartridge.
judge-dredd:
Judge Dredd licenses the 2000 AD comic judge for action games timed with the Stallone film. Super Nintendo and Game Boy carts share the name as movie-era tie-ins from 1995.

Mega-City One, the Lawgiver pistol, and a helmet that stays on are the pieces the license brings from the strip. Each cartridge builds its own rooms around that judge, so the handheld screens are a separate adaptation.

The film's year and the comic's lawman are what the two carts share. The Super Nintendo streets and the Game Boy stages keep different level lists.
final-fight:
Capcom's Final Fight sends Haggar, Cody, and Guy to clean up Metro City. The 1989 arcade cabinet allowed two players at once, and the first Super Nintendo port dropped that co-op and, at first, Guy.

Cody's knife, Guy's speed, and Haggar's pipe handle Mad Gear thugs in a street, an elevator, and a wrestling ring. Bosses such as the Andore family wait at the ends of those districts on the cabinet.

The earliest Super Nintendo cartridge kept Haggar and Cody for a single-player walk. Guy's return, and two-player play, arrived in later revisions and in the console sequels.
terranigma:
Ark leaves an underworld village in Terranigma and must rebuild the surface from a lifeless shell. Quintet and Enix released this action role-playing game in Europe and Japan in 1995, and it never reached North America.

A spear and the crystal at Crysta, the village under the earth, start a journey that resurrects continents, plants, and towns. Side-view fights alternate with an overworld that fills in as life returns.

Soul Blazer and Illusion of Gaia came earlier in Quintet's loose Super Nintendo line. Terranigma is the last of those action role-playing games, and its rebuilding plot stayed out of North American shops.
killer-instinct-1994:
Rare's Killer Instinct (1994) is the arcade fighter Nintendo promoted with combo breakers and a rock soundtrack. The Super Nintendo port is a reduced home version, and Killer Instinct Gold later covered the sequel.

Fulgore, Spinal, and a shadow of the fighter you picked can break a combo if the defender hits the window. The cabinet's announcer and the heavy music sold the spectacle before the home cart trimmed frames.

A Game Boy edition shrinks the roster into a still smaller duel. Gold, on a later Nintendo system, is the home treatment of the sequel rather than of this first cabinet.
mega-man-7:
Bass debuts as a rival in Mega Man 7 (1995), where Capcom moves the classic blue hero onto the Super Nintendo. The plot continues the NES story, on a separate timeline from Mega Man X.

Wily's new robot masters come in batches, and Bass arrives with Treble, a wolf-like partner, between stages. The slide and the charged shot carry over from the later NES games into taller sprites.

Rush still brings adapters for flight and a drill. Bass is the new grudge, and he belongs to this classic line rather than to X's Maverick wars.
urban-strike:
Electronic Arts' Urban Strike brings the Strike helicopter series into a city campaign. This 1994 sequel followed Jungle Strike and still uses that series' mission map between sorties.

A co-pilot, a winch, and a fuel gauge turn each city block into a target list. Ground troops and a terrorist plot replace the jungle canopy of the previous cart.

The selectable mission map is the structure Jungle Strike already used. Urban Strike moves that structure onto streets, rooftops, and a fight over a metropolis.
civilization:
The Super Nintendo Civilization is a console port of Sid Meier's turn-based history game from MicroProse. Technologies still lead toward a spaceship, one more turn at a time, on a smaller home map from 1991.

Settlers found cities, and a science rate decides when the wheel or writing arrives. A rival can demand tribute while advisor screens compress Meier's PC menus onto a controller.

The palace view and the spaceship ending remain the long goals. What changes on the Super Nintendo is the map's size and the way those menus fit a gamepad.
frogger-1981:
Konami's Frogger (1981) hops a frog through traffic and across a river, one of the simple arcade ideas that became universal. Super Nintendo and Game Boy releases are much later ports of that same crossing.

Logs, turtles, and a timer on the far bank decide whether five frogs get home. A car in the first lanes, then a diving turtle in the water, are the hazards the cabinet taught.

The coin-op screen is the original frog. Nintendo home carts replay those lanes with the same goal of five safe pads.
breath-of-fire:
Capcom's Breath of Fire (1993) opens that role-playing line with a hero who can take dragon form. A Super Famicom quest came first, and a Game Boy Advance reissue is how many English-speaking players later met it.

Ryu's breath, a fishing spot, and a party that includes a winged companion give the towns their color. Menu battles and caves that only the dragon body can cross fill the overworld.

Later numbered Breath of Fire games inherit this first transformation. The Advance reissue carried the same quest to a handheld for players who missed the Super Famicom cartridge.
shin-megami-tensei:
Atlus's Shin Megami Tensei walks a demon-haunted Tokyo after the missiles fall. This Super Famicom role-playing game from 1992 descends from the Megami Tensei books and Famicom games, and alignment shapes a bleak apocalypse.

Law, chaos, and a neutral path change which demons will negotiate and which ending the ruins allow. A recruited demon can be fused into a new ally at a cathedral terminal.

A Game Boy Advance reissue later carried that Tokyo to a handheld. The Super Famicom original is where this post-apocalyptic alignment system took the form players still cite.
pitfall-the-mayan-adventure:
Activision's Pitfall: The Mayan Adventure is the sequel to David Crane's Atari 2600 Pitfall, drawn with pre-rendered jungle animation. It debuted on the Genesis and Super Nintendo in the mid-1990s, with 1995 as the year on this record, not the 2600 era.

Pitfall Harry Jr. swings on vines, cracks a whip, and searches Mayan ruins for his father. A crocodile and a crumbling ledge punish a short jump in a denser stage than the 2600's single screen of pits.

A Game Boy Advance port later carried the same ruins. Crane's original pit-jumps live on the 2600, and this adventure is the pre-rendered follow-up.
dragon-quest-v:
Enix's DRAGON QUEST V is famous for a marriage, a playable generation, and monsters you can recruit. This Super Famicom role-playing game from 1992 had no official English release until the Nintendo DS remake.

The hero grows from a child beside his father into an adult who chooses a bride, and the children can later fight. A tamed monster fills a party slot the way a human ally would.

The DS remake finally put an official English script on that family saga. The Super Famicom cartridge is the first version of the wedding and the recruitable monsters.
romancing-saga-3:
Akitoshi Kawazu closed the Super Famicom trilogy with Romancing SaGa 3, Square's last Romancing SaGa on that console. This role-playing game from 1995, like its predecessors, waited many years for an official English edition.

One of several heroes can open the story, and the choice changes which towns feel like home. Techniques spark in battle after a weapon is used enough, a habit Kawazu kept through the trilogy.

Romancing SaGa and Romancing SaGa 2 had already taught that free-form structure. The third cartridge closes the Super Famicom set.
harvest-moon:
Pack-In-Video and Natsume's Harvest Moon runs a farming life on a clock of seasons. Crops, livestock, and town relationships fill the days of this Super Nintendo original from 1996, the cart later handhelds in the series looked back to.

A spring seed dies if summer is neglected, and an unmilked cow changes the money for tools. Festivals and talks with the valley's neighbors turn the calendar into a social season as well as a harvest.

Watering cans and marriage in the handheld sequels grow from this daily loop. The Super Nintendo farm is where soil, animals, and neighbors first shared that clock.
super-punch-out:
Taller sprites and faster tells define Nintendo's Super Punch-Out!!, a career from 1994 that still asks you to read each boxer's cue. This Super Nintendo ladder stands apart from the NES original and from the later Wii game.

Bear Hugger, Bald Bull, and Super Macho Man each flash a tell before the punch that ends a round. Dodging into the opening, then answering, is the lesson a knockdown teaches.

Little Mac's NES climb uses a different camera and a different order of opponents. The Wii revival came later, and the cartridge between them is this Super Nintendo bout.
tales-of-phantasia:
Namco and Wolf Team's Tales of Phantasia is the Super Famicom game that started the Tales series. Real-time battles and a short voice sample were notable on that hardware in 1995.

Cress and the healer Mint fight on a line where steps and attacks share the same moment. A tiny recorded line plays during the story, a rarity on a Super Famicom cartridge.

The Game Boy Advance version later carried the party to a handheld. Linear battles in the Tales style begin with this Namco and Wolf Team collaboration.
syndicate-1993:
Bullfrog's Syndicate (1993) puts a four-agent team on isometric city streets. Researching weapons while those agents walk is part of the computer original's corporate conquest of a world map.

A persuaded civilian can be handed a gun, and a missed shot may hit a bystander the briefing never named. Facing and weapon range matter more, from that overhead angle, than any cockpit view.

The Super Nintendo edition is a later adaptation of Bullfrog's strategy game. The computer version's company-versus-company map remains the signature.
micro-machines-2-turbo-tournament-2:
Codemasters' Micro Machines 2: Turbo Tournament races toy cars across kitchen tables and workbenches. The Genesis J-Cart lets four people play this 1994 sequel without an extra adapter, and the Super Nintendo version is a separate port.

A breakfast table, a garden hose, and a school desk become circuits seen from so high the cars look like toys. A shove off the table's edge eliminates a racer as surely as a crash on a normal track.

The J-Cart's extra sockets are a Genesis feature. Codemasters' Super Nintendo port of the sequel uses that machine's own pads for the miniature race.
kirbys-dream-land-3-1997:
Soft pastel stages and animal friends fill Kirby's Dream Land 3 (1997), HAL's last Kirby for that Super Nintendo generation. It is the last Kirby released for that console generation.

Nago the cat, Pitch the bird, and ChuChu the octopus each change an inhaled ability. A heart gathered for someone in the level can alter the ending, so the walk is also a chain of small favors.

Dream Land 2 on the Game Boy had already introduced animal partners. This pastel adventure closes the generation with those friends still along for the ride.
blackthorne:
Blizzard's Blackthorne, also known as Blackhawk, sends a caped gunman through slow cinematic corridors. The shotgun and the long cape arrived on the Super Nintendo in 1994, before later machines and a Game Boy Advance port.

Kyle Blackthorne takes cover behind a pillar, fires, and plants a bomb on a cracked floor. The framing treats each room like a cut between shots, which is the pace Blizzard used here.

The Advance port carries the same mercenary to a handheld. The Super Nintendo release is where the shotgun and the cape first appeared.
primal-rage:
Atari Games' Primal Rage pits stop-motion dinosaurs and giant apes against one another. This arcade fighter from 1995 carried that prehistoric roster to home ports, the Super Nintendo one included.

Sauron, Blizzard, Chaos, and Armadon each bring a gruesome finishing move, and a tiny worshipper can be eaten. The cabinet's clay animation is what the cartridge sprites are trying to suggest.

A Game Boy edition shrinks those beasts into a smaller duel. The coin-op, with its stop-motion models, is the version the roster was built for.
illusion-of-gaia:
Will crosses ancient ruins in Illusion of Gaia, and his body changes when a fight starts. Quintet and Enix set this 1993 action role-playing game between Soul Blazer and Terranigma in a loose Super Nintendo trilogy.

The boy becomes Freedan, a dark knight, and later Shadow, whose strikes differ from the teacher's blade. Angkor Wat, the Incan ruins, and the Tower of Babel appear along that journey.

Soul Blazer frees captives to restore a world, and Terranigma rebuilds a surface. Illusion of Gaia sits in the middle, with Will's transformations as its combat trick.
tom-jerry:
Household slapstick fills Tom & Jerry on the Super Nintendo, a 1993 cartoon platformer different from the NES game subtitled The Ultimate Game of Cat and Mouse. The chase itself is the whole license.

Jerry rigs a household trap while Tom takes the bruises, and the stages play as a side-view pursuit. An ironing board, a kitchen counter, and a flying pan become the obstacles in that slapstick.

The NES cartridge with the longer subtitle is its own cat-and-mouse product. This Super Nintendo outing builds a separate set of rooms for the same pair.
kirbys-dream-course-1994:
Knocking the pink hero into enemies lowers the stroke count in Kirby's Dream Course (1994), HAL's miniature-golf game. Japan first called this Super Nintendo game Kirby Bowl.

The hole appears only after the enemies on the green are cleared, and a copied ability from the last foe can change the next shot. Wind, a bump, and a star block turn a putt into a puzzle with a par.

Kirby Bowl is the name on the Japanese box. The Western title points at the golf stance, with the same enemy-as-cup rule underneath.
king-of-the-monsters:
SNK's KING OF THE MONSTERS throws giant kaiju into a grappling match inside a city you can smash. This Neo Geo coin-op from 1991 received a Super Nintendo port of that monster-versus-monster fight.

Geon, Woo, and Astro Guy trade suplexes while buildings fall and tiny crowd sprites scatter. A power move can hurl a rival through a block, damaging both the opponent and the skyline.

The Neo Geo cabinet is the original bout. The Super Nintendo cartridge brings those wrestlers and the same crumbling streets home.
demons-crest:
Capcom's Demon's Crest (1994) stars the gargoyle Firebrand in a Super Nintendo action game spun out of Gargoyle's Quest. Elemental crests change how he crosses the gothic stages.

A flame form, a water crest, and an earth-shaking body each open a different path on the same grim map. The crests already found decide whether a later tower will allow Firebrand inside.

Gargoyle's Quest introduced this red demon from Ghosts 'n Goblins on a handheld. The crest system and the Super Nintendo map are what this later cart adds.
grand-theft-auto-1998:
DMA Design's Grand Theft Auto starts as an open-city crime game on PC. The original from 1997 uses top-down streets, and the Game Boy Color cartridge is a later, much smaller adaptation, not those original cities.

Liberty City, San Andreas, and Vice City, in their early flat forms, hand missions to a thief who can abandon the car and walk. Police heat rises with the chaos, which is the loop the computer game made famous.

The color handheld builds a reduced map of its own. The PC cities, with their radio stations and several towns, are the version the name first meant.
pokemon-red:
Satoshi Tajiri spent his childhood collecting insects and later asked Game Freak to turn that habit into Pokemon Red. Kanto's gym circuit is the spine of that walk, from a starter choice to a rival who refuses to stay behind.

Shigeru Miyamoto championed the project inside Nintendo after Tajiri demonstrated a link cable that moved creatures from one handheld to another. The cartridge therefore shipped as a pair: Red and Blue (Green in Japan) hold different wild encounters so friends have a reason to trade.

Ken Sugimori drew the Kanto creatures, and Junichi Masuda wrote the route music that plays while a trainer walks from Pallet Town toward the Indigo Plateau. Eight gyms, a rival, and a team built around a starter defined the loop. The MissingNo glitch and the Elite Four became playground folklore almost immediately.

A following Pikachu arrived later in Yellow. FireRed and LeafGreen rebuilt the same Kanto journey for a newer handheld, and those remakes are separate pages here. Collectors still mean this cartridge when they say they started in Pallet Town.
harry-potter-and-the-philosophers-stone:
Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone is the US title on several different licenses of the first book and film. Game Boy Color, Game Boy Advance, and home-console editions from 2001 were built separately and play as different games.

Hogwarts, a Quidditch pitch, and a dungeon can appear in one edition and take another shape entirely in the next. The Advance outing is a side-view adventure, while a console edition walks rooms in three dimensions.

Philosopher's Stone is the book title used outside the United States. Each Nintendo edition under the Sorcerer's Stone name remains its own adaptation of Harry's first year at the castle.
pokemon-gold:
Pokemon Gold moves the journey to Johto, where a real-time clock changes which creatures are awake. Johto's gym leaders keep different hours, so the same route is a different hunt after dark.

Game Freak, still led creatively by Satoshi Tajiri with music from Junichi Masuda, added breeding, held items, and a day-night cycle the first pair could not show on a monochrome screen. The player starts in New Bark Town, crosses gyms in a new region, and then finds the original Kanto map waiting after the league.

Gold and Silver were sold as a matched pair with different legendary beasts. Crystal later retold the same Johto trip with a playable girl and the Suicune story, and that revision has its own page. HeartGold, years afterward on a dual screen, is a remake rather than this cartridge.

The internal battery that kept the clock running is part of the object's history: when the battery dies, time stops and some events freeze. Collectors still look for carts whose clocks survive.
links-awakening:
Link washes ashore on Koholint in The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening (1993), an island that is not Hyrule, and tries to wake the Wind Fish. Nintendo's Game Boy adventure includes the later color DX edition as the same quest, while the 2019 Switch remake stands apart.

Marin, the Wind Fish's egg, and instruments hidden in dungeons form the path. A side-view chamber and a learned song can open a route the overworld will not show until the tune is played.

The DX edition adds a color dungeon and a camera without rewriting the island's story. The Switch reconstruction is a separate production, and Koholint on the Game Boy is the adventure described here.
super-mario-land:
Super Mario Land gives Mario a pocket journey with its own enemies, vehicles, and ending. Nintendo's first Game Boy outing for him, from 1989, starts the Land line and plays differently from a shrunken Super Mario Bros.

Sarasaland holds Princess Daisy, a submarine, and a plane that shoots balls, with Tatanga the alien as the kidnapper. The usual flagpoles and Bowser's castle do not run this kingdom.

The ending and the enemy list belong to this cartridge. Later Land sequels grow from the first handheld trip through Sarasaland.
super-mario-land-2:
Mario reclaims his castle from Wario in Super Mario Land 2: 6 Golden Coins, hunting six coins hidden in themed zones. Nintendo's second Game Boy Mario Land, from 1992, introduces Wario on a larger map than the first.

A space zone, a giant pumpkin, and a Mario-shaped island each hide a coin that opens the gate. Bunny ears let him glide, a move this cartridge adds on top of the usual jump.

Wario's debut is the plot, with the stolen castle as his prize. Sarasaland, from the first Land game, is a different and smaller journey.
wario-land:
Wario hunts treasure with a shoulder charge in Wario Land: Super Mario Land 3, and the ending changes with how greedy he was. Nintendo's first Wario Land, still numbered as a Mario Land, arrived on Game Boy in 1994.

A helmet blocks falling debris, a thrown foe becomes a projectile, and the coins he hoards steer which finale plays. Captain Syrup's pirates hold the loot he is trying to steal.

The greed of the ending is the story's joke. The Mario Land number on the box keeps this treasure hunt inside that handheld line.
bubble-ghost:
Bubble Ghost asks a specter to puff a fragile bubble through candles and fans. This computer puzzle from 1988 reached the Game Boy later as a port of that ghostly blower.

A breath nudge aims the bubble, and a flame or a spinning fan pops it if the angle is wrong. The ghost cannot touch the hazards; only the bubble's path counts.

The computer rooms came first. The Game Boy cartridge reprints those candlelit chambers for a d-pad and one breath button.
kirbys-dream-land:
Kirby's Dream Land gives the newcomer inhale, spit, and float, with no copy ability yet. HAL Laboratory and Nintendo shipped this first Kirby game on Game Boy in 1992, across five short lands, before Adventure added copy powers.

Whispy Woods and King Dedede wait at the ends of those brief trips. A mint leaf turns Kirby into a puff that crosses a long gap, the power this cartridge offers instead of a stolen move.

Kirby's Adventure on the NES is where an inhaled enemy becomes a sword or a flame. Dream Land on the Game Boy is the earlier float through five lands.
colin-mcrae-rally-1998:
Codemasters' Colin McRae Rally (1998) is a stage-based rally built around the real Scottish driver. The PlayStation original is the known version, and a Game Boy edition is a separate, smaller port.

Gravel, tarmac, and snow ask for a braking point from a pace note rather than a circuit's repeated laps. Damage carries out of a stage, so an early clip of a tree can end the rally.

McRae's name on the box points at that real driver. The handheld edition compresses the stage idea onto a much smaller set of roads.
hugo-1991:
Hugo (1991) stars the troll from ITE's interactive television quizzes, a character Scandinavian kids steered with their TV remotes. Later cartridges, including a Game Boy one, turned those show tasks into a handheld product.

A mine cart, a rope swing, and a falling bridge were the kinds of tasks the television host called. The troll's capture by a witch recurs in the sketches those remote-control games used.

ITE's live broadcast is the origin of the character. The Game Boy cartridge takes the same troll off the air and puts the tasks under a d-pad.
metroid-ii-return-of-samus:
Samus hunts metroids down a vertical nest in Metroid II: Return of Samus, and a battery save was new for the series. Nintendo's Game Boy Metroid from 1991 is the mission that Samus Returns on the 3DS, and later games, revisit.

A counter of remaining creatures drops as each larva falls, and rising lava opens a deeper shaft on SR388. The spider ball joins the morph ball in those tunnels.

The 3DS retelling walks this same hunt with a new camera. The Game Boy cartridge is the first version of the descent.
bugs-life-a:
Disney•Pixar A Bug's Life licenses the Pixar film, and the Nintendo 64 platformer is a different game from the Game Boy versions. Both borrow the movie's insects, and the year on this record is 1998.

Flik's inventions and Hopper's grasshoppers supply the cast, yet a three-dimensional anthill does not share its rooms with the handheld stages. The color and original Game Boy carts are smaller tie-ins with layouts of their own.

The film's ant island is the common license. Each Nintendo edition builds a separate set of challenges around Flik.
kirbys-dream-land-2-1995:
Rick the hamster, Coo the owl, and Kine the fish ride with Kirby in Kirby's Dream Land 2 (1995), HAL's Game Boy sequel. It sits between the first Game Boy Kirby and Super Nintendo Dream Land 3.

An inhaled ability changes when a friend is riding, so a cutter may arc differently on the hamster's back. Dark Matter and a rainbow sword wait for players who find the heart pieces in the levels.

The earlier Dream Land had no animal partners. Dream Land 3 continues the friend idea in pastel, and this Game Boy sequel is the step between them.
asteroids-1979:
Atari's Asteroids (1979), by Lyle Rains and Ed Logg, spins a ship among rocks on a vector screen. Later handheld versions are ports, and the cabinet is the original.

Hyperspace throws the ship to a random point, and a large rock splits into medium ones that still threaten the hull. Wraparound edges and a high-score table belong to that vector display.

Game Boy and Game Boy Advance editions replay the thrust and the split. The glowing cabinet is the machine those ports copy.
pokemon-yellow-version-special-pikachu-e:
Game Freak's Pokémon Yellow Version: Special Pikachu Edition keeps Pikachu outside the ball and follows the anime more closely than Red and Green. Japan received this special edition of the first generation in 1998, and it stays inside Kanto.

Pikachu walks behind the trainer, and Jessie and James appear in scenes the earlier pair staged differently. Gyms still run from Pewter City toward the Indigo Plateau.

Red and Green, and the international Red and Blue pair, are the originals. Yellow dresses that same Kanto journey in the anime's Pikachu and a handful of altered encounters.
missile-command:
Falling warheads threaten six cities in Missile Command, Dave Theurer's arcade defense with a limited stock of interceptors. Atari's trackball cabinet from 1980 is the famous version, and a Game Boy release years later remains a port of that cabinet.

Six cities sit under a cursor, and every interceptor spent is gone for good. A warhead that splits over a skyline costs more shots than a single trail.

The trackball and the city silhouettes belong to Atari's machine. The Game Boy edition reprints that defense on a d-pad.
wario-land-2:
Treasure totals and multiple endings matter more than a life counter in Wario Land II. Nintendo's adventure straddles Game Boy and Game Boy Color, and the color-era release sits with a later generation of Wario in 1998.

A crushed, burned, or inflated Wario becomes a key for a door instead of a game over. Coins still feed a treasure count that steers which finale plays when Captain Syrup's plot is done.

The monochrome and color cartridges share that refusal to tick down lives. Status jokes, not a spare life, are how a stuck room opens.
disneys-pocahontas:
Disney's Pocahontas is a Game Boy tie-in to the animated film, one of several licensed Pocahontas games from the mid-1990s. This cartridge's year is 1996, and it stays a small handheld story beside the larger platformers made for Aladdin or The Lion King.

Meeko, Flit, and Grandmother Willow come from the film, and the stages follow that forest at pocket size. A short hop and a simple obstacle are the scale of the screens.

Aladdin's carpet flights and The Lion King's pride-rock paths live on bigger carts. This Pocahontas release remains a modest Game Boy retelling.
road-rash-old:
A punch from the handlebar defines Road Rash (1991), Electronic Arts' Genesis motorcycle race where police join the chase. That 16-bit game is the series identity, and Game Boy versions are later, smaller offshoots.

A chain or a bare fist comes off the handlebar when a rival pulls alongside. Race winnings buy a faster bike, and an officer on the shoulder can end the run.

The Genesis road, with its roadside weapons, is the one players mean by the name. Handheld editions shrink that punch-and-ride idea onto a narrower street.
the-king-of-fighters-96:
SNK's The King of Fighters '96 is the Neo Geo team tournament that changes bosses and lineups after the previous annual. A Game Boy port exists, the arcade board is the real release, and this record dates it to 1996.

Kyo, Iori, and the Orochi thread continue in three-fighter teams, with a new boss after the last one's defeat. A changed team slot is the kind of yearly tuning SNK did on the cabinet.

The Game Boy conversion compresses those teams onto a small screen. The Neo Geo tournament is the one players count as that year's King of Fighters.
breakout-1976:
Atari's Breakout (1976) clears a brick wall with a ball and a paddle, and Steve Wozniak's prototype for the company is part of its origin story. Any Game Boy edition is a distant port of that arcade idea.

The ball speeds up as bricks vanish, and a missed return costs one of a few turns. Colored rows at the top of the wall score more than the dull bricks near the paddle.

Wozniak's early build and the arcade cabinet are the story's start. The handheld cart replays the same wall without being the machine that introduced it.
the-king-of-fighters-95:
Three-fighter teams return in The King of Fighters '95, SNK's Neo Geo sequel to the first tournament. The Game Boy version is a reduced portable conversion of that arcade game, dated 1995.

Kyo, Benimaru, and a rival trio still enter together, and the boss sequence shifts from the inaugural tournament. A new team and a changed story beat are what the second annual adds on the cabinet.

The handheld build trims frames and backgrounds. Neo Geo remains the machine where this lineup was the current tournament.
castlevania-ii-belmonts-revenge:
Konami's Castlevania II: Belmont's Revenge is the Game Boy sequel to Castlevania: The Adventure. Christopher Belmont climbs four castles in this 1991 cartridge, a different plot from Simon's Quest.

A captured son and Dracula's return frame the choice of which castle to enter. The whip cracks in side view, with movement loosened a little from the stiff Adventure controls.

Simon's Quest on the NES is a day-and-night search with another Belmont. Christopher's four castles belong to this handheld sequel alone.
castlevania-the-adventure-1989:
Konami's first handheld Castlevania, Castlevania: The Adventure (1989), is a stiff whip-platform trek. Longtime fans still rank Christopher Belmont's walk as the series' roughest start.

One hit can knock the whip back a stage of power, and the slow stride leaves little room under a swinging trap. These early corridors offer little subweapon variety to save a bad jump.

Belmont's Revenge, the follow-up on the same handheld, loosens that stiffness. This first cartridge is the awkward opening of Game Boy Castlevania.
final-fantasy-adventure:
Before the Mana series carried that name, Final Fantasy Adventure was Square's Game Boy action role-playing game, released in Japan as Seiken Densetsu. The Western box from 1991 borrows the Final Fantasy name while the hero's sword grows with the road.

A button swings the weapon in real time, and a companion met early changes how a cave puzzle resolves. The sacred tree at the center of the Mana legend waits at the end of that walk.

Secret of Mana on the Super Nintendo is the later, larger sequel. This Game Boy quest is the first Seiken Densetsu story, wearing a Final Fantasy title in the West.
missile-command-1980:
Dave Theurer's arcade classic Missile Command (1980) asks you to shield cities from warheads with a limited stock of interceptors. Atari's trackball cabinet is the machine that name means.

Each battery has only so many shots, and a warhead that splits over a skyline spends them faster than a single trail. The silhouette cities and the trackball are the cabinet's signature.

Handheld editions reprint those cities and that dwindling ammo. The trackball original at Atari is the version the title indicates.
r-type-1987:
Irem's side-scroller R-Type (1987) is remembered for the Force, a detachable pod that shields the ship and powers its shot. The arcade cabinet came first, and home versions followed.

The R-9 docks the Force, then sends it ahead to cover a Bydo creature the main cannon should not face up close. A charge builds while the pod stays attached, the rhythm the opening stage teaches.

Dobkeratops, the battleship-beast at the end of that first run, became the series' postcard boss. Later home carts, handheld ones included, chase the cabinet's Force.
centipede-1981:
Ed Logg and Dona Bailey designed Atari's Centipede (1981), a trackball shooter in a mushroom patch where the insect splits when hit. Spiders, fleas, and scorpions complicate the garden.

A flea plants extra mushrooms as it drops, and a poisoned mushroom sends the centipede diving straight down. The trackball flicks the wand along the bottom of the patch.

The cabinet's ball is the original control. Handheld ports keep the splitting bug and the mushrooms without that ball.
battlezone-1980:
Ed Rotberg's first-person tank duel Battlezone (1980) drew wireframe enemies on a vector screen. Atari's cabinet drew enough notice that the U.S. Army asked about a training variant.

A radar wedge and a slow turret decide whether an enemy tank or a saucer sits in the crosshair. Volcano silhouettes on the horizon give the wireframe field a sense of distance.

The Army's question was about a modified trainer attached to this cabinet's fame. The periscope view and the vector duel are the arcade game itself.
f-1-race:
HAL Laboratory built F-1 Race for Nintendo's Famicom, and it was among the first games to use the console's expansion port for a steering wheel. That wheel turns a simple rear-view race into a hands-on demo of the port, in a release from 1984.

Opposing cars block the lanes, and the wheel's rotation steers more directly than a pad's left and right. The port on the bottom of the Famicom is what made the accessory possible.

A Game Boy edition later carried a similar race to a handheld without the wheel. The Famicom original is the one tied to that expansion-port steering wheel.
new-ghostbusters-ii:
HAL Laboratory's New Ghostbusters II is a license of the film sequel, issued on the NES in Europe and on Game Boy. This cartridge from 1990 never reached North America under that title.

Proton packs and a slimer-like ghost still define the jobs, with Peter and Egon among the team the stages call on. The European NES edition and the Game Boy edition are the two places this particular title appeared.

North American shelves had other Ghostbusters games and skipped this label. HAL's tie-in stays a Europe-and-handheld release of the sequel.
donkey-kong-land:
Rare's Donkey Kong Land is a Game Boy companion to Donkey Kong Country, with its own stages squeezed from pre-rendered artwork. This 1995 trek is separate from the Super Nintendo game it echoes.

Donkey and Diddy still roll and jump, but the barrels, ropes, and cave rooms were drawn for the small screen. The shaded look tries to suggest Country's renders inside a monochrome cartridge.

Country's maps stay on the Super Nintendo. Land is a parallel hike, not a shrunken copy of those same boards.
burgertime-1982:
Data East's BurgerTime (1982) stars chef Peter Pepper, who walks across ingredients to stack burgers while kitchen pests chase him. Ladders link the buns, the lettuce, and the patties.

A pepper shake stuns Mr. Hot Dog, Mr. Egg, and Mr. Pickle long enough for Peter to cross a layer. Dropping a bun onto a patty builds the burger and clears that ingredient from the chase.

The arcade kitchen is the original shift. A Game Boy edition later puts Peter Pepper's ladders on a handheld.
snow-bros:
Toaplan's snowball coin-op reached the Game Boy under the name Snow Bros. Jr, where walking foes get packed into giant snowballs and kicked. That cabinet idea, from 1990, was cut down to fit a cartridge.

Nick and Tom, the brothers in parkas, roll an enemy until the ball bowls through the rest of the floor. A kick that clears a whole platform is the satisfying finish of a room.

The arcade Snow Bros. cabinet is the two-player original. Snow Bros. Jr on Game Boy is the smaller telling of that same roll-and-kick.
boulder-dash-1984:
Peter Liepa's cave puzzle Boulder Dash (1984) sends you digging for diamonds while loose boulders tumble. First Star's original spawned a long line of home ports, Game Boy among them.

A rock balanced over a dug-out space will fall, and a diamond collected under it can trap the digger. Butterflies and amoebas in some caves add creatures that change the soil.

The cave-in logic is Liepa's puzzle. Handheld and computer ports keep that diamond hunt and those falling stones.
real-bout-fatal-fury-special:
SNK's Real Bout Fatal Fury Special is a Neo Geo revision in the Fatal Fury line, tuned as an arcade fighter. Plane-switching scraps, hopping between foreground and background, define this 1997 edition.

Terry Bogard and Geese Howard return to South Town with that two-lane movement. A special that changes planes can slip an attack that would have landed on the near lane.

Earlier Fatal Fury cabinets had already taught the lane swap. Real Bout Special is a tuned Neo Geo version of the same South Town idea.
super-star-wars-return-of-the-jedi:
Sculptured Software and LucasArts closed their 16-bit trilogy with Super Star Wars: Return of the Jedi. This Super Nintendo run from 1994 includes a speeder-bike chase and Millennium Falcon stages beside the platforming.

Luke, Han, and Chewbacca trade the lead while the sail barge and Endor's forest moon supply set pieces. The speeder run through the trees plays nothing like the on-foot lightsaber rooms.

Super Star Wars and The Empire Strikes Back on the Super Nintendo are the earlier thirds. Return of the Jedi finishes that run with the Falcon and the speeder.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-fall-of-the:
Konami's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Fall of the Foot Clan is the turtles' Game Boy debut, a short side-scroller about reaching April. This 1990 cartridge points ahead to the handheld follow-up Back from the Sewers.

Leonardo's katanas, Donatello's bo, Raphael's sai, and Michelangelo's nunchaku each change the reach. Shredder's Foot soldiers fill the rooms between the brothers and April O'Neil.

The NES turtles game is a longer, separate mission. This handheld debut is the short walk that Back from the Sewers continues.
true-lies:
True Lies is an action license of James Cameron's spy film, and each home edition adapts the movie on its own terms. Game Boy is one of those editions, and the license sits in 1994.

Harry Tasker's double life, a chase, and a terrorist plot are the scenes those editions pick from. The Game Boy screens choose a pocket-sized slice of that film.

Cameron's picture is the shared source. The handheld version builds its own string of stages from Tasker's mission.
lemmings-2-the-tribes:
Polar, circus, and medieval marchers carry different skills in Lemmings 2: The Tribes, DMA Design's sequel. The puzzle still asks you to save a set quota, and this sequel dates to 1993.

A polar tribe, a circus tribe, and a medieval tribe carry tools the original toolbox lacked. A pole vault or a fan's blast can cross a gap a plain builder cannot.

The exit quota is the win DMA Design used in the first game. Tribes are the addition, and each one changes which skills the level offers.
the-lost-world-jurassic-park:
Several unrelated products share the name The Lost World: Jurassic Park, from a Sega light-gun cabinet to separate home adaptations of Spielberg's sequel. The shared title clusters in 1997, and the products are not one campaign.

A rail shooter asks for raptors in the sights, while a handheld edition may play as a small side-view trek on Isla Sorna. Dinosaurs from the film are the overlap you can count on.

Spielberg's sequel is the license. Each cabinet or cartridge under that title was built as its own adaptation.
tetris-attack:
Nintendo sold Panel de Pon in the West as Tetris Attack, a rising-stack match puzzle restyled around Yoshi. Tetrominoes never fall, and the Western cartridge arrived in 1995.

Blocks push up from below, and swapping two neighbors to align three or more clears them. Yoshi and his island friends replace the fairies of Japanese Panel de Pon.

A cursor and a swap are the whole move. Falling four-block pieces belong to Tetris, a different puzzle whose name this cart borrowed.
casper:
The friendly-ghost film spawned Casper on separate Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges in the years after the movie. They are licensed adaptations, not one shared quest, and this record uses 1997.

Whipstaff Manor, the uncles, and Kat's friendship with the ghost come from the film. Each handheld builds its own rooms in that house.

The monochrome cart and the color cart can both wear Casper's name. Their mansion layouts stay separate jobs.
bonks-adventure:
Hudson Soft's PC Engine mascot, also called PC Genjin, debuts in Bonk's Adventure (1989), and his oversized head is the weapon. A Game Boy port came after the TurboGrafx-16 original.

A headbutt stuns a dinosaur, and a slab of meat powers that bonk further. The smiling caveman was Hudson's console hero, charging through prehistoric stages on the PC Engine.

TurboGrafx-16 players met the headbutt first. The Game Boy cartridge is a later, smaller reprint of that debut.
double-dribble-1987:
Konami's basketball game Double Dribble (1987) cuts to a close-up dunk when a shot drops. That spectacle, on the arcade cabinet and the NES, became the signature.

A play chosen from a small set, then a made basket, triggers the zoomed-in slam. The rest of the court stays a plainer five-on-five until that moment.

Fans remember the close-up more than any season schedule. A Game Boy edition that reuses the name is chasing the dunk the cabinet and the NES already showed.
battle-arena-toshinden:
Tamsoft's weapons fighter Battle Arena Toshinden arrived with the early PlayStation, published by Takara. Blade duels in three dimensions are what the name refers to, and the game dates to 1995.

Eiji Shinjo's katana and a rival's long weapon circle a ring that can throw a loser off the edge. The camera sits near the blade, part of that early PlayStation showcase.

A Game Boy listing under the same name is a different, smaller product. The three-dimensional weapon fights are the battles the title means.
zen-the-intergalactic-ninja:
Konami published Zen: Intergalactic Ninja on Game Boy in 1993, a side-scroller drawn from the small-press comic about an alien warrior. A bo staff and a pollution-fighting plot fit that comic's hero.

Zen reaches through short stages a pocket screen can hold, bonking foes with the staff. The indie comic's environmental ninja is the license Konami put on the cartridge.

Those comic pages, not a toy line or a television season, are the source. The Game Boy version is a compact run with that alien in the lead.
gargoyles-quest:
Capcom's Gargoyle's Quest (1990) stars Firebrand, the red demon from Ghosts 'n Goblins, on a Game Boy map of side-view fights. The hero is a gargoyle on his own quest, not a Belmont.

Wings carry Firebrand across gaps, and a breath attack replaces any whip. Towers on a gloomy overworld open into those side-view battles.

Ghosts 'n Goblins treats this demon as an enemy to dodge. Here Firebrand is the one crossing the map.
pinocchio-1996:
Disney's animated film about the wooden puppet became the license for Pinocchio (1996), and each home version retells the story in its own way. The Game Boy edition is one of those retellings.

Geppetto's workshop, Jiminy Cricket, and Monstro the whale supply scenes a handheld can shrink. Pleasure Island may be a short stage here and a longer chapter on another machine.

The growing nose and the whale are the film's markers. Each cartridge picks its own order and scale for those scenes.
zool:
Gremlin Graphics pitched Zool as an Amiga mascot, a ninja from the Nth dimension racing through themed worlds. Console and Game Boy ports followed that computer debut from 1992.

A sweet world, a music world, and a tool world each change the pests the ninja kicks. Speed and a double jump were Gremlin's bid in the mascot races of that computer era.

The Amiga version is the one the Nth-dimension pitch was built around. Handheld and console ports carry the same ninja onto later machines.
bionic-commando-1987:
Capcom's arcade original Bionic Commando (1987) introduced the grappling-arm soldier that the NES game, where he cannot jump, made famous. A later handheld cartridge reused the name for a different release.

The arm latches a ceiling and swings the commando across a gap no hop could cover. Enemy soldiers and a sci-fi fortress fill the arcade stages that taught that swing.

The NES adaptation, with its no-jump rule and its own plot, is the home game many players mean. The arcade cabinet is where the bionic arm first showed up.
star-wars-1983:
Atari's vector cabinet Star Wars (1983) seats you in an X-wing for the Death Star trench. It is a film-based arcade game, built years before the side-scrolling home licenses.

A tower on the surface, then the trench itself, asks for shots on targets while TIE fighters cross the wireframe view. The Death Star's exhaust port is the last target that vector sequence offers.

Later side-scrolling Star Wars games on home consoles tell their scenes another way. This cabinet is the wireframe trench run.
chuck-rock:
Core Design's caveman Chuck Rock belly-slams through an Amiga platformer. Console ports and a Game Boy version carried the same prehistoric joke, and the original dates to 1991.

A beer belly stuns a dinosaur, and a thrown rock clears a ledge the stomach cannot reach. Chuck crosses those slapstick stages to get back someone the dinosaurs carried off.

The Amiga belly-slam is the original gag. Later ports, the Game Boy one included, keep Chuck and that same stomach attack.
fifa-1993:
Known in full as FIFA International Soccer, FIFA (1993) is EA's first entry in that long soccer line. An isometric pitch, looking down on the grass at an angle, defined the early annuals.

National teams fill the match, and a through-ball reads from that elevated camera rather than from a sideline broadcast. Later editions kept the angle for a while before the series moved on.

International Superstar Soccer is Konami's separate approach to the sport. This isometric debut is the cartridge that opened EA's FIFA line.
donald-in-maui-mallard:
Europe's name for Disney's platformer is Donald in Maui Mallard. North America called the console versions Maui Mallard in Cold Shadow, with Donald as a shirt-wearing detective, and the European title sits on a 1995 release.

A staff and a bug-loaded gun, the detective's two stances, are the moves the console game is known for. The Game Boy edition under the European name is a smaller pocket take on the same duck.

Cold Shadow is the subtitle North American boxes preferred. Donald in Maui Mallard is how Europe labeled that hard-boiled disguise.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-ii-back-fro:
Konami followed Fall of the Foot Clan with Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: Back from the Sewers. This Game Boy side-scroller from 1991 sends Leonardo and his brothers back through the pipes after April.

Shredder's forces occupy the tunnels, and each turtle's weapon still changes an attack's reach. The stages run longer than the very short debut they continue.

Fall of the Foot Clan is the preceding handheld mission. Back from the Sewers is the return trip, with a deeper set of tunnels for the same four brothers.
xenon-2-megablast:
The Bitmap Brothers followed Xenon with Xenon 2: Megablast, a vertical shooter whose soundtrack came from Bomb the Bass. The Amiga original was ported widely, Game Boy included, after a debut in 1990.

A shop between waves sells weapons, and the bass-heavy track keeps going over that upgrade screen. Power-ups stack on a ship seen from above, a different view from the first Xenon.

Bomb the Bass gave Megablast the music players attach to the name. The Game Boy port is one of many homes for that Amiga shooter.
mega-man-dr-wilys-revenge:
Capcom's first Game Boy Mega Man, Mega Man: Dr. Wily's Revenge, remixes robot masters from the first two NES games. The cartridge from 1991 is its own adventure, ending in a fortress built for this handheld.

Cut Man's scissors and Elec Man's beam return on a small screen, and a new boss waits after the familiar ones. This remix still leans on the earliest NES tools.

Mega Man 2's robot masters supply the other half of the borrowed roster. Wily's handheld fortress, with new encounters inside, keeps the cart from being a straight port of either NES number.
gauntlet-ii:
Cursed food labeled It appears in Gauntlet II, Atari Games' arcade sequel, along with new classes in the four-player dungeon crawl. This cabinet from 1986 lets heroes pick colors and keeps the generator-smashing of the first Gauntlet.

The morsel labeled It can stun or transform whoever eats it, hidden among ordinary turkey legs. A wizard, an elf, a valkyrie, and a warrior still hold exits while generators spawn grunts.

The first Gauntlet established the four heroes and the health that drains with time. It, the cursed bite, is the sequel's nasty extra in that same maze.
krustys-fun-house:
Audiogenic designed Krusty's Fun House for Acclaim, and the job is herding rats into a machine inside the clown's fun house. This Simpsons puzzle from 1992 shipped on the NES, the Super Nintendo, the Genesis, and Game Boy.

A block, a fan, or a trampoline steers a rodent toward the pipe that feeds the grinder. Krusty's pie can stun a rat that wandered the wrong way.

Bart's other Simpsons carts tend to be side-view adventures. Krusty's Fun House is the rat puzzle, repeated on those formats with the clown as host.
castlevania-legends:
Konami's Game Boy game Castlevania Legends stars Sonia Belmont. Koji Igarashi later set this story outside the timeline he treated as official, and the cartridge dates to 1997.

Sonia's whip and a magical fire companion shape a side-view climb toward Dracula. Burning Mode, a brief surge of power, is one ability this handheld plot gives her.

Igarashi's later account of the series left Sonia aside. The Game Boy cartridge remains the story of that Belmont.
klax:
Dave Akers designed Klax for Atari Games, catching colored tiles off a conveyor and stacking them into lines. Ports reached almost every home format of the period, and the cabinet dates to 1989.

A tile that misses the paddle falls away, and three of one color in a row vanish for points. The belt speeds up until the paddle at the bottom is a frantic sorter.

The arcade stack is the original. Game Boy and Game Boy Color editions are among the many ports of Akers's conveyor.
james-pond-2-codename-robocod:
Millennium's fish agent stretches up a shaft in James Pond 2: Codename Robocod, wearing a robotic suit. The sequel to James Pond became a staple of Amiga and console play, and this record places it in 1993.

The suit lets Pond's body extend to a high ledge in a toy factory. Penguins, presents, and a factory boss replace the first game's underwater spy work.

James Pond began as a fishy secret agent. RoboCod's stretch and the toy plant are the sequel's own playground.
gremlins-2-the-new-batch:
Sunsoft's license of Joe Dante's film sequel is Gremlins 2: The New Batch, with separate NES and Game Boy cartridges. The two versions play differently, and both belong to 1990.

Gizmo stays gentle while a new batch overruns a building, and each cartridge stages that overrun on its own map. Clamp Center's chaos in Dante's film is the license they share.

The NES rooms and the Game Boy rooms are two adaptations. Sunsoft did not tie them together as one continued quest.
super-dodgeball:
Technos turned its Kunio arcade dodgeball into Super Dodge Ball (1988), a cult NES sports game full of super throws. The Famicom original sits in the same late-1980s window the title's digits name.

A charged throw crosses the court in a flaming arc, and a teammate can catch and return without a bounce. Kunio and his rivals bring Technos brawler faces onto the court.

Those NES super throws built the cult reputation. A Game Boy edition later echoes the flaming ball on a smaller court.
dragon-warrior-monsters:
Enix's Game Boy spinoff Dragon Quest Monsters reached the West as Dragon Warrior Monsters. Breeding and battling creatures is the loop, a pocket cousin of the main series, dated 1998.

Two parent monsters yield an offspring with inherited skills, and a tournament gate wants that bred team. The journey hops gates rather than walking the long overworld of a numbered Dragon Quest.

Dragon Warrior was the Western name Enix used for the main line then. This breeding cart is the pocket cousin, not a numbered chapter.
donk-kong-94:
The familiar girders open Donkey Kong, and after four stages the game becomes a puzzle of flips and handstands. Nintendo's Game Boy release from 1994 is a separate work from the 1981 arcade cabinet and from Donkey Kong Country.

Pauline waits above the first construction site, then Mario hunts keys and switches with a handstand jump. A triple jump and a flip off a wire are the tools those later worlds demand.

The 1981 cabinet ends once the girders are clear. Country is Rare's side-scroller about another Kong, while this cartridge continues into puzzle rooms.
the-blues-brothers:
Titus built The Blues Brothers as a platformer about the Belushi and Aykroyd revue. Computer, console, and Game Boy editions share the license, and the game dates to 1991.

Jake and Elwood, in hats and sunglasses, jump stages set to the spirit of that act. A speaker stack or a road case can block the way to the exit.

The film and the musical revue supply the black suits. Titus's editions put the same pair on computers, consoles, and Game Boy.
marios-picross:
Jupiter and Nintendo's Mario's Picross is a Game Boy logic book that fills grids from number clues while Mario hosts. Japan and Europe received this puzzle in 1995, and North America waited on later reissues.

A row clue of three, then one, means three filled cells, a gap, and a single cell, and a mistake spends time. Mario's hammer chips the grid until a mushroom or a star appears.

Later Picross books carried the same clues forward. This first Mario-hosted volume is the Game Boy release Japan and Europe got before a wider reissue.
bubsy-2:
Accolade's sequel Bubsy 2 put the bobcat back on the Super Nintendo and the Genesis. Larger stages and the same talkative mascot define the follow-up, which arrived in 1994.

Bubsy's glide and a remark after a hit carry into those wider levels. The bobcat's mouth, more than any new mechanic, is what players associate with the sequel.

The first Bubsy cartridge established the comments and the glide. This follow-up stretches the stages and keeps Accolade's mascot talking.
yoshis-cookie:
Bullet-Proof Software, Nintendo's Tetris partner, co-made Yoshi's Cookie. Matching cookies in a row on Game Boy and the NES clears the board, and the puzzle dates to 1992.

A cursor slides a row or a column until identical treats line up, and Mario can show up among them. Yoshi hosts while the board refills with a fresh mix.

Tetris, the falling-block game Bullet-Proof brought to Nintendo, moves pieces downward. Yoshi's Cookie slides what is already on the table until a line matches.
mighty-morphin-power-rangers-the-movie:
Bandai's Game Boy tie-in to the Rangers feature is titled Mighty Morphin Power Rangers: The Movie (BG). This movie license from 1995 is a side-scroller of its own, apart from the television-season cartridges.

Ivan Ooze and the film's ninja-clad team give the stages a movie-specific set of foes. Morphing still changes a ranger's strength on a short map built for the feature.

Weekly-villain carts follow the television show. The Movie (BG) label marks Bandai's separate side-scroller for the feature film.
super-off-road:
Leland's arcade racer Super Off Road puts three trucks on an overhead dirt oval under Ivan Stewart's name. A Game Boy port was among the many home versions, and the cabinet dates to 1989.

A nitro burst and a tight oval turn decide which truck takes the flag. The view stays above the track so all three vehicles remain on screen.

Ivan Stewart's name on the marquee ties the cabinet to a real off-road driver. Home ports, the Game Boy one included, keep that overhead dirt oval.
toxic-crusaders:
The Troma cartoon spun from The Toxic Avenger licensed Toxic Crusaders for a run of games. Bandai's Game Boy cartridge from 1992 stars those mop-wielding mutants.

Toxie and his friends swing cleaning tools through side-view stages of slime and corporate goons. The cartoon's gross-out jokes shrink onto short handheld levels.

The Toxic Avenger film is the older, harsher source. Toxic Crusaders is the cartoon license, and Bandai's cart is the Game Boy telling of those mop heroes.
the-amazing-spider-man-1990:
Rare built LJN's Game Boy release The Amazing Spider-Man (1990) as a side-scroller of wall climbs and street fights. It is the first handheld Spider-Man, separate from later Super Nintendo and PlayStation games.

A web line between buildings and a punch for a sidewalk thug share the same short stages. Doctor Octopus can close a level on a screen far smaller than those later consoles.

The Super Nintendo and PlayStation Spider-Man productions came afterward as different games. This Rare and LJN cartridge is the pocket debut.
kid-icarus-of-myths-and-monsters-2:
Nintendo and Tose made Kid Icarus: Of Myths and Monsters for Game Boy, a sequel to the NES angel-archer. It reached North America and Europe in 1991 and skipped Japan at the time.

Pit climbs vertical chambers again, and a stronger bow still depends on keeping his health up. New fortresses and a different final threat replace the underworld egg of the NES quest.

The NES Kid Icarus is the ascent this handheld continues. Japan missed Of Myths and Monsters in that first window, while North America and Europe received it.
final-fantasy-legend-ii:
Square's second SaGa game is Final Fantasy Legend II in the West. The Game Boy party still mixes mutant, human, and monster members, and Japan saw the cartridge in 1990.

A mutant eats meat to shift stats, a human buys gear, and a monster transforms by devouring a defeated foe. The group climbs a fresh tower of worlds rather than repeating the first SaGa path exactly.

The Final Fantasy label on the Western box is branding laid over SaGa. This second cartridge is the one with that food-and-form party.
turrican:
Manfred Trenz's run-and-gun Turrican debuted on the Commodore 64 and the Amiga, famous for a transforming wheel. A Game Boy port followed the computer original, which arrived in 1990.

The hero curls into a wheel that rolls under spikes, then stands to fire a spread of shots. A long beam and a mine round out the arsenal on those large computer maps.

The wheel is the move players cite when they name Trenz's game. The Game Boy port carries that curl-and-shoot onto a smaller screen.
the-battle-of-olympus:
Infinity's NES action game The Battle of Olympus, published by Broderbund, sends a Greek hero through side-view fights often set beside Zelda II. A Game Boy port later appeared in Europe, and the NES release dates to 1988.

Orpheus seeks Helene, and the gods hand him tools that open new stretches of the mythic map. A sword swipe and a life bar are the combat people compare with Zelda II's side view.

The European Game Boy port retells that same walk. Broderbund's NES edition is the one Infinity built first.
gargoyles-quest-ii:
Capcom moved Firebrand to the NES for Gargoyle's Quest II, a larger follow-up to the Game Boy original. Japan knew the NES game as Red Arremer II, and that release dates to 1992.

The red demon's wings and breath cover a wider gloomy realm than the handheld quest. Extra crests and a longer overworld give the NES cart its size.

Red Arremer II is the title on the Japanese Famicom edition. The Game Boy Gargoyle's Quest is the smaller adventure Firebrand had already finished.
speedball-2-brutal-deluxe:
A steel ball and legal injuries define Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe, the Bitmap Brothers' armored Amiga sequel to Speedball. Ports spread it far beyond that computer after a debut in 1990.

A steel ball thrown into a high goal scores more than a simple carry, and injuring a rival is legal. A bribe between matches can buy a star or sabotage the other side.

The first Speedball set the armored rules. Brutal Deluxe, with its metal pitch, is the sequel those ports carried to consoles and handhelds.
ultima-old:
Richard Garriott's first role-playing game in the line is what Ultima (Old) points at, the Apple II original that opened the series. That computer quest dates to 1981 and begins the Britannia saga the later games expand.

A top-down party, a dungeon stair, and the wizard Mondain set a pattern the numbered sequels elaborate. Sosaria's dark floors on that Apple II disk are the rooms the series grows out of.

Later Ultimas add virtues, a living countryside, and the name Britannia in full. Ultima (Old) is the label for that Apple II start.
mega-man-ii:
Capcom's second Game Boy Mega Man is labeled Mega Man II(3Ds/GB). The cartridge from 1991 continues the handheld remix line rather than porting one NES number straight across.

Robot masters drawn from more than one home game return, and a new Wily stage caps the mix. The small screen matches Dr. Wily's Revenge more than it matches any single NES cart.

Mega Man 2 on the NES is a complete roster with its own fortress. This second handheld chapter borrows and rearranges under the II(3Ds/GB) label.
tintin-in-tibet:
Infogrames' Tintin in Tibet turns Hergé's album about a mountain rescue into a platformer. Super Nintendo, Game Boy, and other versions retell that climb, and the game dates to 1995.

Tintin searches for Chang after an air crash, with Snowy and Captain Haddock on the snowy path. A yeti and a rope bridge supply the album's Himalayan hazards.

The comic's lost friend is the story every version adapts. Each format, from the Super Nintendo to Game Boy, stages the rescue in its own rooms.
street-racer:
Vivid Image's Street Racer is a cartoon kart racer on the Super Nintendo and the Genesis, built to sit beside Mario Kart. Ubisoft published it in 1994.

A rumble mode lets the cars brawl as well as finish, and another mode uses the same vehicles to kick a ball. Caricatured drivers give the tracks a different face from Mario's cups.

Mario Kart remains Nintendo's own series of cups and shells. Street Racer is Vivid Image's neighbor, with fighting and a ball game added to the laps.
mtvs-beavis-and-butt-head:
Couch gags sell MTV's Beavis and Butt-Head, one of several versions of the cartoon licensed that season. The duo's faces are the hook, and the license dates to 1994.

Beavis and Butt-Head wander stages built from the show's gross-out jokes, with a television and a sofa as props. A Game Boy edition shrinks those two faces onto a pocket screen.

Other consoles received their own versions in the same window. The cartoon's laugh and the pair's names are what every edition is selling.
donkey-kong-land-2:
Diddy and Dixie carry Rare's Donkey Kong Land 2, the Game Boy companion to Donkey Kong Country 2, across a new handheld map. It is a fresh layout rather than a compressed port of the Super Nintendo game, and it dates to 1996.

Dixie's helicopter hair and Diddy's cartwheel return, while the boards themselves were built for the small screen. Kaptain K. Rool waits at the end of a pirate trek that uses its own rooms.

The earlier Donkey Kong Land accompanied the first Country game. Land 2 does that job for Diddy and Dixie's adventure, with a map drawn for Game Boy.
mr-nutz:
Ocean's squirrel platformer Mr. Nutz started on the Amiga and the Super Nintendo. A Game Boy version carried the same acorn-hoarding hero, around a debut in 1994.

A thrown nut and a tail attack clear forest, ice, and a volcano. The squirrel's design was Ocean's try at a mascot hop on those machines.

Amiga and Super Nintendo editions came first. The Game Boy cartridge keeps the acorns and the same squirrel on a smaller map.
the-final-fantasy-legend:
Square's first SaGa game reached the West as The Final Fantasy Legend. Japan called it Makai Toushi SaGa, the Final Fantasy wording was Western branding, and the Game Boy release dates to 1989.

A party climbs a tower of worlds, a monster member changes by eating foes, and a human buys better steel. The creator waiting at the top closes that first SaGa pilgrimage.

Makai Toushi SaGa is the name on the Japanese box. The Final Fantasy wording on Western shelves does not turn the cart into a numbered Final Fantasy.
who-framed-roger-rabbit:
Toontown ink and a live-action detective share Who Framed Roger Rabbit, the Touchstone film's licensed case. Home versions, including a Game Boy game from Capcom in some regions, adapt that mystery from 1988.

Eddie Valiant, Roger, and Jessica Rabbit lead, with Judge Doom as the figure to reach. The dip that can destroy a cartoon is one movie detail those games borrow.

Capcom's regional Game Boy edition is one adaptation among several. The film's mixed animation is the case they retell.
kid-dracula:
A cartoon count who learns spells headlines Konami's Kid Dracula, the Western Game Boy release of a Castlevania parody. The Famicom original, Akumajo Special: Boku Dracula-kun, came first, and the handheld Western release dates to 1993.

Projectiles and bright boss jokes replace a straight Belmont duel. Familiar monsters show up as gags rather than as a gothic climb.

Boku Dracula-kun on the Famicom is the earlier version of the joke. Kid Dracula on Game Boy is the later Western cartridge.
asterix:
Getafix's potion fuels Asterix (1993), one of Infogrames' platformers drawn from the Goscinny and Uderzo comics. The digits inside this title pick out that particular release.

Obelix's menhir and a Roman camp supply the jokes the stages run on. Asterix punches legionaries while the village fence stays in the background of the albums.

Other Infogrames carts adapt the same Gauls on other machines. This labeled release is the one whose title carries that date on its own.
mega-man-iii:
Snake Man and Spark Man join other borrowed bosses in Capcom's Mega Man III, a Game Boy remix tied to the NES Mega Man 3 and Mega Man 4 rosters. A new Wily capstone follows them, and the cartridge arrived in 1992.

The remix habit continues from Dr. Wily's Revenge and from the second handheld chapter. Small-screen corridors replace the full fortresses of those NES games.

Mega Man 3 and Mega Man 4 on the NES remain complete adventures of their own. Mega Man III borrows their robot masters and builds a different castle.
pokemon-puzzle-challenge:
Intelligent Systems recast Panel de Pon with pocket monsters for Pokémon Puzzle Challenge, a Game Boy Color stack-matcher. Japan sold it as Pokemon de Panepon, and the Western cart dates to 2000.
