Blocks rise under a partner's portrait, and swapping two tiles sends an attack at the rival stack. A league of puzzle matches replaces the Yoshi framing used in Tetris Attack.

Panel de Pon is the Japanese puzzle Intelligent Systems started from. This cartridge keeps the rising stack and dresses it in pocket monsters.
fifa-road-to-world-cup-98:
Qualifying matches fill EA Sports' FIFA: Road to World Cup 98, the soccer annual aimed at the tournament those digits name. Nintendo 64 and Game Boy were among the versions, and the annual dates to 1997.

National squads march through a structure built around that World Cup. The Nintendo 64 edition uses a three-dimensional pitch, while the Game Boy edition is a much smaller handheld season.

EA's annual put that march on a long list of machines. Nintendo's pair, the big console and the pocket cart, each got a version.
bomb-jack:
Tehkan's arcade platformer Bomb Jack scores extra for lighting bombs in the right order before they blow. Home computers picked the idea up quickly, and the cabinet dates to 1984.

Jack's cape lets him hover, and the sequence bonus multiplies a careful route. A sphinx backdrop and a castle backdrop are among the screens those bombs sit on.

The arcade order bonus is the original rule. Home ports, and later a Game Boy edition, chase that hovering hero and those lit fuses.
kirbys-pinball-land-1993:
Whispy Woods, Kracko, and King Dedede crown the tables in Kirby's Pinball Land (1993), HAL Laboratory's Game Boy pinball game. The pink hero is the ball, and three themed boards lead upward.

Launching Kirby into a boss at the top of a table starts the fight. Poppy Bros. bounce between the bumpers on the way up those boards.

The layout is a handheld original, not a port of a Super Nintendo Kirby sport. Dedede's table is the last flipper challenge of the run.
tecmo-bowl-1990:
Calling a play from a small playbook is what made Tecmo's Tecmo Bowl (1990) famous on the NES. That coaching choice, more than any single machine, is the public memory.

Running and passing options scroll before the snap, and the defense tries to guess which one is coming. Bo Jackson and other licensed stars made a broken tackle feel huge on that field.

Fans imitate the playbook screen when they remember the game. A Game Boy edition later carries the same pre-snap choice.
boxing-1980:
Bob Whitehead designed Activision's Atari 2600 cartridge Boxing (1980), a two-player bout from the company's early sports line. Two fighters seen from above trade punches until one drops.

A glove extended at the right moment scores, and the crowd is a simple border around the ring. Whitehead's Activision sports carts favored this kind of small, readable contest.

The 2600 ring is the original bout. A later handheld edition under a plain boxing name looks back at that Activision cartridge.
final-fantasy-legend-iii:
Time travel frames Square's third SaGa, sold in the West as Final Fantasy Legend III. Japan received the Game Boy party in 1991, still under a Final Fantasy label abroad.

A flooded future and a visitable past change which towns are under water. Body parts installed on the heroes replace the meat-eating transformations of the earlier SaGa carts.

The Western box keeps the Final Fantasy Legend name. This third cartridge is the time-travel chapter of the line.
stargate-1995:
Daniel Jackson's portal trip is the image behind Stargate (1995), licensed from Roland Emmerich's film. Acclaim's home versions sit with that movie, whose date is already part of this title.

A soldier stepping through the ring, then a desert world with its guards, supplies the scenes the games borrow. The god-king on the far side of the gate is the figure those stages build toward.

Acclaim's editions adapt the film on the home hardware of that moment. The stone ring from Emmerich's picture is the prop every version chases.
pocket-monsters-pokemon-green-version:
Japan's first retail pair was Red together with Pocket Monsters (Pokemon Green Version). The later Japanese Blue, not this green cart, supplied more of what international Red and Blue became, and the pair dates to 1996.

Bulbasaur, Charmander, and Squirtle still leave Professor Oak's lab in Pallet Town. Version-exclusive creatures in the tall grass are the reason two friends would trade.

Japan's Blue revision adjusted encounters after the green release. International Red and Blue drew more heavily from that later blue cart.
kick-off:
Dino Dini's Kick Off is the Anco soccer game whose speed on the Amiga and the Atari ST made it a rival to later Sensible Soccer. A Game Boy version exists, and the computer original dates to 1989.

The ball leaves the foot quickly, so a pass can race ahead of the player who kicked it. That pace, more than a televised camera, is what Amiga clubs argued about.

Sensible Soccer arrived afterward with its own overhead style. Kick Off is Dini's earlier, faster Anco game, with a handheld port among its offshoots.
metal-gear-solid-1:
Shadow Moses is the infiltration in Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear Solid, the first Metal Gear in three dimensions. A later Game Boy Color cartridge used this same title in the West for a different story, Ghost Babel, and the PlayStation game dates to 1998.

Solid Snake calls Campbell, Meryl, and Otacon on a codec while a radar and a cardboard box shape the sneak. Boss fights break the usual gunfight, including a duel that asks the player to change how the console is used.

Ghost Babel is a separate handheld mission that borrowed the Western title. Kojima's Shadow Moses disc is the three-dimensional game the name first identified.
grand-theft-auto-2-1999:
Gang respect meters steer DMA Design's Grand Theft Auto 2, which stays top-down. The computer game from 1999 adds those faction scores, and the Game Boy Color cartridge is a smaller, separate city.

Jobs for the Zaibatsu, the Loonies, or the Yakuza change how the districts treat the thief. A respected gang opens work the others will not offer.

The original cities of the first game are a different map. This sequel's handheld version builds yet another reduced town, not a photocopy of the computer sectors.
alone-in-the-dark-the-new-nightmare:
Edward Carnby returns in Infogrames' Alone in the Dark: The New Nightmare, a survival-horror sequel. The Game Boy Color edition is its own flat game, apart from the console release, and the sequel dates to 2001.

A flashlight beam and scarce ammo define Carnby's search through a shadowed mansion. Aline Cedrac investigates the same grounds on a parallel route in the fuller version of the story.

The console release uses three-dimensional rooms. The Game Boy Color cart retells the nightmare as a separate two-dimensional trek.
driver:
Tanner's undercover driving in Reflections' Driver (1999) turned film-style car chases into a PlayStation hit. A later Game Boy Color version is a much smaller take on the same premise.

The cop behind the wheel must finish a felon's job without wrecking the car the gang expects. A replay camera and a long take through traffic sell the cinematic chase on PlayStation.

The color handheld keeps the undercover idea and shrinks the streets. Reflections' PlayStation original is the chase with that film camera.
pokemon-crystal:
Suicune's pursuit runs through Johto in Pokemon Crystal, with animated battle sprites Gold and Silver lacked. Game Freak and Nintendo's third version of that generation stays on Game Boy Color, dated 2000.

A trainer can start as a girl, an option the earlier pair did not open, and the legendary beast's story threads the towns. Moving sprites play when a move is called.

The Battle Tower adds a challenge room on top of the league. Johto, the Elite Four, and the Kanto epilogue still sit underneath on the same color handheld.
heroes-of-might-and-magic:
Towns and creature stacks fill New World Computing's Heroes of Might and Magic: A Strategic Quest, the first Heroes game. A Game Boy Color version arrived years later, and the computer original dates to 1995.

A hero rides an adventure map, claims mines, and leads peasants or dragons into a hex fight. Each town alignment builds dwellings that produce those stacks.

The computer campaign is the original strategic quest. The Game Boy Color edition is a much later, smaller adaptation of that hero-and-town loop.
rayman:
Mr. Dark menaces the limbless world Michel Ancel introduced in Ubisoft's Rayman, first shown on the Atari Jaguar. Later Game Boy Color and DS cartridges reuse the name with stages of their own, and the debut dates to 1995.

Helicopter hair and a detached punching fist carry Rayman across lands where friends have no limbs either. Freeing a cage of Electoons opens the way toward the next territory.

The Jaguar showing is where that limbless run began. The Game Boy Color and DS carts that share the title build different stages around the same hero.
oracle-of-ages:
Past and present reshape Labrynna in The Legend of Zelda: Oracle of Ages, and puzzles depend on the era under your feet. Flagship and Nintendo released this Game Boy Color quest in 2001, with secrets that link it to Oracle of Seasons.

The Harp of Ages turns a sapling into a climbable tree when the century shifts. Veran, sorceress of shadows, is the figure those era changes are meant to undo.

A password carried from Seasons plants a linked secret in Labrynna. The two color adventures were built to be finished as a pair.
oracle-of-seasons:
Winter can freeze a lake that summer opens when the rod is used in The Legend of Zelda: Oracle of Seasons. Flagship and Nintendo aimed this Game Boy Color half at action more than Ages' puzzles, and shipped it in 2001.

Holodrum changes under Din's season rod, and Onox, a general in dark armor, is the threat those shifts uncover. Combat-leaning dungeons are this sibling's emphasis.

Linked secrets travel by password toward Oracle of Ages. The two quests were meant to be played beside each other.
catwoman:
Patience Phillips's whip leads Electronic Arts' Catwoman, the tie-in to the Halle Berry film. GameCube carries a three-dimensional version, Game Boy Advance a separate side-scroller, and the license dates to 2004.

Rooftop climbs follow the film's cat-suited lead, with claws and a jewel heist among the images. Cube rooms move in depth, while the Advance stages stay on a flat plane with another level list.

The movie's suit is the shared costume. Each Nintendo edition builds a different set of rooms for that tie-in.
pokemon-trading-card-game:
Energy cards and a prize pile teach a deck in Pokemon Trading Card Game, a campaign of battles rather than a grass-patch league. Hudson Soft and Nintendo's Game Boy adaptation of the tabletop game sits beside Red and Blue, dated 1998.

A bench of basic monsters and a stack of energy reproduce the table rules on a handheld. Club masters on an island challenge the deck the player has built.

Red and Blue remain the role-playing pair about tall grass and gym badges. This Hudson cartridge is the card campaign next to them, not the next numbered region.
fifa-2000:
EA Sports named the soccer annual FIFA 2000 for the season ahead and shipped that box in 1999, beside console and PC copies. A Game Boy Color edition put the same season's clubs into a pocket match.

You still choose a side, push a tiny squad up the pitch, and take a set piece before the half ends. The handheld field cannot copy a television broadcast, so the tactics stay simple and the matches stay short.

Collectors file the cartridge with the sports line from that shipping season, even though the title looks one year further on. It is the pocket FIFA of that cycle, built for quick halves rather than a full broadcast presentation.
gex-enter-the-gecko:
Crystal Dynamics brought the television-quoting lizard back in Gex: Enter the Gecko (1998), chasing him through movie-set rooms on PlayStation beside the Nintendo 64 release. The Game Boy Color cartridge is a separate flat version of that gecko, not those roomy sets squeezed down.

Gex tail-whips through movie-channel rooms while firing quips at the camera. Remote gags and costume worlds are the joke, and the 3D editions let a camera follow him into those sets.

The color handheld redraws the same wisecracking hero as flat stages. Players who quote the voice lines usually mean the console adventure, while the cartridge keeps the character without those 3D rooms.
donald-duck-goin-quackers:
Ubisoft's chase Donald Duck: Goin' Quackers sends Donald after Daisy, while Europe titled that adventure Quack Attack in its 2000 release. Nintendo 64, GameCube, and Game Boy Color each received a version, and they do not play as one build.

A temper meter pushes Donald from a slow walk into a furious sprint on the console stages. Merlock's kidnapping plot supplies the slapstick, with Huey, Dewey, and Lou still orbiting the Disney frame.

The color cartridge compresses that rescue into a smaller side view. Moving from the Nintendo 64 stages to the GameCube ones changes the camera and the layout, so each box is its own Donald chase.
vigilante-8:
Luxoflux set armed muscle cars loose on an alternate 1970s highway in Vigilante 8, a demolition derby that reached PlayStation and Nintendo 64 during 1998 with named drivers. A Game Boy Color adaptation followed, carrying that armed-car idea onto a small screen.

You pick a vehicle, bolt on a weapon, and try to be the last wreck still rolling. Named drivers turn a desert road into a duel, with missiles and rams replacing any ordinary race position.

The handheld edition keeps the armed-car fantasy without the console draw distance. Collectors treat that cartridge as its own small adaptation of the Coyote-and-vigilante war, not as the 3D arenas squeezed flat.
lego-racers:
High Voltage Software built LEGO Racers in 1999 for LEGO Media, a kart racer whose cars are made of bricks. Nintendo 64 received that game, and Game Boy Color received a smaller circuit set.

You assemble a minifigure driver and a brick chassis, then line up against LEGO champions. Studs and spare pieces change the car between heats, which is the toy-box hook a plain kart game never had.

The console cup has the fuller track list. The color cartridge trims the calendar of races while still using those minifigure rivals, so the two editions share a garage fantasy and not a single course list.
road-rash-ii:
Electronic Arts added split-screen to motorcycle combat in Road Rash II, the Genesis sequel to Road Rash from 1993 where a punch still counts during a heat. Punching a rival while you hold the racing line remains the point of every lap.

Two players can share one television on that Genesis version and swing between corners. Chains and clubs sit in the same violent toolkit as a well-timed fist, and a crashed rider has to run back to the bike.

A Game Boy Color edition carries the sequel's name without becoming that split-screen living-room match. Knocking someone off a bike and taking the finish is still the identity that separates this entry from a clean racing sim.
jet-set-radio-2012:
Smilebit's inline crews tag a living city in Jet Set Radio, the Dreamcast game from 2000 drawn in cel shading to a pirate-radio beat. Rival gangs and a DJ call the next graffiti target while the police meter climbs.

You skate, grind, and spray a tag across Tokyo-to districts before the authorities close in. The look is a cartoon broadcast, with thick outlines and a soundtrack that behaves like a station you cannot quite tune away from.

The Nintendo listing here is the Game Boy Advance release of that name. The cel-shaded Dreamcast original is the pirate-radio game players mean when they talk about those tagging crews.
doom-ii:
id Software moved the invasion into city streets with DOOM II, the 1994 sequel subtitled Hell on Earth. Office blocks and a downtown siege replace the chained labs of the first Mars episode.

The super shotgun is the weapon players remember from those urban maps, and the Icon of Sin waits once the city is pushed back. Secret rooms and a larger enemy mix make the sequel meaner than a simple second episode of the same base.

A Game Boy Advance port years later cut the episode down so a cartridge could hold it. That handheld Hell on Earth is a shortened campaign, not the full PC map list.
need-for-speed-underground-2-2:
EA Black Box opened a whole city for car customization in Need for Speed: Underground 2, the street-racing sequel from 2004 that lets you drive between shops. GameCube keeps that free-roam structure, while the Game Boy Advance cart is a separate racer.

You drive into shops, fit a body kit, and take races that sprawl across one connected map on the console. Sponsor offers and a garage full of parts are the night-to-night loop, not a menu of disconnected cups only.

Bayview is the city those free-roam nights are actually crossing, and a Nintendo DS listing sits beside the other editions. Players who describe free-roam nights and deep visual tuning mean the Black Box city, not the closed courses on the handheld cartridge.
splinter-cell:
Ubisoft introduced Sam Fisher in Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell, a stealth game that started on Xbox during 2002 under the Third Echelon banner. GameCube received those missions, and the Game Boy Advance edition is a separate flat mission set.

A light meter decides whether a guard sees the spy or walks past a shadow. Third Echelon sends Fisher to grab a foe, force a code, and leave the lights broken behind him.

The handheld missions keep the Fisher name and redraw the sneaking as flat corridors. Anyone who remembers the sticky shadows and the goggles wants the console infiltration, not the pocket crawl.
need-for-speed-carbon:
Canyon duels and a racing crew follow Most Wanted in Need For Speed Carbon, EA's street sequel from 2006 that treats a canyon drop as a loss. GameCube, Wii, and Nintendo DS versions were sold, and the handheld ones were built as their own games.

You draft teammates, then take a canyon sprint where one bad line drops the car. Territory and crew roles matter on the home versions that inherited the earlier blacklist structure.

A Game Boy Advance edition is another separate build under the Carbon name. The canyon crews and the territory map belong to the console game, not to the pocket cartridge.
sonic-the-hedgehog:
Sonic Team built a speedy answer to Mario in Sonic the Hedgehog (1991), Sega's Genesis mascot debut. Later Wii and Nintendo 3DS reissues are that 16-bit game, not a new adventure, and a Game Boy Advance listing carries the same debut.

Green Hill Zone opens on loops, rings, and Dr. Robotnik's badniks. The spin dash is not in this original run, so speed comes from holding a slope rather than from a move Sonic gained afterward.

A reissue still ends at Robotnik's zones and the chaos emeralds of this first quest. Nobody booting the Wii or 3DS version is starting a fresh story with new stages.
worms-blast:
Team17 left turn-based artillery behind for Worms Blast, a 2002 puzzle closer to block-clearing than to a Bazooka duel. GameCube and Game Boy Advance both got versions of that shift.

You fire at colored clusters and try to keep a rising waterline from swallowing the boat. Worms still crew the cannon, but the goal is a cleared stack rather than a last worm standing on an island.

That break from the usual deathmatch is why an afternoon with this entry feels like a different series. Disc and cartridge both ask for the same aim-and-clear idea, even when their stage lists diverge.
marvel-ult-alliance:
Raven Software's hero-swapping brawler Marvel Ultimate Alliance is Activision's team fighter from 2006, built so you can change heroes inside one scrap. Wii has that console game, and Game Boy Advance has a smaller separate one on the same Marvel name.

You pause mid-fight, change from a bruiser to a flyer, and chain their specials against one mob. Comic villains supply the bosses while several teams share a single roster you can rebuild between missions.

The Wii disc is the home game with that swapping. The handheld cartridge uses a much smaller mission set, so the two boxes are not interchangeable copies of one brawl.
pokemon-firered:
Game Freak remade the Kanto journey as Pokemon FireRed, a 2004 cartridge with the advance generation's mechanics and a post-game island. LeafGreen is the paired remake, and this is not Pokemon Red.

Abilities and a running pace sit on top of Brock's gym, the old rival, and a professor's parcel. After the league, the Sevii Islands open a chain of areas the 1996 quest never had.

Linking with LeafGreen changes which creatures you can finish. Anyone hunting the original red cartridge wants that older Kanto release, because this box is the later retelling.
pokemon-ruby:
Contests, secret bases, and Groudon's drought define Pokemon Ruby, Game Freak's Hoenn journey from 2002 and one half of a matched pair. Sapphire is the other half, Emerald is the third version, and Omega Ruby on Nintendo 3DS is a later remake.

Groudon waits while the region's story bakes under drought. Contest ribbons and a base you decorate give the walk something besides gym badges and a rival on Route 103.

Mixing records with a friend shares bases and contest data. The 3DS remake retells Hoenn much later, so this cartridge is the original ruby-version adventure with its own legendary.
the-sims-2:
Maxis added life stages and aspirations in The Sims 2, the PC sequel from 2004 whose Sims age from toddler toward elder. GameCube and Game Boy Advance releases are separate console games, not that computer simulation shrunk down.

On the PC, a Sim ages from toddler to elder and chases a lifetime want. The Nintendo editions build their own neighborhoods and goals instead of copying the computer neighborhood screen.

A player who wants the aging clock and the aspiration meter wants the computer game. The Nintendo boxes share the dollhouse name, then follow scripts written for their own machines.
minish-cap:
Ezlo the talking cap shrinks Link in The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap, the complete 2004 adventure Flagship made with Nintendo. Towns and dungeons change scale at Minish size, and this quest is not a port of an earlier console Zelda.

Vaati's curse starts the trouble, and the Picori legend explains why the tiny people can help. A gust jar and four sword-clone copies open paths that exist only while Link is small.

Wii U and Nintendo 3DS later reissued this same cap-and-curse story. The dungeon map is its own Zelda, not a cut of Ocarina of Time and not a remake of A Link to the Past.
phoenix-wright-ace-attorney-2001:
Capcom's courtroom debut Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney first shipped on the Game Boy Advance in Japan during 2001, with Phoenix objecting through testimony. The Nintendo DS version that traveled worldwide adds a bonus case and touch-screen evidence.

You press a witness, find the contradiction, and present the right document from the court record. Maya Fey assists Phoenix while Miles Edgeworth tries to close the trial in a guilty verdict.

Wii and Nintendo 3DS releases later carried those cases onward. The bonus DS episode is the piece that separates the worldwide touch-screen release from the original Japanese script.
comix-zone-1995:
Sketch Turner punches through living panels in Comix Zone, Sega's Genesis brawler from 1995 in which the artist Mortus draws the enemies. A Wii Virtual Console release later reissued that same comic fight, and a Game Boy Advance listing points at it too.

You shred a page border to reach the next frame while the artist Mortus draws fresh enemies onto the paper. Sketch's rat Roadkill can be thrown as a weapon or sent to sniff out a health pack.

The Wii reissue is that Genesis page-hopper, not a new brawler with new villains. Roadkill, Mortus, and the panel borders are the pieces players still remember.
rayman-raving-rabbids:
Ubisoft turned a platformer into a living-room party in Rayman Raving Rabbids, the 2006 Wii disc of motion minigames. Game Boy Advance and Nintendo DS copies are separate products, and Wii U later carried the party version too.

You shake a remote for plunger pulls, cow launches, and other rabbid stunts while Rayman stays their prisoner. The screaming rabbits replaced the long side-scrolling quest the project started as.

Handheld boxes use the rabbid license for their own smaller games. Anyone remembering the living-room noise means the Wii party disc, not the cartridge.
oddworld-munchs-oddysee-2001:
Oddworld Inhabitants paired Abe with a Gabbit ally in Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee (2001), an Xbox adventure that a later Game Boy Advance version retells in 2D. Munch can swim where Abe still chants to possess factory guards.

The pair try to stop a scheme aimed at Gabbits and Mudokons. Possession, chanting, and Munch's water routes are the console tools, framed by Oddworld's industrial cruelty.

The flat handheld retelling keeps both heroes and drops the 3D camera. Players who remember the Xbox journey should not expect that same viewpoint on the cartridge.
spider-man-2:
Treyarch's open-city web-swinging tie-in to Sam Raimi's second film is sold as Spider-Man 2: The Game. The 2004 GameCube version is that sandbox, and Game Boy Advance is a side-scroller, with Nintendo DS as a further separate edition.

You shoot a web at a corner, swing down a Manhattan block, and peel off toward a mission marker. Doc Ock supplies the film's threat while pedestrians react to the swinging.

The side-scroller keeps the movie villain and drops the free-roam map. The city where a single swing can cross several streets is the GameCube game.
king-kong:
Ubisoft alternates a scarce-ammo explorer with the ape in Peter Jackson's King Kong: The Official Game of the Movie, the 2005 tie-in to Peter Jackson's film. GameCube has the main design, while Game Boy Advance and Nintendo DS editions are separate.

Jack Driscoll survives Skull Island with a gun that runs dry, then the player smashes a V-Rex as Kong. The film's island set pieces structure the console campaign, not a wrestling moveset.

Handheld editions retell the same movie under their own rules. The scare of an empty firearm belongs to the GameCube design.
splinter-cell-pandora-tomorrow:
Spies-versus-mercenaries multiplayer first appears in Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell: Pandora Tomorrow, Ubisoft's sequel from 2004 that still sends Sam Fisher through fresh cities. GameCube has that game, and Game Boy Advance has a flat side story starring the same spy.

Sam Fisher still hugs shadows while a new terrorist plot moves him through fresh cities. The online mode pits stealth operatives against armed mercenaries, a match the first game did not ship.

The side-story cartridge keeps Fisher in flat corridors. Anyone hunting the mercenary multiplayer wants the console edition, where those two sides actually meet.
final-fantasy:
Square opened its line with Final Fantasy, the 1987 NES quest in which four jobs cross a cursed world through menu-driven battles. Garland's kidnapping of Princess Sara starts the search for darkened crystals.

A party of fighters, thieves, black mages, and white mages fights from a command list rather than from an action stick. Chaos and a time loop wait once the four crystals are restored, and that structure became the template later numbered entries kept rewriting.

Game Boy Advance and Wii releases later carried this same first quest. Every sequel assumes this job party and this crystal crisis already happened.
harry-potter-and-the-order-of-the-phoeni:
Spellcasting inside Hogwarts drives Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix, Electronic Arts' tie-in from 2007 to the fifth book and film. Wii, Nintendo DS, and Game Boy Advance each got a version fitted to that hardware.

Dolores Umbridge and Dumbledore's Army give the school year its villain and its student club. You learn a gesture or a button for a spell, then face scenes that reach the Ministry as well as the castle corridors.

The Wii version leans on motion for the wand, while the handheld editions map the same book onto smaller controls. None of those three is a straight copy of another format's castle.
ultimate-spider-man:
Treyarch let you switch to Venom in Ultimate Spider-Man, a 2005 open-city game based on the Ultimate comics. GameCube has the 3D version, and the Game Boy Advance and Nintendo DS editions are separate.

Peter Parker swings the streets, then the black symbiote takes over for a meaner fight. This Venom comes from the Ultimate comic line, not from Sam Raimi's films.

The city where that switch happens is the GameCube game. Handheld boxes tell smaller stories under the same comic name without the free-roam toggle.
need-for-speed-porsche-unleashed:
EA traced a career through Porsche history in Need for Speed: Porsche Unleashed, sold in Europe under the name Porsche 2000 with air-cooled cars at the start of the timeline. The Game Boy Advance cartridge keeps the badge and strips that timeline structure down.

Evolution and Factory Driver modes on the big versions move you from early air-cooled cars toward later supercars. The factory timeline is the career, organized as events rather than as one endless city.

The handheld cart puts Porsche badges on a much simpler racer. It is not the full timeline career, only the marque and the name.
metroid-zero-mission:
Nintendo retold the first Metroid as Metroid: Zero Mission, a 2004 remake with a map, shinespark tricks, and a stealth ending the NES game did not have. The NES original keeps its own identity beside this Game Boy Advance telling.

Samus loses the Power Suit in Chozodia and must sneak past Space Pirates in the Zero Suit. A shinespark charges off a slope, and the map marks items the original left hidden in unlabeled shafts.

Chozo statues still grant missiles and bombs, yet the route and the ending infiltration are new. Players who remember only Tourian from the NES cartridge meet an extra stealth chapter here.
tron-20:
Monolith set disc combat and light cycles inside the computer world of Tron 2.0, a PC sequel from 2003 on the Tron license. The Game Boy Advance release is a separate action game, not that PC campaign copied down.

Jet, son of Alan Bradley, moves through programs, corrects permissions, and fights with an identity disc. Light-cycle stretches break up the corridor fights on the computer version.

The cartridge uses the Tron name for its own action scenes. It does not contain Jet's PC permissions puzzle or those cycle stretches.
metroid-fusion:
Metroid Fusion puts a voice, the computerized Adam, in Samus's ear and still hides missiles off the path that voice recommends. The station marks an objective and then still hides tanks in rooms the marker never mentions.

Nintendo released it in the same season as Metroid Prime, with Yoshio Sakamoto directing the handheld half. Samus is infected by the X parasites, confined to a suit that talks, and hunted by the SA-X, a copy of her fully powered self, aboard the B.S.L. research station.

The map marks an objective, which the earlier Metroids refused to do, yet the station is still full of optional tanks and a navigation room that lies about how trapped you are. The final choice about the station and the X is the story beat Fusion is remembered for.

Metroid Dread continues directly from this ending. Prime is the other half of that return to the series and has its own page. This entry is Metroid Fusion.
lego-star-wars:
Traveller's Tales retold the prequel trilogy in bricks with Lego Star Wars: The Video Game, their first Lego Star Wars, released in 2005 with Qui-Gon among the minifigures. GameCube supports co-op, and Game Boy Advance has a simpler tie-in.

You smash props for studs, then swap from Qui-Gon to a droid to open a door. Episodes I through III supply the levels, played for slapstick rather than for a strict film recap.

Two players can share the GameCube story. The handheld tie-in keeps the minifigure Jedi and drops that shared-screen co-op.
the-lord-of-the-rings-he-return-of-the-k:
EA staged the third Jackson film as a hack-and-slash in The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King, with two-player co-op on GameCube during 2003 amid the Pelennor crowds. The Game Boy Advance version covers the same war from the side.

Aragorn, Legolas, and Gandalf carve through crowds at the Pelennor and along the Paths of the Dead. The Black Gate is among the film scenes the console version turns into a brawl you can share.

The side-view cartridge follows that war with its own levels. It is a companion retelling, not the co-op disc squeezed into a smaller box.
castlevania-aria-of-sorrow:
Konami lets a future protagonist drink enemy souls in Castlevania: Aria of Sorrow, the 2003 castle you map at your own pace. Players often set it beside Symphony of the Night because both reward wandering instead of a stage select.

Soma Cruz steals a soul and turns it into a bullet, a summon, or a stat change. The 2035 castle is Dracula's power in a new host, and the map fills only where you choose to walk.

A Wii U reissue later carried this same soul-collecting castle. The backtracking, not a linear whip march, is why the Symphony comparison sticks.
shrek-2:
Activision tied a game to the DreamWorks sequel and called it Shrek 2: The Game, a 2004 license with different GameCube and Game Boy Advance versions. Fairy Godmother's potion plot and the trip to Far Far Away supply the movie beats both editions draw on.

Shrek, Donkey, and Puss in Boots appear, yet each machine builds its own stages around them. A move you learn on the disc is not guaranteed on the cartridge.

The shared piece is the ogre's second-film story, not a single level list. Buying one box does not hand you the other edition's camera.
phoenix-wright-ace-attorney-trials-and-t:
The third Ace Attorney casebook, Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney − Trials and Tribulations, debuted on the Game Boy Advance in Japan during 2004, with Godot's mask waiting in court. DS, Wii, and Nintendo 3DS releases later carried those trials onward.

Godot prosecutes with coffee and a mask, while the story reaches back into Mia Fey's past. Dahlia Hawthorne's scheme ties the cases into one long grudge rather than three unrelated clients.

Presenting evidence still means catching the lie in a testimony. The later ports keep that Japan-first script, mask, coffee, and all.
phoenix-wright-ace-attorney-justice-for-:
Capcom's second courtroom game, Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney − Justice for All, arrived on the Game Boy Advance in Japan during 2002, still built as four cross-examinations. The Western DS release came later with those same four cases, and a Wii release carried that quartet too.

Franziska von Karma brings a whip to court, and the opening case gives Phoenix amnesia before he can remember how a cross-examination works. Pearl and Maya still pull the investigation screens between testimonies.

A circus and a kidnapped assistant sit among the four trials. Outside Japan, the DS edition is how most players first met that whip and that memory loss.
madagascar:
Activision sent zoo animals through New York in Madagascar, the 2005 tie-in to the DreamWorks film. GameCube, Game Boy Advance, and Nintendo DS each shipped their own version of that escape.

Alex the lion, Marty the zebra, Melman, and Gloria are the four leads, from the Central Park opening toward a later shipwreck. A minigame on one format is not guaranteed on the next.

What the three boxes share is the zoo quartet, not a single set of levels. Each machine rebuilds the film's beats with its own stages.
lego-star-wars-2-the-original-trilogy:
Minifigure trench runs define Lego Star Wars II: The Original Trilogy, Traveller's Tales' retelling from 2006 of the first three films. GameCube has co-op, and Game Boy Advance has its own version.

You fly a minifigure run at the Death Star trench, then hunt studs on Hoth and Endor. Character tokens unlock Darth Vader, a stormtrooper, and a crowd of extras once those story beats are finished.

Two players share the console adventure. The handheld version retells the trilogy without that same shared-screen co-op.
final-fantasy-ii:
Square's Famicom sequel FINAL FANTASY II raises stats by using weapons and spells, with no experience points, and it first appeared in 1988 under an emperor's shadow. Game Boy Advance and Wii releases later reissued that use-based growth.

Firion, Maria, and Guy learn a sword or a cure only by spending it in battle, so a spell you never cast stays weak. The Emperor of Palamecia is the tyrant, and Leon's absence drives the party forward.

Keyword talks with townspeople open the next town. The reissues keep that use-based growth instead of bolting on a normal experience ladder.
tony-hawks-underground-2:
Neversoft leaned into a stunt-tour story for Tony Hawk's Underground 2, the skate sequel from 2004 whose World Destruction Tour steps off the board. GameCube has that campaign, and the Game Boy Advance cart is a separate adaptation.

You step off the board for prank gags, then return to a gap or a manual in cities on the World Destruction Tour. Bam Margera's brand of stunt comedy frames the console story between the actual lines.

The handheld cart uses the sequel's name for its own smaller sessions. The tour structure, off-board gags included, belongs to the GameCube campaign.
tony-hawks-pro-skater-4:
Neversoft dropped the two-minute run timer for open goals in Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 4, the skate entry from 2002 that lets you talk to a pro mid-level. GameCube uses that structure, and Game Boy Advance has a different skate game under the name.

You stay in a level, talk to a pro, and clear goals in any order instead of racing a clock that dumps you out. Career cash still buys decks and stats, but the timer that defined the first three Pro Skater games is gone on the console.

The handheld release does not copy those open goals. It borrows the name for a separate session.
fifa-07:
A PlayStation 3 launch slot accompanied FIFA 07, the EA Sports annual covering the 2006 season on older consoles too. GameCube, Game Boy Advance, and Nintendo DS carried editions beside the older consoles.

You set a formation, call a through ball, and chase a league table the way the television season expects. The new-console launch copy sat beside older-engine versions rather than erasing them.

Handheld editions compress that season into their own match engines. The shared label is the squad list from that campaign, not one identical set of rules.
crash-of-the-titans:
Radical Entertainment let Crash grab oversized enemies and turn them in Crash of the Titans, the 2007 entry that puts a mutant under his feet. Wii, Nintendo DS, and Game Boy Advance versions differ from one another.

You stun a titan, hop on, and spend its attack on the next wave. Cortex still schemes over the island, but jacking a beast replaces crate-hopping as the headline move.

A trick shown on the Wii is not promised on the cartridge. Each machine builds its own titan encounters around that grab.
broken-sword-the-shadow-of-the-templars:
Revolution Software dropped an American tourist into a Templar plot in Paris with Broken Sword 1 - The Shadow of the Templars, the 1996 point-and-click. A Game Boy Advance port arrived later.

George Stobbart watches a clown bomb a café, then follows Nico Collard through crypts and manuscripts. Conversation icons and close-up inventory pieces carry the mystery from that sidewalk to a buried order.

The handheld port keeps the café conspiracy on a small screen. It is the first Broken Sword story, the clown and the Paris crypt, not a later chapter in the series.
mario-and-luigi-superstar-saga:
AlphaDream and Nintendo opened the Mario & Luigi series with Mario & Luigi: Superstar Saga, a 2003 comedy about timed jumps and hammers in a neighboring kingdom. A Nintendo 3DS remake exists as its own later entry.

Cackletta steals Princess Peach's voice and flees to the Beanbean Kingdom. The brothers stack, swing hammers on a beat, and press a button just before a hit lands to bounce it back.

Bros. Attacks spend Bros. Points on combined moves such as a splash or a swinging knock. The 3DS retelling of Beanbean came afterward, so this cartridge is the original handheld comedy.
ratatouille:
THQ followed a rat through a Paris kitchen in Ratatouille, the 2007 tie-in to Pixar's film. GameCube, Game Boy Advance, and Nintendo DS were sold as separate games.

Remy guides Linguini inside Gusteau's restaurant while trying not to be seen by the humans. Cooking challenges and chase scenes from the movie are rebuilt differently on each machine.

The disc does not contain the cartridge's levels. What they share is Remy, the kitchen, and that restaurant, not a common stage list.
mother-3:
Nintendo, Brownie Brown, and HAL Laboratory told Mother 3 in chapters with rhythm-timed battles, releasing it in Japan during 2006 and never officially localizing it then. It is the Game Boy Advance sequel to EarthBound and the last Mother game.

Lucas swings on the beat, and a combo grows only if the next press matches the music. Tazmily Village gives way to a Pigmask invasion as the chapters move from family loss toward a darker island.

Porky ties the ending back to the villain EarthBound players already feared. The cartridge's script is the Japanese text, because no official translation shipped with it then.
avatar-tla-tbe:
THQ's second tie-in Avatar: The Last Airbender - The Burning Earth covers the Earth Kingdom war in a 2007 release split across two handhelds. Game Boy Advance and Nintendo DS each have a version.

Aang, Katara, Toph, and Sokka bend or strike through stages based on that war. The Fire Nation's push supplies the season these levels are dramatizing, from sieges to chases across earthbending country.

The two handheld builds do not share one map. Each retells that Earth Kingdom stretch with its own stages and its own controls.
golden-sun:
Camelot's Djinn reshape both puzzles and classes in Golden Sun, the 2001 role-playing game that opens the series. The Lost Age continues the same story, so a clear from this cartridge can matter later.

Isaac's party leaves Vale when alchemy is threatened, and each Djinn you set changes a field spell and a character class. Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Mercury djinn shift stats the moment you assign them.

A dungeon puzzle often needs the same Psynergy you cast in battle. The sequel expects this party's progress, which is why players kept their passwords.
fire-emblem:
Intelligent Systems and Nintendo brought permadeath tactics to North America with Fire Emblem, the 2003 grid campaign Japan knows as The Blazing Blade. A fallen unit is gone for the rest of the story.

Lyn, Eliwood, and Hector each lead a stretch of the war. The weapon triangle of sword, lance, and axe decides a duel before the damage numbers resolve, and supports grow when allies fight side by side.

Importers already knew that permadeath from earlier Japanese Fire Emblem games. This was the first time that rule and those three lords reached a wide North American shelf.
wizardry-proving-grounds-of-the-mad-over:
Andrew Greenberg and Robert Woodhead sent parties into Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord, Sir-Tech's Apple II maze from 1981, with Werdna waiting below. Japanese Game Boy Color releases later carried the early scenarios.

Fighters, priests, and mages descend while you map a wireframe corridor by hand, because the screen will not draw the graph for you. Werdna waits under the maze, and a dead body needs a temple or it stays lost.

Those color handheld editions brought the same early scenarios to Japanese players long after the Apple II disks. A careful paper map is still part of surviving the proving grounds.
nhl-2000:
One-timers across three periods define NHL 2000, the hockey annual EA Sports shipped in 1999 under the following year's name. A Game Boy Color edition was made for that season's clubs.

You skate a line, call a one-timer, and try to hold a lead across three periods. Playoff pushes and real NHL teams are the modes an annual like this is built to offer, even when the sprites are tiny.

The cartridge is the pocket edition of that season, not a later era of the series with a different rules rewrite. Smaller teams still stand in for the clubs of that hockey year.
moorhuhn-3:
Germany's Crazy Chicken fad continued with Moorhuhn 3, a 2001 entry in a deliberately silly hunting series. A Game Boy Color version put that barnyard joke on a cartridge.

You aim at absurd birds and other targets that refuse to behave like a serious hunting sim. The chicken is a cartoon pest, and the score climbs for ridiculous shots rather than for a clean field craft.

The handheld edition keeps the gag. It belongs to the German Moorhuhn line, not to a realistic outdoors sport.
perfect-dark-2000:
Rare built stealth-leaning missions for Joanna Dark in Perfect Dark (GBC), a 2000 Game Boy Color companion to the Nintendo 64 shooter. It is not that console campaign cut down to fit a pocket.

Gadgets and quiet takedowns matter more than a loud firefight on the small screen. dataDyne is still the corporation she is sent against, while the Carrington Institute remains her side of the fiction.

The Nintendo 64 story is a different campaign with a different shape. This cartridge writes its own mission list around the same agent.
rainbow-islands-the-story-of-bubble-bobb:
Taito replaced bubbles with climbable rainbows in Rainbow Islands: The Story of Bubble Bobble 2, the Bubble Bobble follow-up whose 1987 cabinet stars Bub and Bob. Home versions followed that upright, including a later Game Boy Color release.

Bub and Bob show up as boys who throw rainbows as platforms and as weapons. Collapse a rainbow from the top of the screen and it crushes the monsters underneath.

Diamonds on the arcade design change which ending you can reach. The color cartridge carries the rainbow-climbing idea away from the cabinet without becoming a new Bubble Bobble sequel of its own.
frogger-2-swampys-revenge:
Hasbro put a named villain in the title of Frogger 2: Swampy's Revenge, the 2000 sequel to the Frogger revival, and added more obstacle courses. Game Boy Color was one of the versions.

Swampy the crocodile holds the grudge, while Frogger still hops traffic, water, and themed hazards. Extra characters and branching lanes expand the single-road idea of the revival that came before.

The color cartridge is one edition of that revenge plot. Hop timing stays the skill, now with Swampy's traps mixed into the lanes.
mega-man-xtreme-2000:
Capcom remixed stages from the first two Mega Man X games for Mega Man Xtreme, a Game Boy Color X entry that North America received in 2001 with Sigma-era rooms rearranged. Armor parts and boss weapons still transfer, arranged into a new order.

X faces a motherboard crisis built from Sigma-era stages you may already know. A Maverick room returns in a handheld layout, which is the remix rather than a new numbered console sequel.

Zero's presence and the familiar boss weapons make it feel like the X series even on a small screen. The cartridge is its own X episode, not Mega Man X3 and not a plain port of the Super Nintendo games.
test-drive-off-road-3:
Accolade kept the dirt-racing line going with Test Drive: Off-Road 3, the off-road entry from 1999 that swaps sports cars for trucks and buggies. A Game Boy Color edition was issued under that same off-road name.

Trucks and buggies replace the paved sports cars of the parent Test Drive games. Courses run through mud, hills, and desert instead of street circuits and closed asphalt loops.

The handheld edition keeps the dirt theme on a small screen. It is the third off-road entry, not one of the road-going Test Drive boxes that never left the pavement.
resident-evil-gaiden:
A cruise-ship outbreak with a timing gauge is Resident Evil Gaiden, Capcom's side story from 2001 built outside the main survival-horror team. It does not port any console Resident Evil.

Leon Kennedy and Barry Burton are pulled onto the liner. Fights resolve by stopping a gauge, not by a tank-controlled camera inside a mansion.

A separate team means the ship does not match the PlayStation Spencer estate or later over-the-shoulder campaigns. The cartridge is its own ocean detour.
wwf-attitude:
Stone Cold and The Rock headline WWF Attitude, Acclaim's wrestling game from 1999 covering the Attitude Era on Nintendo 64 and PlayStation. Game Boy Color has a reduced take on that license.

Entrances follow that television era, and the console versions add a create-a-wrestler career beside exhibition matches. The squared circle is still the whole sport.

The color cartridge trims the presentation into a smaller card. It uses the Attitude license without the full Nintendo 64 feature set.
mega-man-xtreme-2-2001:
A parts menu and bosses from Mega Man X3 define Mega Man Xtreme 2, Capcom's Game Boy Color follow-up from 2001 that stayed handheld-only. X and Zero can both take the stages.

Equipped parts change a room, and those X3 Mavericks return inside a new crisis rather than as a port of the Super Nintendo game. No home-console twin shipped beside the cartridge.

Players seek this second Xtreme box for the parts menu and that boss cast. It is an X episode that never left the color handheld.
army-men-sarges-heroes-2:
Green plastic soldiers meet the tan army again in Army Men: Sarge's Heroes 2, the 3DO sequel from 2000 that sends Sarge through household worlds. Nintendo 64 has the 3D game, and Game Boy Color has a separate version.

A kitchen or a desk becomes a battlefield, and General Plastro's tan side is still the enemy color. The console camera walks those rooms in depth.

The cartridge does not shrink the Nintendo 64 levels. It is its own green-versus-tan mission set under the same subtitle.
wizardry-ii-the-knight-of-diamonds:
Imported veterans hunt the knight's armor in Wizardry II: The Knight of Diamonds, Sir-Tech's shorter scenario from 1982 on the Apple II line. A fresh party is not the intended start.

Heroes from the Mad Overlord's maze descend again, and the goal is tighter than that first proving ground. Traps still punish a careless paper map.

Japanese Game Boy Color releases later touched these early Wizardry scenarios. The diamond armor only makes sense if the first party is still alive to import.
kirby-tilt-n-tumble:
A tilt sensor inside the cartridge steers Kirby Tilt 'n' Tumble, the HAL and Nintendo toy from 2000 that makes you pitch the whole handheld. That gimmick is the game, because a directional pad never replaces the sensor.

Marble-like courses ask you to roll Kirby up ramps and away from holes. Tip too hard and the pink ball leaves a cloud path.

Later Kirby games rarely ask you to physically pitch the hardware this way. The cartridge itself is the joystick.
looney-tunes-racing:
Bugs and Daffy take the wheel in Looney Tunes Racing, Infogrames' kart racer from 2000 with a Game Boy Color version beside the PlayStation release. Gags replace plain missiles.

Cartoon sets frame the tracks, and a power-up can turn a rival into a joke. Warner's cast is the roster, not a generic driver list.

The color cartridge is the smaller circuit version of that cast. The PlayStation disc is the bigger sibling, not a requirement for the handheld heats.
toki-tori-2001:
Two Tribes made a limited-move egg hunt in Toki Tori (2001), a Game Boy Color original about a small chick whose later Wii and Nintendo 3DS releases are remakes. Each level hands you a counted set of bridges or freezes.

Spend the last bridge on the wrong gap and an egg stays out of reach. The chick cannot hop a pit the way a platform hero would.

Forethought is the whole contest. Those later remakes redraw this same egg hunt rather than inventing a new bird.
rampage-2-universal-tour:
George, Lizzie, and Ralph leave Earth in Rampage 2: Universal Tour, Midway's follow-up from 1999 that smashes cities on other worlds. You still climb a facade, jab it into rubble, and eat between soldier shots.

The tour sends the trio toward alien skylines instead of only repeating American downtowns. Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color both carried that off-world destruction.

The three named monsters are why the sequel exists. A skyline that is no longer one country's streets is the new joke.
disneys-dinosaur:
Aladar's herd trek licensed Disney's Dinosaur in a wave of home versions from 2000, and the Game Boy Color cartridge is one of them. Lemurs and carnotaur threats mark the film beats those editions share.

You guide the iguanodon through hazards based on the migration. Other home boxes sat beside the cartridge for people who had just seen the movie.

The pocket version is not the only one stores sold. What they share is Aladar's walk, not one identical set of levels.
test-drive-le-mans:
Infogrames built the French day-long race into Test Drive Le Mans, also sold as Le Mans 24 Hours, an endurance racer from 2000 whose night stints matter. A Game Boy Color version carries the same Sarthe event.

Rain and pit decisions replace a three-lap dash on the big versions. Circuit de la Sarthe is the course the license points at.

The handheld edition keeps the Le Mans badge and a shorter reading of that day. It is still the endurance idea, not a city street circuit.
hugo-black-diamond-fever:
The Danish television troll returns in Hugo: Black Diamond Fever, a 2001 entry from Interactive Television Entertainment's long Hugo line. Game Boy Color is one of many Hugo cartridges, and Scylla's black-diamond scheme is the plot.

Kids once shouted jump and duck at Hugo on a call-in show, and the games grew from that. This cartridge is one European stop, not a Nintendo-born adventure.

The troll, the witch, and the diamonds are the recognizable pieces. Plenty of other Hugo boxes sit beside this fever episode.
daikatana-2:
John Romero's Ion Storm shooter Daikatana is the PC game from 2000 whose long delay became infamous, with Hiro Miyamoto carrying a time-shifting sword. The Game Boy Color release is a separate action game, not that first-person project.

Sidekicks on the PC are people you are expected to protect across eras. The troubled development followed the name more loudly than any single level.

The cartridge does not contain those first-person eras. It uses the sword's name for its own handheld action and puzzles.
yars-revenge-2:
Howard Scott Warshaw's insect-versus-shield duel Yars' Revenge became one of the Atari 2600's biggest original sellers after its 1982 release, built around a Yar and a Qotile. The Neutral Zone is the stripe where the enemy swirl cannot kill you.

You nibble a shield, then fire at what sits behind it. A Game Boy Color release later revisited that same shield-eating fight.

The famous version remains the 2600 cartridge Warshaw designed. Later revisits inherit the insect, the shield, and that safe stripe.
the-lion-king-simbas-mighty-adventure:
Activision followed the earlier platformer with The Lion King: Simba's Mighty Adventure, a 2000 continuation into scenes past the first film. PlayStation and Game Boy Color both had versions.

Pride Rock and the animal cast still frame the jumps, including moments that earlier platformer did not stage. The two versions are separate builds of that continuation.

Neither box replaces the 16-bit Lion King game that came before. Simba's later scenes are the reason this subtitle exists.
wizardry-iii-legacy-of-llylgamyn:
Descendants close the Apple II trilogy in Wizardry III: Legacy of Llylgamyn, Sir-Tech's third scenario from 1983, where alignment changes how the maze treats you. Llylgamyn is the threatened land.

You bring children of an earlier party rather than the same veterans who finished the knight's quest. The scenario is shorter and stranger than a straight repeat of the first corridors.

Japanese color-handheld releases later carried these early chapters. This third scenario ends the original trilogy.
pokemon-puzzle-challenge-2000:
Panel de Pon returns wearing Pokémon faces in Pokémon Puzzle Challenge (2000), Intelligent Systems' stack-clearing contest and the color-handheld cousin of Pokémon Puzzle League. It is not a Red or Blue adventure.

You swap panels to chain a crash while a trainer portrait reacts. The puzzle underneath belongs to Panel de Pon, with a Pokémon coat instead of fairies.

There is no gym circuit and no capture. The match ends when the stack clears, which is why it sits nearer Puzzle League than beside a Kanto quest.
harvest-moon-gb:
Victor Interactive made the first handheld farm as Harvest Moon GB, a 1997 sim of crops, livestock, and town visits that Natsume published in the West. You plant, water, and ship produce before the season turns.

Animals need daily care, and villagers can be befriended between chores. The pocket calendar is smaller than the home-console farms that preceded it, yet the work is the same rural loop.

Later color sequels grow the town. This cartridge is the first pocket farm.
f1-racing-championship:
Ubisoft put an official Formula 1 license on Nintendo 64 as F1 Racing Championship, a season racer from 2000 with a simpler Game Boy Color edition under the same name. Real teams and a grid are what the console license is for.

Car setup matters more on that Nintendo 64 season than on the handheld. The color cartridge keeps the championship name and trims the simulation.

It is not the console season copied pixel for pixel. A shorter race is the pocket reading of that license.
dragon-ball-z-legendary-super-warriors:
Banpresto retold major fights with cards in Dragon Ball Z: Legendary Super Warriors, a Game Boy Color strategy game from 2002 that Infogrames published in the West. Goku and Vegeta appear as faces on that hand of attacks.

Energy, movement, and a super attack share the card space instead of a pure fighting-game input. The show's big confrontations supply the duels.

The Western box is Infogrames' edition of Banpresto's handheld retelling. Building the hand is the strategy.
azure-dreams:
Konami's tower climb reached color handhelds as Azure Dreams GB, a 1999 companion to the PlayStation release where random floors and egg hatching remain the loop. The Monster Tower forgets its layout when you leave.

A failed run can still leave a hatched ally for the next climb. The disc has the fuller town, while this cartridge keeps the eggs and the shifting floors in a smaller frame.

It is a handheld cousin, not a replacement for the PlayStation tower. Hatching and climbing are the reasons to return.
donkey-kong-land-iii:
Dixie and Kiddy star in Donkey Kong Land 3, Rare's companion from 1997 to Donkey Kong Country 3, with animal buddies along their route. Color hardware makes that trek easier to read than the monochrome Game Boy original.

It is a companion quest, not the Super Nintendo game copied into a cartridge. The twin Kongs distinguish it from the first two Land adventures.

On a color screen the trek is easier to read than it was in monochrome. The pieces you hunt still sit off the main path the way Country 3 taught players to look.
kirikou:
Michel Ocelot's French animated film licensed Kirikou, a Game Boy Color release from 2001 aimed at European players. It is a cartoon adaptation, not a Nintendo adventure.

The small hero of that West African story is the lead, and the cartridge speaks to audiences who already knew the film. European shelves are where this box was meant to sit.

Nothing about the village tale comes from a Mario or Zelda template. The film is the source, and the handheld is one adaptation of it.
mickeys-speedway-usa:
Pete's theft of Pluto starts Mickey's Speedway USA, Rare's kart racer from 2000 for Nintendo 64 starring Mickey and the Disney cast. The Game Boy Color version is a separate top-down circuit game.

Power-ups and Mickey's friends fill the console's American-themed tracks. The color cartridge looks down on simpler circuits instead of using Rare's polygonal roads.

Both boxes share the Speedway name and do not share a camera. The Pluto chase is the excuse for the race.
nascar-heat:
Hasbro's stock-car license NASCAR Heat covers that NASCAR season in a release from 2000 for PlayStation, PC, and Game Boy Color. You draft in a pack, pit, and run an oval the way the badge expects.

Bigger editions push a fuller race weekend, while the cartridge simplifies the same stock-car idea. It is a season-specific Heat title, not a generic arcade kart.

The three editions share the NASCAR badge and differ in how deep a race goes. Ovals, not city streets, are the point.
harvest-moon-2-gbc-1999:
Natsume's sequel Harvest Moon 2 GBC (1999) builds a bigger town and more villagers than Harvest Moon GB, sitting between that first pocket farm and Harvest Moon 3 GBC. You still raise crops and animals, now with a wider street of neighbors to court.

Festivals give the days more appointments than the first cartridge had. Tools and conversations fill the gaps between shipping produce.

Players sorting the color trilogy put this box in the middle. The expanded village is the reason to pick it up after the original farm.
harry-potter-quidditch-world-cup:
Broomstick matches from the books become Harry Potter: Quidditch World Cup, EA's sports game from 2003 with a Snitch to chase. GameCube has the fuller pitch, and Game Boy Advance has a simpler adaptation.

You chase the Snitch, score through the hoops, and play as a house side. The console match has the fuller pitch, while the cartridge trims the same sport.

It is Quidditch, not a Hogwarts walking adventure. The Golden Snitch ends a match the way the books say it should.
tony-hawks-underground:
Neversoft let you step off the board in Tony Hawk's Underground, the skate game from 2003 that adds a story. GameCube has that campaign, and Game Boy Advance is a separate skate title.

You walk to a mission, then pop back on the deck for a line. The console story is the one with that on-and-off structure.

The handheld borrows the name for its own sessions. Stepping off the board is the console campaign's new trick.
fire-emblem-the-sacred-stones:
A smaller cast and a world map of optional fights distinguish Fire Emblem: The Sacred Stones, the campaign from 2004 by Intelligent Systems and Nintendo. It is the other widely released Game Boy Advance Fire Emblem, separate from the first Western release.

Eirika and Ephraim split the war against Grado's monsters. Optional skirmishes on the map let you fight or walk past, a rhythm the tighter first Western campaign did not offer in the same way.

Permadeath still removes a fallen unit. The twin lords and the roaming monsters set this war apart from The Blazing Blade.
final-fantasy-tactics-advance:
Clan laws and a snow-globe world of jobs fill Final Fantasy Tactics Advance, Square's handheld tactics game from 2003 built for short maps. It is a spin on the earlier PlayStation Tactics, not that game's port.

Marche falls into Ivalice, where a Judge can forbid a weapon mid-battle. Clans dispatch units across small maps you can finish away from a television.

The PlayStation game's long political war is a different story. Laws, judges, and the snow globe are this cartridge's own Ivalice.
james-bond-007-nightfire:
Eurocom's Bond shooter James Bond 007: NightFire follows Agent Under Fire with a gadget-heavy plot from 2002 on the main console. GameCube holds those missions, and Game Boy Advance is a separate first-person take.

Gadgets and a set-piece plot still frame Bond after that previous shooter. The console missions are the primary campaign.

The handheld is its own first-person reading of the NightFire name. It does not shrink the GameCube level list into a cartridge.
kingdom-hearts-chain-of-memories:
Sora climbs Castle Oblivion on a card deck in Kingdom Hearts: Chain of Memories, the entry Square Enix and Jupiter released in 2004 between the first two Kingdom Hearts games. A later PlayStation 2 remix rebuilds that memory journey in 3D.

Sora climbs Castle Oblivion while cards decide which attack or friend appears. Riku's path is the other side of the memory story.

The 3D remix is a rebuild, not this cartridge. Sleight combinations on the deck are the handheld combat.
toy-story-2-buzz-lightyear-to-the-rescue:
Buzz crosses film sets in Toy Story 2: Buzz Lightyear to the Rescue, the 3D platformer Traveller's Tales made for Activision in 1999 from the Pixar sequel. Nintendo 64 received that console game, with Buzz hunting for Woody.

Zurg and the toy-store beats supply the stages. The Nintendo 64 camera follows Buzz through those rooms rather than along a flat run.

A Game Boy Advance listing also sits beside that console adventure. The living-room version players mean is the Nintendo 64 rescue.
baldurs-gate-dark-alliance:
Snowblind Studios made a Forgotten Realms hack-and-slash called Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance, a console brawler from 2001 separate from BioWare's PC Baldur's Gate. GameCube got a port, and a Game Boy Advance game later used the name.

You pick a hero and carve through dungeon crowds rather than pausing for the computer saga's dialogue trees. Loot and co-op brawling are the console point.

The handheld title that borrowed the name is not that dungeon crawl copied down. BioWare's computer story stays on the PC.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-2003:
Konami's beat-em-up on the cartoon that premiered alongside it is Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (2003), with the four brothers in the streets. GameCube has the 3D brawler, and Game Boy Advance has a side-scrolling counterpart.

Leonardo, Raphael, Donatello, and Michelangelo fight Foot soldiers in the show's style. The console camera circles the brawl, while the cartridge watches from the side.

The two editions share the cartoon and not a camera. Foot clan grunts are the crowd both of them clear.
pokemon-mystery-dungeon-blue-rescue-team:
Chunsoft wakes a human inside a Pokemon body in Pokémon Mystery Dungeon: Blue Rescue Team, a rescue-job story from 2005 that can link work with a partner cart. Mystery floors and bulletin missions replace any gym circuit.

You accept a bulletin mission, crawl a mystery floor, and try to bring the client home. The transformation premise replaces any gym challenge.

Friend rescues pass between this team and the red partner cart. Waking up in a new body is the start of every run.
medal-of-honor-underground:
Manon's French resistance campaign is Medal of Honor: Underground, the PlayStation sequel DreamWorks Interactive set in 2000 during World War II. The Game Boy Advance release is a later, separate shooter.

Resistance missions replace a more familiar front. Manon's story is the campaign the PlayStation disc is telling.

The handheld shooter uses the Underground name without being that PlayStation mission set. Occupied France is still the setting both point toward.
colin-mcrae-rally-20:
Stage clocks and the Scottish champion define Colin McRae Rally 2.0, the Codemasters rally from 2000 built on pace notes. A Game Boy Advance version followed as a handheld adaptation of those gravel stages.

You learn a pace note, commit to a corner, and try not to lose the split. Gravel and tarmac stages are the career, not a closed oval.

The cartridge is the pocket reading of those stage clocks. McRae's name on the box is the license, and the times are the score.
the-lord-of-the-rings-the-two-towers:
Helm's Deep anchors The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers, EA's action game from 2002 of the second Jackson film. GameCube has the 3D battles, and Game Boy Advance has its own side-view campaign.

You hold the wall while Uruk-hai push against Aragorn or another hero of that film. The console battles are the big-screen version of the siege.

The side-view cartridge retells the same war from the flank. It is not the GameCube siege squeezed into a smaller camera.
advance-wars:
Andy, Max, and Sami each bend a shared army in Advance Wars, the strategy game Intelligent Systems and Nintendo released in 2001 for a wide new audience. A much later Switch collection revisits those early maps.

Andy, Max, and Sami change range, firepower, or movement on a shared roster. Fog, funds, and a captured factory still decide a map.

A CO power makes two players with the same tanks fight differently. The Switch collection is a later revisit, not this cartridge.
worms-world-party:
Sheep, girders, and bazookas fill Worms World Party, Team17's party-minded worm battles from 2001 on a small screen. Teams still take turns blowing holes in a landscape.

Teams take turns on a destructible landscape, and the small screen holds that artillery duel. It is a party-minded entry rather than a block-clearing cousin like Worms Blast.

The cartridge is the pocket version of those worm teams. Craters and sudden girders are the jokes between explosions.
madden-nfl-07:
PlayStation 3's launch window included Madden NFL 07, the EA Sports football annual for the 2006 season beside older consoles. GameCube and Game Boy Advance carried editions of that same campaign.

You call a play, read a coverage, and manage the clock the way a Madden year expects. The new-console copy did not erase the older-engine boxes.

Handheld playbooks compress the season. The shared piece is that year's roster, not one identical engine.
ford-racing-3:
A licensed Ford lineup fills Ford Racing 3, the racer from 2005 whose Game Boy Advance and Nintendo DS versions are the handheld editions. Mustangs and other Blue Oval badges stock the garage.

You pick a Ford and run the license's events rather than a fictional manufacturer. Each handheld builds its own reading of that garage.

It is the third box in the Ford Racing line, aimed at the badge. The two pocket editions do not share one track list.
pirates-of-the-caribbean:
Disney's pirate license reached the Game Boy Advance as Pirates of the Caribbean in a handheld adventure from 2003, the year the first film opened. Swords and ships supply the fantasy the cartridge is selling.

The box matches that first movie's arrival rather than a later sequel's plot. You get a small-screen pirate story under the film's name.

Swordplay is the adaptation. It is not a museum of every later voyage in the series.
mario-party:
Four players, one television, and a dice roll open Mario Party, the Hudson Soft and Nintendo board from 1998 that starts the series. Stars and coins decide the winner after a string of minigame interruptions.

Stars and coins decide the winner after a set run of turns. The living-room television is part of the design, not an optional extra.

A Game Boy Advance listing came later, but this shared board is the original. Later handheld parties are follow-ups, not this four-player table.
castlevania-harmony-of-dissonance-2:
Juste Belmont explores a twin castle in Castlevania: Harmony of Dissonance, Konami's Game Boy Advance follow-up from 2002 to Circle of the Moon. It is a brighter, larger handheld original.

Two overlapping castles make the map a puzzle of which version of a hall you are in. Juste's spell books replace Nathan Graves' card magic from the previous cartridge.

The brighter palette is deliberate next to that earlier entry. Walking both castles, not picking a stage from a list, is the journey.
mario-kart-super-circuit:
Cups borrowed from Super Mario Kart sit inside Mario Kart: Super Circuit, Nintendo's small-screen racer from 2001 with extra tracks of its own. The flat courses belong between the earlier dimensional Kart and the pocket sequels that followed.

You drift a tiny kart on those familiar tracks plus new cups made for the small screen. A link race is part of how a session with friends can feel.

The flat courses are a choice, not a failed copy of the Nintendo 64's dimensional tracks. Super Mario Kart's cups are the nostalgia half of the menu.
the-incredibles:
Bob Parr's family powers The Incredibles, THQ's tie-in from 2004 to Pixar's superhero film. GameCube has the console adventure, and Game Boy Advance has a separate side-scroller.

Mr. Incredible, Elastigirl, and Dash each change how a room is crossed on the console. The cartridge watches the same family from the side and builds its own stages.

Syndrome's threat comes from the film. The two boxes do not share a level list.
2006-fifa-world-cup:
National teams in Germany fill 2006 FIFA World Cup, EA Sports' official tournament game. GameCube and Game Boy Advance each received an edition.

You pick a country, play the bracket, and chase the trophy rather than a club season. The handheld edition is its own match engine under that tournament name.

The Germany setting is the point of this box. It is a World Cup tournament, not the ordinary club season of a domestic annual.
the-legend-of-zelda-four-swords:
Vaati splits one hero into four in The Legend of Zelda: Four Swords, packed by Nintendo and Capcom in 2002 beside A Link to the Past. Later DS and Nintendo 3DS releases revisited that four-hero idea.

Vaati splits Link, and friends each take a color to pull switches a solo hero cannot. The original packaging was a bonus beside that port, not a standalone console epic.

Later revisits keep the four-sword idea on new hardware. A switch that needs more than one Link is the multiplayer joke.
wario-land-4:
A jewel hunt whose timer starts only after you choose to escape is Wario Land 4, Nintendo's handheld from 2001 that is louder and more animated than the color Wario games. You grab the treasure, then the clock begins.

Princess Shokora's pyramid frames the levels. Frog, snowman, and other transformations change how Wario fits through a gap on the way out.

The escape timer is the twist. Earlier color Wario adventures did not hinge on that decision to turn around and run.
open-season:
Boog and Elliot leave town rules behind in Open Season, Ubisoft's tie-in from 2006 to the Sony hunting-season cartoon. Boog's forest stages were rebuilt separately for the disc and for each pocket machine.

The film's hunted-become-hunters joke supplies the pair. Each machine builds its own stages around that forest duo.

A minigame on the disc is not the cartridge's level. The shared piece is the cartoon, not one camera.
castlevania-circle-of-the-moon-2:
Pairing two cards is the magic of Castlevania: Circle of the Moon, a launch castle Konami shipped in 2001 with Nathan Graves inside. Japan sold it as Akumajo Dracula: Circle of the Moon, outside the usual numbering.

Nathan Graves combines two cards for a spell while exploring that launch castle. The card pairs are the system, not a soul steal from a later entry.

Launch timing is part of its story, because it was there when the handheld arrived. The Japanese title sits outside the numbered line many players expected.
bionicle-heroes:
Eidos published Bionicle Heroes as an action game from 2006 based on LEGO's Bionicle toys. GameCube, Game Boy Advance, and Nintendo DS each use that license differently.

Toa heroes and mask powers supply the fantasy. The toys' canister sets are the source, not a film script.

Buying the disc does not give you the cartridge's stages. The shared badge is the Bionicle line itself.
madden-nfl-06:
A quarterback vision cone hides receivers outside the passer's view in Madden NFL 06, the EA Sports annual released in 2005 with that cone as the headline rule. You see what the quarterback sees, and a receiver in the blind spot vanishes until the view swings.

GameCube and Game Boy Advance editions carry the season beside the bigger consoles. Play-calling still fills the downtime between snaps.

The cone is what separated this annual from the previous Madden box. Snap decisions now include whether the target is even visible.
kirby-and-the-amazing-mirror:

tomb-raider-legend:
Lara Croft's reboot under Crystal Dynamics is Tomb Raider: Legend, that studio's first Tomb Raider, released in 2006 with a GameCube port of the console adventure. A grappling hook and a motorcycle set piece mark the new Lara.

Ancient puzzles interrupt the gunfights, and the story chases a myth rather than a single mansion. The studio change is the reason this Lara feels restarted.

The GameCube disc is that adventure on Nintendo hardware. It is not the original Core Design chronology continued without a break.
star-wars-jedi-knight-ii-jedi-outcast:
Kyle Katarn takes a lightsaber back up in Star Wars Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast, the 2002 shooter Raven Software made and LucasArts published. A GameCube version shipped with that return, and a Nintendo Switch release later carried it too.

Desann's threat pulls Kyle out of a quieter life and back into Force powers. Gunplay gives way to saber combat once the story allows the blade.

The console missions, including the Nintendo ones, are that Katarn comeback. It is not a podrace and not a fleet battle.
prince-of-persia-the-sands-of-time:
Farah and the Dagger of Time star in Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time, Ubisoft Montreal's 2003 revival of Jordan Mechner's series. Wall runs feel fair only because a few seconds can rewind.

Wall runs and pillar leaps only work if the rewind can save the attempt. The Sands turn the palace's guards into the enemy sand army.

GameCube received that palace among the console versions. The rewind is the mechanic every later Sands story is answering.
need-for-speed-most-wanted:
Rockport's blacklist is the ladder inside Need For Speed: Most Wanted, and every cop chase raises the heat that unlocks the next rival. EA Black Box built that 2005 street campaign so the city, not a menu of closed circuits, decides when Razor Callahan's crew will race you.

Pursuit breakers drop from billboards onto cruisers, and bounty cash buys the parts that turn a junkyard wreck back into a competitive car. Milestones only clear after enough police cars are wrecked to force a one-on-one against the name painted on the board.

The cube disc carries that same Rockport pursuit, sirens included, rather than a side story. Pink slips from the earlier underground career are gone, and the prize here is a face on the most-wanted wall.
prince-of-persia-warrior-within:
Dahaka hunts the prince through Prince of Persia: Warrior Within, a darker sequel that trades the hourglass charm of The Sands of Time for heavier swordplay. Ubisoft sent him back along a doomed timeline in 2004, with the Dahaka as a beast that cannot be bargained with.

Wall runs still cross the island fortress, but sand-time powers now feed combos, and the prince can seize an enemy weapon mid-swing. Kaileena's presence in the fortress pulls the story toward a choice the first game never staged.

The cube release is that same fortress campaign, acrobatics and all. Players who only knew the kind prince meet a harder, more violent fighter on these corridors.
prince-of-persia-the-two-thrones:
Babylon's streets open Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones, the closing chapter of the Sands trilogy, where the prince shares a body with a darker self. Ubisoft mixed the old acrobatics with speed kills in 2005, letting a stealth kill from a ledge replace a long courtyard fight.

Chariot chases cut through the city between rooftop runs, and the Dark Prince's chain becomes a weapon and a swing line when the transformation hits. Farah is back in the story after the island detour of the previous game.

The cube disc is the original release of that Babylon ending, and a later motion-console build followed the same campaign. Speed kills and the inner voice are the point of this chapter, not a new hourglass tutorial.
crazy-taxi:
Axel's fare meter is the whole contest in Crazy Taxi (1999), a clock race about delivering passengers before the timer hits zero. Sega's Hitmaker cabinet became a Dreamcast favorite, and the cube disc is a home port of that same arcade design.
