Intelligent Systems and Nintendo released the Wii game in 2007. Count Bleck's Void is why the flip exists. Mario, Peach, Bowser, and Luigi each take a chapter's hero slot, with Tippi the Pixl and Count Bleck's Void driving the plot.

The Thousand-Year Door on GameCube remains the turn-based predecessor. Here a flip finds a door painted on a surface the flat view cannot enter.
punch-out-wii:
Little Mac's tells return, glass jaw and all, in Punch-Out!!. Doc Louis still shouts from the corner, and a star punch still answers a pattern Glass Joe or King Hippo has already shown.

Next Level Games and Nintendo revived the NES career on Wii in 2009. Bald Bull's charge still needs the star punch. Motion controls can be turned down so the fight stays on the buttons, which keeps Bald Bull's charge readable without a mandatory swing of the remote.

It is a boxing revival, not a new sport with teams and a season. The career order of papercraft chins is the NES ladder rebuilt.
monster-hunter-tri:
Underwater fights set Monster Hunter Tri apart from the earlier hunts. Lagiacrus patrols a flooded zone, Moga Village is the hub, and Capcom used the Wii entry to bring the series to a wide Nintendo audience.

The village and Loc Lac city frame gathering, cooking, and the Cha-Cha mask in a loop released in 2009. Lagiacrus under Moga's waves is the hunt the camera was rebuilt for. Great Jaggi on the beach is the teaching hunt; the leviathan below the waves is the one the controls were rebuilt to allow.

Later portable Monster Hunter games are separate. The underwater camera and Moga's dock belong to this Wii chapter.
fire-emblem-radiant-dawn:
Three armies rotate the save file in Fire Emblem: Radiant Dawn. Micaiah's Dawn Brigade, Ike's returning mercenaries, and a third force continue the Path of Radiance war, and the cast is among the largest the series had fielded.

Intelligent Systems and Nintendo released the direct GameCube sequel on Wii in 2007. Micaiah's Dawn Brigade opens the war before Ike returns. Tellius laguz and beorc still share chapters, with ledges and height changing how a tide of units approaches.

Part shifts hand the lord's seat to a different commander. A unit benched in Micaiah's opening can become essential once Ike's half of the war resumes.
sin-and-punishment-star-successor:
A partner joins the rail in Sin & Punishment: Star Successor. Treasure's Wii follow-up keeps the stick-aim idea from the Nintendo 64 game and lets the player swap who leads the shot.

Released in 2009, it is not a remake of the 2000 original. Isa and the partner share a score attack that scrolls whether or not the reticle is ready, and the Wii remote can place shots the stick also covers.

The Nintendo 64 game remains the first incarnation of that control scheme. Star Successor's dual leads and its later-era stages are the sequel's own run.
the-last-story:
Cover commands shape the fights in The Last Story. Zael directs a mercenary band through Lazulis Island, a city losing its magic, and battles use line of sight rather than a free-roaming turn grid.

Mistwalker's late Wii RPG, published by Nintendo in the West, arrived in 2011 alongside that era's Xenoblade Chronicles and Pandora's Tower. Gathering circles change the terrain mid-fight, and Calista's place in the dying magic is the plot's hinge.

The mercenary jobs between story chapters pay for the swords. It is a Wii role-playing game with a cover button, not an open continent in Shulk's style.
pikmin-3:
Juice rations limit the day in Pikmin 3. Alph's juice meter drops until fruit comes home. Alph, Brittany, and Charlie split squads across a garden, and the fruit they carry home is both food and the clock.

Nintendo released the Wii U adventure in 2013. Rock Pikmin crack a crystal the red ones only stare at. Rock Pikmin and Winged Pikmin join the older colors, and a GamePad map lets one captain be aimed while another is already hauling.

The later Deluxe release, with extra difficulties, has its own Switch page. The three captains and the juice meter are the Wii U expedition.
splatoon:
Turf War ends when the paint is counted in Splatoon. Inklings shoot ink, swim through their own color as squids, and lose if the opposing team owns more ground when the timer stops.

Nintendo's Wii U original, released in 2015, set Inkopolis, Judd the cat judge, and the Zapfish news broadcasts around that mode. Rollers and chargers change how ground is claimed, but the score is still coverage, not a kill total.

Splatoon 2 and Splatoon 3 are Switch sequels. The first Inkopolis plaza and its ranked ladders belong to the Wii U game.
super-smash-bros-for-wii-u:
Larger stages mark the home half of Super Smash Bros. for Wii U. Eight fighters on one television need the larger stage. Bandai Namco, Sora Ltd., and Nintendo shipped it as the television partner to a 3DS version, and the Wii U stages use the extra screen space.

The pair arrived in 2014. Ultimate's physics are a later argument. Eight-player brawls and the bigger stage list belong on this console edition, while the 3DS cartridge is a separate page and Ultimate on Switch is a later game with its own physics and roster.

Amiibo fighters and the stage builder use the Wii U hardware. A Final Destination match here is not the handheld's smaller take on the same idea.
xenoblade-chronicles-x:
Planet Mira is the frontier, and a Skell is the ride, in Xenoblade Chronicles X. Elma's Skell license is earned on Mira, not on the Bionis. A customizable avatar joins BLADE in New Los Angeles, and the doll-like mech transforms between a walking frame and a flight mode.

Monolith Soft and Nintendo released this Wii U spin in 2015, separate from the numbered story that follows Shulk. Elma's team, the FrontierNav map, and the alien continents are not the Bionis.

A later Definitive Edition is its own page. The Wii U expedition is the one where the avatar's Skell license is earned on Mira.
yoshis-woolly-world:
Yarn balls hide the secrets in Yoshi's Woolly World. Good-Feel built craft-textured stages where a yarn Yoshi unravels a wall or throws a wool ball of yarn at a shy guy.

Nintendo published the Wii U game in 2015. A wool skein in the background is often the real road. Two Yoshis can share a stage, and the skeins stitched into the background are often the real path.

A 3DS version with Poochy followed. The home-console original is the wool garden before that handheld follow-up added the pup.
nintendo-land:
GamePad attractions fill a theme park in Nintendo Land. A ghost house hides the seeker from the television, and Luigi's Ghost Mansion uses the same asymmetric idea with a different costume.

Nintendo's Wii U launch compilation, released in 2012, was packed in with many deluxe sets. Mario Chase, Metroid Blast, and Animal Crossing's Sweet Day each teach a different way to look at the pad versus the TV.

Takamaru's ninja castle and Donkey Kong's Crash Course sit in the same plaza. The attractions are demos of the new controller, not a single campaign with one ending.
splatoon-note-star-fox-zero:
Cockpit drawings disagree with the television in Star Fox Zero. The GamePad shows Fox McCloud's view from the Arwing while the TV shows a chase camera, and the two pictures do not always match.

Nintendo and PlatinumGames released this Wii U retelling in 2016, late in the console's life, and it is not Star Fox 64. The Gyrowing hovers where the Arwing cannot. The Walker transformation, the Gyrowing, and the Landmaster return as mission tools rather than as a straight replay of the Nintendo 64 routes.

Falco, Slippy, and Peppy still call targets. The skill is flying while glancing down at the cockpit, which the earlier on-rails runs never required.
paper-mario-color-splash:
Huey's paint restores Prism Island in Paper Mario: Color Splash. Battles spend cards instead of the old partner turns, and a hammer swing is aimed at a thing-card the player has painted into the deck.

Intelligent Systems and Nintendo released the Wii U game in 2016, between Sticker Star and The Origami King on Switch. Port Prisma is the hub, and unpainted spots on the island are the reason to keep walking.

The partner system of the first two Paper Mario games is not the battle model here. Paint capacity and the card hand are.
the-wonderful-101:
Drawing a shape builds the weapon in The Wonderful 101. Wonder-Red scratches a fist and the crowd becomes one. Wonder-Red's crowd of heroes unites into a giant fist, sword, or gun when the gesture matches the form.

PlatinumGames published it with Nintendo on Wii U in 2013. The GEATHJERK invasion is the operation on the title card. Operation 001 against the GEATHJERK asks the player to scratch the Unite Morph on the GamePad while the television shows the resulting giant tool.

A later remastered edition exists. The Wii U original is the one where that scratch was drawn on the GamePad.
hyrule-warriors:
Battlefield crowds, not dungeon keys, carry Hyrule Warriors. Omega Force and Team Ninja crossed Zelda characters with musou sweeps, and Link, Impa, and Zelda clear hundreds of officers on maps that are not the mainline quests.

Nintendo published the Wii U crossover in 2014. A fallen keep hands the base to the other army. Cia and Lana pull warriors from several eras onto the same field, with keeps that change owner when a base falls.

Definitive Edition on Switch is a separate, expanded page. The Wii U original is the first of those battlefield crossovers.
nintendogs:
Stylus strokes and a spoken command train the puppy in Nintendogs. The clock runs in real time, so a Labrador, a dachshund, or a chihuahua from the different breed packs gets hungry while the handheld is closed.

Nintendo's DS pet simulation, a launch-era phenomenon, arrived in 2005. A spoken name makes the puppy turn its head. The microphone hears a call, the touch screen throws a disc, and contests award prizes that buy a bigger room.

Nintendogs + Cats on 3DS is a sequel. The original breed packs and the microphone tricks belong to the DS cartridges.
pokemon-diamond:
The physical-special split rewrites moves in Pokemon Diamond. A move's category, not only its type, decides whether attack or special attack lands, and Sinnoh's gyms are where that new math first matters.

Game Freak and Nintendo released Diamond as one half of the 2006 pair. Dialga is the cover legendary, Pearl keeps Palkia, and Platinum is the third version. Brilliant Diamond on Switch is a remake with its own page.

Mt. Coronet splits the region. Underground digging and the split damage categories are the generation's new tools, not a Johto reunion.
pokemon-soulsilver:
A following creature walks behind the trainer in Pokemon SoulSilver. The paired remake of Silver matches HeartGold's companion and its two regions, Johto first and Kanto after the league.

Game Freak and Nintendo released this other 2009 DS remake with the Pokewalker in mind. Lugia is the version legendary, and the walking partner is a creature from the party, not a fixed mascot.

It is not the 1999 cartridge and not a new generation. The dual-region map and the follower are the remake's promises, shared with HeartGold and distinguished by the legendary.
pokemon-white:
Zekrom fronts the paired Unova journey in Pokemon White. A different legendary from Black's Reshiram, and a city that changes after the story, set the version apart while Team Plasma and N remain the shared conflict.

Game Freak and Nintendo released this other 2010 DS edition beside Black. Castelia's studios and the Plasma story are the same plot skeleton, with version-exclusive encounters filling the routes.

One Unova city changes once the credits have rolled, on top of the version-exclusive encounters. White is not a remake of Johto and not Black 2's later time skip.
pokemon-black-2:
Two years pass inside Unova before Pokemon Black 2 begins. Game Freak and Nintendo had not previously built a paired edition as a direct sequel, and this DS follow-up to Black is that sequel, not a remake.

The new protagonists walk a changed region in 2012. Kyurem's fusion is the threat the two-year gap was building. Kyurem's fusion plot, Pokestar Studios, and the Pokemon World Tournament sit on top of a map players of Black already knew.

White 2 is the partner version. Black 2's towns remember the earlier Plasma crisis instead of pretending the first Unova journey never happened.
mario-luigi-bowsers-inside-story:
Bowser's body is the dungeon in Mario & Luigi: Bowser's Inside Story. Mario and Luigi platform through the koopa king's insides on the touch screen while Bowser fights on the top screen.

AlphaDream and Nintendo released the DS game in 2009. Fawful's Blorbs are why the brothers fell in. Fawful's Blorbs plot forces the brothers down Bowser's throat, and giant battles enlarge Bowser until the top screen cannot hold him.

A 3DS remake later revisited the same body. The original dual-screen split, brothers below and Bowser above, is the DS structure.
kirby-canvas-curse:
Drawn ink is the control stick in Kirby: Canvas Curse. Kirby is a ball, and the player paints a path for him to roll along instead of walking him with a pad.

HAL Laboratory and Nintendo built the DS game entirely around the touch screen in 2005. Drawcia's curse is why the hero is a ball. Drawcia cursed Kirby into that rolling form, and medals reward a line that also collects the stage's treasures.

Rainbow lines fade, so a long stroke is a timed platform. No other Kirby of its era asks the player to be the floor.
chrono-trigger-ds:
Lost Sanctum and an Arena extend the timeline on the DS release of Chrono Trigger. Square Enix's dual-screen reissue adds those sites, plus a map spread across both screens, which the Super Nintendo cartridge did not contain.

Crono, Marle, Lucca, and the Millennial Fair still open the journey, and Lavos still waits at the end of the eras. The 2008 reissue keeps the field battles and the tech combinations while parking the new dungeon and the monster arena off the original path.

The SNES original remains a separate entry. Players who want the Lost Sanctum's reptite quest are holding the dual-screen edition, not the first cartridge.
phoenix-wright-ace-attorney:
Courtroom objections share a cartridge with crime-scene searches in Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney. Point at a contradiction, shout the objection, and the cross-examination breaks, then the investigation half sends Phoenix back to the scene.

Capcom's DS release in 2005 is the first Ace Attorney many players outside Japan could buy. Mia Fey, Miles Edgeworth, and Maya Fey carry the early cases, and Rise from the Ashes, the fifth case, uses the touch screen for evidence the Game Boy Advance original never had.

The steel samurai and the spirit mediums are the tone. Later numbered trials are sequels; this is the first widely released DS set of cases.
elite-beat-agents:
Suited agents fix a stranger's crisis by hitting marks in Elite Beat Agents. iNiS built touch-screen rhythm scenes where a song's beats are the only way the story moves, from a ballroom panic to a sports meltdown.

Nintendo published the Western sibling of Ouendan on DS in 2006. The Commander's bark drops if the marker is missed. The Commander barks orders, the agents dive in sunglasses, and a missed marker drops the crowd's morale until the number fails.

Ouendan remains the Japanese predecessor with its own soundtrack. Elite Beat Agents is the localization's scenario, not a menu of the same songs.
advance-wars-dual-strike:
Two commanding officers share one battle in Advance Wars: Dual Strike. Each CO owns a front, the DS shows both screens at once, and a tag power spends the meters they have filled together.

Intelligent Systems and Nintendo released the follow-up to the Game Boy Advance pair in 2005. A tag power spends both meters on one split map. Black Hole returns, and newer officers join Andy, Nell, and the earlier cast for dual fronts that a single GBA map could not show.

A CO's power still changes the math of a whole turn. The new trick is firing two of those powers across a split battlefield.
tears-of-the-kingdom:
The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom takes the Hyrule of Breath of the Wild and adds a sky, a depths, and a glue. A rocket on a shield is a legal solution, which is the design speaking out loud.

Hideto Fujibayashi directed the sequel. Ultrahand, Fuse, Ascend, and Recall let the player build a bridge, stick a rocket to a shield, or rewind a falling stone. The tutorial islands float above the clouds, and the first dive back to the surface is the moment the old map becomes unfamiliar.

Zonai devices, the Light Dragon, and a story about Rauru and the imprisoning war sit under the building toys. The depths are a dark mirror of the surface, explored with brightbloom seeds, and the sky islands are sparse on purpose so the journey between them matters.

It is not a mode inside Breath of the Wild. That game remains its own page. This page is Tears of the Kingdom.
mario-kart-8-deluxe:
Mario Kart 8 Deluxe reopened the Wii U racer on Switch and replaced the weak battle mode with balloons and dedicated arenas. Inklings join the grid, and battle mode finally has arenas built for balloons.

Nintendo EPD shipped it with Inklings on the roster, a smarter item system for computer racers, and every DLC character from the Wii U version included. Gold Mario and a second set of gold parts reward high rankings instead of a single limited-time cart.

Years later the Booster Course Pass added cups built from older Mario Kart tracks, which turned one disc into a long-running online lobby. The physics, the anti-gravity sections, and the 200cc class still belong to the Mario Kart 8 design, but the battle arenas and the extra cups are why this edition is not the same product.

The Wii U Mario Kart 8 has its own page. Booster Course cups and the rebuilt battle arenas are the reasons Deluxe stayed in the dock for years.
animal-crossing-new-horizons:
Animal Crossing: New Horizons starts with a deserted island, a tent, and a debt to Tom Nook that you pay by shaping the land. A tent becomes a house only after the island starts to look like a place someone chose.

Katsuya Eguchi and Hisashi Nogami's team at Nintendo EPD built it around a real-world clock: shops close, birthdays land on the calendar, and snow falls in January even if you would rather it didn't. Mystery islands, reached with a ticket, are how new neighbors and new fruit enter the town. Nook Miles pay for recipes and for tickets to mystery islands where the fruit and the villagers are a gamble.

A free update added terraforming, so cliffs and rivers became something the player sculpts rather than something the island arrived with. Redd's art boat, the museum's fossils, and K.K. Slider's Saturday concert are the rituals that make a town feel occupied.

The GameCube, DS, Wii, and 3DS Animal Crossing games are other towns with their own pages. This one is Animal Crossing: New Horizons.
metroid-dread:
EMMI patrols force a retreat in Metroid Dread. Samus slips past robots she cannot destroy yet, then returns with the temporary cannon that makes a rematch possible, on the planet ZDR.

MercurySteam and Nintendo released this Switch side-view follow-up to Fusion in 2021. An EMMI grab sends Samus back to the checkpoint. ADAM still advises, Raven Beak waits at the end of the station-to-planet escalation, and the EMMI zones are the rooms where stealth replaces a missile dump.

It is a Switch original, not a port of Fusion. The checkpoint after an EMMI grab is the new punishment for being seen.
tom-clancys-rainbow-six:
Planning the breach comes before the trigger in Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six. Red Storm's tactical shooter makes the player sketch the entry, then carry that plan into the building, where a wrong door order empties the team.

The Nintendo 64 version followed the computer original. In 1998 the loop was already plan, execute, and accept that a single lost operative fails the mission description.

Rainbow's roster is a kit of specialists, not a run-and-gun avatar with a bottomless clip. A heartbeat sensor and a door charge matter more than a circular arena.
mortal-kombat-trilogy:
Three tournaments share one roster in Mortal Kombat Trilogy. Midway packed the first three games together, and the Nintendo 64 cartridge held a larger fighter list than the PlayStation disc.

Shao Kahn, Motaro, and the hidden palette swaps sit beside the living roster in a compilation released in 1996. Motaro's inclusion is the cartridge's roster boast. Fatalities still end the round, but the reason to own this cart is the headcount, not a new realm's story.

The PlayStation release trimmed names the cartridge kept. A mirror match against a boss the disc omitted is the Nintendo 64 edition's boast.
re-volt:
Toy cars take the racing line through a kitchen in Re-Volt. Acclaim's remote-control racer runs those miniatures across houses and streets, where a table leg is a wall and a sidewalk is a highway.

The Nintendo 64 edition shares that scale with the other versions. In 1999 the PC release also included a track editor, a tool the cartridge does not need in order to hide a shortcut under a sofa.

Batteries and pickups decide a toy's pace. The fantasy is a living-room grand prix, not a licensed touring car on a closed circuit.
conkers-bad-fur-day:
Rare scrapped a gentler squirrel and shipped Conker's Bad Fur Day. The foul-mouthed platformer replaced that abandoned family tone with a war chapter, a heist, and a boss fight against the Great Mighty Poo.

The Nintendo 64 game arrived in 2001, with context-sensitive buttons that turn a puddle or a beer keg into the solution. Berri and the Panther King sit in a story that would not have fit the cute pitch Rare first showed.

Multiplayer modes, including a beach assault, share the cartridge with the solo chapters. The humor is the texture; the platforming still asks for a timed jump.
fighting-force:
Belt-scrolling brawls step into polygonal streets in Fighting Force. Core Design tried to carry the arcade beat-em-up into 3D, with weapons lifted off the pavement and rooms that break when a body hits a crate.

The 1997 release reached the new disc consoles and the Nintendo 64. A crate breaks when the body hits it. Four fighters work the same city blocks, and a boss at the end of a district replaces the next wave of identical thugs.

It is a punch-and-throw tour, not a one-on-one duel with special-move motions. The camera sits behind the brawler so a crowd can surround the avatar the way a flat belt-scroller once did.
pokemon-stadium-2:
Gold and Silver teams step into 3D rings in Pokémon Stadium 2. A Transfer Pak cup is not a wild-grass route. A Transfer Pak moves the handheld party onto the Nintendo 64, where gym leaders and rented teams fight under a cup bracket.

Japan received the battle game in 2000. Johto levels get a polygon body in that castle. Minigames and the Gym Leader Castle sit beside the imported Johto roster, which the earlier stadium game could not read from those color cartridges.

It is a fight venue, not a wild-grass journey. The creatures still gain their levels on the Game Boy Color; this cartridge is where those levels get a polygon body.
kirby-64-the-crystal-shards-2000:
Crystal shards hide on every planet Kirby visits in Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards. HAL Laboratory's Nintendo 64 platformer, released in 2000, lets two inhaled powers fuse, so a bomb-spark mix or a stone-cutter mix becomes the key.

Ribbon carries the shattered crystal while Dark Matter hops worlds. Pop Star is only the first stop; later planets change which fusion opens the door.

Combining powers is the puzzle the shards are counting. A player who treats every inhale as a simple replacement, the way earlier Kirby games allowed, will leave half the crystal behind.
yoshis-story-1997:
Pre-rendered dioramas frame the fruit hunt in Yoshi's Story (1997). A melon outscores a trail of apples on the right page. Nintendo followed Yoshi's Island with a side-scroller whose goal is collecting fruit on short pages, and the scenery looks molded rather than hand-tiled.

Six Yoshis still differ by the snack they prefer. A melon on the right page outscores a trail of common fruit, which makes the route a menu choice as much as a jump path.

Baby Bowser's storybook is scored and brief. The SNES island's longer transformation puzzles are a different Yoshi adventure from these layered, pre-rendered pages.
mario-party-3:
Story duels arrive with the Millennium Star in Mario Party 3. The Millennium Star's duel can ignore the four-player couch. Hudson's board game, released in 2000, was the last Mario Party of its kind on the Nintendo 64, and Daisy and Waluigi join the playable roster for those duels.

Partner battles and item shops change a star chase that the first two boards resolved mostly by minigames and coins. A one-on-one story match can ignore the four-player living room and still use the same dice.

Later party games moved to other consoles. The Millennium Star's campaign and the duel maps close the Nintendo 64 run.
mario-tennis-2000:
Tournament brackets share a roster with character growth in Mario Tennis (2000). A trainable backhand stays with one athlete across the bracket. Camelot's Nintendo 64 game mixes cup tennis with stats that change how a fighter covers the court, and a separate Game Boy Color game uses the same title for a school story.

Waluigi's twisted swing and Peach's reach are readable before any stat screen. The charge shot still ends a rally, but the growth system asks a player to stay with one athlete across events.

The color handheld's rookie campaign is not this cartridge. Home-console brackets and the trainable roster are the Nintendo 64 mix.
the-world-is-not-enough:
Eurocom's first-person missions follow the film, and they are not the PlayStation tie-in, in 007: The World is not Enough. The Nintendo 64 shooter uses Bond's gadgets on routes written for that hardware.

Released in 2000, it shares a movie with a different game on the other console. A corridor cleared with the Nintendo 64 control stick is not a level from the PlayStation disc that used the same title footage.

Pierce Brosnan's outing supplies the set pieces. The cartridge's objective list is Eurocom's, which is why the two tie-ins should not be saved as one product.
fifa-98-road-to-world-cup:
Qualifying matches, not a finished World Cup bracket, structure FIFA '98: Road to World Cup. EA themed the soccer annual around the road to the tournament and shipped that edition in 1997.

National teams fight through the qualifying groups the later knockout tournament assumes are already decided. The '98 in the name points at the finals; the cartridge's modes spend their time getting there.

Indoor stadiums and the usual EA pass meter still decide a goal. The campaign's prize is a place in the finals, which a plain exhibition friendly never tracks.
army-men-sarges-heroes:
Plastic soldiers shrink into a kitchen in Army Men: Sarge's Heroes. 3DO took the tan-versus-green army into a third-person shooter in 1999, and Sarge walks the human world where a cereal box is cover.

Portals between the plastic battlefield and the backyard are the level transitions. A toy tank that was scenery on the green table becomes a vehicle once the scale flips.

The Green army is still the enemy. The new map is the household, which the flat plastic campaigns never entered.
destruction-derby:
Wrecking the grid scores more than finishing first in Destruction Derby. Reflections' combat racer, from 1995, awards points for the damage you deal, and it became an early PlayStation staple.

The bowl and the street courses exist so cars can trade paint. A clean qualifying lap matters less than the moment a rival's hood folds.

The Nintendo 64 listing sits beside that reputation. The design is still the demolition score, not a lap-time simulation of an open-wheel season.
nightmare-creatures:
Monster-haunted London is the street map in Nightmare Creatures. Kalisto's 1997 action game plays as a weapon-based brawler, with cobbles, fog, and creatures that close distance faster than a pistol duel would allow.

Blades and kicks answer the things climbing out of the alley. The setting is Victorian gothic, and the camera stays close enough that a swing has to be aimed, not sprayed.

It is a brawler wearing a horror neighborhood. Exploration is the gap between fights, not a quiet investigation with a notebook.
mortal-kombat-mythologies-sub-zero:
Sub-Zero leaves the tournament for a side-scrolling mission in Mortal Kombat Mythologies: Sub-Zero. Midway's 1997 prequel follows the Lin Kuei assassin through traps and bosses, including Quan Chi's interest in a stolen amulet.

Ice moves still freeze a corridor, but the camera and the ladders belong to a platformer. The fighting-game rounds of the main tournaments are not the structure.

Shirai Ryu rivalry hangs over the errand. A fatality prompt never replaces the next ledge.
robotron-2084:
Twin sticks split movement from aim in Robotron: 2084. Grunts pour in from every edge of the room. Eugene Jarvis and Larry DeMar's Williams arcade game, from 1982, asks the player to rescue the last humans while robots flood the room.

Every human saved is a detour from the shot. The grunts, hulks, and brains enter from the edges, and standing still is how a run ends.

The Nintendo 64 library lists the name among its titles. The design people mean is still that arcade twin-stick rescue, not a later 3D cousin with a different subtitle.
f-zero-x-1998:
Nintendo EAD put a huge field on the grid in F-Zero X. Death Race folds the ribbon into a shape Mute City never had. The 1998 futuristic racer is remembered for speed and for track design that folds into cylinders, loops, and ribbons with almost no roadside clutter.

Captain Falcon is one entry on a machine select that scrolls for a long time. Death Race and the X Cup punish a pilot who only practiced the standard Grand Prix lanes.

Mute City returns as a name, then drops the field into a shape the SNES circuit never drew. The Nintendo 64 hardware's willingness to draw that many machines at once is the engineering bet.
mario-golf-1999:
Stroke play shares a menu with a role-playing mode in Mario Golf (1999). A created golfer's approach still obeys the wind. Camelot's Nintendo 64 game lets a created golfer build stats beside the Mario roster's exhibition rounds, and a separate Game Boy Color version carries the same name.

Club choice and wind still decide an approach before any experience point is spent. The RPG mode is a career wrapper, not a battlefield.

The color handheld's story links are a different cartridge. Putting greens and the trainable golfer are the home version's pair of ideas.
vigilante-8-2nd-offense:
Weaponized cars keep an alternate 1970s war going in Vigilante 8: 2nd Offense. Luxoflux followed its vehicular combat game with this 1999 sequel, still a fight between armed vehicles rather than a clean race.

Special weapons mounted on the chassis replace a pit stop. Arenas built from desert diners and half-finished highways are the laps.

The first Vigilante 8 set the decade and the guns. 2nd Offense adds machines and maps without leaving that car-war premise.
south-park-1998:
Snowballs are the ammunition in South Park (1998). Cartman's snowball is a worse joke than a clean aim. Acclaim's first-person shooter, based on the Comedy Central show, puts Cartman, Stan, Kyle, and Kenny in levels that were widely panned when the game launched.

Cows, aliens, and the boys' voices carry the license. Aim is clumsy enough that the joke of the show arrives louder than the shooting.

It is not the later quiz party hosted by Chef. This is the first-person outing, and the reception followed it from the start.
extreme-g-2:
Anti-gravity bikes return armed in Extreme-G 2. A mine on the neon tube is also a racing line. Acclaim's futuristic motorcycle sequel, released in 1998, continues the weaponized races of the first Extreme-G rather than starting a street-legal series.

A boost along a neon tube is also a shot window. Opponents drop mines, and the track can loop overhead while the bike's weapons recharge.

The first game's machines are the precedent. Extreme-G 2's new circuits are still anti-gravity duels, not a muddy rally stage.
rampage-world-tour:
George, Lizzie, and Ralph punch skylines again in Rampage World Tour. Midway revived the gorilla, the lizard, and the wolf for a 1997 city-smashing sequel to the arcade monster game.

Buildings fall when the same wall is hit enough times, and a snatched soldier is a health snack. New cities extend the tour beyond the original arcade's shorter list of blocks.

The Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color releases share those three monsters. Climbing a facade and eating the roof fixtures is still the verb.
bomberman-64-1997:
Polygonal stages and a rescue plot share Bomberman 64 (1997). A thrown bomb can turn a polygonal corner. Hudson moved the series off the flat grid, adding a single-player story about saving people beside the usual blasting.

Gold bombs and kicked explosives still clear a room, but the camera sits inside a 3D space where a bomb can be thrown around a corner. The rescue targets give the solo mode a reason to visit each world.

Multiplayer blasting remains the party. The cartridge's new claim is the polygonal rescue, which the earlier flat puzzles did not stage.
1080deg-snowboarding-1998:
Board weight and landing windows define 1080° Snowboarding (N64). Nintendo EAD's snowboard simulation arrived in 1998 and stayed a favorite of the console's sports line for how heavy a trick feels.

A grab has to be held through the rotation, and a race against another rider punishes a flourish that does not point downhill. Crystal Lake's gates and the steeper caves ask for different lines.

Match race, time attack, and contest share one rider select. The simulation's mass is the reason players kept returning to the same slope.
gex-3-deep-cover-gecko:
Television channels are the worlds in Gex 3: Deep Cover Gecko (1999). A hidden remote opens a channel the trilogy had not used. Crystal Dynamics closed the gecko trilogy with another platformer built on those TV jokes, tail attacks, and remote-control stage selects.

Gex whips with his tail and quotes his way through a channel's set dressing. Rez's media empire is the villainous frame the earlier gecko games already used, and this one spends it on a last set of parody rooms.

Secret remotes hide extra channels. The joke density, not a new move set, is what the trilogy's last cartridge adds.
jet-force-gemini:
Juno, Vela, and Lupus share an insect war in Jet Force Gemini. Rare's 1999 third-person shooter puts the brother, the sister, and their dog against the Drone army on the Nintendo 64.

Each character opens a different slice of the same planets. Tribal allies and the Mizar plot wait behind gates that may require a second hero's weapon.

The dog's route is not a joke slot. Ammunition types and the rescued Tribals make the campaign a scavenger hunt between the firefights.
harvest-moon-64-1999:
Crops, livestock, and town visits fill the days in Harvest Moon 64 (1999). The shipping bin turns a season of crops into cash. Natsume's Nintendo 64 farm simulation is a localization from the Bokujou Monogatari line, and the shipping bin is where a season's work becomes money.

Tools wear down, festivals interrupt the calendar, and the townspeople remember whether you showed up. Marriage candidates and barn animals extend the loop past the first harvest.

It is a farm calendar, not a combat quest. The Bokujou Monogatari source is the reason the chores feel like a life rather than a score attack.
international-superstar-soccer-64:
Through balls and a sharp camera made International Superstar Soccer 64 the one called the best there. A one-two pass beats a special meter on that pitch. Konami released it in 1997, without needing a mascot roster to sell the match.

Player runs and one-two passes reward a timed press more than a special meter. The hexagonal pitch markings and the crowd noise frame a simulation-minded match.

Exhibition and tournament modes use national sides. The reputation came from how the ball left the foot, which rival soccer carts on the same console did not match.
beetle-adventure-racing:
Hidden gates cut the lap in Beetle Adventure Racing. Paradigm's 1999 arcade racer uses Volkswagen's New Beetle, and the shortcuts are buried in barns, castles, and cliffs rather than painted as an obvious racing line.

Crates along the detour pay a risk that the main road does not. Australia received the same race as HSV Adventure Racing, a rename that kept the beetles and the secret doors.

Nitro pads still reward the bold line. The New Beetle's shape is the car; the discovery is the hole in the scenery.
space-station-silicon-valley:
Possessing robot animals is the move set in Space Station Silicon Valley. DMA Design's 1998 puzzle-platformer lets a chip hop from a mouse body to a sheep body while exploring a stranded station.

Each animal's physics solves a different gap. A flying form crosses a fan shaft that the wheeled form can only stare at.

The station's robots are both the tools and the obstacles. Evo's lost body is the reason the chip keeps changing hosts.
hey-you-pikachu:
Players talk to the partner through a headset in Hey You, Pikachu! Nintendo's Nintendo 64 Voice Recognition Unit hears simple requests, and the Japanese release arrived in 1998.

Pikachu reacts to a called name and to activity prompts rather than to a button-mapped attack. Fishing, a walk, and a small errand are scenes the microphone can push forward.

The cartridge is useless without that microphone accessory. A standard controller never became the way this Pikachu listened.
nba-live-2000:
The season after the lockout is the one simulated in NBA Live 2000. The lockout's aftermath is the roster this annual simulates. EA's annual basketball game shipped in 1999, with NBA teams, a season mode, and the usual live-series presentation.

Roster spots reflect the campaign that followed the shortened year, not a fantasy draft of cartoon athletes. Franchise tools and an exhibition tip-off share the same player ratings.

It is not NBA Live 99's lockout-year edition. The 2000 naming covers the season that came next.
winback-covert-operations:
Leaning out of cover is the shot in Winback: Covert Operations. Omega Force and Koei built the 1999 third-person shooter around that peek, years before cover buttons became common.

A laser sight overheats if the trigger stays down. Corridors are designed as slices of wall, so a stand-up charge is how a life ends.

The hero's mission is a rescue under fire, not an open desert. The lean is the mechanic the later cover shooters would be compared against.
v-rally-1997:
Off-road stages established a series in V-Rally (1997). Gravel changes the slide a tarmac stage would forgive. Infogrames' rally racer helped plant that name on PlayStation, and later ports and sequels kept using it.

Gravel, tarmac, and snow change how a slide should be caught. Co-drivers and checkpoint times are the rally language, not a closed oval's lap counter.

The Nintendo 64 release sits among those later arrivals. Those PlayStation races are what made the name a series rather than a one-off billboard.
wwf-no-mercy:
Create-a-wrestler is the tool players still cite inside WWF No Mercy. AKI and THQ's wrestling game, released in 2000, is remembered as a high point of the genre, especially that editor.

Entrances, ladders, and a deep grapple list sit under the created star. SmackDown-era WWF names fill the default roster, but a custom wrestler can main-event a pay-per-view the real card never booked.

The AKI engine's timing is the feel. A reversal window this tight is why the cartridge outlasted the license printed on the box.
star-wars-episode-i-battle-for-naboo:
Naboo's N-1 starfighter, not an X-wing, leads Star Wars Episode I: Battle for Naboo. Factor 5 followed Rogue Squadron with this Nintendo 64 flight shooter in 2000, telling the film's battle from the Naboo side.

Theed, Trade Federation control ships, and ground targets share a mission select. The same technical showpiece that made Rogue Squadron readable returns for a different army.

It is not the Rebel campaign. The yellow fighter and the palace plaza mark whose war this disc is simulating.
chameleon-twist:
A long tongue swings, swallows, and poles in Chameleon Twist. Japan System Supply's 1997 platformer gives the hero that elastic reach, so a distant bar is a grapple point and an enemy can be eaten and spat.

The tongue's length is the jump stat. Levels are built as poles and gaps that a normal hop cannot cross.

A swallowed foe becomes ammunition. The Nintendo 64 camera follows a body whose main limb is the mouth.
the-powerpuff-girls-chemical-x-traction:
Chemical X is the power named in the title of The Powerpuff Girls: Chemical X-traction. The Cartoon Network series became a fighter in 2001, with Blossom, Bubbles, and Buttercup throwing that energy at Mojo Jojo and the other villains.

Arenas quote Townsville rather than a tournament bracket from a fighting-game lineage. A special move spends Chemical X, which is the resource the show already used as the girls' origin.

It is a licensed fighter, not an episode you watch. The three sisters are the roster's center, and the substance in the title is their meter.
custom-robo:
Outfitting a toy fighter is the preparation in Custom Robo. Guns, bombs, pods, and legs snap onto a small robot before the battle, and the series began on the Nintendo 64 in Japan in 1999.

A GameCube game carried the short title west in 2004. Legs and guns snap on before the toy robot ever fires. The Nintendo 64 origin is the Japanese toy-robot battler; the later home release is how many players outside Japan met the name.

Parts change a hover and a shot pattern. The fight is short, and the editing of the little machine is the long part.
dr-mario-64:
Four players drop capsules on shared wells in Dr. Mario 64, and Wario joins that story lineup. Nintendo brought the pill-matching puzzle to the console in 2001.

Viruses still vanish when three matching colors line up. Megavitamins fall as two-tone pills, and a versus rule can dump garbage onto a neighbor's bottle.

Wario's inclusion is the story's twist on the classic clinic. The four-player bottle is the reason to bring the puzzle off the handheld.
clayfighter-63-13:
Clay limbs deform instead of bruising in ClayFighter 63⅓. A squashed clay body is the hit spark. Interplay's claymation fighter arrived on the Nintendo 64 in 1997 as a numbered sequel in the ClayFighter series.

Stop-motion looking models throw specials in 3D arenas. A hit squashes the clay rather than flashing a bruise, which is the visual joke the series is built on.

Earlier ClayFighter games supplied the gooey cast. This numbered Nintendo 64 bout is the one with the fraction in its name and a polygonal ring.
mega-man-64-2001:
Mega Man Volnutt explores a 3D town, not a side-view stage select, in Mega Man 64 (2001). Kattelox Island replaces the Robot Master select. Capcom's Nintendo 64 port of Mega Man Legends swaps the classic run-and-gun for a hub on Kattelox Island.

Roll, the Servbots, and the Flutter airship support a scavenger plot about refractors. The buster still fires, but conversation and a locked door in the city matter as much as the next boss room.

It is the Legends adventure on a cartridge. Side-scrolling Robot Master ladders are a different Mega Man.
body-harvest:
Giant insects occupy open maps across several eras in Body Harvest. DMA Design's 1998 shooter, published by Gremlin, lets the player commandeer cars and trucks while fighting those bugs in wide areas rather than corridors.

A time period changes the vehicles parked on the road. Greece's early streets and a later city's highways are both insect warzones with room to drive around a flank.

The mission is extermination with a steering wheel nearby. Gremlin's publishing and DMA's open lots are the combination the Nintendo 64 version is known for.
superman-the-new-superman-adventures:
Fog rings became the notorious obstacle in Superman: The New Adventures. Titus's 1999 game, better known as Superman 64, puts the hero through those hazy corridors and landed on worst-of lists for how the flight feels.

Lex Luthor's virtual Metropolis is the frame. A ring dive that should be a simple flight lesson instead fights the camera, which is the complaint that followed the cartridge.

It is not a side-scrolling comic adaptation. The fog course and the nickname Superman 64 are what players mean when they bring the game up.
cruisn-world:
Globe-trotting courses follow Cruis'n USA in Cruis'n World. Midway's arcade racer, released in 1998, sends exotic cars through international stages rather than staying on the first game's American roads.

Checkpoints and a boost button keep the lap loud. A landmark from another country is the backdrop, and traffic is an obstacle to shove aside.

The Nintendo 64 port carries that world tour home. Cruis'n Exotica, the later fantasy sequel, is a different set of roads.
bio-freaks:
Limbs come off and bolt back on during Bio F.R.E.A.K.S. A bolted-on arm changes the stance mid-round. Midway's 1998 weapons fighter lets a combatant tear an arm away and mount a replacement without waiting for the next round.

The arena is a floating fight, not a best-of-three mat. A lost limb changes the available weapon until a new one is grabbed from the scrap.

Digitized-looking cyber bodies sell the gore of the swap. The mid-battle rebuild is the mechanic Mortal Kombat's finishing moves never offered as a continuing stance.
south-park-chefs-luv-shack:
Chef hosts the questions in South Park: Chef's Luv Shack. Acclaim turned the Comedy Central show into a quiz-and-minigame party in 1999, with the cafeteria cook running the board.

Trivia about the series sits between short competitive bursts. Cartman, Kyle, Stan, and Kenny are the seats at the board, not first-person avatars in a snowball fight.

The earlier South Park shooter is a different cartridge. Luv Shack is the party night, and Chef's voice is the host track.
snowboard-kids-2:
New riders and new courses continue the cartoon hill in Snowboard Kids 2. An item tossed downhill is the sequel's new trick. Atlus's sequel, released in 1999, keeps item-throwing races where a snowboard is also a weapon platform.

Gates and jumps share the slope with pickups that stun the leader. The cast is still kids on bright boards, not a weighty simulation of a real mountain.

The first Snowboard Kids set the tone. This follow-up's claim is the added roster and the added tracks, still in that exaggerated downhill fight.
power-rangers-lightspeed-rescue:
The rescue team from the television season becomes playable in Power Rangers Lightspeed Rescue. The 2000 action game is one of many licensed Power Rangers titles of that era, built around the Lightspeed crew rather than an earlier Ranger generation.

Demons supply the fights, and the show's rescue framing is the license on the box. A morphing hero clearing a stage is the expected loop, shared with other Ranger games and tied here to this season's cast.

Mariner Bay's team is the roster. It does not try to retell Mighty Morphin from the beginning.
nfl-blitz-1998:
Late hits are legal, and a play can catch fire, in NFL Blitz (1998). A flaming ball carrier is the arcade rule, not a salary cap. Midway's arcade football game is known for exaggerated violence, not for a league simulation of downs and salary caps.

Seven-a-side chaos and huge tackles replace a playbook's nuance. A pass can be launched from anywhere once the arcade rules take over.

It is not Madden's season mode. The Nintendo 64 cabinet-style match is the late hit and the flaming ball carrier.
ridge-racer-64:
Drift courses from two Namco games share Ridge Racer 64. Revolution's corners sit beside the first game's roads. Nintendo Software Technology's 2000 release is the Nintendo 64 chapter of the series, built from Ridge Racer and Ridge Racer Revolution tracks.

A powerslide through a corner is still the skill. Boost pads and the nameless rival cars keep the arcade timing Namco's cabinets taught.

Revolution's layouts sit beside the first game's roads. The Nintendo 64 chapter is that mix, developed at Nintendo's American studio rather than as a straight cabinet dump.
road-rash-64:
Chains and kicks share the bike in Road Rash 64. A chain swung from the bike is not an EA course. THQ's 1999 motorcycle brawler was made for the Nintendo 64 apart from Electronic Arts' earlier Road Rash games.

A punch can knock a rival off the lane while traffic closes in. The weapon in hand matters as much as the throttle, which is the series idea this separate production kept.

EA's original rash of races is a different lineage. This cartridge's courses and its roster were built for Nintendo's hardware without being those earlier discs.
mission-impossible-1998:
Stealth objectives follow Ethan Hunt in Mission: Impossible (1998). A blown alarm restarts the embassy room. Ocean's tie-in is based on the 1996 film, and the Nintendo 64 version is the one the game is best known for.

Disguises, alarms, and a failed sneak restart a room. The embassy and the CIA-flavored infiltration quote the movie without becoming a shooter that rewards every alarm.

Other platforms received the license too. Players who remember the sticky stealth checkpoints usually mean the Nintendo 64 cartridge.
wcw-mayhem:
Television names fill the roster of WCW Mayhem. Electronic Arts' 1999 wrestling game uses the WCW license, so the Monday-night stars are the reason to pick a match.

Entrances and signature moves stand in for a created universe. A title match can book the show's headliners without leaving the WCW banner for a rival promotion.

It is not THQ's Nitro game and not an AKI grappler. EA's presentation of that roster is the cartridge's identity.
turok-rage-wars:
Arena score replaces the Lost Land trek in Turok: Rage Wars. Acclaim's 1999 spin drops most of the exploration and focuses on multiplayer fights in the Turok setting.

Weapons and dinosaur-era maps become deathmatch kits. A campaign of long corridors is what the earlier Turok games asked for; this one asks who controls the pickup.

The rifle and the alien gun still feel like Turok hardware. The mode select is the change: rounds, not a map full of keys.
nba-live-99:
The lockout-shortened season is the one on the cover of NBA Live 99. That abbreviated NBA year is the roster on the box. EA shipped the basketball annual in 1998, tying the rosters to that abbreviated NBA year.

Fewer games on the real calendar did not remove the season mode. Exhibition tip-offs still use the same live-series player ratings and team playbooks.

NBA Live 2000, named for the year that followed, is a different annual. This edition is the lockout year's teams.
namco-museum-1995:
Cabinet art surrounds the coins in Namco Museum (1995). Pac-Man's maze sits in the same hallway as Galaga. PlayStation owners got Namco's arcade set, including Pac-Man, Galaga, and Dig Dug, presented with museum plaques rather than as a bare high-score table.

The mazes, the formations, and the digging dirt play by their coin-op rules. A gallery between games is the compilation's extra room, a walk past the cabinets.

Other Namco Museum volumes picked different lineups. This first gathering is the one with those three marquee machines in the same hallway.
madden-nfl-2001:
Another August kickoff in a long annual line is Madden NFL 2001. John Madden's name still sits over the August kickoff. EA's football game reached stores in 2000, with NFL teams, playbooks, and John Madden's name still on the box.

Season mode and exhibition share the same ratings pile. A created player can sit on a depth chart the real camp never posted.

A pocket edition on Game Boy Color keeps the same NFL depth chart. The Nintendo 64 season is one more year in that unbroken Madden NFL march, not a new sport.
war-gods:
Digitized fighters carry weapons in War Gods. Midway's 1996 3D weapon fighter followed Mortal Kombat in spirit, from the same publisher, with gods battling over a power instead of a tournament trophy alone.

A staff or a blade replaces the bare-handed special. Ring movement in three dimensions changes how a jump-in looks compared with the earlier side-view kombat.

It is not a Mortal Kombat roster with new costumes. The divine cast and the weapon set are the difference Midway shipped.
duke-nukem-64:
Extra stages arrived with the trimmed chaos of Duke Nukem 64. An extra map the PC episode never shipped is on the cart. The cartridge port of Duke Nukem 3D, which reached players in 1997, cut some of the violence for Nintendo and added levels the PC release did not ship.

Duke's boots, the aliens, and the one-liners still structure the corridors. A jetpack section and a shrunk room remain the kind of set piece the build is known for.

The PC shareware episode is not this layout. The cartridge's quieter gore and its extra maps are the Nintendo-specific cut.
international-track-field:
Button-mashing decides the sprint in International Track & Field 2000. Sydney's branding covers the same mash-the-button wrists. Konami's Olympic sequel is themed to the Sydney Games and follows the 1996 International Track & Field.

Swimming, throwing, and track events share a timing bar. A mash that peaks too early wastes the jump, which is the skill the series keeps testing.

Sydney's branding is the new coat. That earlier button-masher is the ancestor, and this edition moves the same wrists to a later Games.
san-francisco-rush-2049:
Airborne lanes and underground cuts push the city forward in San Francisco Rush 2049. A flying gap between towers replaces a simple hill shortcut. Atari sent the arcade city racer into the future in 2000, adding those tracks beyond the original hill streets.

Stunt gaps between buildings replace a simple shortcut through a construction site. The future cars still trade paint on Rush-style roads, only the altitude changed.

The future city also fits on a Game Boy Color cartridge beside the tower gaps. The Nintendo 64 future tour is the one with the flying gaps and the tunnels under the bay.
rocket-robot-on-wheels:
Physics toys fill the first world Sucker Punch shipped, Rocket: Robot on Wheels. The 1999 platformer showed off a Nintendo 64 engine full of swinging parts and stackable objects, before the studio moved on to Sly Cooper.

Rocket the robot solves gaps by grabbing, throwing, and riding contraptions rather than only by jumping. A misplaced crate is a failed puzzle, not background.

Sly Cooper's stealth heists came later and elsewhere. The robot's theme-park machinery is this debut's playground.
puzzle-bobble-2:
Bub and Bob's bubbles gain a sequel in Puzzle Bobble 2. Bust-a-Move II prints the same well under another name. Taito's aiming-and-matching puzzle, also widely sold as Bust-a-Move II, continues the arcade original's shot from the bottom of the well.

A cluster falls when the connected colors lose their anchor. The 1996 follow-up adds boards without changing that clear-the-ceiling goal.

Versus garbage still drops when a large group pops. Bust-a-Move II is the same puzzle under the name many cabinets printed in the West.
wwf-war-zone:
Full-motion entrances introduce a created wrestler in WWF War Zone. Acclaim's 1998 wrestling game is remembered for that create-a-wrestler and for the video entrances that play before the bell.

Grapples and a cage match sit under the WWF roster. A custom star can steal the entrance lighting the real lineup also uses.

AKI's later No Mercy editor is a different engine. War Zone's claim is Acclaim's creation suite and those filmed walkouts.
hot-wheels-turbo-racing:
Orange track and die-cast speed define Hot Wheels Turbo Racing. Stormfront Studios' 1999 arcade racer is a Mattel license built around Hot Wheels cars, loops, and boost pads rather than a touring-car season.

A toy car that leaves the plastic strip for a shortcut still looks like something from the carpet at home. Opponents draft and bump on courses sized like a giant playset.

The Mattel badge is the license. Stormfront's handling is what makes the loop a race instead of a commercial.
nagano-winter-olympics-98:
Skiing and skating share an official license in Nagano Winter Olympics '98. A downhill gate uses a different timing bar from the skate. Konami's sports game shipped in 1997, with those events and other winter disciplines under the Nagano name.

A downhill run and a short-track skate use different timing. The Olympic rings and the Japanese host city are the packaging around the button-timed sports.

It is a licensed multi-event disc, not a single-discipline career. Nagano's slopes are the brand on every menu.
wipeout-64:
Anti-gravity teams race an exclusive chapter in Wipeout 64. Feisar's livery marks a ship built for this hardware. Psygnosis brought the series to the Nintendo 64 in 1998, and this chapter did not ship as a straight copy of the PlayStation seasons.

Weapons and boost pads line circuits built for the cartridge. Feisar and the other team liveries still mark the ships, while the track design is this hardware's own.

Later Wipeout games returned to other platforms. The Nintendo 64 season is the exclusive one, with its own ship balance and its own corners.
iggys-reckin-balls:
Spiked balls climb obstacle towers in Iggy's Reckin' Balls. Iguana's 1998 party racer rolls characters inside those balls through Nintendo 64 courses where a bump is both an attack and a steering error.

Vertical progress matters as much as a lap. A popped rival drops down the tower, which a flat kart race would not do.

The spikes are the body. Iguana built the party mode around colliding spheres rather than around a road's racing line.
wwf-wrestlemania-2000:
AKI's editor grew again for WWF WrestleMania 2000. No Mercy's editor is the aisle this game was paving. THQ shipped the wrestling game in 1999, and it set up the more celebrated No Mercy that followed, still on the same grappling engine.

Entrance gear, a story of WWF calendars, and a large create-a-wrestler share the cartridge. SmackDown names fill the default card while a custom star can be given a finisher the television roster did not use.

Game Boy Color received a smaller sibling. The Nintendo 64 game is the one that paved the aisle toward No Mercy's deeper creation suite.
madden-nfl-2002:
One of the last Madden seasons on the hardware is Madden NFL 2002. This season feels like a farewell kickoff on that hardware. EA's football annual, released in 2001, still offers NFL teams and playbooks on the Nintendo 64 near the end of that console's sports line.

A season can be simulated week by week. John Madden's name remains the brand, and the ratings updates are the ritual the series had already trained players to expect.

Game Boy Color got a companion edition. Later Madden years left the Nintendo 64 behind, which is why this season feels like a farewell kickoff.
wcw-nitro:
Monday Nitro is the television show tied to WCW Nitro. Inland Productions and THQ released the wrestling game in 1998, using the WCW banner and the night of the week the program owned.

Matches book the show's stars rather than a cross-promotion dream card. Strikes and pins follow the license, with the Nitro name promising the Monday roster.

EA's WCW Mayhem is a different publisher's take. This THQ cartridge is the one stapled to the weekly show's title.
san-francisco-rush-extreme-racing:
Hidden ramps started the city series in San Francisco Rush: Extreme Racing. Atari Games released the shortcut-filled racer in 1997, sending cars over the hills where a billboard can hide a leap.

Alcatraz sightlines and downtown drops reward a driver who leaves the marked road. Crash damage and a loud boost are the arcade language the later Rush games inherited.

Rush 2049 pushed the same idea into the future. This first Extreme Racing is the present-day hills and the original secret doors.
international-superstar-soccer-2000:
Konami kept the kickoff going with International Superstar Soccer 2000. A runner off the ball is still the camera's subject. The series reached the Nintendo 64 in 1999, still a national-team match without leaning on a mascot cast.

Through balls and set pieces carry the play. A tournament bracket of countries sits beside a friendly, and the camera stays interested in the runner off the ball.

The earlier International Superstar Soccer 64 is a different season. This 2000-named edition is the later Nintendo 64 continuation, also seen on Game Boy Color.
ms-pac-man-maze-madness:
Dot-munching becomes a 3D walk in Ms. Pac-Man Maze Madness. Namco's 2000 adventure sends Ms. Pac-Man through maze worlds instead of offering a straight port of the arcade board.

Ghosts still chase, but keys, switches, and a moving camera turn the pellets into a path through rooms. Four maze themes replace the single scrolling board.

It is not a high-score loop of the original cabinet. The Nintendo 64 journey uses the bow and the ghosts as characters in a stage list.
cruisn-exotica:
Fantasy roads replace the world tour in Cruis'n Exotica. Midway's third Cruis'n arcade racer arrived in 2000 with courses beyond the earlier real-world cities, including tracks that leave ordinary geography behind.

A boost through a themed set piece matters more than a national landmark. Traffic and checkpoints stay, but the skyline can be a ruin or a dream rather than a capital.

Cruis'n World handled the globe. Exotica is the one that stopped pretending every stage was a real country.
puyo-puyo-sun:
A sun meter charges the chain in Puyo Puyo SUN. Compile's 1997 puzzle keeps the colored-blob clears and adds that meter, which powers up a well-timed pop.

Arle still drops the blobs, and a group of the same color vanishes when it touches a matching neighbor. The sun sits over the well as a resource the earlier Puyo games did not hang there.

Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color both received the sunny rules. Garbage sent to an opponent still depends on the size of the chain, only now the meter can amplify it.
madden-nfl-2000:
Playbooks open another NFL August in Madden NFL 2000. Depth charts for that camp are not the next season's roster. EA released the football annual in 1999, one more season in the Madden NFL line, with John Madden's name over the same weekly ritual.

Teams, depth charts, and exhibition kicks share the disc or cartridge. A franchise week still asks which player is healthy enough to start.

Madden NFL 2001 and Madden NFL 2002 are neighboring seasons, not this roster. The 2000 edition is its own camp and its own ratings.
mace-the-dark-age:
Fantasy weapons clash in 3D arenas in Mace: The Dark Age. Atari's 1997 fighter pits those combatants against each other in arcades and on the Nintendo 64, with blades and spells instead of a modern street.

A ring-out or a heavy swing ends the round. The dark-fantasy cast, including fighters who do not look like digitized actors, separates it from Midway's weapon gods.

Cabinets and the Nintendo 64 share the move lists. The arena's edge is as dangerous as the opponent's sword.
chameleon-twist-2:
New rooms keep the elastic tongue busy in Chameleon Twist 2. A swallowed foe is still ammunition on the new poles. Japan System Supply continued the Nintendo 64 platformer in 1998, still swinging from poles and swallowing foes with the same long reach.

The sequel's layouts change which gap the tongue must bridge. A swallowed enemy remains ammunition, and the camera still chases a hero whose mouth is the grappling hook.

The first Chameleon Twist introduced the limb. This follow-up spends it on a second set of poles, pits, and targets.
nascar-2000:
Stock cars circle another EA season in NASCAR 2000. Daytona's banking shares a weekend with the shorter ovals. The annual reached players in 1999 as one entry in the long EA Sports NASCAR line, with licensed stock-car racing rather than a fantasy vehicle.

Drafting on a superspeedway and a pit stop for tires are the season's verbs. Daytona's banking and the shorter ovals share a weekend structure of practice and race.

NASCAR 99 is the earlier annual. This 2000-named edition is the next garage, not a rally detour.
monaco-grand-prix:
The harbor circuit is the subject of Monaco Grand Prix. Ubisoft's 1999 street racer focuses on the famous race around the principality and was also sold under a Racing Simulation name.

The tunnel, the swimming pool chicane, and the barriers leave little runoff. A qualifying lap on that layout is the mode the title promises, more than a globe of unrelated tracks.

The alternate Racing Simulation branding wrapped the same streets. Monaco's barriers, not an oval, are the test.
knockout-kings-2000:
Licensed professionals fill the ring in Knockout Kings 2000. Jab timing and a stamina meter replace a cartoon windup. EA's boxing game shipped in 1999 as part of the Knockout Kings series of real fighters, with jab timing and a stamina meter rather than a cartoon windup.

A career can move a boxer up a card of those licensed names. The corner's advice and the punch stats sit under a simulation of rounds, not a single special-move duel.

Later Knockout Kings seasons changed the roster. This 2000-named edition is the camp EA released at the end of the decade.
wheel-of-fortune-old:
Spinning for consonants is the whole turn in Wheel of Fortune (Old). The early home version of the television quiz, dated 1988, lets players spin a wheel and call letters against a puzzle board.

A bankrupt wedge still ruins a hot streak. The host's wheel and the letter board are the show, translated into a game that does not need a new plot.

Later television seasons changed sets and prizes. This older home edition is the wheel-and-letter ritual from the dated release, before the show's later stage designs.
top-gear-rally:
Weather moves across the stage in Top Gear Rally. Boss Game Studios and Kemco released the Nintendo 64 rally racer in 1997, and the courses are noted for rain and snow that change grip mid-race.

A slide on a drying line is a different car from the same machine in clear air. Rally timing and service intervals frame the weather, rather than a closed-oval draft.

Game Boy Color received a related version. The Nintendo 64 storms are the ones players remember when the name comes up.
puzzle-bobble-3:
A third ceiling of bubbles continues the shot in Puzzle Bobble 3. A new bubble type interrupts a simple color match. Taito's matcher, also sold under the Bust-a-Move name, follows Puzzle Bobble 2 without abandoning the aim-from-below clear.

New bubble types interrupt a simple color match. The 1997 entry still drops a cluster when its anchor pops, and versus play still punishes a small clear.

Bub and Bob remain the mascots on the well. Bust-a-Move players met the same third round under the Western title.
wetrix:
Raised earth is the only bowl in Wetrix. Zed Two's puzzle makes you lift and lower terrain so falling water does not spill off the map, and it became a known Nintendo 64 puzzle release.

A lake that breaches a low wall ends the board. Fire and ice pieces complicate the plumbing, but the failure is always a spill.

The 1997 idea is landscaping under pressure. Points come from the water you manage to keep, not from a line of matching tiles.
shadowgate-64-trials-of-the-four-towers:
Torches still burn down inside a polygonal castle in Shadowgate 64: Trials of the Four Towers. Kemco's 1999 adventure retells the 1987 castle quest in 3D, with the four towers as the structure of the exploration.

A skull, a lever, and a dying flame remain the kind of threat the point-and-click original used. The Nintendo 64 camera walks the halls the older illustrated rooms only showed as stills.

The 1987 story is the plot being retold. This edition's claim is the 3D trial through those towers, not a new kingdom.
nascar-99:
An earlier garage in the same annual line is NASCAR 99. Caution flags already structure this earlier Sunday. EA's stock-car game shipped in 1998, before the later numbered editions, with superspeedways and pit strategy already in place.

Drafting packs and caution flags structure a Sunday. The car numbers and the ovals mark it as stock-car racing, not an off-road stage.

NASCAR 2000 is the next season's product. This one is the prior year's garage, still under EA's NASCAR banner.
ecw-hardcore-revolution:
Tables and the promotion's reputation define ECW Hardcore Revolution. Acclaim's 2000 wrestling game uses the Extreme Championship Wrestling license and the hardcore-match image that license carried.

Weapons at ringside matter more than a clean pin sequence. The ECW roster is the card, and a brawl that leaves the ring fits the name on the box.

A smaller hardcore card on Game Boy Color carries the ECW license too. It is not a WCW television sim and not AKI's WWF engine.
blues-brothers-2000:
Jake and Elwood share a platforming job in Blues Brothers 2000. Sunglasses and suits keep Jake and Elwood moving. The game follows the brothers and is tied to the film of the same name, with sunglasses, suits, and a mission that keeps moving them forward.

Jumps and hazards sit under the musical license. A set piece quotes the movie's pair rather than inventing a new duo.

The film's title is the game's title. Playing it means steering Jake and Elwood, not watching the concert from a menu.
f-1-world-grand-prix:
A full calendar of circuits makes a season in F-1 World Grand Prix. Video System's 1998 Nintendo 64 simulation runs Formula 1 across real-world tracks, with practice and race weekends rather than a single fantasy oval.

Monaco's barriers and Monza's straights can appear on the same schedule. Car setup and a qualifying lap change the grid before the lights go out.

It is a season, not a mini-game of one famous corner. Video System's handling model is what the Nintendo 64 weekend uses.
battletanx-global-assault:
Rival tanks roll through another ruined map in BattleTanx: Global Assault. 3DO followed its tank combat game with this 1999 Nintendo 64 shooter, still a war of armored vehicles rather than infantry corridors.

A campaign of rival machines gives the sequel its targets. Turrets and pickups decide a street that the first BattleTanx already taught players to fear.

The global name widens the theaters. It remains a tank duel, with the sequel's maps as the new cities to flatten.
buck-bumble:
An armed bee patrols the garden in Buck Bumble. Argonaut's 1998 shooter puts the player in control of that insect on the Nintendo 64, with guns mounted on a body the size of a flower.

Blades of grass become walls. Enemy insects fill the backyard, and the bee's weapons are the joke and the aiming challenge at once.

Argonaut's tiny protagonist is not a jet. The garden scale is the level design.
automobili-lamborghini:
Italian badges line the grid in Automobili Lamborghini. Titus's 1997 Nintendo 64 racer is built around those sports cars and was called Super Speed Race in Japan.

A high-speed license plate matters more than a story. Corners and a boost ask the car to behave like the badge on the hood, which is the fantasy the Japanese title also sold.

Super Speed Race is the same machine under another name. The Nintendo 64 grid is Lamborghini's, not a fictional prototype studio's.
nba-hangtime:
Exaggerated dunks succeed NBA Jam in NBA Hangtime. Midway's 1997 arcade basketball game keeps those oversized slams and adds a create-a-player on top of the two-on-two chaos.

A player on fire still changes the shooter's confidence. The create-a-player lets a custom face join the NBA roster the arcade cabinet already shouted out.

It is not EA's season simulation. Hangtime's verb is the dunk, and the new face is the mode Jam's first cabinets lacked.
polaris-snocross:
Polaris sleds hit snowmobile gates in Polaris SnoCross. Vicarious Visions' 2000 racer carries that brand onto the Nintendo 64, with snocross whoops and icy berms instead of asphalt.

A bad landing in the whoops costs more than a wide line. The Polaris name on the hood is the license, and the track is built for skis and a track, not tires.

Those Polaris sleds also race on Game Boy Color, whoops included. The Nintendo 64 snow is the one with the full whoop sections.
hybrid-heaven:
Limb-targeted blows feed the stats in Hybrid Heaven. Konami's 1999 Nintendo 64 game mixes role-playing numbers with close-quarters fighting in a science-fiction bunker.

A punch aimed at an arm can weaken the next grapple. Experience changes which strikes exist, so the fight is not a fixed special-move list.

The setting is a future facility, not a fantasy town. Konami's combination of menus and melee is the oddity the cartridge is remembered for.
aero-fighters-assault:
Jets leave the flat cabinet for large sorties in Aero Fighters Assault. Paradigm and Video System took the shooter series into 3D with this 1997 Nintendo 64 entry.

A lock-on and a canyon run replace a vertically scrolling formation. The Aero Fighters name, also known from the Sonic Wings cabinets, supplies the pilots while the geometry is new.

Ground targets and rival aces share a mission. The 3D assault is the chapter that stopped being a single-screen swarm.
scooby-doo-classic-creep-capers:
The Mystery Machine crew hunts a culprit in Scooby-Doo! Classic Creep Capers. THQ's 2001 adventure is a 3D take on the Hanna-Barbera cartoon, with Fred, Daphne, Velma, Shaggy, and Scooby searching for clues.

A mask coming off is still the punchline the show trained viewers to expect. The Nintendo 64 rooms are explored rather than watched, and a scared dash from Shaggy can be the fail state.

The gang's roles stay familiar. It is a mystery walk, not a fighter wearing the same dog.
pokemon-pinball:
Catching happens on the playfield in Pokémon Pinball. Jupiter and HAL Laboratory's 1999 Game Boy Color game puts Pokemon on pinball tables, and a well-aimed hit sends one into the ball for a capture.

The red and blue tables echo the paired versions' mascots. Evolution and a Pokedex fill up from successful catches between the bumpers, which a plain high-score table never tracked.

Nintendo published the cartridge. It is a pinball table with a Pokedex, not a gym challenge that happens to use a flipper.
102-dalmatians-puppies-to-the-rescue:
Oddball and her brother Domino carry 102 Dalmatians: Puppies to the Rescue, the chase spun from the film sequel. Cruella de Vil has caged the rest of the litter, so the stages are a rescue rather than a stroll through town.

A puppy's kit is a bark, a shove, and a short hop. Toy rooms, alley walls, and a factory of cages turn the kidnapping plot into obstacles a dog the size of a boot can clear.

The parent picture is itself a follow-up to the famous Dalmatian story, and this 2000 tie-in keeps that sequel's spotless puppy in front. Clearing a room means finding the stolen pups, not racing a clock for its own sake.
xena-warrior-princess:
Lucy Lawless's syndicated hero reached living rooms again when Xena: Warrior Princess became a 1999 action game, and Titus later shipped a separate handheld version. Gabrielle's road companion and the chakram belong to the television warrior, not to a generic sword fighter.

The PlayStation release and the smaller cartridge do not share a camera. One is a 3D brawler built around the show's fights, while the handheld keeps Xena in a tighter side view with the same leather-and-steel silhouette.

Callisto, Ares, and the gods of that series are the kind of opposition the license implies, and the handheld does not pretend to be the disc. Titus treated the color cart as its own outing rather than a squeezed copy of every PlayStation stage.
croc-2:
Baron Dante's crocodile returns in Croc 2 still looking for the Gobbos and, this time, for the parents he never met. Fox Interactive's 1999 sequel leaves the first island's simple rescue-and-exit rhythm for villages that hand out errands.

The little crocodile still beats enemies with a tail swipe and rides geysers between ledges. Swap-in helpers and a wider map distinguish the follow-up from Croc: Legend of the Gobbos, where the job was mostly freeing the small furry captives.

A color handheld edition shrinks that village-and-quest structure into a flatter run without abandoning the search. The Gobbos remain the neighbors worth saving, and the missing family is the reason the journey continues past the first adventure.
army-men:
Green plastic faces tan plastic in Army Men, the 1998 opener of a long toy-soldier line from 3DO. Sarge and his squad treat a kitchen, a yard, and a picnic table as a war zone sized for figures that stand an inch tall.

The fantasy is the scale. A garden hose is a river, a birthday candle can be cover, and the tan army's machines are molded from the same bin as the green rifles.

Sequels kept coming after this first clash, some squad-sized and some later real-time. The original joke still sticks: a serious campaign fought by toys that look like they came from a hardware-store bag.
super-mario-bros-deluxe:
Challenge scores and a linked versus race sit beside the familiar pipes in Super Mario Bros. Deluxe. Nintendo's 1999 cart holds the original side-scroller, material from the Japanese Lost Levels, and a set of extra trials that ask for more than a straight run to the flagpole.

Boo can chase Luigi across a course in the versus option, and a toy box of extras sits outside the stages. Hidden coins and a print-ready album give the small screen reasons to revisit a level the living-room original finished in a few minutes.

World 1-1's goombas and Bowser's false bridges remain the spine. What the color cart adds is the second quest's harder layouts and the challenge targets, so a player who has already saved the princess still has a reason to keep the cartridge in the slot.
x-men-mutant-academy:
Danger Room style sparring is the frame for X-Men: Mutant Academy, Activision's 2000 one-on-one fighter. Wolverine's claws, Cyclops's optic blast, and Storm's weather sit on a versus roster instead of inside a scrolling brawl.

Marvel's students and teachers take turns as playable fighters, and a short story mode sends them through academy matches rather than through a single mutant's solo hunt. The combo timing is the skill, not a long walk between bosses.

A later Academy sequel continued the same versus idea. This release is the first of those fighter carts, the one that put the team into direct matches instead of a side-view march.
metal-gear-ghost-babel:
Solid Snake infiltrates Galuade in Metal Gear: Ghost Babel, and the mission is not a replay of Shadow Moses. Konami's 2000 stealth game was retitled Metal Gear Solid outside Japan, yet the story stands apart from the PlayStation episode.

A top-down radar, a cardboard box, and a codec call are the tools, squeezed onto a small screen that still wants the player to avoid a guard's cone. The outer-heaven fortress, the new Metal Gear, and a different cast of rivals keep the plot from being a portable summary of the disc.

Western boxes borrowed the Solid name because that was the brand shoppers knew. Inside, the infiltration is its own what-if, with Snake sneaking through a fortress the PlayStation game never mapped.
blade:
Wesley Snipes's daywalker carries the sword in Blade (2000), cutting through vampires that hate his sunlight. The handheld hunt keeps the coat and the blade rather than every scene of the film.
