Whistler's world of serum and silver is the backdrop, while the stages put Blade in alleys and nests where a firearm and a blade take turns. The tie-in does not retell every scene of the movie; it keeps the hunt and the leather coat.

A later film and a later console game expanded the same character. This cart is the small-screen version of that first movie's premise: one immune hunter against a city of vampires.
moorhuhn-2:
Pheasants explode out of a countryside scene in Moorhuhn 2, the sequel Germany already knew under the Crazy Chicken name. The 2000 follow-up keeps the joke of the original casual hit: a cursor, a gun, and a sky full of birds that deduct points if the wrong thing is hit.

Antlers, aircraft, and bonus targets interrupt the flock so a round is not only a matter of speed. The humor is local and broad, which is why the series traveled under two titles depending on the shelf.

Point-and-shoot rounds made the first pheasant game a phenomenon on home computers, and the sequel adds busier scenes without changing the rule. Empty the sky, mind the penalty targets, and the round ends when the clock does.
lego-island-2-the-bricksters-revenge:
Pepper Roni pedals after an escaped convict in LEGO Island 2: The Brickster's Revenge. The 2001 sequel starts from the jailbreak that ended the first island story and sends the pizza-delivery kid across themed lands built from bricks.

Castle gates, adventurer ruins, and a spaceport each change the vehicle and the puzzles, while the Brickster stays one step ahead with a stolen construction. Minifigure scale means a door is a stack of bricks and a bridge can be rebuilt if the right pieces are found.

The home-computer adventure is the wide version of that chase. A smaller cart tells the same escape with tighter stages, still starring Pepper, the Brickster, and the island that cannot hold its villain.
hugo-the-evil-mirror:
A witch's curse splits a family across glass in Hugo: The Evil Mirror, a 2002 stop on the long trail of the Danish television troll. Children had shouted moves at Hugo for years on a live show; this entry turns that troll into a side-view runner.

Mirrors are the stages' logic. Hugo hops, throws, and hunts for the relatives trapped behind the glass, while the curse is the reason the forest no longer behaves.

The series had already jumped from studio audiences to home screens many times before this one. What marks the mirror story is the rescue of Hugo's own household, not another round of the show's minigames.
mat-hoffmans-pro-bmx:
Vert ramps carry the name of a real rider in Mat Hoffman's Pro BMX, Activision's 2001 trick game from the same boom as Tony Hawk. Hoffman, nicknamed the Condor, is the marquee pro, and the sessions are about air, grinds, and a score rather than a finish line.

A handheld edition flattens the parks into a side view where the stick still times a tailwhip. The home versions had room for larger bowls; the small cart keeps the rider, the sponsors' feel, and the two-minute run.

Tony Hawk's skate games had already taught players a trick grammar. This BMX set borrows that grammar for pegs and dirt, with Hoffman's name on the box as the proof it is not another skateboard.
mr-driller:
Susumu Hori's air meter is the real opponent in Mr. Driller, Namco's 2000 descent through colored blocks. Drill a connected group of the same color and it vanishes; drill carelessly and the shaft above collapses onto the little driller.

Pockets of air refill the meter, which is always draining. The deeper the hole, the stranger the color patterns, and a missed capsule ends the run faster than any monster would.

Taizo's son, heir to a digging legacy, is a puzzle character rather than an explorer with a map. That release made the single-screen panic a series: color, oxygen, and the next block down.
test-drive-6:
Licensed metal and a police radar define Test Drive 6, Accolade's 1999 street-racing stop on a series that had been selling point-to-point courses for years. The courses run from city to city rather than around a closed oval, and the cars wear real manufacturer badges.

Traffic, a checkpoint clock, and a patrol car that takes offense at a high speed are the hazards. A handheld version keeps the same fantasy, a named sports car and a road with an end, even when the scenery is reduced to a strip.

Earlier Test Drive games had already made the license the selling point. This sixth entry refreshes the garage and the map without turning the series into a circuit championship.
dave-mirra-freestyle-bmx:
X Games dirt and a side-view trick line meet in Dave Mirra Freestyle BMX, Acclaim's 2000 debut built around the real rider and other pro BMX names. The home versions on PlayStation and Dreamcast are 3D park sessions; the color handheld cart is a smaller profile view, not that 3D game squeezed until it fit.

Manuals, grinds, and a clock still decide a run on the small screen. Mirra's name sits on the box because the license, not a fictional mascot, was the draw in that skate-and-bike season.

Dave Mirra Freestyle BMX 2 is the sequel, with a larger roster and new parks on the home consoles. The first cart, especially the flat handheld edition, is the one that introduced the rider before the follow-up arrived.
buzz-lightyear-of-star-command:
Emperor Zurg, not Andy's toy box, is the threat in Buzz Lightyear of Star Command. Disney's television spinoff, rather than the Toy Story films alone, supplies this 2000 platform chase, with Star Command's ranger in the lead.

Mira Nova, Booster, and XR belong to that show's crew, and the stages send Buzz through alien corridors with a laser and a jump. The movie's bedroom is not the map; the cartoon's space ranger duty is.

A film about a doll who thinks he is a ranger came first. This cart plays the assignment the cartoon gave him, Zurg included, without requiring the player to have watched Woody's side of the story.
the-grinch:
Whoville's presents are the target in The Grinch, the platform tie-in to Ron Howard's film of the Dr. Seuss book. The 2000 cart puts the green grump on rooftops and in toy shops, stealing and sneaking in the movie's spirit.

Max the dog and the mayor's inflated Christmas are part of that Seuss town, and the stages turn the heist into jumps, gadgets, and a sack. Cindy Lou Who's holiday is the thing being ruined, which keeps the plot pointed at the mountain above town.

Other Seuss games have starred the Cat or the Lorax. This one is only the Howard film's Grinch, mean on purpose, working through a town of Whos before any change of heart.
walt-disney-world-quest-magical-racing-t:
Space Mountain and the Haunted Mansion become laps in Walt Disney World Quest: Magical Racing Tour. Eidos published the 2000 kart race set inside the Florida resort, with Disney characters driving instead of watching a parade.

Gates, themed hazards, and a boost tied to the park's own attractions are the racing language. A haunted foyer, a jungle cruise, and a tomorrowland straight each ask for a different line, and the karts are sized like ride vehicles.

Florida's actual park map is the license. The game is not a generic castle circuit with mouse ears pasted on; the courses are the resort's lands, which is the reason the title bothers to name the place.
chicken-run:
Ginger's pie-machine escape is the plot of Chicken Run, the 2000 tie-in to Aardman's stop-motion film. Mrs. Tweedy's farm is a prison, Rocky is the circus rooster who claims he can fly, and the chickens are building a way out.

Stealth, fetching parts, and avoiding dog and human patrols fit a story about a breakout rather than a straight brawl. The clay look of the movie is the reference point: huts, fences, and the dreadful machine in the barn.

Aardman's chickens are not cartoon birds in a generic yard. The tie-in keeps Tweedy's farm, the coop, and the plan to leave before anyone becomes a pie.
bust-a-move-4:
Bub and Bob aim upward again in Puzzle Bobble 4, the Taito matcher also sold as Bust-a-Move. The 1998 console entry adds bubble types and a ceiling that creeps down when the player hesitates.

Matching three or more of a color drops every bubble hanging from that cluster. New bubble types in this installment change how a chain falls, so a shot that only matched in the earlier games can now bounce into a larger collapse.

The dinosaurs from Bubble Bobble are still the operators of the cannon. What players remember is the ceiling, the aim, and the last bubble that either clears the round or ends it.
wacky-races-1991:
Dick Dastardly's Mean Machine belongs to the cartoon, but Wacky Races (1991) is a computer platformer from Hi-Tec Software, not a lap around those deserts. Hanna-Barbera's racers are the cast, and the Amiga and the Commodore 64 are among the machines where that version lived.

Penelope Pitstop, Muttley, and the other drivers arrive as cameos from the Saturday cartoon, while the play is jumping and dodging rather than steering the Compact Pussycat through a finish banner. Dastardly's sabotage survives as hazards instead of as race position.

A later racing game reused the same cartoon. Hi-Tec's older release is the side-view one, the odd case of a famous motor derby turned into ledges and enemies.
hype-the-time-quest:
A stone knight wakes in the wrong century in Hype: The Time Quest, Ubisoft's 1999 action role-playing game. Hype, the knight, has been thrown through time, and each era changes the enemies and the tools he carries back to the fight.

Real-time sword swings share the screen with a party of companions met along the way. Medieval yards, later cities, and a future that does not belong to a fairy tale are the stops, so the inventory has to make sense in more than one age.

Ubisoft framed the whole trip around that one displaced knight. The time jumps are the campaign, not a bonus stage bolted onto a single castle.
rampart-1990:
Ship fire knocks holes in a fortress during Rampart (1990), then a clock demands the walls be rebuilt. Atari Games alternates cannon defense with a building phase, and later home ports kept that two-beat round.

Tetris-like pieces drop so a gap in the curtain wall can be plugged before the next fleet arrives. Fail to enclose a castle and the round is already lost, no matter how many ships the cannons sank.

The arcade cabinet made the alternation famous, and later machines from computers to consoles copied it. Placing the wall, then answering the fleet, is the entire argument of the design.
milons-secret-castle-1986:
Bubbles are the key and the weapon in Milon's Secret Castle (1988), Hudson Soft's maze of hidden doors. The adventure debuted on the Famicom Disk System in 1986 and reached the NES under this title, with a boy who pops bubbles to open a castle that will not label its rooms.

Shops hide behind ordinary bricks, and a boss waits where a bubble revealed a ladder. Queen Eliza's captivity is the reason to keep searching, but the castle rarely says which wall is fake.

Hudson's habit of secret rooms is the difficulty. Players traded rumors about which brick to strike, because the map itself refuses to be a guide.
tomb-raider-curse-of-the-sword:
Lara Croft's pistols meet a cursed blade in Tomb Raider: Curse of the Sword, the 2001 handheld adventure Core Design made and Activision published. It is a sequel to the earlier handheld Tomb Raider, still a side-view trek rather than the 3D tombs of the home console games.

Levers, ledges, and a weapon that is also a problem push Lara through ruins and streets. The sword of the title is the story's complication, not a simple damage upgrade, and the small screen keeps the climbing readable.

Core had already defined Lara on PlayStation and Saturn. This cart continues the pocket line those studios' handheld sequel started, with the curse as the new reason to raid.
lufia-the-legend-returns-2001:
Ancient Sinistrals haunt the party in Lufia: The Legend Returns (2001), a pocket journey of towns and turn-based battles. The small screen still has to hold a full group of allies between dungeons.

Recruitable allies, far more than a fixed party of four, distinguish this chapter from a straight retelling of the fortress stories on home consoles. Random encounters, spells, and equipment shops are the rhythm between story scenes.

Earlier Lufia games had already made the Sinistrals a recurring doom. This chapter keeps that lineage and spends its novelty on who can join and how a battle fits in a pocket.
stuart-little-2:
Margalo the canary and a falcon pull Stuart into the city in Stuart Little 2, the 2002 tie-in to the second film. The mouse of the house is the playable lead, with Snowbell the cat still part of the family the movie assembled.

Rooftops, model planes, and rooms that are huge because the hero is small define the obstacles. The falcon is the kidnapper the plot has to answer, so the stages move from the Littles' home toward a rescue.

E.B. White's mouse had already been filmed once. This follow-up game sticks to the second picture's bird, the falcon, and the mouse who treats a toy airplane as a serious vehicle.
survival-kids:
Hunger and a handmade axe matter more than a sword in Survival Kids, Konami's 1999 island story, also called Stranded Kids. Children washed onto a hostile shore have to fish, build, and read the weather if they want to see another morning.

Day and night change which animals move, and a tool made from beach scrap opens a path a bare hand cannot. The hostile island is the antagonist: snakes, cliffs, and an empty stomach, not a dark lord with a speech.

Konami aimed the loop at patience. Eat, craft, explore, and sleep, then repeat, until the shore offers a way home.
megami-tensei-gaiden-last-bible:
Demon partners fill the party in Megami Tensei Gaiden: Last Bible, the Game Boy spinoff that opened the Last Bible line. A 1994 monster-collecting role-playing game wearing the Megami Tensei name, it sends a young hero out to recruit the very creatures other games would only have fought.

Talking a demon into joining, then fusing that roster into something stronger, is the loop beneath the turn-based fights. Towns still sell herbs and rumors, but the encyclopedia of monsters is the real equipment list.

Later Last Bible chapters continued the same recruiting. This first one is the spinoff that proved the Megami Tensei habit of negotiation could live on a pocket cartridge.
harvest-moon-3-gbc-2000:
Crops and livestock fill the days in Harvest Moon 3 GBC (2000), the third color-handheld entry after Harvest Moon GB and Harvest Moon 2 GBC. A town remembers how the farmer treats it, and the daylight still runs out too soon.

Watering, shipping produce, and brushing an animal are the morning. Festivals and courtship fill the evening, with a bachelor or bachelorette whose heart meter moves when the farmer shows up with the right gift.

The series had already taught players that a farm is a calendar. This third pocket chapter adds another valley, another set of neighbors, and the same risk of letting the turnips die.
redline-racer:
Superbike lean is the whole camera in Redline Racer, and it is Criterion Games' first release. The 1998 motorcycle racer is an early step for the studio later known for Burnout, already obsessed with speed and a road that punishes a bad line.

A tucked rider, a cockpit rush, and courses built for top speed are the contents. There is no combat power-up fantasy here; the crash is what happens when the racing line fails.

Burnout's later crash cinema grew out of a team that had already shipped a bike game about velocity. This debut is that bike game, the one that put Criterion on a road before the takedown series existed.
warriors-of-might-and-magic:
Hack-and-slash corridors, not a hero grid, are the battlefield in Warriors of Might and Magic. 3DO's 2000 spinoff is an action role-playing game, deliberately separate from the turn-based Heroes strategy games that share the license.

A single champion clears dungeons, gains levels, and manages a bar of health and mana while enemies rush in real time. Castles and creature names echo Might and Magic, but there is no weekly hero moving across an overland map.

Heroes of Might and Magic kept the turn order and the castle sieges. This warrior's outing is the other shelf: one body, one weapon, and rooms full of the franchise's monsters.
lego-stunt-rally:
Brick-built ramps are the courses in LEGO Stunt Rally, a 2000 racer whose tracks are assembled from LEGO pieces. Cars made of the same studs jump gaps, and a bad landing scatters the tidy geometry the course was built from.

Studs, slopes, and loop shapes replace asphalt and guardrails. The license is not only the minifigure in the driver's seat; the road itself looks like a table covered in construction toys.

Other brick games of that season explored islands or agents. This one stays on the stunt track, with the pieces doing the work of both the car and the corner.
woody-woodpecker-racing:
A laugh and a beak lead the grid in Woody Woodpecker Racing, the 2000 kart racer headlined by Universal's cartoon bird. Other licensed characters from that studio's cartoons share the cups, so the woodpecker is the star rather than the only driver.

Power-ups, a three-lap circuit, and a course dressed in cartoon props are the racing. Woody's peck and the rival birds' gags decide who leaves the last corner with a boost.

Universal had a bench of theatrical cartoons to draw from. The kart uses that bench, with Woody's name large on the box and the rest of the roster filling the starting lights.
deja-vu:
A bathroom stall, a headache, and a murder charge open Deja Vu: A Nightmare Comes True. ICOM Simulations' 1985 MacVenture is a point-and-click noir about an amnesiac in Chicago, played through windows of verbs rather than a walking avatar.

Examine, open, take, and hit are the commands, aimed at a briefcase, a gun, and a city that already thinks the hero is guilty. The 1940s streets and a body the protagonist cannot remember are the mystery's engine.

Later ports carried the same windowed investigation onto consoles and handhelds. The case itself stays Chicago, the stall, and the missing memory.
spider-man-n64:
Webs replace stairs in Spider-Man (2001), one of the action games from the wave of Spider-Man titles just before the 2002 film. Marvel's wall-crawler swings, punches, and sticks to brick while a city of familiar enemies waits below.

Doctor Octopus, street thugs, and a skyline of fire escapes give the swing a reason to exist. A camera that follows the web line is what the larger versions of that wave were built around, and the mask's quips keep the fights from feeling like a silent beat-em-up.

A movie in 2002 would soon fix one actor's face to the mask. This earlier outing still belongs to the comics wave that came just before that film, with the web as the way across town.
deer-hunter:
A tree stand and a deer call are the equipment in Deer Hunter. The budget hunting sim became a surprise PC hit in 1997, and later follow-ups stretched a quiet wait into a long line of hunts.

Tracks, wind, and a rifle scope replace a health bar. The deer is not a boss with a pattern so much as an animal that spooks if the hunter moves wrong, which is why the game found an audience far outside the usual enthusiast shops.

No blockbuster campaign explains that hit. A low price, a recognizable hobby, and a stand in the woods were enough, and the sequels spent years subdividing the same hunt.
spider-man-2-the-sinister-six:
Doctor Octopus, Mysterio, Electro, the Vulture, Sandman, and a sixth schemer share the marquee of Spider-Man 2: The Sinister Six. Torus Games' 2001 handheld pits the wall-crawler against that villain team, and it is not the later movie game that reused a similar numeral.

Side-view punches, web shots, and a boss at the end of a stretch of thugs are the rhythm. Each member of the six brings a gimmick, so a sand storm and an illusion are not the same fight as a tentacle grab.

Activision's movie tie-ins came afterward and told a different story. Torus's cart is the comics team-up, the one whose title names the Sinister Six outright.
wings-of-fury-1987:
A carrier deck is home base in Wings of Fury (1987), and the plane must strafe ships before it lands. Broderbund's side-scrolling World War II sortie spends its bombs on vessels and shore guns, then asks for the deck again.

Torpedoes, bombs, and machine guns are separate tools, and an enemy battleship is a different problem from a shore gun. The Pacific setting stays in profile, so altitude is a lane and the carrier is a moving runway at the edge of the screen.

Apple II players met the sortie first, and other home computers followed. Takeoff, attack, and a careful return to the deck are the loop the title never abandons.
alleyway:
Mario's head is the paddle in Alleyway. Nintendo's brick-breaker from the Game Boy's early shelf in 1989 follows the Breakout tradition of a ball, a wall of bricks, and a bat that has to keep the ball alive.

Bonus stages freeze the destruction and arrange bricks into pictures, including ships and creatures a player can clear for the shape rather than the score. The ball speeds up, and a missed return ends the ball just as it would in the arcade original.

Launch-window shelves needed a game anyone could read in a second. Bricks and a familiar face did that job, with Mario as the bat instead of a nameless rectangle.
earthworm-jim-menace-2-the-galaxy:
Psycrow's grudge follows the worm into Earthworm Jim: Menace 2 the Galaxy, the 1999 handheld platformer from Crave and IMS Productions. It is a later, smaller entry in the Earthworm Jim series, a pocket run rather than a new full-size episode.

The super suit, a blaster, and a worm who whips his own head are still the moves. Princess What's-Her-Name remains the reason the galaxy is in trouble, and the jokes stay broad even when the stages are short.

Shiny's original console games had already set the weird tone. This cart keeps the worm, the suit, and the menace, scaled down by Crave and IMS for a screen that cannot hold those older stages whole.
toobin:
Inner tubes and a handful of cans send Bif and Jet downriver in Toobin'. Atari Games' 1988 arcade game dodges logs, alligators, and fishermen while the riders toss cans at obstacles that will not move on their own.

Branches, fishing lines, and a party beach full of thrown objects make the current a course. Steering is a lean left or right in the tube, and the score favors a rider who hits the gates and still has a can left for a hazard.

The cabinet's joke is the leisure object treated as a vehicle. A tube is not a car, the river forks, and the can is both ammunition and the thing that keeps a run alive.
pokemon-trading-card-game-2:
New duelists and a larger card pool arrive in Pokemon Trading Card Game 2, the Japanese sequel to the first card adventure. It came out in 2001 and did not receive an official English release at the time.

Deck building, element weaknesses, and a story island of opponents are the play, with the cards themselves as the party. A win still depends on energy, a bench, and the prize cards, just as a table match would.

Importers met the set years afterward. On release, the sequel's new cards and its island of duels belonged to the Japanese cartridge alone.
harry-potter-and-the-sorcerers-stone-200:
Hogwarts is a turn-based journey in Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone (GBC), Griptonite's 2001 role-playing take on the first story. It is separate from the console action games, which put Harry in a 3D castle instead of a party battle.

Spells are commands, a classmate can stand in the party, and classes in charms or potions feed the next fight. The stone of the title sits at the end of a school year that also includes corridors, a forbidden forest, and a troll who does not belong in a dungeon.

Philosophers and sorcerers share the book's two titles depending on the country. This cartridge uses the sorcerer's name and plays as a role-playing game, not as the home-console leap across moving staircases.
new-york-race:
Flying traffic over a future Manhattan is what survived of a canceled movie license in New York Race. Kalisto's 2001 futuristic racer began as a Fifth Element game and shipped without that film's name, so Leeloo and Korben never became the official drivers.

Lanes stacked above streets, a boost, and rival craft replace yellow cabs. The skyline is still recognizably New York, which is the joke of a tie-in that had to drop the film and keep the city.

Luc Besson's picture had the multipass and the opera singer; the released racer has neither on the box. What remains is the traffic in the air and Kalisto's decision to ship the city anyway.
titus-the-fox-1991:
Suzy has been taken toward Marrakech, and the rescuer is a fox who throws crates, in Titus the Fox (GB, GBC). The handheld port follows a platformer about that journey. The computer original is from 1992, and the Game Boy edition followed in 1993.

Boxes, balls, and other objects become ammunition and stepping stones. North African streets, rugs, and rooftops are the scenery, with the publisher's own name doubled as the hero's.

Titus the company and Titus the fox are the same word on purpose. The pocket edition keeps the throw-and-stack climb that the computer version used to cross a city toward Marrakech.
star-wars-yoda-stories:
A fresh little map appears every time Yoda gives an errand in Star Wars: Yoda Stories. LucasArts' 1997 desktop game builds a short randomized adventure around the Jedi master, closer to a desktop toy than to a filmed trilogy you replay scene by scene.

Luke's era, a lightsaber, and a scattering of Imperials and wildlife fill whatever layout the generator dealt. Because the paths change, a walkthrough for one afternoon is useless the next morning.

Indiana Jones had a sibling in the same desktop-adventure line. This one swaps the hat for Yoda's hut and keeps the promise that a session will be short and different.
shin-megami-tensei-devil-children:
Children sign pacts with demons in Shin Megami Tensei: Devil Children. Atlus aimed the spinoff at a younger audience in 2000, pairing kids with demon partners instead of leaving negotiation to adult heroes alone.

Recruiting, fusing, and battling still descend from the parent series, but the heroes are school-age. A partner demon walks with the child, and the story treats that bond as the point.

Black Book and Red Book are the paired cartridges of the same season, each with a different child. This broader name is the line those two routes belong to, the one that let a kid hold the leash.
lego-alpha-team:
Gadgets and a ticking contraption define LEGO Alpha Team. The PC puzzle adventure from 2000 sends agents to take apart the Brickster's machines, room by room, in a chain of bricks, lasers, and fans.

Dash Justice leads the squad, directing teammates whose tools only work on a specific part of the trap. A door will not open because a hero walked up to it; it opens because a crane, a fan, or a mine was placed on the right stud.

The Brickster is the same villain the island stories use. Here he is an engineer of deathtraps, and the agents are puzzle pieces with helmets.
shin-megami-tensei-devil-children-black-:
Setsuna's route is the one sealed in Shin Megami Tensei: Devil Children: Black Book. Atlus sold it in 2000 as one of two paired cartridges, alongside a Red Book with its own path and its own child.

A demon partner, fusion, and a story that does not simply mirror the other cart are the reasons to own this half. Link play between the books was part of the pitch, so a friend with the opposite color could trade what this route never gives away.

Mirai's story lives in the red cart. Black Book keeps Setsuna, his pact, and the battles that only his version stages.
shamus-1982:
A detective's pistol faces a maze of robots in Shamus (1982), the Atari favorite William Mataga wrote for Synapse. Color-coded doors and a short supply of shots make each life a scavenger hunt.

Shadowed corridors, color-coded doors, and a limited supply of shots make each life a scavenger hunt. The inspiration sits near other maze shooters of the home-computer boom, but the fedora and the case file are Shamus's own costume.

Case II continued the detective later. This first labyrinth is the Atari original, the one Synapse put Mataga's name on, full of robots and one investigator.
batman-chaos-in-gotham:
Gotham's rogues spill into the streets in Batman: Chaos in Gotham, a 2001 handheld action game drawn from the animated-series era of Batman licenses. The cowl and the gadgets belong to that drawn Batman, not to a later film's armor.

Side-view punches, a batarang, and a boss pulled from the cartoon's gallery structure the levels. The title's chaos is the excuse to move from rooftop to warehouse without a long detective novel between fights.

Animated-series games had already multiplied across handhelds. This one keeps the name of the city in the title and the animated Bat on the box, fighting through a Gotham that will not stay quiet.
suzuki-alstare-extreme-racing:
A factory team, not a fictional mascot, is the license in Suzuki Alstare Extreme Racing. The 1999 bike racer puts Suzuki machines and the Alstare squad on courses where lean angle and braking decide the place, not a projectile.

Superbike silhouettes, a tachometer, and a pack of sponsored riders make the grid look like a paddock. The name on the box is the racing team's, which is a different kind of endorsement from a celebrity athlete's trick game.

Corner speed is the skill the courses test. Alstare's colors and Suzuki's bikes are why the cart exists, and a missed apex still costs the place.
shanghai:
Matching tiles vanish in pairs in Shanghai. Activision published Brodie Lockard's mahjong solitaire in 1986, and a stacked dragon of tiles has to be cleared by removing free pairs before a buried tile can move.

The layout, not a timer alone, is the opponent. Seasons, dots, and honors only leave if both copies are exposed, so a greedy first match can seal a tile the player needed at the end.

Lockard's computer version turned a table game into a solitaire of height and access. Later ports kept the dragon and the rule that a covered tile is not yet a move.
dropzone-1984:
A jetpack hangs over a single screen in Dropzone (1984), where Archer MacLean follows the Defender tradition. Scientists wait on the ground while aliens swarm the moment a rescue hesitates.

Thrust, a laser, and a grab are the controls, and the ground is where the people you are saving stand. Lose them, or crash the pack into the dirt, and the wave has already won.

MacLean's precision is the reputation: tight gravity, a crowded screen, and no scrolling world to hide in. Defender's sweep is the ancestor; the jetpack and the Atari keyboard scene are this game's own life.
the-black-onyx:
A black gem at the bottom of a dungeon is the prize in The Black Onyx. Henk Rogers' 1984 computer role-playing game is often credited as the commercial role-playing game that opened Japan's home-computer market to the genre.

Parties, first-person corridors, and a quest built around that gem gave Japanese PC players a dungeon they could buy rather than type in from a magazine. The title is the treasure, so the goal is never abstract.

Rogers later became famous for other Japanese game business, but this dungeon is the credit the blurb preserves. The gem, the corridors, and the market it helped open are the story.
disneys-atlantis-the-lost-empire-the-los:
Milo Thatch's expedition becomes a run of stages in Disney's Atlantis: The Lost Empire. The 2001 action tie-in follows the animated film's dive toward a living city, with Kida's people and the submarine voyage as the reason the platforms exist.

Levers, spears, and collapsing bridges stand in for the movie's set pieces. Rourke's greed and the crystal at the heart of Atlantis are the stakes, even when a stage only asks for a jump.

Disney's picture was a pulp adventure in animation. The tie-in keeps the lost city, the explorer, and the descent, rather than inventing a new island for a mascot.
balloon-kid-1990:
Alice stays aloft with the balloons in her hands in Balloon Kid (1990), pumping a new one whenever one pops. Nintendo's follow-up to Balloon Fight sends her scrolling across the sky after her brother Jim.

Birds, lightning, and a long horizontal trip replace Balloon Fight's single-screen duel. The balloons are both the jump and the life pool: lose them and Alice drops.

Balloon Trip's endless scroll is the ancestor of the travel. Alice, Jim, and the spare balloons she carries are what make this chapter a story instead of another versus match.
nicktoons-racing:
Rugrats, Hey Arnold, and other Nickelodeon stars share a starting grid in Nicktoons Racing. The 1999 kart racer puts several of the network's cartoons on the same tracks, so a toddler and a football-headed kid can draft one another.

Themed courses, a projectile gag, and a cup structure are the racing. Each driver brings a cartoon's prop rather than a generic mascot, which is the license doing its job.

Nickelodeon had spent the decade filling a schedule with distinct shows. This kart is the crossover that puts those shows' heroes on one circuit.
magical-drop:
Columns of color fall, and a jester throws them back, in Magical Drop. Data East's 1995 puzzle game has the player catch falling drops and hurl them upward to clear a stack before the pile reaches the bottom.

Grabbing one color, stacking it, and releasing it into a matching run is the verb. Chains clear faster than single matches, and the opponent on the other side of the screen is filling your well while you fill theirs.

Tarot-like character art frames the versus mode. The skill is still the grab and the throw, the trick that separates this column game from a matcher that only aims a cannon.
quest-for-camelot:
Kayley's chase after Excalibur is the spine of Quest for Camelot, the 1998 action tie-in to Warner Bros.' animated film. Camelot's stolen sword, a two-headed dragon, and a forest full of obstacles turn the movie's journey into stages.

Garrett's falcon and the steel blade everyone wants give the levels their landmarks. The play is running, striking, and clearing a path toward the sword rather than sitting through the songs.

Warner Bros. put the feature's title on the box and little else in the way of a new plot. Kayley, the sword, and the road back to Camelot are the tie-in's entire map.
shadowgate-classic:
A torch burns down while you stand still in Shadowgate Classic. ICOM's 1987 MacVenture is the point-and-click castle adventure that later traveled to many home computers and handhelds, and the flame is a clock.

Examine, open, and use apply to a skull, a bridge, and a warlock lord who must not be allowed to summon his beast. Click the wrong fixture and the castle kills you outright, which made the guide a companion people kept beside the keyboard.

The windowed verbs are the same MacVenture language as the Chicago mystery from the same studio. Here the rooms are stone, the light is finite, and the warlock is the reason to hurry.
harry-potter-and-the-chamber-of-secrets-:
A basilisk in the pipes waits at the end of Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (GBC). Griptonite followed its first handheld role-playing game with this 2002 sequel, again separate from the console action game of the same book.

Tom Riddle's diary, a petrified classmate, and spells learned in class feed turn-based fights through Hogwarts. Harry still walks a school year, but the mystery is the chamber under the castle rather than a stone hidden in a mirror.

The home-console version of the story leaps and duels in a modeled castle. Griptonite's cart keeps the party's commands, the diary, and the snake.
star-ocean-blue-sphere:
A private planet and a returning crew define Star Ocean: Blue Sphere. tri-Ace and Enix released it only in Japan, in 2001, as a follow-up set after Star Ocean: The Second Story.

Real-time battles and a science-fantasy ship full of the previous game's faces carry the combat. Because no official English edition appeared with that first release, the planet's proper names stayed in Japanese for years.

The Second Story had ended on a larger scale. Blue Sphere picks up the same company for a smaller, Japan-only episode rather than retelling the whole war.
the-dukes-of-hazzard:
The General Lee's horn is the fantasy in The Dukes of Hazzard, a game based on the CBS series about cousins Bo and Luke Duke. Their orange car, Hazzard County, and a sheriff who cannot quite catch them are the ingredients the show never changed.

Jumps, roadblocks, and Boss Hogg's schemes translate the chase into play. Rosco P. Coltrane's patrol car is the obstacle, and the bridge the cousins fly off is the set piece players expect from the title.

The television cousins made a stripped Dodge famous. Any game under this name has to answer that car, that county, and those two drivers.
lego-alpha-team-2001:
Agents still wear the helmets in Lego Alpha Team (2001), but the puzzles are not the computer adventure's chain of gadgets. The handheld starring that squad plays differently from the PC game released the year before.

Brick traps, a short route, and a direct order to a teammate fit the small screen. Dash Justice's squad is still dismantling the Brickster's work, yet the interface is not the desktop chain of gadgets.

Owning the computer adventure does not solve this cart. The same villains and the same team show up, and then the handheld asks for its own kind of solution.
pokemon-gold-version:
Johto's gyms open at odd hours in Pokémon Gold Version, because a clock inside the cartridge changes the route. Game Freak's pair reached Japan in 1999 and the West in 2000, and day or night decides which creatures are awake.

New Bark Town, a fresh set of gym leaders, and a later trip into Kanto after the league make the map larger than the first generation. Breeding, held items, and the Pokégear are tools the red-and-blue cartridges could not run.

Ho-Oh on the box is the legendary this version features, opposite Silver's beast. Crystal retold Johto afterward, and HeartGold is a much later remake, not this cartridge's battery-backed clock.
xtreme-sports-2000:
Boards, bikes, and a snowfield share one cartridge in Xtreme Sports (2000), WayForward's multi-event handheld. A single save moves the athlete from one discipline to the next.

Tricks, a judged run, and a course that is not a Mario-style lap are the common language. The events change the vehicle under the athlete's feet while the score still cares about style.

WayForward's later reputation came from other genres. This cart is their multi-event sports assortment, a pocket meet rather than one long season of a single sport.
pocket-bomberman:
White Bomberman jumps in profile in Pocket Bomberman, and the maze battle is gone. Hudson's 1997 release turns Bomberman into a side-scrolling platformer, with bombs as tools for cracking blocks and clearing a path instead of as arena weapons.

Ladders, pits, and a fuse you have to outrun replace the four-player grid. A bomb is still round and still explodes in a cross, but the camera follows one Bomberman through a stage.

Hudson's arena games remained the famous form. This pocket outing is the odd one that asks the mascot to jump.
oddworld:
Mudokons still need a chant, and Sligs can still be possessed, in Oddworld Adventures 2, the handheld follow-up drawn from Abe's Exoddus. SoulStorm brew covers the factory floor of this 2001 cart, rather than only the first game's meat plant.

Abe talks, sneaks, and pulls a lever that only a possessed guard can reach. Rescuing his fellow Mudokons, or letting them come to harm, is the moral score the series already used.

Exoddus on a home console is the wide version of this plot. The pocket follow-up keeps Abe, the chant, and the brew, scaled to a screen that shows one corridor at a time.
x-men-mutant-wars:
A scrolling fight, not a versus round, is the shape of X-Men: Mutant Wars. Marvel's mutants appear in this 2000 side-view action game, a different title from the one-on-one Mutant Academy fighter released around the same time.

Claws, optic blasts, and a march through enemy waves replace a fighting-game health bar and a best-of-three. The team is the license; the camera is a side scroller's.

Academy matches ask who wins a duel. Mutant Wars asks whether the mutants can cross a stage, which is why the two carts do not substitute for each other.
x-men-wolverines-rage:
Adamantium claws lead every screen in X-Men: Wolverine's Rage, the 2001 handheld built around Marvel's berserker. Healing and a short temper are the character's whole combat loop, aimed at the color handheld rather than at a team roster.

Side-view slashes, a lunge, and a boss who can outlast the healing factor structure the stages. Logan is not sharing the buttons with Storm or Cyclops here; the cart is his name and his grudge.

Other mutant games of the season split the team into fighters or squads. This one stays on Wolverine, the rage in the title included.
spongebob-squarepants-legend-of-the-lost:
A golden spatula, not a secret recipe, is the quest in SpongeBob SquarePants: Legend of the Lost Spatula. One of the earliest games from the Nickelodeon cartoon, this 2001 platformer sends the fry cook through Bikini Bottom after a utensil with a legend attached.

Jellyfish Fields, Patrick's rock, and the drop toward the Chum Bucket's neighborhood become the obstacles. A jump and a spin attack carry SpongeBob between the pineapple and the deeper sand.

Later SpongeBob games filled home consoles with movie plots. This early cart is the small one about the spatula, the fry cook, and Bikini Bottom.
hamtaro-ham-hams-unite:
Western shelves met the hamster club through Hamtaro Ham-Hams Unite! The cartoon's pocket adventure came west in 2001, with the Ham-Hams, Hamtaro's circle of hamster friends, as the neighbors who need visiting.

Bijou, Boss, and the other Ham-Hams each hide a small errand behind a sunflower seed or a shared phrase. The play is an adventure of conversations and tiny problems, not a race around a wheel.

Japanese audiences had the hamsters first. The western cart is the one that introduced that club, and the title's demand is that the Ham-Hams get together.
pong-the-next-level:
Power-ups stuck to a paddle are the update in Pong: The Next Level. Hasbro took the 1972 paddle game and, in 1999, added balls that curve, paddles that stretch, and boards that are no longer an empty court.

Atari's original needed two bats and a dot. This sequel keeps that duel and then breaks it with obstacles, so a point can be won by a trick the 1972 cabinet did not have.

Hasbro Interactive was collecting classic names in that era. The next-level subtitle is honest about the trick: Pong, plus the gadgets.
game-watch-gallery-2:
Parachute, Helmet, Chef, and Vermin sit beside Mario redraws in Game & Watch Gallery 2, Nintendo's second collection of the old liquid-crystal games. The color edition of those Mario versions arrived in 1998.

A classic screen keeps the monochrome alarm-clock look, while the Mario screen turns Chef into a cook flipping food and Helmet into a Mario who still has to dodge falling objects. The score attack is the same; the costume changes.

Gallery collections became a way to keep the wrist-game era playable. This second set is those four LCD games plus the Mario versions, not a new platformer wearing an old title.
legend-of-zelda-links-awakening-dx:
Koholint Island washes Link ashore in Legend Of Zelda: Link's Awakening DX. The 1998 color update rebuilds the 1993 adventure with color, a photo feature, and an extra Color Dungeon the monochrome cartridge never had.

Marin, the Wind Fish, and a camera shop that feeds the photo album are the reasons to wander between dungeons. Instruments still wake the island, and the Color Dungeon adds a tunic reward for players who only knew the first release.

The photo feature wants a printer attachment and a spare shot of a boss or a neighbor. Color, that album, and the extra dungeon are what separate this update from the original gray adventure.
microsoft-pinball-arcade:
Real cabinets, not fictional tables, are the attraction in Microsoft Pinball Arcade. Microsoft's 1998 collection recreates a set of actual pinball machines for play at home, with flippers, bumpers, and rule cards that belong to those tables.

A nudge can tilt the machine, and a skill shot still depends on the plunger. Because the tables existed in arcades and bars first, the digital versions are trying to keep each one's ramps and drop targets honest.

Microsoft put its name on a museum of steel balls. The play is still a flipper and a tilt, applied to tables a player could once have found in a bowling alley.
shin-megami-tensei-devil-children-red-bo:
Mirai's pact is the campaign inside Shin Megami Tensei: Devil Children: Red Book. The companion cartridge shipped in 2000 beside Black Book, the other half of Atlus's paired Devil Children release.

Her demon partner, her route, and the fusions that route allows are not a palette swap of Setsuna's story. Owning both books was the way to see the whole season, and a link between them could move a demon the other cart never recruits.

Atlus sold the pair as twins on purpose. Red Book is Mirai's half, the one that does not make sense as a mere costume change on the black cart.
conkers-pocket-tales:
A gentle squirrel, not a foul-mouthed one, stars in Conker's Pocket Tales. Rare's 1999 adventure sends Conker after stolen presents and a kidnapped Berri, years before the adult humor of Bad Fur Day.

Overworld paths, small foes, and a tone aimed at a younger player define the cart. The Evil Acorn's mischief is a fairy-tale problem, and Conker solves it without the later game's jokes.

Rare already had the squirrel in a racing cameo and a platform project that changed direction. This pocket tale is the sweet version, the one Bad Fur Day deliberately left behind.
ronaldo-v-football:
The Brazilian striker, not the later Portuguese star, is the face of Ronaldo V-Football. Infogrames' 2000 soccer game carries his endorsement, and in the United States the same game is known as Ronaldo V-Soccer.

Clubs, a whistle, and the number-nine fantasy of that era's Inter and Barcelona forward are the contents. It is a simulation of matches, not a trick-sport minigame with his name pasted on a skateboard.

Two famous Ronaldos have confused box art ever since. This endorsement belongs to the Brazilian, the one Infogrames put on a soccer cover at the turn of that career.
ultimate-fighting-championship:
The octagon, not a temple, is the ring in Ultimate Fighting Championship. An early licensed fighting game from 2000 borrows the mixed-martial-arts promotion, so strikes and takedowns share one ruleset instead of a fireball contest.

Grappling on the mat and a stand-up exchange are both legal, which is the promotion's whole identity. A health bar still ends the bout, but the moves are elbows, shoots, and a cage rather than a cartoon special.

Later UFC games grew a larger roster and a heavier presentation. This early license is the one that first put the promotion's cage into a fighting game.
resident-evil-code-veronica:
Claire Redfield's search for her brother lands her on Rockfort Island in Resident Evil Code: Veronica. Capcom's 2000 Dreamcast game is a mainline entry even though it sits outside the numbered titles, with Alfred and Alexia Ashford as the island's keepers.

Fixed cameras, a limited inventory, and a second half that finally brings Chris in are the survival-horror grammar. Antarctica and the Ashford family plot push the story past Raccoon City without turning it into a spinoff.

Numbered sequels kept Leon or a new outbreak. Veronica is still canon, the chapter where Claire is the prisoner and the Ashfords are the reason.
army-men-rts:
Plastic rifles take real-time orders in Army Men RTS. In 2002 the toy soldiers moved into base-building strategy, commanding Sarge's green troops across oversized household battlefields.

A kitchen counter is high ground, a tan plastic factory is the enemy base, and a resource node might be a pile of beads. The camera looks down on a backyard the way other strategy games look down on a continent.

Earlier Army Men games had been squad shooters in the same giant house. This one hands Sarge a command map and keeps the war green against tan.
disneypixar-cars-2:
Radiator Springs, not a spy sequel, is the map in Disney•Pixar Cars. THQ's 2006 racing game is the tie-in to the first Pixar film, and Lightning McQueen's rookie season is the story it uses.

Mater, Doc Hudson, and the town's shops turn a race into a hub between events. Piston Cup laps and a desert highway are the driving, with McQueen's rust-red paint as the car the camera follows.

A later film sent the same cars overseas on a spy plot. This tie-in stays home with the first movie, the town, and the cup.
worms-3d:
Bazookas leave the side-on trench in Worms 3D. Team17 took the artillery series fully into 3D in 2003, so a worm can walk around a hill instead of only along a flat strip of land.

The ninja rope, the wind, and a sheep still decide a turn, but the camera has to be aimed before the shot. Cover is a real boulder, and a teammate can be stranded on a ledge the old side view would have shown in one glance.

Earlier Worms games made the profile battlefield famous. This entry's argument is the extra dimension, and the ways a familiar weapon misbehaves when the target can hide behind the camera.
true-crime-streets-of-la:
A badge and a bad temper share Nick Kang's car in True Crime: Streets of LA. Luxoflux's 2003 open-world game sets the cop in Los Angeles, with a meter that tracks whether he stays clean while the case pulls him through the city.

Driving, shooting, and a street fight are all legal ways to reach the next informant. The good-cop meter is the distinctive rule: brutality closes doors that a cleaner arrest would open.

Later True Crime moved the badge to another city. This first one is Kang, Los Angeles, and the meter that judges the drive over.
second-sight:
John Vattic wakes with a headache and a power he does not remember earning in Second Sight. Free Radical Design, the TimeSplitters studio, released the psychic action game in 2004, splitting stealth guns and telekinesis across one conspiracy.

A crate lifted without hands, a guard put to sleep, and a rifle for when the trick fails are the options. The plot folds back on an experiment, so the powers are clues as well as weapons.

TimeSplitters had been a costume party of a shooter. Second Sight is the same studio playing a straight face, with Vattic's mind as the special move.
true-crime-new-york-city:
Manhattan replaces the west coast when Marcus Reed takes the case in True Crime: New York City. Luxoflux moved the open-world cop series there in 2005, and Reed's history with the street is the reason the precinct bothers to use him.

Borough traffic, a subway entrance, and a shootout that can spill into a store are the city's grain. The series' mix of driving and on-foot enforcement stays, now under a skyline of towers rather than palm-lined boulevards.

Nick Kang's Los Angeles game is the previous chapter. This one belongs to Reed, the boroughs, and a department that does not trust its new man.
tony-hawks-american-wasteland:
Los Angeles refuses a loading screen between spots in Tony Hawk's American Wasteland. Neversoft set the 2005 skate game in that city and linked its skate areas into one continuous map, so a manual can carry a combo out of one district and into the next.

Hollywood, the downtown hills, and a makeshift park share one story about a skater new to town. Classic mode still offers the two-minute score attack when the story goals are not the session you wanted.

Earlier Hawk games had been a menu of levels. The wasteland's trick is the joined-up city, and the bail that happens when the manual between neighborhoods fails.
sonic-3d-blast-1996:
Flickies are the birds worth saving in Sonic 3D Blast (1996), Traveller's Tales' isometric Genesis game. A Saturn edition shipped beside it, and Doctor Robotnik is still stuffing wildlife into machines.

The isometric angle makes a loop harder to read than in the side-view games, and a shield or a speed shoe still hides in a corner of the island. Special stages differ between the Genesis and Saturn editions, but both are about freeing the birds.

Sonic's usual run is a profile of springs and loops. Blast turns that run into a diagonal maze of Flickies, which is why players still describe the camera first.
metal-gear-solid-the-twin-snakes:
Shadow Moses returns with a new camera in Metal Gear Solid: The Twin Snakes. Silicon Knights remade the 1998 stealth game for the GameCube in 2004, with new cutscenes directed by Ryuhei Kitamura.

Solid Snake, Meryl, and Liquid still fight over the nuclear walking tank, but first-person aiming and Kitamura's action-film staging change the feel of a corridor. The cardboard box and the codec remain, now under cutscenes that dive and spin more than the original boards.

The PlayStation game is the story's first telling. Twin Snakes is the remake that keeps the island and recuts the cinema, Kitamura's name included.
crash-bandicoot-wrath-of-cortex:
Crunch, a brute built to match the bandicoot, debuts in Crash Bandicoot: The Wrath of Cortex. Traveller's Tales' 2001 platformer is the fourth main Crash game, with Doctor Neo Cortex still funding the disaster and elemental masks stirring the islands.

Crates, a spin, and a chase level between the platforming are the familiar verbs. Crunch is the new body in the boss slots, a rival designed as Crash's opposite rather than another scientist in a lab coat.

Naughty Dog had already left the series by this point. Traveller's Tales kept the crates and added Crunch, the muscle Cortex had been missing.
sonic-riders:
Extreme Gear, a hoverboard, replaces the footrace in Sonic Riders. Sonic Team's 2006 racing game drafts behind a rival to refill air, and the Babylon Rogues, led by Jet the Hawk, are the reason the boards exist.

Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles still run, but a grind rail and a turbulence pocket matter more than a spin dash. Courses in the city and the desert are race tracks first, and running out of air is how a board drops out of the pack.

Earlier Sonic racing had been cars or shoes. Riders commits to the board, the air meter, and Jet's crew of thieves.
shadow-the-hedgehog:
A firearm and a branching conscience define Shadow the Hedgehog. Sega gave the black hedgehog guns and a hero-or-villain story in 2005, with Black Doom's alien army as the invasion that forces the choice.

Chaos Emeralds, a dark mission, and a hero mission can split the same level into different endings. Vehicles and a weapon wheel sit beside the usual homing attack, which is why fans of the speed alone often bounced off the combat.

Sonic's team games had kept Shadow as a rival in someone else's plot. This one hands him the guns, the aliens, and a last decision about which side the black hedgehog takes.
def-jam-fight-for-ny:
Hip-hop names fill the locker room in Def Jam: Fight for NY. AKI and EA's 2004 fighter is the sequel to Def Jam Vendetta, and the roster is a lineup of rappers rather than a pantheon of invented martial artists.

New York venues, a create-a-fighter story, and a Blazin' mode that spends momentum on a cinematic hit are the extras around the brawling. The crowd is part of the weapon set, because a fighter can be thrown into the front row.

Vendetta had already proved the license could box. Fight for NY widens the boroughs, the story, and the list of MCs who show up to swing.
the-legend-of-zelda-four-swords-adventur:
Four tunic colors and four Game Boy Advance cables are the requirement in The Legend of Zelda: Four Swords Adventures. Nintendo's 2004 multiplayer Zelda links those handhelds to the console so four Links can split Hyrule's screens.

Vaati and Shadow Link supply the villains, while a force gem and a cooperative puzzle keep a solo player from treating the others as decoration. The sword that duplicates Link is the premise inherited from the handheld Four Swords.

A single television is not enough for the full trick. The console reads the handhelds, and the adventure is built so the four Links have to share items instead of racing one another to Ganon.
call-of-duty-finest-hour:
Soviet, British, and American squads share one disc in Call of Duty: Finest Hour. Spark Unlimited brought the World War II shooter to consoles for the first time in 2004, after the series had begun on the PC.

Eastern Front snow, a North African approach, and a Western European push give each army its own weapons and radio chatter. The console aim is slower and more guided than a mouse, which was the adjustment Spark had to make.

Infinity Ward's original PC campaign is a different product. Finest Hour is the first time the series' war fit on a console pad, with three nations' missions on the disc.
mortal-kombat-deception:
Chess pieces that punch and a falling-block board sit beside the fatalities in Mortal Kombat: Deception. Midway followed Deadly Alliance with this 2004 fighter, adding Chess Kombat and Puzzle Kombat to the usual one-on-one bouts.

A large roster returns characters the previous game had removed, and a Konquest walk through the realms frames the story between matches. The puzzle mode drops fighters as blocks, while Chess Kombat turns a board into a squad of the same kombatants.

Deadly Alliance had already changed the 3D camera and killed a pair of heroes. Deception's extra modes, the chess board and the puzzle well, are what the subtitle is selling besides another fatality.
timesplitters-2:
Cortez hops centuries in TimeSplitters 2, and each mission is a different decade's gunfight. Free Radical's 2002 shooter is remembered for those time-hopping assignments, a map maker, and multiplayer that outlasted the story for a lot of households.

A Western street, a sci-fi lab, and a 1920s nightclub can sit on the same disc because the plot is a chase through time. The arcade league and the challenge rooms train the tricks the story missions then demand.

The map maker lets a player place bots, weapons, and doors, which is why custom nights lasted longer than the campaign. Free Radical's sequel is the one people mean when they talk about the series' editor and its costume box.
x-men-legends-2-rise-of-apocalypse:
Apocalypse's machines are the dungeons in X-Men Legends II: Rise of Apocalypse. Raven Software's squad action role-playing game, published by Activision in 2005, is the sequel to X-Men Legends, built for up to four mutants at once.

Skill trees, a shared loot pile, and a mutant power that has to combo with a teammate's power are the systems. The villain in the title is the campaign's end, with the Age of Apocalypse tone coloring the zones.

The first Legends game had already proved a comic team could loot like an action role-playing party. This sequel raises Apocalypse and keeps the four-player couches.
skies-of-arcadia:
Air pirates and a sky full of islands carry Skies of Arcadia. Overworks' 2000 Dreamcast role-playing game follows Vyse, Aika, and Fina among the floating continents, and a later GameCube edition was titled Legends.

Ship-to-ship cannon fire, a moon crystal, and a Blue Rogue crew distinguish a random battle from the discoveries on the world map. Finding a new island fills a blank chart, which makes exploration a reward of its own.

Legends adds scenes and extras around the same pirates. The Dreamcast telling is this name, Vyse's ship, and the sky that replaced an ordinary overworld.
tales-of-symphonia-2003:
Lloyd Irving's twin blades open Tales of Symphonia (2003) on a console that had the journey to itself at launch. Namco's action role-playing game uses the series' real-time battles, so where a fighter stands changes what a strike can hit.

Colette's pilgrimage, the Desians' human ranches, and a world that is not the only world sit under the fights. Linear-motion combat lets a player run behind an enemy instead of choosing a spell and waiting on a still menu.

Later ports carried Lloyd's party off the GameCube. At launch the journey was exclusive to that console, which is the fact the original audience lived with.
timesplitters-future-perfect:
Four players can walk the story together in TimeSplitters: Future Perfect. Free Radical closed the trilogy in 2005, adding that cooperative campaign and console online play to Cortez's time war.

A past mission and a future mission still share one sergeant, and the tools include a split-screen editor for people who never touch the plot. Online matches brought the same bots-and-costumes chaos to a wire instead of only a couch.

The second game had the map maker and the best reputation. Future Perfect is the one that lets friends share the campaign and, for the first time in the trilogy, take the match online.
resident-evil-code-veronica-x-2:
Extra scenes lengthen Claire's imprisonment in Resident Evil - Code: Veronica X, the expanded cut of Code Veronica. It spread widely on PlayStation 2 in 2001 and later reached the GameCube.

Rockfort Island, Alfred Ashford, and Chris's arrival remain the spine, with the new footage filling gaps rather than replacing the outbreak. A player who only knew the Dreamcast release meets additional cinema in this cut.

Veronica without the X is the original chapter. The X cut is the one that traveled, scenes added, onto the PlayStation 2 and then the cube.
sonic-spinball-1993:
Flippers launch the hedgehog in Sonic Spinball (1993), a Genesis machine built around his speed. Robotnik's fortress supplies the tables, and missing a flipper costs a life.

Toxic caves, a lava works, and a final showdown table each hide a route to a Chaos Emerald. Bumpers, a plunger, and a drain that costs a life replace the usual side-view loops, though a spin still fits the pinball fantasy.

The main Genesis platformers were already a trilogy by the time this experiment arrived. Spinball is the odd machine in that family, the one where missing a flipper is the death.
call-of-duty-2-big-red-one:
The U.S. 1st Infantry Division's nickname is the title of Call of Duty 2: Big Red One. Treyarch's 2005 console shooter follows that division and was not a PC expansion of the computer game that shares the numeral.

North Africa, Sicily, and the push into Europe give one squad a continuous war instead of a montage of unrelated heroes. The "Big Red One" shoulder patch is the through-line, so the player stays with the same unit's campaign.

Other Call of Duty stories jumped nation every few missions. This console campaign sticks with the American division whose nickname is painted on the box.
hulk:
Bruce Banner sneaks, and then the creature finishes the room, in The Hulk. Radical Entertainment's 2003 film tie-in switches between rampaging as the green giant and playing as Banner when a door is too small or a guard must not be alerted.

The Ang Lee film's split personality is the mechanic. Banner's stealth sections are quiet and fragile; Hulk's are about throwing a truck and ignoring the bullets.

Other Hulk games have been only the smash. Radical's tie-in insists on both bodies, which is the movie's point turned into a level change.
crash-tag-team-racing:
Two cars lock together mid-lap in Crash Tag Team Racing. Radical Entertainment's 2005 mix of karts and on-foot platforming lets vehicles fuse in the middle of a race, combining weapons while the track is still moving.

Von Clutch's MotorWorld is the park that needs its stolen power gems back, and between races Crash walks the midway to find them. A platforming detour is not a menu; it is how the next car part and the next clue show up.

Earlier Crash racing was karts alone. The fusion, the park, and the walking sections are this one's extra machinery.
ssx-3:
Three peaks of one mountain replace the course menu in SSX 3, EA Canada's connected snowboard descent. A rider in the 2003 entry can drop from the summit toward the village without loading a separate run.

Tricks, a boost meter, and rival boarders still score the descent. Lodges on the way down are both checkpoints and the place a new board gets bought, which makes the mountain a place rather than a loading screen with snow.

Earlier SSX games picked a track and then raced it. The third entry's map is the whole alp, and bailing near the bottom means a long climb back in spirit if not on foot.
mario-party-4:
Four controllers share one television in Mario Party 4, Hudson's first party on the GameCube. The 2002 boards and minigames keep the format the Nintendo 64 games had already drilled in.

Mario, Peach, Wario, and the rest still roll a die, land on a space, and then play a short contest for coins. New boards change the gimmick, while the star someone has to buy remains the argument of the afternoon.

Hudson had already shipped three living-room parties. This fourth one moves the same die, the same star, and a fresh set of minigames onto the new console.
star-fox-adventures:
Dinosaur Planet was the project before Fox McCloud inherited it, and the finished game is Star Fox Adventures. Rare's 2002 adventure recast that dinosaur story around the Star Fox pilot, with a staff in his hands more often than an Arwing.

Prince Tricky, a triceratops child, and Krystal join a quest of puzzles, combat, and a limited stretch of flying. The SharpClaw and a broken-up world of dinosaurs are the enemies and the map, leftovers of the game it used to be.

Star Fox fans who wanted only space combat met a role-playing trek instead. Rare's recasting is the history: Dinosaur Planet's bones, Fox's face, and Tricky's commentary.
viewtiful-joe-2003:
Slow motion and Mach Speed are film tricks Joe spends like ammo in Viewtiful Joe (2003), Clover Studio's side-scroller. Hideki Kamiya's hero gets those VFX powers from Captain Blue.

Silvia gets captured into Movie Land, so the stages are reels: a city street, a spaceship, and a boss who only staggers when the stylish meter is full. VFX is both the attack and the score, because playing plainly does less damage.

Kamiya's team at Clover treated the camera as a weapon. Joe's red helmet and the V-watch are the tools, and a stylish dodge is worth more than a plain punch.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-mutant-mele:
Four turtles and a pile of Foot soldiers enter one arena in Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Melee. Konami's 2005 brawler is a fighting spinoff of the cartoons, not a story platformer that walks the sewers scene by scene.

Leonardo's swords, Raphael's sai, Donatello's staff, and Michelangelo's nunchaku still mark the brothers, while Shredder's side can join the free-for-all. Items drop into the pit so a match is not only footsies and a special.

The cartoon platformers tell an episode. Mutant Melee throws the cast into a room and lets them hit each other, which is the spinoff's entire point.
spyro-enter-the-dragonfly:
Scattered dragonflies are the collectible Spyro has to recover in Spyro: Enter the Dragonfly. After Insomniac left the series, this 2002 adventure arrived under Universal and launched to a notoriously rough reception.

A new breath type, a hover, and a home that has lost its dragonflies are the ideas on paper. Players met crashes, thin worlds, and a short list of the insects the title promises, which is the reputation that stuck to the disc.

Insomniac's earlier Spyro games had been the polished trilogy. Enter the Dragonfly is the first step after that studio left, and the rough launch is part of how people still describe it.
medal-of-honor-rising-sun-2003:
Pearl Harbor opens the campaign in Medal of Honor: Rising Sun. EA moved the series from Europe to the Pacific theater in 2003, so the first mission is a battleship morning rather than a French hedgerow.

The Philippines, a raid involving a carrier, and a Pacific island assault follow that harbor for the Marine at the center of the story. Period weapons and a squadmate replace the European towns of the earlier medals.

Rising Sun's theater change is the point of the subtitle. Europe had been the default front; this entry starts at the harbor and stays in the Pacific.
hobbit-the-2003:
Bilbo's contract with the dwarves drives Hobbit, The (2003), Sierra's adaptation of Tolkien's novel. The road belongs to the book rather than to the later Hobbit films.

The Shire, Gollum's riddle game, and a long walk toward Smaug's mountain structure the levels. Gandalf appears as the wizard who will not stay for the whole road, which matches the book's habit of leaving Bilbo to the problem.

Peter Jackson's Hobbit pictures arrived years afterward. Sierra's game belongs to the novel and to that earlier window, with the ring and the burglar still the center.
mario-party-5:
Capsule items replace the old inventory in Mario Party 5, and Hudson throws them onto the GameCube boards. The 2003 party lets a player plant a capsule on a space and change the next roll.

New boards, a set of minigames, and the same star-buying contest keep the party recognizable. A capsule might grow a plant, spring a trap, or move a star, so the board itself becomes the weapon between minigames.

Mario Party 4 had brought the format to the console without this item system. The fifth entry's capsules are the rule change, and the boards are built around them.
barnyard:
Otis the cow walks upright through Barnyard, the 2006 tie-in to Nickelodeon's film about a farm of animals who misbehave when the farmer looks away. Chores, a race, and a party in the barn are the kinds of scenes the movie already staged.

The bullies are coyotes, and the farmer must not catch the animals standing. Minigames break up the yard exploration, which fits a film that was already a pile of gags rather than one long quest.

Nickelodeon's picture gave the cow a secret life. The game uses that secret, Otis's voice and his friends, as the excuse for the activities in the yard.
mario-power-tennis:
A charged shot that belongs to one character, not a generic smash, is the gimmick in Mario Power Tennis. Camelot added those special shots to the Mario tennis formula in this 2004 GameCube game, so Peach's power is not Mario's fire.

Gimmick courts tilt, speed up, or flood, and a pair of players can trigger the charge only after a rally earns it. Bowser's shot and Waluigi's trick are comedy as well as points.

Camelot had already made a Mario tennis game without the power system. The charged shots and the strange courts are what the "power" in the title adds.
ice-age-2-the-meltdown:
A flood chasing the herd is the timer behind Ice Age 2: The Meltdown. The Blue Sky film sequel received this 2006 platform tie-in, with Manny, Sid, Diego, and Scrat each causing a different kind of trouble on the way to higher ground.

Scrat's acorn obsession and the melting valley are the jokes turned into pits and moving ice. The play is a run, a jump, and a set piece copied from the picture's disaster.

The first Ice Age film had already been tied to games. This one follows the sequel's melt, the herd, and the squirrel who will not drop the nut.
medal-of-honor-european-assault:
Europe is the front again in Medal of Honor: European Assault. EA returned the series to that theater in 2005, after the Pacific-set Rising Sun, and the missions move through several famous operations rather than one harbor.

A squad can be ordered to cover a street, and the player's soldier still carries the series' first-person rifle. The subtitle's "assault" is the pace: several landings and pushes instead of Rising Sun's ocean war.

Rising Sun had been the Pacific detour. European Assault puts the medal back among hedgerows, rivers, and the western campaign's set pieces.
dragon-ball-z-budokai:
Beam struggles and a saga recap open the 3D era in Dragon Ball Z: Budokai. Dimps started its long line of anime fighters with this 2002 game, covering the show's fights from the Saiyan arrival through later enemies.

Goku, Vegeta, and a capsule system for building a move list give the roster more than a single special. Story mode follows the anime's duels, while a versus match ignores the plot and just charges a blast.

Later Budokai sequels added more of the cast and flashier team attacks. This first one is the Dimps model: 3D arena, anime story, and a custom set of techniques.
driver-san-francisco:
John Tanner's coma is the reason a driver can change bodies in Driver San Francisco. Ubisoft Reflections built the 2011 game around Shift, a power that jumps the player from car to car across an open city.

A chase that is going badly can be saved by shifting into the car ahead and moving it out of the way. The story treats the shift as a dying detective's vision of San Francisco, with Jericho as the man Tanner is trying to stop.

Earlier Driver games were about one car and a getaway. Shift makes the whole traffic jam a set of vehicles the player might become before the corner.
alone-in-the-dark:
Central Park, split into episodes, replaces the old mansion in Alone in the Dark (2008), Eden Games' reboot. Edward Carnby walks that park with fire as a tool and the case broken into chapters.

The 1992 original had defined the fixed-camera mansion crawl. This reboot lets Carnby combine objects, burn a fissure, and watch the plot arrive in episodes rather than as one continuous tape.

Carnby is still the investigator's name. The park, the flames, and the episode breaks are what Eden changed when it started the series over.
sonic-the-hedgehog-4-episode-1:
Splash Hill's loops announce a side-view return in Sonic the Hedgehog 4 - Episode I, a Dimps and Sonic Team follow-up. Doctor Eggman drops badniks into short zones, and the episode reached players in 2010.

A homing attack sits on top of the old spin, and Casino Street, Lost Labyrinth, and Mad Gear Zone follow the grassy opener. A second episode continued the serial later; this first chapter is the test of whether a Sonic sold in parts could still feel like the old run.

The Genesis trilogy had ended on a different scale. Episode I is the short revival, four zones and a familiar doctor, offered as the start of a serial rather than one long cartridge.
metal-slug-x:
Marco and Tarma get a cleaner board in Metal Slug X, SNK's rebalanced revision of the second arcade mission. The 1999 changes ease the slowdown that hurt that earlier hardware.

Prisoners still yell for a gun, the Metal Slug tank still rolls over infantry, and General Morden's army is still the target. New weapon balance and fewer choked frames are the reason to pick this revision when both boards are available.

Metal Slug 2 is the game this one repairs. X keeps the jokes, the POWs, and the tank, and it tries to make the busiest screens playable.
metal-slug:
The SV-001 tank and a very small squad open METAL SLUG. Nazca's 1996 Neo Geo run-and-gun launched the series, with chunky vehicles and Marco and Tarma against General Morden's rebellion.

A grenade arc, a hostage who tosses you a weapon, and a vehicle you can lose in one bad turn are the systems. The animation's bulk is the style: rifles, jeeps, and a boss that fills the screen without becoming a polygon showcase.

Later numbered missions added more soldiers and wilder vehicles. This first board is Morden's debut, the tank's debut, and Nazca's debut of the whole joke.
sega-bass-fishing:
A lure and a motion-controlled rod are the tackle in SEGA Bass Fishing. The 2008 Wii release brings Sega's arcade fishing game, originally Get Bass, onto those motion controls.

Choosing a lure, reading the water, and fighting a bass that can snap the line are the rounds. The arcade cabinet had a physical rod; the home version asks the controller to fake that tug.

Get Bass is the name the arcade crowd used. The Wii release keeps the lake, the lures, and the fight, and it puts the cast in the player's hands.
call-of-duty-3:
Normandy's breakout is the war told in Call of Duty 3, Treyarch's console shooter. The 2006 campaign did not receive a PC version at launch.

American, British, Canadian, and Polish units each take a stretch of the 1944 fight after D-Day. Hedgerows, a tank push, and a close ambush are the missions, with the series' first-person rifle still the main tool.

Earlier Call of Duty games had a computer home. This third entry stayed on consoles at the start, telling the breakout through more than one nation's squad.
la-mulana:
Tablets and a father who disappeared inside the ruins drive La-Mulana. Nigoro's explorer homages MSX action adventures, began as freeware in 2005, and a remake reached more players around 2012.

Lemeza Kosugi whips traps, reads a stone that rewrites an earlier room, and dies to a puzzle that was never marked as a puzzle. The Mother, a presence under the ruins, is the secret the tablets are circling.

The freeware original is the cult MSX-styled trek. The remake is the version more people could finish, or fail, without hunting that first release.
bittrip-beat:
CommanderVideo's body is the paddle in BIT.TRIP BEAT. Gaijin Games opened the BIT.TRIP series on WiiWare in 2009 with this rhythm game, bouncing a dot back to the beat until the pattern becomes a wall of notes.

Miss the beat and the mode drops toward a flatter, harsher soundtrack. The dot, the bat, and the music are the entire screen, which makes the later games in the series look busy by comparison.

Gaijin's CommanderVideo went on to other rhythm challenges. Beat is the first, the one that is honestly a paddle and a pulse.
destroy-all-humans:
Crypto-137 lands a saucer in a paranoid decade in Destroy All Humans! Pandemic's 2005 invasion casts the Furon alien as a 1950s body-snatcher harvesting human brains.

A ray that pulls a human off the sidewalk, a disguise that only works until someone screams, and a saucer that levels a fairground are the tools. Santa Modesta and the other towns are B-movie America, complete with men in hats who already suspect the new neighbor.

The title's exclamation is the tone. Crypto is not a sympathetic visitor; the mission is the brain, the probe, and the lawn he scorches on the way out.
fifa-10:
Licensed clubs and a new season of kits fill FIFA 10, the annual soccer game from EA Sports. It shipped in 2009 as another season of the long-running series on consoles and PC.

Formations, a whistle, and the league tables players expect from the real calendar are the simulation. The roster moves with the transfers of that season, which is why last year's disc stops being the one people bring to a couch match.

EA's series had already been an annual habit for a long time. This season's cover and its squads are what separate the disc from the year before it and the year after.
tales-of-monkey-island-complete-pack-cha:
Merfolk and a spreading curse strand the pirate in Tales of Monkey Island Complete Pack: Chapter 2 - The Siege of Spinner Cay. Telltale's second episode of the 2009 season leaves Guybrush on Spinner Cay while the Pox of LeChuck keeps moving from victim to victim.

Elaine is still part of the season's trouble, and the island's scale-folk have their own politics about the disease. Puzzle conversations, not sword grades, are how a Telltale chapter advances.

This is one WiiWare chapter of a five-part revival, not a LucasArts Monkey Island. Spinner Cay, the merfolk, and the pox are this episode's whole island.
